The Post-Buyback Announcement confirmed that BSE was the designated exchange, demat accepted shares were credited to the company's demat account on Thursday, 20 June 2024, unaccepted demat shares were returned/lien removed the same day, no physical shares were tendered, and if a depository transfer instruction was rejected the shares would move to the shareholder broker's depository pool account.
review_notes: Settlement-flow details (Company Broker SW Capital, funds via Clearing Corporation, demat movement to Company Demat Escrow Account) are supported by LoF chunks 22 and 289-292; Post-Buyback PA confirms actual June 20 transfers and shareholder-broker fallback. Broader mechanical focus than run-20's settlement-schedule question.

question: Beyond the common exclusions of not being a record-date shareholder or bidding more than the record-date holding, what other rejection grounds does the Letter of Offer list for demat and physical tenders? What actual rejection data did the post-buyback announcement report?
answer_summary: For demat tenders, additional rejection grounds included: non-receipt of the completed Tender Form and documents from physical holders who bid in demat form; name/PAN mismatch in the demat account; court or competent-authority restraint; and disputed or unclear title. For physical tenders, the list added: documents not received by the Registrar by 5:00 p.m. on 13 June 2024; another company's or invalid share certificate enclosed; transmission not completed; physical certificate not received; signature mismatch on the Tender Form/Form SH-4; self-attested PAN of the shareholder/joint holders not submitted; and duplicate bid. The Post-Buyback Announcement reported that 270 bids were rejected for not being record-date shareholders, excess bids by 100 reserved-category and 34 general-category shareholders over their record-date holdings were excluded, and no physical shares were tendered.
review_notes: Rejection-criteria checklist for demat and physical tenders is supported by LoF section at chunks 297-299, and Post-Buyback PA supplies actual rejection/absence data (270 non-record-date bids, excess-bid exclusions, no physical tenders). Distinct from run-20's record-date/excess/zero-entitlement focus.

question: Mukesh Chauradiya’s accounts were attached under Recovery Certificate No. 7426 of 2023 on June 13, 2024, and SEBI issued a remittance order about a month later. Did the attachment notice impose a complete freeze on those accounts, and what did the remittance order change about the bank’s obligation toward the balances?
answer_summary: The attachment notices did not impose a total freeze. They prohibited debits to the extent of the total dues in bank accounts and prohibited any debit from demat accounts or mutual fund folios, while expressly allowing credits to continue. The July 15, 2024 remittance order converted the freeze into an active collection step: it directed banks and mutual funds to remit the outstanding amount lying in the defaulter’s accounts forthwith by EFT/NEFT/RTGS to SEBI’s designated ICICI Bank account and to intimate the remittance particulars by e-mail to recoverywro@sebi.gov.in.
review_notes: Answer directly supported by attachment notices (No Debit but credits allowed, chunks #2/#10) and remittance order (directed EFT/NEFT/RTGS to ICICI + email intimation, chunk #1). True two-document contrast; distinct freeze-to-collection memory target.

question: Both the attachment and remittance notices in RC 7426 told banks and mutual funds that Mukesh Chauradiya might not hold an account with them. Under what exact circumstances could an intermediary stop responding, and what presumption applied only at the attachment stage?
answer_summary: At the attachment stage, if the intermediary had no account or folio for the defaulter, it need not inform SEBI; moreover, if no response was received within 15 days from the date of receipt of the attachment notice, it would be presumed that the defaulter held no account or balance with that intermediary. The July remittance order retained only the no-account safe harbour — if the defaulter had no account or folios, the intermediary need not inform SEBI — but it did not repeat or carry forward the 15-day presumption.
review_notes: Supported by attachment chunks #4/#10 (15-day no-response presumption; no-account safe harbour) and remittance chunk #4 (no-account safe harbour only, no 15-day presumption carried forward). Strong negative-presence/diff trap.

question: After the June 13, 2024 attachment notice in RC 7426, a bank discovers that Mukesh Chauradiya has opened a new savings account. Is the bank required to freeze that new account, and does the July 15 remittance order retain that same forward-looking duty?
answer_summary: Yes. The attachment notices required the intermediary to immediately attach any new bank account, demat account or mutual fund folio opened or created for the defaulter after the notice was issued, and to intimate the details to the Recovery Officer. The July 15 remittance order did not repeat or modify that ongoing surveillance duty; it simply directed institutions holding attached balances to remit the then-outstanding amount to SEBI’s designated account.
review_notes: Attachment chunks #4/#10 require immediate attachment of new accounts/folios and intimation. Remittance chunk #1 imposes no ongoing surveillance duty. Good applied compliance scenario with forward-looking duty check.

question: SEBI copied Mukesh Chauradiya on both the RC 7426 attachment notices and the remittance order. Did the defaulter face the same personal direction in both documents?
answer_summary: No. The attachment notices included a personal direction to Mukesh Chauradiya stating that he was not to receive, recover or demand the proceeds or money held or to be held in the attached accounts. The July 15 remittance order copied him, but contained no equivalent personal prohibition; it only ordered banks and mutual funds to remit the attached amount and noted that intermediaries with no account or folio need not respond.
review_notes: Attachment chunk #5/#11 includes the personal direction to Mukesh Chauradiya not to receive/recover/demand proceeds. Remittance chunk #4 copies him without that direction. Clean document-diff target.

question: The RC 7426 proceeding issued Attachment Proceeding No. 12187 for banks and No. 12188 for demat and mutual fund folios, yet the July remittance order addressed both groups in a single letter. Why was the attachment split into two notices while the remittance was combined?
answer_summary: The attachment had to freeze two distinct asset classes held by different intermediaries: bank accounts are maintained by banks, while demat accounts and mutual fund folios are maintained by depositories and asset management companies. Therefore, two notices were issued with distinct proceeding numbers. Because the July remittance order operated on balances already attached under both proceedings, SEBI could consolidate its directions in one order addressed to all banks and all mutual funds, citing both AP 12187 and AP 12188 and providing a single SEBI bank account for the remittance.
review_notes: Attachment chunks #0/#6 show separate AP 12187 (banks) and AP 12188 (demat/MF). Remittance chunks #0/#1 cite both AP numbers in one consolidated letter. Distinct procedural-structure question.

question: Anand Rathi Wealth's 2024 buyback was priced at ₹4,450 per equity share. According to the Letter of Offer, over which market benchmarks and at what premia was the buyback price justified, what was the face value of each share, and does the post-buyback announcement confirm that the same price and total amount were actually paid?
answer_summary: The Letter of Offer set the buyback price at ₹4,450 per equity share (face value ₹5 each) for up to 3,70,000 shares, aggregating to ₹164.65 crore excluding transaction costs. The price was justified against three benchmarks: (i) a premium of 31.95% on NSE and 36.76% on BSE over the volume-weighted average market price during the three months preceding Monday, April 8, 2024 (the intimation date); (ii) a premium of 22.56% on NSE and 22.46% on BSE over the closing price on Friday, April 5, 2024 (the day before the intimation date); and (iii) a premium of 11.00% on NSE and 10.86% on BSE over the closing price on the board-meeting date, Friday, April 12, 2024. The post-buyback announcement confirms that 3,70,000 shares were actually bought back at ₹4,450 each, for a total amount of ₹164.65 crore excluding transaction costs.
review_notes: Supported directly by cited LoF and post-buyback PA chunks: LoF states the ₹4,450 price and the three NSE/BSE premium benchmarks with exact percentages; the PA confirms the same price, face value, shares bought back and ₹164.65 crore total. Teaches a distinct pricing-justification memory target not covered in prior accepted rows.

question: Why did Anand Rathi Wealth say the 2024 buyback was necessary, and what did the Letter of Offer predict would happen to profitability, return ratios and capital structure? Did the post-buyback announcement confirm that the expected amount was ultimately deployed?
answer_summary: The Letter of Offer states the buyback was undertaken after taking into account the Company's medium-term strategic and operational cash requirements, and to return surplus funds to shareholders efficiently. The stated reasons were: returning surplus cash broadly in proportion to shareholding, optimising capital structure, reserving shares for small shareholders, improving financial ratios such as earnings per share, return on capital employed and return on equity, and giving shareholders liquidity/optionality. Management believed the buyback would not materially affect profitability or earnings except for the loss of investment income on the deployed cash, would likely improve return on net worth/return on equity, would not impair growth opportunities or operating cash needs, and would not result in a change of control. The post-buyback announcement confirms that the full expected amount of ₹164.65 crore (excluding transaction costs) was utilised.
review_notes: LoF sets out the management rationale and projected impact on profitability/return ratios/capital structure; the post-buyback PA confirms the expected amount was deployed. Distinct memory target.

question: Which statutory auditor and partner certified that Anand Rathi Wealth had adequate firm financial resources to meet its buyback obligations, on what date, and which key statutory checks did the auditor's report perform—particularly the debt-to-capital-and-free-reserves test? What amount was actually spent according to the post-buyback announcement?
answer_summary: kkc & associates llp, Chartered Accountants, the Company's statutory auditors, certified adequate and firm financial resources through partner Devang Doshi (Membership Number: 140056) in a certificate dated May 21, 2024. The auditor's report (under Schedule I clause (xi) of the SEBI Buyback Regulations) performed several procedures: examined the permissible capital payment under Section 68(2)(c) of the Companies Act; inquired into the state of affairs from audited standalone and consolidated financials as at March 31, 2024; traced paid-up capital and retained earnings; verified arithmetical accuracy of Annexure A; checked Articles of Association authorisation; examined that the debt-to-capital-and-free-reserves ratio after buyback would not exceed 2:1; confirmed that all buyback shares were fully paid-up; and obtained management representations. The post-buyback announcement confirms that ₹164.65 crore (excluding transaction costs) was actually spent.
review_notes: LoF identifies kkc & associates llp and Devang Doshi as the certifying statutory auditor and lists the schedule-I(xi) checks performed; PA confirms the amount spent. Differs from the raw leverage question.

question: The Letter of Offer projected how the buyback would affect book value per share, basic earnings per share, and return on net worth on a standalone basis. What were the projected pre- and post-buyback figures, and did the post-buyback announcement disclose any actual post-buyback EPS or return-on-net-worth numbers?
answer_summary: On a standalone basis, the Letter of Offer projected: book value per share at March 31, 2024 of ₹141.90; basic EPS rising from ₹53.05 to ₹53.52 (assuming full acceptance); and return on net worth increasing from 37.31% to 51.63%. The post-buyback announcement does not update any of these projected financial parameters: it reports the amount spent, number of shares bought back, and the post-buyback shareholding pattern, but it does not disclose any actual post-buyback EPS or return-on-net-worth figure.
review_notes: LoF projects standalone book value, EPS, and return-on-net-worth figures; the post-buyback PA only repeats capital-structure data and does not update EPS/RONW. Negative-absence claim verified against the cited PA chunks.

question: What was the change in Anand Rathi Wealth's issued, subscribed and paid-up capital between the Letter of Offer and the post-buyback announcement, and how many equity shares were extinguished?
answer_summary: Both the Letter of Offer and the post-buyback announcement record the same pre- and post-buyback capital structure. Authorised share capital remained unchanged at 5,00,000 equity shares of ₹5 each (₹2,500.00 lakhs). Issued, subscribed and paid-up capital fell from 4,18,28,297 equity shares of ₹5 each (₹2,091.41 lakhs) to 4,14,58,297 equity shares of ₹5 each (₹2,072.91 lakhs), reflecting extinguishment of 3,70,000 equity shares.
review_notes: LoF presents the pre-/post-buyback capital structure; the post-buyback PA confirms the same issued/paid-up capital and extinguishment of 3,70,000 equity shares.

question: According to the Letter of Offer, what restrictions apply to Anand Rathi Wealth issuing new equity or raising further capital after the buyback closes, and what exceptions allow such issuances? When did the buyback period close, as reported in the post-buyback announcement, so that the six-month and one-year clocks start running?
answer_summary: The Letter of Offer provided three restrictions: (1) under Regulation 24(i)(b), the Company shall not issue any new equity shares or other specified securities (including by way of bonus) until closure of the buyback period; (2) under Section 68(8) of the Companies Act, the Company shall not make any further issue of the same kind of shares or other specified securities within six months after completion of the buyback, except by way of bonus shares or equity shares issued to discharge subsisting obligations such as conversion of warrants, stock option schemes, sweat equity, or conversion of preference shares or debentures; and (3) the Company shall not raise further capital for one year from closure except to discharge such subsisting obligations. The post-buyback announcement states the buyback closed on Thursday, June 13, 2024.
review_notes: LoF quotes the Regulation 24(i)(b), Section 68(8) and one-year capital-raising restrictions with subsisting-obligation exceptions; the PA provides the June 13, 2024 closing date that anchors the clocks.

question: What restriction did the Letter of Offer place on the Promoter and Promoter Group's dealing in Anand Rathi Wealth shares during the buyback period, and when did that restriction end according to the post-buyback announcement?
answer_summary: The Letter of Order provides that the Promoter and Promoter Group shall not deal in the Company's equity shares on the stock exchange or off-market, including by way of inter-se transfers among themselves, during the period from the date of passing of the special resolution approving the buyback until the closing of the buyback. The post-buyback announcement records that the buyback opened on Friday, June 7, 2024 and closed on Thursday, June 13, 2024, so the dealing restriction ended on June 13, 2024.
review_notes: LoF restricts Promoter/Promoter Group dealings until the buyback closes; the PA reports the open/close dates, so the restriction ends on June 13, 2024.

question: According to the Letter of Offer, what statutory and regulatory approvals were required for the buyback, and were any approvals said to be still pending? Which stock exchange was designated for the offer according to the post-buyback announcement?
answer_summary: The Letter of Offer states the buyback required approval of shareholders by special resolution (which was obtained by postal ballot), and that the buyback was subject to approvals from SEBI and the stock exchanges (NSE and BSE) as may be required under applicable law. As of the date of the Letter of Offer, no other statutory or regulatory approval was required. Participations by non-resident shareholders were additionally subject to FEMA and the Income Tax Act. The post-buyback announcement confirms that BSE Limited was the designated stock exchange for the buyback.
review_notes: LoF lists shareholder special-resolution, SEBI, NSE/BSE approvals and says no other approvals were pending; PA confirms BSE was the designated stock exchange.

question: Section 68(2)(d) of the Companies Act requires that, after a buyback, a company's aggregate secured and unsecured debts not exceed twice its paid-up equity share capital and free reserves. What was Anand Rathi Wealth's latest reported total-debt-to-equity ratio, how much cash was ultimately spent, and why does this show the company was comfortably within the statutory threshold?
answer_summary: The Letter of Offer discloses that, as at March 31, 2024, the Company's total-debt-to-equity ratio was 0.01 on both a standalone and consolidated basis. The post-buyback announcement confirms the Company spent ₹164.65 crore (excluding transaction costs) to buy back 3,70,000 shares. Even after reducing reserves by the buyback amount, the Company's debt of about ₹8-9 crore is far below twice its remaining paid-up capital and free reserves, so the statutory threshold was comfortably satisfied.
review_notes: LoF discloses the 0.01 total-debt-to-equity ratio and Section 68(2)(d) ceiling; PA confirms the spent amount. The answer's headroom inference is consistent with the cited data.

question: Soumen Mitra and Sanjoy Kumar Dey were each fined ₹6,00,000 in the V B Industries adjudication order dated January 31, 2023, then obtained a remand from the Securities Appellate Tribunal in Appeal No. 370 of 2023. What was the final adjudication outcome after the remand, and what happened to Soumen Mitra's recovery certificate as a result?
answer_summary: The fresh Adjudicating Officer disposed of the proceedings against both Soumen Mitra and Sanjoy Kumar Dey without imposing any penalty (order dated March 20, 2025). Because the underlying adjudication order fell away, Recovery Certificate No. RC6489 of 2023 dated May 3, 2023 issued against Soumen Mitra was cancelled on August 13, 2024.
review_notes: Fresh AO and RC6489 cancellation both support the answer: SAT Appeal No. 370/2023 led to a fresh AO disposing of proceedings without penalty, and Soumen Mitra's RC6489 was cancelled on 13 Aug 2024.

question: On 13 August 2024 SEBI issued two recovery-side orders concerning Soumen Mitra after the SAT remand. What did the cancellation order do, and what did the release order direct banks, depositories and mutual funds to do?
answer_summary: The cancellation order cancelled Recovery Certificate No. RC6489 of 2023 dated May 3, 2023, exercising powers under section 28A of the SEBI Act. The release order, issued the same day, directed all banks, NSDL/CDSL and mutual funds to release the bank accounts/lockers, demat accounts and mutual fund accounts of Soumen Mitra that had been attached under notices dated May 30, 2023.
review_notes: Cancellation order cancels RC6489 under section 28A; release order directs banks/depositories/MFs to free attached accounts. Both documents are needed to distinguish the two orders.

question: Soumen Mitra's recovery certificate RC6489 of 2023 demanded Rs. 6,31,000, although the original Adjudicating Officer penalty in the V B Industries matter was only Rs. 6,00,000. What makes up the balance of Rs. 31,000?
answer_summary: The Rs. 6,31,000 figure in RC6489 of 2023 is the aggregate of the Rs. 6,00,000 penalty plus further interest, costs, charges and expenses incurred in the recovery proceedings. The order drawing the certificate explicitly describes the amount as the penalty "along with further interest, all costs, charges and expenses".
review_notes: RC6489 states Rs. 6,31,000 includes further interest, costs, charges and expenses; the AO order cites the original Rs. 6,00,000 penalty. Clean amount-reconciliation target.

question: Soumen Mitra and Sanjoy Kumar Dey were jointly noticees in the V B Industries AO order and in SAT Appeal No. 370 of 2023. How did the SAT outcome separately affect each noticee's recovery proceedings?
answer_summary: Both noticees were ultimately exonerated: the fresh Adjudicating Officer disposed of the proceedings against them without penalty on March 20, 2025. Their separate recovery certificates—RC6489 of 2023 for Soumen Mitra and RC6493 of 2023 for Sanjoy Kumar Dey—were cancelled on August 13, 2024. In addition, Soumen Mitra's attached bank, demat and mutual fund accounts were released under Attachment Proceeding Nos. 10301 and 10302 of 2023.
review_notes: Requires the fresh AO, both cancellation orders, and the release order to map how the SAT outcome separately touched Soumen Mitra (RC6489 + release of attachments) and Sanjoy Kumar Dey (RC6493).

question: On remand, why did the fresh Adjudicating Officer decide not to impose any penalty on Soumen Mitra and Sanjoy Kumar Dey under the V B Industries AO proceedings, and what recovery action followed from that conclusion?
answer_summary: The fresh AO found that the DIR-12 filings for Goldensight Vinimay Pvt. Ltd. and Onceover Dealtrade Pvt. Ltd. did not contain the noticees' signed consent letters; the attached DIR-2 forms were in the names of other persons and were unsigned, with no board resolutions supporting the appointments. Because the Show Cause Notice had not invoked Section 27(1) or any other provision for directors' vicarious liability, the AO held the notices could not be deemed guilty and disposed of the proceedings without penalty. The Recovery Officer had already cancelled Soumen Mitra's RC6489 of 2023 and released his attached accounts on August 13, 2024.
review_notes: Findings in the fresh AO explicitly cite unsigned/wrong-name DIR-2 consents, missing board resolutions, and the non-invocation of Section 27(1); cancellation order shows RC6489 was already cancelled. Distinct evidentiary-reasoning target.

question: Before cancelling RC6489 of 2023, SEBI had attached Soumen Mitra's bank and demat accounts on May 30, 2023. After the SAT remand, what did the Recovery Officer direct intermediaries to do, and under which attachment proceeding numbers?
answer_summary: Vide the release order dated August 13, 2024, the Recovery Officer directed all banks, mutual funds, NSDL and CDSL to release the bank accounts/lockers, demat accounts and mutual fund accounts of Soumen Mitra that had been attached under Attachment Proceeding Nos. 10301 and 10302 of 2023.
review_notes: Release order supplies AP 10301 & 10302 of 2023 and the direction to release bank/demat/MF accounts; cancellation order anchors the SAT-remand context. Narrow operational-detail target.

question: After HUL demerges its ice-cream business into Kwality Wall’s (India) Limited, an acquirer announces a mandatory open offer for KWIL. What corporate event made the open offer mandatory, what share of KWIL voting capital was offered for, and at what price?
answer_summary: The open offer was mandatory because the demerger first allotted KWIL shares to HUL shareholders in a 1:1 ratio, so HUL’s existing promoters (the Sellers) became holders of 61.90% of KWIL. Magnum HoldCo then entered into a share purchase agreement to acquire those 145,44,12,858 shares (61.90% of Voting Share Capital) with control. Crossing the 25% threshold with control triggered Regulations 3(1) and 4 of the SEBI (SAST) Regulations, requiring the acquirer and PACs to make an open offer for up to 61,08,93,729 KWIL shares, representing 26.00% of the Voting Share Capital, at ₹21.33 per share.
review_notes: Both cited docs support the 1:1 mirror allotment trigger, the 61.90% promoter block, and the 26%/INR 21.33 open offer terms.

question: The HUL demerger scheme expressly says no separate valuation was carried out for the share entitlement ratio, yet the KWIL open offer relies on independent valuation reports to set the offer price. Why does the open offer need a valuation when the demerger did not?
answer_summary: The scheme was exempt from a full valuation because the share entitlement ratio was 1:1, so KWIL’s shareholding mirrors HUL’s and no value exchange between shareholders is required. However, KWIL shares had no trading history before the public announcement—listing and trading approval were received on February 12, 2026, and trading began on February 16, 2026—so they were not “frequently traded” under Regulation 2(1)(j) of the SEBI (SAST) Regulations. Therefore, the offer price had to be determined under Regulations 8(1) and 8(2) using valuation reports dated February 13, 2026, from Bansi S. Mehta Valuers LLP and PwC Business Consulting Services LLP.
review_notes: Directly contrasts HUL scheme's no-valuation rationale with the SAST infrequent-trading valuation requirement; both document sets support it.

question: The HUL demerger scheme states that KWIL shares issued to HUL shareholders will remain frozen in the depositories until listing permission is granted. When did KWIL actually secure listing and trading approval, and how did that timing affect the open offer pricing method?
answer_summary: The scheme provides that Resulting Company New Shares shall remain frozen in the depository system until listing/trading permission is granted by the designated stock exchange. KWIL received listing and trading approval from BSE and NSE on February 12, 2026, and trading commenced on February 16, 2026. Because there had been no prior trading history, the shares were not treated as “frequently traded” under the SEBI (SAST) Regulations, so the open offer price of ₹21.33 was determined by independent valuation reports dated February 13, 2026, instead of relying on market price.
review_notes: Scheme freeze condition and KWIL listing/trading approval date are both supported; explains pricing-method consequence.

question: HUL’s promoters were described as promoters of KWIL immediately after the demerger, but the KWIL open offer says they will be reclassified as public after selling control. How does the demerger make them promoters of KWIL in the first place?
answer_summary: Because the HUL scheme allotted KWIL shares to all HUL shareholders in the same proportion as their HUL holdings, HUL’s existing promoters (the Sellers) automatically held 61.90% of KWIL after the record date of December 5, 2025. The open offer public announcement treats them as KWIL’s promoters because they acquired that stake through the mirror-allotment and controlled KWIL. After Magnum HoldCo acquires their 61.90% stake and control, the Sellers will cease to be in control and intend to be reclassified from “promoter” to “public” under Regulation 31A of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations.
review_notes: Supports the promoter status via mirror shareholding and the planned Regulation 31A reclassification to public.

question: The SPA through which Magnum HoldCo buys control of KWIL is signed before the open offer. What milestones from the HUL demerger scheme must occur before the SPA acquisition can close and the open offer can proceed?
answer_summary: The SPA, dated June 25, 2025, is conditional on: (i) the HUL demerger scheme becoming effective, with the ice-cream business transferring to KWIL; (ii) KWIL issuing and allotting its equity shares to HUL shareholders in the 1:1 ratio contemplated by the scheme; and (iii) KWIL’s equity shares receiving listing and trading approval on the stock exchanges. Once these scheme outcomes are satisfied, the Acquirer acquires 61.90% of KWIL with control, triggering the mandatory open offer under Regulations 3(1) and 4 of the SEBI (SAST) Regulations.
review_notes: SPA conditions precedent map cleanly to the scheme milestones in both documents.

question: Boards approved the HUL demerger on January 22, 2025, and the scheme became effective on December 1, 2025, yet the KWIL open offer public announcement is dated February 16, 2026. Why could the open offer be announced only after the demerger was already effective?
answer_summary: The SPA acquisition that triggers the open offer is conditional on the scheme becoming effective, KWIL shares being allotted to HUL shareholders, and KWIL shares being listed on the stock exchanges. The scheme notice makes the scheme itself subject to subsequent NCLT and regulatory approvals, and fixates the 1:1 share entitlement and listing application. It was only after the scheme took effect on December 1, 2025, and after KWIL received listing and trading approval on February 12, 2026, that Magnum HoldCo’s acquisition of control actually triggered Regulations 3(1) and 4 of the SEBI (SAST) Regulations, making the open offer announcement possible on February 16, 2026.
review_notes: Timeline sequencing is supported: board approval, scheme effective date, KWIL listing date, and the February 16 public announcement.

question: A shareholder sees only the newspaper advertisement for the HUL scheme meeting and wants the full set of papers before deciding how to vote. What does the advertisement say about where to find the documents, and how does the formal notice define the full pack?
answer_summary: The newspaper ad states that the advertisement appeared in Business Standard (All Editions) and Loksatta-Mumbai on July 9, 2025. It repeats the August 12, 2025 meeting date, cut-off dates, and e-voting windows, and says the notice, scheme, and explanatory statement were dispatched on July 7, 2025 to shareholders as of June 23, 2025, with copies available on HUL’s website, the BSE and NSE websites, and NSDL’s e-voting site; physical copies could be obtained from HUL’s registered office or by e-mailing levercare.shareholder@unilever.com. The formal notice defines the complete meeting pack as the Notice, Explanatory Statement, Scheme of Arrangement, and Annexures 1 through 14E, which include the share entitlement ratio report, fairness opinion, stock exchange observations, financial statements, and disclosure documents.
review_notes: Newspaper ad and formal notice are both used; the channel list and the complete document set are supported.

question: The HUL scheme freezes KWIL shares and prohibits any change in shareholding pattern or control from the record date until listing. If accepted in full, the KWIL open offer would leave public shareholders holding far less than 25%. How do the two documents reconcile these conflicting positions?
answer_summary: The no-change restriction in the scheme applies only between the record date (December 5, 2025) and the listing/trading of KWIL shares. KWIL received listing and trading approval on February 12, 2026, and trading commenced on February 16, 2026. The open offer therefore occurs after the restriction ends. The public announcement acknowledges that full acceptance could cause public shareholding to fall below the minimum public shareholding requirement under Rule 19A of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Rules, 1957 read with Regulation 38 of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, and states that the Acquirer and PACs will ensure KWIL complies with the minimum public shareholding requirements in the manner and timeline prescribed by law.
review_notes: Reconciles the scheme's temporary no-change freeze with the post-listing open offer and acquirer's MPS compliance undertaking.

question: Under the RC 7426 attachment notice, what information must a bank provide to SEBI within 15 days, and does the July 15 remittance order supersede that reporting obligation?
answer_summary: The June 13, 2024 bank attachment notice requires the bank to provide within 15 days: (a) details of all accounts including lockers held by Mukesh Chauradiya; (b) account statements for the latest one year; (c) confirmation of attachment; and (d) complete details of all loan/advance accounts along with assets charged. The July 15 remittance order does not repeat that 15-day reporting package; it converts the bank’s duty to remitting any amount lying in the defaulter’s accounts forthwith by EFT/NEFT/RTGS to SEBI’s designated ICICI account and emailing the remittance particulars.
review_notes: Supported by cited chunks: bank attachment notice lists the 15-day reporting package and the remittance order shifts the duty to immediate remittance by EFT/NEFT/RTGS. Two documents are materially needed to resolve the superseding/alteration point.

question: Almost seven months after the RC 7426 demand notice, SEBI attached Mukesh Chauradiya’s accounts. What factual finding let SEBI move from demand to attachment, and what did the remittance order do once the attachment was already in place?
answer_summary: The attachment notices state that no amount had been paid by the defaulter and that SEBI had sufficient reason to believe he might dispose of amounts in bank accounts or securities in demat accounts/mutual fund folios, which would delay or obstruct recovery. That unpaid-plus-risk premise justified the attachment. The July 15 remittance order treated the attachment as already in place and directed the banks and mutual funds holding balances to remit the outstanding amount forthwith to SEBI’s designated ICICI account.
review_notes: Directly supported: attachment notice states non-payment plus risk of disposal, while the remittance order assumes the attachment and directs banks/MFs to remit. Both docs needed.

question: Mukesh Chauradiya’s penalty in the Hiran Orgochem GDR matter went unpaid after the Adjudicating Officer’s order. Trace SEBI’s recovery chain from that AO order through to the remittance order, giving the date and principal direction of each step.
answer_summary: Step 1: Adjudicating Officer order dated July 11, 2023 (Order/AK/AJ/2023-24/28034-28035) imposed a Rs. 20 lakh penalty in the Hiran Orgochem matter. Step 2: Recovery Certificate 7426 of 2023 was drawn up on December 1, 2023 with total dues of Rs. 21,21,000 (penalty plus interest plus cost) and a Notice of Demand was issued. Step 3: On June 13, 2024, attachment notices (AP 12187 for bank accounts and AP 12188 for demat/MF folios) prohibited debits, required reporting of details within 15 days, and directed Chauradiya not to recover proceeds. Step 4: On July 15, 2024, the remittance order consolidated AP 12187 and AP 12188 and directed banks/mutual funds to remit the outstanding Rs. 22,61,000 by EFT/NEFT/RTGS to SEBIRRD PEN7426 of ICICI Bank (IFSC ICIC0000106) and to email particulars to recoverywro@sebi.gov.in.
review_notes: AO order date/order-number/penalty, RC/demand date and amount come from attachment notice chunks; remittance order supplies the next step’s date, outstanding amount, and principal direction. Multi-document procedural-chain memory target supported.

question: Intermediaries receiving the RC 7426 attachment notice were given 15 days to respond, while the remittance order says to act ‘forthwith’. What is each deadline for, and what relief applies if the intermediary does not hold any account or folio for Mukesh Chauradiya?
answer_summary: The attachment notice gives the intermediary 15 days from receipt to provide details/statements/confirmations; if no response is received in that time, it is presumed that the defaulter has no account/balance with that intermediary. If the intermediary holds no account at all, it need not inform SEBI. The remittance order replaces that 15-day reporting phase with an immediate (‘forthwith’) duty to remit any amount lying in the defaulter’s account by EFT/NEFT/RTGS to SEBI’s ICICI account and to email the particulars; again, if no account/folio exists, the intermediary need not respond.
review_notes: Deadlines and no-account/no-folio relief are clearly stated in both cited documents. The attachment-remittance contrast is genuine and both docs are required.

question: What information does the RC 7426 attachment notice require a depository participant or mutual fund to provide, and how does the later remittance order alter that obligation?
answer_summary: The demat/MF attachment notice directs the intermediary to provide immediately: (a) details of all accounts/folios held by the defaulter; (b) copy of account statement(s); and (c) confirmation of attachment. Like the bank notice, it freezes debits (but allows credits), attaches new accounts/folios, and presumes no account if no response is received within 15 days. The July 15 remittance order does not ask for that documentary package again; instead it orders the intermediary to remit any amount lying in the defaulter’s accounts forthwith by EFT/NEFT/RTGS to SEBIRRD PEN7426 of ICICI Bank (IFSC ICIC0000106) and to email the remittance details.
review_notes: Distinct asset-class counterpart to q01: demat/MF attachment notice requires account/folio details, statements, and confirmation; remittance order converts this into an immediate remittance duty. Supported by cited chunks.

question: Our close-ended AIF's tenure ends in July 2025. If unit holders approve a two-year extension in June 2025, will the scheme be exempt from the February 2025 dematerialisation circular entirely, and can it still make new portfolio investments during the extended tenure?
answer_summary: No; the blanket exemption from holding investments in dematerialised form under paragraph 21.4.2 applies only to schemes that were already in extended tenure as on February 14, 2025. Because the extension is approved after that date, the scheme must still dematerialise pre-July 2025 investments covered by the investee-law or control conditions by October 31, 2025, and investments made on or after July 1, 2025 must be held in dematerialised form. However, the Sundaram informal guidance confirms that AIF Regulations do not expressly prohibit fresh investments during extended tenure, provided the PPM or other fund documents do not restrict them and appropriate disclosures are made when seeking extension.
review_notes: Directly supported by cited chunks: para 21.4.2 demat exemption is only for schemes already in extended tenure as of Feb 14, 2025; Sundaram guidance permits fresh investments in extended tenure subject to PPM/disclosures. Strong two-doc date/exception trap.

question: Our AIF plans to file its PPM under the April 2026 fast-track mechanism in May 2026 and expects to appoint a new compliance officer later this year. Who bears responsibility for PPM accuracy, and what qualification must the compliance officer hold from 2027?
answer_summary: Under the fast-track mechanism, the Merchant Banker and the Manager of the AIF are responsible for ensuring the accuracy and completeness of all disclosures in the PPM and in declarations submitted to SEBI. Submission of the PPM is not SEBI approval and does not make SEBI responsible for the disclosures. Separately, from January 1, 2027, only persons who have passed the NISM Series-III-C Securities Intermediaries Compliance (Fund) Certification Examination may be appointed or continue as compliance officers of AIF managers.
review_notes: Well supported: fast-track circular places accuracy/disclosure responsibility on merchant banker and AIF manager; compliance-officer circular requires NISM Series-III-C certification from Jan 1, 2027. Useful regime-crossing calendar question.

question: A Category II AIF wants to offer a co-investment vehicle (CIV scheme) inside the AIF structure. Can it use the April 2026 fast-track PPM process for the CIV shelf placement memorandum, and what structural restrictions still apply to the CIV?
answer_summary: Yes. The fast-track mechanism applies to Angel Funds and AIF schemes other than Large Value Funds for accredited investors (LVFs). A CIV is itself a scheme within the AIF structure, so its shelf placement memorandum may be filed under the fast-track route, allowing the scheme to be launched 30 days after filing (subject to first-scheme timing and a first close within 12 months of launch eligibility). The co-investment framework still requires each CIV to have separate bank and demat accounts, ring-fenced assets, and limits co-investments by an accredited investor across CIV schemes to three times that investor's contribution in the related AIF scheme investment, with the usual carve-out for multilateral/bilateral DFIs, SIDCs, government-owned or controlled entities, central banks and sovereign wealth funds.
review_notes: Cited chunks support that fast-track route covers non-LVF AIF schemes, and CIV framework treats a CIV as a scheme with a shelf PPM plus separate accounts/3x cap/carve-outs. Both documents are necessary to answer.

question: Both the March 2026 AIF regulatory-reporting circular and the December 2025 compliance-officer certification circular became effective immediately. For a manager planning the compliance calendar, what are the actual future deadlines under each?
answer_summary: The Regulatory Reporting circular is effective immediately. The first Annual Activity Report, for the year ending March 2026, must be submitted by May 31, 2026, and the first limited Quarterly Activity Report is for the quarter ending June 2026 and is due within 15 calendar days of quarter end. The Compliance Officer Certification circular is also effective immediately, but the qualification deadline is January 1, 2027: from that date only persons who have passed the NISM Series-III-C Securities Intermediaries Compliance (Fund) Certification Examination may be appointed or continue as compliance officers of AIF managers.
review_notes: Both circulars effective immediately; reporting circular specifies first Annual Activity Report by May 31, 2026 and first quarterly report for Jun-2026 quarter within 15 days; certification circular fixes Jan 1, 2027 qualification deadline.

question: A compliance team is mapping the legal effect of SEBI updating the FPI Master Circular. How does the savings clause in the May 2024 Master Circular compare with the savings clause in the December 2025 draft when prior registrations, pending applications, penalties, and proceedings are involved?
answer_summary: Both circulars preserve actions taken under the rescinded documents, but the wording and the layer of the circular lineage differ. The May 2024 Master Circular rescinded the earlier circulars listed in Annexure A and provided that anything done or action taken under those rescinded circulars before rescission is deemed to have been done under the corresponding provisions of the May 2024 Master Circular; pending applications are also deemed to have been made under corresponding provisions; and the previous operation, rights, obligations, liabilities, penalties, and proceedings remain unaffected as if the rescinded circulars had never been rescinded (clf-hdsv9cdor3l7icrwk9jpxrnd#3, #4). The December 2025 draft similarly rescinds the May 2024 Master Circular and listed circulars, deeming anything done under the rescinded Master Circular before rescission to have been done under the corresponding provisions of the draft, and pending applications to have been made under corresponding provisions; for rights, liabilities, penalties, and proceedings it states they are not affected by the rescission and remain enforceable as if the rescinded Master Circular had continued to be in force (clf-ghmxirkc1v5r3wlb69830lte#3, #4, #5, #6). Practically, continuity is maintained, but the 2025 draft shifts to a 'continued in force' formulation and also rescinds the 2024 Master Circular itself.
review_notes: Cited savings clauses in May 2024 MC (clf-hdsv9cdor3l7icrwk9jpxrnd#3,#4) and Dec 2025 draft (clf-ghmxirkc1v5r3wlb69830lte#3-#6) directly support the comparison of continuity language and the added rescission of the 2024 MC itself. Truly multi-document, distinct memory target.

question: The December 2025 draft of the reviewed FPI Master Circular has a different subject line than the May 2024 Master Circular. What category of investors present in the May 2024 circular appears to be excluded from the draft, and where does this show up in both documents?
answer_summary: Eligible Foreign Investors (EFIs) appear to be dropped from the consolidated draft. The May 2024 Master Circular is titled 'Master Circular for Foreign Portfolio Investors, Designated Depository Participants and Eligible Foreign Investors' and contains a dedicated Part E titled 'Guidelines for participation/functioning of Eligible Foreign Investors (EFIs) in International Financial Services Centre (IFSC)' (clf-hdsv9cdor3l7icrwk9jpxrnd#2, #6, #9, #153). The December 2025 consultation draft is titled 'Master Circular for Foreign Portfolio Investors ("FPIs") and Designated Depository Participants ("DDPs")'; its table of contents lists Parts A-E covering registration, post-registration activities, KYC, investment conditions, additional disclosure framework, and ODIs, with no Part E for EFIs (clf-ghmxirkc1v5r3wlb69830lte#3, #7, #8, #9, #10). The subject line and structural table of contents together show the narrower proposed scope.
review_notes: May 2024 MC title and Part E on EFIs (clf-hdsv9cdor3l7icrwk9jpxrnd#2,#6,#9,#153) contrast with Dec 2025 draft title and TOC that omits EFI Part E (clf-ghmxirkc1v5r3wlb69830lte#7-#10). Clean negative/scope-change target.

question: An FPI restructures its legal form from a corporate to a trust. After the June 2024 amendment, how must the FPI report this change, within what timeframe, and what must the DDP do? Why can this not be answered from the May 2024 Master Circular alone?
answer_summary: Restructuring of legal form/sub-category (e.g., corporate to trust) is classified as a Type I material change. It must be reported as soon as possible and within seven working days of occurrence, with supporting documents provided within 30 days (clf-pu60x04n5n46q8l7hoc4q1rm#2, #3; clf-ghmxirkc1v5r3wlb69830lte#48, #49, #50). The DDP must examine all material changes and reassess eligibility, but for Type I changes listed in items I to VI—which include restructuring of legal form/sub-category—it must mandatorily require the FPI to seek fresh registration (clf-pu60x04n5n46q8l7hoc4q1rm#4; clf-ghmxirkc1v5r3wlb69830lte#51). The May 2024 Master Circular's Para 14 did not yet divide material changes into Type I and Type II and did not prescribe a seven-working-day deadline or mandatory fresh-registration categories; the June 2024 circular introduced that classification by modifying the Master Circular (clf-pu60x04n5n46q8l7hoc4q1rm#0, #1). Therefore answering the question requires both the June 2024 amendment and the December 2025 draft that preserves the new classification.
review_notes: Corporate-to-trust restructuring is Type I material change under June 2024 circular (clf-pu60x04n5n46q8l7hoc4q1rm#2-#4) and preserved in Dec 2025 draft (clf-ghmxirkc1v5r3wlb69830lte#48-#51); May 2024 MC lacked Type I/II split. Strong applied compliance question with multi-doc necessity.

question: The May 2024 FPI Master Circular listed several prior circulars in Annexure A that stood rescinded. If implemented, which circulars would the December 2025 draft rescind that were issued after May 30, 2024, and why were they not in the May 2024 rescission list?
answer_summary: The May 2024 Master Circular's Annexure A rescinded circulars up to March 20, 2024, including the January 25, 2024 DDP/custodian reporting circular, the March 20, 2024 additional-disclosures amendment, the 2023 LEI and RFQ circulars, and the December 19, 2022 FPI Master Circular (clf-hdsv9cdor3l7icrwk9jpxrnd#155, #156, #157). The December 2025 draft's rescission list covers everything the May 2024 Master Circular rescinded plus the circulars issued after May 30, 2024, namely: June 5, 2024 material-changes (CIR/2024/76), June 5, 2024 flexibility-after-expiry (CIR/2024/77), June 27, 2024 IFSC-NRI/OCI participation (CIR/2024/89), August 1, 2024 additional-disclosures amendment (CIR/2024/104), October 22, 2024 CAF modification (CIR/2024/145), November 11, 2024 reclassification-to-FDI (CIR/2024/152), November 12, 2024 simplified-registration (CIR/2024/156), December 17, 2024 ODI arbitrage (CIR/2024/176), April 9, 2025 additional-disclosures amendment (CIR/2025/52), May 16, 2025 ODI-implementation extension (CIR/2025/71), September 10, 2025 GS-FPI ease circular (CIR/2025/127), and the May 2024 Master Circular itself (clf-ghmxirkc1v5r3wlb69830lte#150, #151, #152, #153, #154). They could not appear in the May 2024 list because they had not yet been issued (clf-ghmxirkc1v5r3wlb69830lte#0, #1).
review_notes: May 2024 Annexure A lists pre-May circulars (clf-hdsv9cdor3l7icrwk9jpxrnd#155-#157); Dec 2025 draft rescission list adds all post-May circulars plus the May 2024 MC (clf-ghmxirkc1v5r3wlb69830lte#150-#154). Exhaustive filter is well-supported and explains why the later circulars could not be in the earlier list.

question: An intern is comparing the structure of the May 2024 FPI Master Circular with the December 2025 draft and cannot find the DDP investor-charter requirement in the same Part. Where does each document place the obligation on DDPs to publish the investor charter and monthly complaint data?
answer_summary: In the May 2024 Master Circular, the DDP Investor Charter and monthly complaint disclosure obligations are located in Part F, 'Publishing of Investor Charter and Disclosure of Complaints by DDPs on their websites'; the charter is Annexure H and the complaint format is Annexure I (clf-hdsv9cdor3l7icrwk9jpxrnd#9, #154, #169). In the December 2025 draft, the same content is moved into Part B 'Post registration activities' as Paragraph 13, with the title unchanged, the charter now placed in Annexure F and the complaint data format in Annexure G (clf-ghmxirkc1v5r3wlb69830lte#7, #8, #57, #58, #164). The relocation is part of the draft's streamlining effort, folding DDP conduct and disclosure duties into the post-registration section instead of keeping a separate Part F.
review_notes: DDP investor-charter and complaint-disclosure obligation moves from Part F/Annexures H,I in May 2024 MC (clf-hdsv9cdor3l7icrwk9jpxrnd#9,#154,#169) to Part B/Annexures F,G in Dec 2025 draft (clf-ghmxirkc1v5r3wlb69830lte#7,#8,#57,#58,#164). Distinct structural-relocation target.

question: After distributing most proceeds, our AIF retains a small amount beyond the permissible fund life to cover expected operational expenses. How must that retained money be invested, what substantiation is required, and by when must valuations based on the investees' audited March 31 accounts be reported?
answer_summary: Retained money must be invested strictly in accordance with Regulation 15(f) of the AIF Regulations, i.e., only in permitted liquid instruments such as liquid mutual funds, bank deposits, Treasury bills, triparty repo, commercial paper and certificates of deposit. Amounts kept for operational expenses must be substantiated through invoices, supporting documents or comparable prior-year expenses, and the proposed retention period for operational expenses must not exceed three years. For valuation, the September 2024 circular extends the timeline for reporting valuation based on audited March 31 data from six months to seven months, i.e., by October 31 each year.
review_notes: Retained-money rules (Reg 15(f), invoice substantiation, 3-year cap) are supported by the winding-up consultation paper, and the Oct 31 audited-data valuation deadline is supported by the Sept 2024 valuation circular. The two docs are only loosely coupled, but each teaches a separate memory target.

question: An HUL shareholder becomes a KWIL shareholder because of the demerger and assumes that only shareholders recorded on the demerger Record Date can participate in the KWIL open offer. Is she correct, and what is the actual cut-off date used when sending the Letter of Offer?
answer_summary: No. The demerger Record Date only identified which HUL shareholders would receive KWIL shares, and the KWIL open offer uses a separate 'Identified Date'. The Identified Date is defined as the date falling on the tenth working day prior to the commencement of the Tendering Period. For this open offer, the Identified Date is Wednesday, April 8, 2026. That date is used solely to decide to whom the Letter of Offer is sent; even shareholders who acquired KWIL shares after the Identified Date remain eligible to tender during the offer period.
review_notes: Verified: Record Date is defined in the scheme (HUL notice #154/#1181); Identified Date is 10 working days before the Tendering Period (LOF #38/#10/#212/#216) and all public shareholders, even those acquiring after the Identified Date, may tender (#216). Two-doc necessity is strong; human-shaped misconception.

question: The HUL demerger scheme meeting and the KWIL open offer each required newspaper publication. Which newspapers/editions carried each announcement, and why do the language mixes differ at the two stages?
answer_summary: The HUL scheme meeting advertisement was published in Business Standard (All Editions) and Loksatta-Mumbai on July 9, 2025. The KWIL open offer Detailed Public Statement was later published in Financial Express (English, All Editions), Jansatta (Hindi, All Editions) and Navshakti (Marathi, Mumbai Edition). Both are public-disclosure requirements for their respective corporate actions, but the scheme ad was aimed at HUL shareholders voting on the demerger while the open offer public statement was aimed at KWIL public shareholders; the choice of English, Hindi and Marathi editions reflects the broader public-shareholder outreach needed for an open offer.
review_notes: Verified: scheme ad in Business Standard (All Editions) and Loksatta-Mumbai on Jul 9, 2025 (ad #0/#12); open offer DPS in Financial Express (English, All Editions), Jansatta (Hindi, All Editions) and Navshakti (Marathi, Mumbai) on Feb 20, 2026 (LOF #79). Distinct channel/language comparison across stages.

question: Only an equity-shareholder meeting was convened for the HUL demerger scheme. Why did the NCLT dispense with separate creditors' meetings, and who was appointed to chair and scrutinize the shareholder meeting?
answer_summary: The NCLT dispensed with separate meetings of the secured and unsecured creditors of HUL and separate meetings of KWIL shareholders because the scheme did not involve any compromise or arrangement with creditors, did not modify creditor rights and was not prejudicial to them. As at the relevant date HUL and KWIL had no secured creditors and KWIL had no unsecured creditors. The Tribunal appointed Mr. Ferdino Rebello, retired Chief Justice of the Allahabad High Court, as Chairperson of the meeting and Mr. Ashwini Ramakant Gupta, Company Secretary (COP 18163), as Scrutinizer of the e-voting process.
review_notes: Verified: NCLT dispensed with separate creditor meetings (ad #3) and the scheme explains no compromise/arrangement with, or prejudice to, creditors (notice #94); chairperson and scrutinizer appointments are in both the notice (#16) and ad (#9). Slight factual inference on secured/unsecured creditors is consistent with the cited rationale but not word-for-word.

question: Which SEBI-registered intermediary appears with the same registration number in both the HUL demerger scheme pack and the KWIL open offer documents, and what were its contrasting roles?
answer_summary: Kotak Mahindra Capital Company Limited, SEBI registration number INM000008704, appears in both stages. In the HUL scheme circular it acted as an independent Category-I merchant banker and issued the Fairness Opinion dated January 21, 2025. In the KWIL open offer it acted as the Manager to the Open Offer. KFin Technologies Limited served as Registrar to the Offer for the open offer, while the HUL scheme meeting used NSDL to provide the remote e-voting and e-voting-during-meeting facilities.
review_notes: Verified: Kotak Mahindra Capital Company Limited, SEBI Reg. INM000008704, acted as independent Category-I merchant banker / Fairness Opinion issuer in the scheme circular (notice #4/#16) and Manager to the Open Offer in the LOF (#6/#7). Good cross-document actor memory.

question: At the time the HUL scheme meeting notice was issued, which regulatory approvals had already been obtained and which were still pending? Trace the subsequent milestones through which the scheme became effective and the KWIL Letter of Offer was finally issued.
answer_summary: When the HUL scheme meeting notice was issued, BSE and NSE had already given their observation letters on May 14, 2025, conveying no adverse observations/no objection. The NCLT order directing the meeting was dated June 11, 2025. The scheme still required the Tribunal's final sanction and other statutory approvals. The effective date of the scheme was December 1, 2025, KWIL shares were allotted on the Record Date of December 5, 2025, KWIL obtained listing and trading approvals on February 12, 2026 and trading began on February 16, 2026. The public announcement of the open offer was also made on February 16, 2026, the controlling SPA was consummated on March 30, 2026, and the final Letter of Offer was dated April 10, 2026.
review_notes: Verified: BSE/NSE observation letters dated May 14, 2025 and NCLT order of Jun 11, 2025 in notice (#125/#139); scheme effective Dec 1, 2025, record date Dec 5, 2025, listing/trading approval Feb 12, 2026, trading commencement Feb 16, 2026 (PA #8/#9/#12); SPA consummated Mar 30, 2026 and final LOF dated Apr 10, 2026 (LOF #190/#39). Strong timeline spanning three documents.

question: A depository participant started applying the new BSDA charge structure to accounts opened in July 2024, referring to the circular issued on June 28, 2024. Is the July start date correct, and what does the earlier consultation paper show about when SEBI originally intended the circular to take effect?
answer_summary: No, the July start is premature. SEBI Circular SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD-PoD1/P/CIR/2024/91 dated June 28, 2024 states that it shall come into effect from September 01, 2024. The June 5, 2024 consultation paper (Annexure A) had left the effective date as a placeholder "DD-MM-YYYY". The final circular therefore resolved that placeholder by choosing September 01, 2024 as the operative date.
review_notes: Effective-date placeholder (DD-MM-YYYY) in the June 5 consultation paper's Annexure A and the fixed September 01, 2024 date in the June 28 circular are both directly cited and supported. Distinct date-trap/memory target.

question: A DP argues that the BSDA cap applies only to annual maintenance charges, so it can impose higher transaction, pledge, or dematerialisation charges on BSDA holders than on regular account holders. Does the June 28, 2024 circular support this, and how did its stance differ from the draft circulated for public comments?
answer_summary: The DP's argument fails. Paragraph 2.3(b) of the June 28, 2024 circular expressly states that, other than the AMC specified in the slab, "BSDA shall be treated at par with non-BSDA for the purpose of levying charges for various other services and DPs shall not levy higher charges to BSDA." The June 5, 2024 consultation paper's draft circular did not include this explicit at-par/non-higher emphasis; it only said other regular-account conditions continued to apply. The final circular therefore added a clearer anti-discrimination rule for non-AMC charges.
review_notes: Paragraph 2.3(b) of the final circular adds explicit at-par/non-higher charge language that the draft only expressed generically in para 2.4(c); both documents are needed to see the shift. Distinct from the other two rows.

question: Before finalising the June 2024 BSDA circular, SEBI invited public comments on three specific threshold and pricing design choices. What were those choices, and which of them appeared unchanged in the final circular issued less than four weeks later?
answer_summary: The June 5, 2024 consultation paper asked stakeholders: (i) whether the BSDA limit should be enhanced above the proposed ₹10 lakh; (ii) whether separate limits for debt and other-than-debt securities should be retained instead of a combined ₹10 lakh fungible limit; and (iii) whether AMC should be NIL, ₹100, or ₹500. The June 28, 2024 final circular retained the ₹10 lakh combined limit and the NIL/₹100 AMC structure; it did not raise the limit above ₹10 lakh, did not retain separate debt/equity limits, and did not introduce the ₹500 AMC option.
review_notes: The three public-comment design choices (limit enhancement, combined vs separate limits, AMC options) are enumerated in the consultation paper and mapped correctly to the final circular's retained structure. Distinct option-selection memory target.

question: The HUL demerger scheme states that KWIL's entire pre-scheme paid-up share capital (held by HUL) will be cancelled and reduced when the scheme becomes effective. What provision allows this reduction to happen without a separate Section 66 proceeding, and why does KWIL not have to add 'And Reduced' to its name? How do the open offer documents confirm that the reduction does not prevent KWIL from being listed?
answer_summary: The cancellation/reduction is treated as an integral part of the scheme sanctioned under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013. Because of the explanation to Section 230(12), the provisions of Section 66 do not apply to any consequential cancellation of share capital under the scheme. Stakeholder consent given through the scheme is deemed sufficient, and the NCLT order sanctioning the scheme is deemed to be the Section 66 confirmation order. Clause 10.3 of the scheme expressly provides that KWIL is not required to add 'And Reduced' as a suffix to its name. The open offer documents confirm KWIL became a listed company: the Public Announcement states KWIL received BSE/NSE listing and trading approval on February 12, 2026 and trading commenced on February 16, 2026, and the Letter of Offer notes KWIL's shares are listed on BSE and NSE with a corresponding update of its CIN/status from unlisted to listed.
review_notes: Directly supported by cited chunks (HUL scheme clauses 10.1-10.3, PA #12, LOF #28). Three-document angle is coherent and adds a distinct scheme-law memory target.

question: An HUL shareholder holds shares in physical form and does not give her demat account details to the company at least seven days before the demerger record date. What does the scheme say will happen to the KWIL shares she is entitled to, and can she still tender those shares in the mandatory open offer?
answer_summary: The scheme provides that KWIL shares will be issued in dematerialised form to eligible shareholders who hold HUL shares in dematerialised form. A physical shareholder must provide demat details at least seven days before the record date; if she does not, KWIL will keep her shares in abeyance, in an escrow account or with a trustee until the details are provided. Shares corresponding to HUL shares held in the unclaimed suspense account or the IEPF are similarly channelled into a new KWIL unclaimed suspense account or the IEPF. The Letter of Offer clarifies that all public shareholders, whether registered or unregistered and holding shares in dematerialised or physical form, are eligible to participate in the open offer during the tendering period. A physical holder must complete the Form of Acceptance and normally dematerialise the shares in time to tender.
review_notes: Cited HUL chunks (213-215) clearly cover the abeyance / escrow / IEPF rule and LOF chunks (13, 254, 255) cover eligibility and physical-holder tender procedure.

question: The KWIL open offer identifies seven Sellers who together hold 61.90% of KWIL before the sale of control. How did those Sellers come to hold that block, and why does their combined holding equal HUL's promoter shareholding percentage?
answer_summary: The Sellers are Unilever PLC, Unilever Group Limited, Unilever Overseas Holdings AG, Unilever UK&CN Holdings Limited, Unilever South India Estates Limited, Unilever Assam Estates Limited and Unilever Overseas Holdings B.V. They acquired their KWIL shares as the HUL promoter group under the 1:1 share entitlement ratio on the demerger record date of December 5, 2025. Because HUL's promoters collectively held 61.90% of HUL, the same mirror shareholding was allotted to them in KWIL. The HUL scheme notice discloses that these Unilever Group Shareholders executed the SPA to sell the entire block to Magnum HoldCo, and the Letter of Offer breaks down each Seller's pre-transaction holding totalling 145,44,12,858 shares (61.90%).
review_notes: LOF Sellers table (147-150) supports names and 61.90% aggregate. HUL chunk 122 supports SPA disclosure. Exact record date is not in the cited chunks (but is in broader scheme/offer text), so evidence score is trimmed slightly.

question: The SPA through which Magnum HoldCo buys control of KWIL implies a per-share value of about INR 20.61, yet the mandatory open offer is priced at INR 21.33. Why must the acquirer pay public shareholders a higher price than it negotiated with the Sellers?
answer_summary: The open offer price is fixed as the highest of the parameters under Regulations 8(1) and 8(2) of the SEBI (SAST) Regulations. The negotiated SPA price of INR 20.61 is only one input; it is derived by converting the Euro-denominated SPA consideration at the RBI reference rate of EUR 1 = INR 107.6218 on February 13, 2026. Because KWIL shares had no trading history before the Public Announcement and were not frequently traded, Regulation 8(2)(e) required an independent registered valuer's price. The higher of the two independent valuations, INR 21.33 by Bansi S. Mehta Valuers LLP, became the offer price.
review_notes: Clean support in PA #16 (FX conversion) and LOF #194-197 (Regulation 8 price table, independent valuation floor at INR 21.33). Good multi-document price-calculation target.

question: The KWIL open offer Public Announcement is dated February 16, 2026, but the Letter of Offer is dated April 10, 2026 and can be dispatched to shareholders as late as April 16. What disclosure and regulatory steps must occur between the public announcement and the start of tendering?
answer_summary: Between the PA and tendering, the SAST Regulations require: (i) publication of the Detailed Public Statement within five working days of the PA (published on February 20, 2026, before the February 24 deadline); (ii) filing of the Draft Letter of Offer and receipt of SEBI observations (actual SEBI observations received by April 6); (iii) determination of the Identified Date (April 8, 2026) for sending the LOF; (iv) dispatch of the LOF by April 16, 2026; and (v) an offer-opening public announcement before the Tendering Period begins on April 23, 2026. The Letter of Offer schedule records both the indicative original dates and the actual revised dates.
review_notes: Timeline / deadline chain is broadly right and verifiable, but the answer's DPS publication date (Feb 20, 2026) is not in the cited PA #29 / LOF #10-13 chunks. The fact is present elsewhere in the LOF, so the row is accepted with a citation-gap note.

question: The HUL demerger scheme transfers all ice-cream intellectual property to KWIL, but the open offer says KWIL is actually using the India Ice Cream IP under a transitional sub-license. What happens to that licence once Magnum HoldCo completes its acquisition of control?
answer_summary: Although the scheme vests all ice-cream business assets (including Intellectual Property) in KWIL, the operational India Ice Cream IP sits in Magnum IP Holdings B.V. Magnum IP licensed it exclusively to Unilever IP Holdings B.V. on a transitional basis, and that licence was sub-licensed to HUL and then transferred to KWIL. The Public Announcement states that the Ice Cream IP Sub-License and the UIPH Licence will terminate on completion of the SPA transaction, after which Magnum IP will grant a new licence for the India Ice Cream IP to KWIL. The Letter of Offer confirms that, as of the LOF date, those transitional licences had terminated and discussions on commercial terms for the new licence were underway.
review_notes: Nicely combines scheme IP transfer clause (HUL #145), PA licence-termination/reg-grant statement (#22-23), and LOF confirmation (#101) that licences had terminated.

question: If the KWIL open offer is fully accepted, the public shareholding will fall well below 25%. Does the acquirer intend to delist KWIL, and what undertaking has it given about the minimum public shareholding requirement?
answer_summary: No. The acquirer and PACs state in the Public Announcement that they have no intention to delist KWIL. They also confirm that the open offer is not conditional on any minimum level of acceptance. Both the Public Announcement and the Letter of Offer acknowledge that full acceptance of the open offer (together with the SPA) could cause public shareholding to fall below the 25% minimum required under Rule 19A of the SCRR read with Regulation 38 of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, and the acquirer undertakes to ensure that KWIL meets the minimum public shareholding requirement in the manner and timeline prescribed by law.
review_notes: Supported by PA #24/#30 and LOF #28/#74. There is some overlap with previously accepted kimi_run_000029_q08 (freeze-to-listing vs MPS reconciliation), but this row targets the separate 'delisting intent + MPS undertaking' memory point, so it is kept.

question: Compare the property listed as 'S No B6' in the March 2024 and July 2024 Bishal Group sale confirmation orders. Are the two listings the same piece of land, and how can you tell from the property descriptions?
answer_summary: No. Although both orders use the serial number B6, they describe different land. The March 2024 listing is vacant land at LR Khatian No 400, Plot Nos (R.S. & L.R.) 251 & 243 and other plots, in Mouza Mayakol, P.S. Dhubulia, Dist. question: The July 2024 Bishal Group sale confirmation order states that the highest bidder for 'S No B7' defaulted. Does the March 2025 Bishal Group sale confirmation order confirm that property?

question: What payment schedule and fee must a successful Bishal Group bidder satisfy before the sale can be confirmed, and what final amount did Progressive Vanijya deposit for property B6 in July 2024?
answer_summary: The notice of sale requires the successful bidder to pay 25% of the bid amount (inclusive of the EMD already paid) immediately — within 48 hours of being declared successful — and the balance amount plus a poundage fee of 1% of the bid amount within 15 days from the auction. question: What statutory provision does the Recovery Officer rely on to confirm the Bishal Group auction sales, and what condition regarding applications to set aside the sale is recorded as satisfied?
answer_summary: The confirmations are made under section 28A of the SEBI Act, 1992 read with Rule 63(1) of the Second Schedule to the Income-tax Act, 1961. Each order records that no application was made before the Recovery Officer for setting aside the sale under Rule 60 of the Second Schedule, and because the full purchase money had been paid, the sale was confirmed and became absolute. This wording is consistent across the March 2024, July 2024 and March 2025 orders.
review_notes: Statutory basis and no-set-aside condition repeated and supported across the three orders.

question: Three 2026 commodity-derivatives initiatives—a capacity circular, a Core SGF coverage update, and an early-pay-in draft clarification—were each reviewed with input from a different advisory body or working group. Map each initiative to the body whose advice SEBI cited.
answer_summary: The February 2026 capacity-planning circular for commodity derivatives was reviewed by SEBI in consultation with the Technical Advisory Committee (TAC) and a public consultation paper dated June 30, 2025. The March 2026 Core SGF coverage circular cited recommendations of the Risk Management Review Committee (RMRC) and public comments. The May 2026 early-pay-in draft clarification was recommended by the Working Group on Review of current regulatory framework of delivery and settlement applicable to Agricultural Commodity Derivatives Segment and was endorsed by the Commodity Derivatives Advisory Committee (CDAC) in its February 26, 2026 meeting.
review_notes: Supported: TAC + June 2025 consultation for capacity (ph1#2); RMRC + public comments for Core SGF (foetslkry#1); WG on delivery/settlement + CDAC Feb 26 2026 for early pay-in (qsc#2-3). Multi-doc advisory-body mapping, distinct intent.

question: Each of the three 2026 commodity-derivatives circulars or draft circulars amends a different provision of the SEBI Master Circular for Commodity Derivatives Segment dated August 4, 2023. Identify the provision each one changes.
answer_summary: The February 2026 capacity-planning circular supersedes Clause 16.1.2 of Chapter 16 (trading-system capacity). The March 2026 Core SGF coverage circular modifies Part C ('Coverage') of paragraph 22 ('Standardized Stress Testing for Commodity Derivatives') in Annexure O, replacing the earlier coverage calculations. The May 2026 early-pay-in draft circular revises paragraph 11.3.1 of Chapter 11 (Early Pay-in Facility) so it covers derivatives contracts more broadly and assigns the facility to Clearing Corporations.
review_notes: Supported: capacity circular supersedes Clause 16.1.2 of Chapter 16 (ph1#4); Core SGF modifies Part C of paragraph 22 of Annexure O (foetslkry#1); early-pay-in draft revises paragraph 11.3.1 of Chapter 11 (qsc#3, #5-6).

question: The February 2026 capacity-planning circular applies the December 10, 2024 general MII capacity framework to the Commodity Derivatives Segment, but it makes two headline carve-outs for commodity MIIs. What are they?
answer_summary: Most paragraphs of the December 10, 2024 circular apply mutatis mutandis. The two commodity-specific adjustments are: (i) the installed-capacity multiplier is raised to at least 2 times projected peak load, whereas the general framework requires at least 1.5 times; and (ii) when actual capacity utilization exceeds 75% of installed capacity, the commodity MII must take immediate action and its Standing Committee on Technology (SCOT) must oversee the action, with the framework for augmentation included in the MII's Capacity Planning and Real Time Performance Monitoring Policy.
review_notes: Supported: Dec 2024 general framework requires 1.5x installed capacity (p8qbnpp#2); Feb 2026 commodity circular raises it to 2x (ph1#3). General 75% trigger enhanced by SCOT oversight/policy inclusion in commodity circular (ph1#3-4). Two-doc delta with consequence.

question: Two of the 2026 commodity-derivatives documents assign a new or reserved role to a regulator or market infrastructure institution. Under the May 2026 early-pay-in draft, which entity would provide the early-pay-in facility, and what discretionary power does the March 2026 Core SGF circular reserve to SEBI?
answer_summary: The May 2026 early-pay-in draft circular shifts responsibility for providing the early-pay-in facility to Clearing Corporations (rather than Stock Exchanges) and extends it to relevant derivatives contracts sold. The March 2026 Core SGF coverage circular inserts a clause that permits SEBI, after due deliberation, to grant exemptions or relaxations from strict enforcement of SGF provisions in the commodity derivatives segment on a case-by-case basis, considering prevailing market conditions, the adequacy of the risk-management framework and investor protection.
review_notes: Supported: early-pay-in draft shifts provider from Stock Exchanges to Clearing Corporations and broadens to relevant derivatives contracts sold (qsc#1 vs #6); Core SGF circular reserves SEBI exemption/relaxation power (foetslkry#2-3).

question: The February 2026 capacity circular, the March 2026 Core SGF circular and the May 2026 early-pay-in draft circular all invoke the same statutory authority. What is it?
answer_summary: Each of the three circulars is issued in exercise of the powers conferred under Section 11(1) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with Regulation 51 of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) (Stock Exchanges and Clearing Corporations) Regulations, 2018.
review_notes: Supported: all three instruments cite Section 11(1) of SEBI Act 1992 read with Regulation 51 of SCR(SECC) Regulations 2018 (ph1#5, foetslkry#3, qsc#7). Academic citation match but multi-document supported and distinct from other rows.

question: The March 2026 Core SGF circular sets a new coverage calculation, while the February 2026 capacity-planning circular sets a new utilization trigger. If a clearing corporation asks whether SEBI can relax either requirement, what is the difference between the two circulars?
answer_summary: The Core SGF circular explicitly allows SEBI to grant exemptions or relaxations from strict enforcement of SGF coverage provisions on a case-by-case basis, taking into account prevailing market conditions, risk-management adequacy and investor protection. The capacity-planning circular contains no comparable waiver; it requires the MII to take immediate action when utilization exceeds 75% of installed capacity, with SCOT overseeing the action and the augmentation framework recorded in the MII's Capacity Planning and Real Time Performance Monitoring Policy.
review_notes: Supported: Core SGF circular contains explicit SEBI exemption/relaxation route (foetslkry#2-3), while capacity circular mandates immediate action and SCOT oversight at >75% utilization with no waiver (ph1#3-4). Negative-comparison target distinct from q04.

question: Our CRA has been approached to rate short-term debt instruments that fall under RBI guidelines. A partner argues that the July 2025 CRA Master Circular already authorizes this because it directs CRAs to align rating scales with other financial-sector regulators. Is the Master Circular the right source for permission, and when does the relevant authority become effective?
answer_summary: No. The July 2025 Master Circular only operationalizes the rating-scale alignment mentioned in Regulation 9(f); it does not itself authorize a CRA to rate instruments governed by another regulator. The authority comes from the SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) (Amendment) Regulations, 2026, which substitute Regulation 9(f) and come into force on the date of their publication in the Official Gazette. The amended clause permits a CRA to carry out any other activity specified by SEBI or to rate financial instruments under the purview of another financial-sector regulator or authority as specified by SEBI, and the new Explanation clarifies that such ratings must follow the respective regulator's guidelines and remain under that regulator's purview.
review_notes: Supported by both cited docs. Master Circular only aligns scales under Reg 9(f); 2026 Amendment supplies authority and effective date. Applied compliance scenario with effective-date trap.
