question: While updating our standard CRA rating agreement, the legal team wants to cite the 2026 CRA Amendment as the source for the seven-day information-supply clause and the requirement that issuers disclose prior non-cooperation with another CRA. Is that sourcing correct, and where do those agreement clauses actually come from?
answer_summary: No. The 2026 Amendment is narrowly limited to substituting Regulation 9(f) regarding additional activities and ratings under other financial-sector regulators; it does not introduce rating-agreement clauses. The clauses are found in the 2025 Master Circular for Credit Rating Agencies. The Master Circular requires the rating agreement to include an undertaking that the issuer will disclose the history and status of any prior rating relationship, including non-cooperation, and an undertaking to provide information sought by the CRA within seven days (immediately if there is a delay or default in servicing debt obligations).
review_notes: Supported. Amendment is limited to Reg 9(f) substitution; rating-agreement clauses are in the Master Circular (disclosure of prior non-cooperation and seven-day information supply). Clean negative/source-check.

question: The November 18, 2024 circular amended Para 15 of the CRA Master Circular then in force by deleting the term 'technical default' from the list of scenarios. Does the July 2025 Master Circular still use that term, and does the 2026 CRA Amendment alter the post-default curing rule?
answer_summary: No to both. The November 2024 circular omitted 'technical default' from Para 15.3 and modified sales scenario list. The July 2025 Master Circular reflects this deletion: Para 15.3 now refers only to scenarios such as change in management, acquisition, sizeable inflow of long-term funds, or benefits from a regulatory action. The 2026 Amendment only substitutes Regulation 9(f) concerning additional activities and ratings under other regulators; it does not touch the post-default curing rule, which remains as consolidated in the 2025 Master Circular.
review_notes: All three cited docs are needed: Nov 2024 circular omits 'technical default'; July 2025 Master Circular reflects the deletion; 2026 Amendment does not touch the cure rule. Minor wording around 'sales scenario list' is loosely paraphrased but the core lineage is solid.

question: How does the December 2024 ODI arbitrage circular change the additional-disclosure test for FPIs with segregated portfolios, and did the April 2025 threshold amendment alter that portfolio-level treatment?
answer_summary: For FPIs with segregated portfolios, the December 2024 circular provides that the additional-disclosure criteria apply individually to each segregated portfolio, with each portfolio treated as a separate FPI for compliance. If a segregated portfolio breaches the concentration criteria, any liquidation requirement applies only to that portfolio. The April 2025 amendment raised the size threshold from INR 25,000 crore to INR 50,000 crore but did not change this portfolio-level mechanics.
review_notes: Cited chunk #23 directly states SP-level disclosure/liquidation mechanics; April amendment chunk #1 confirms threshold rise to INR 50,000 crore and does not modify the SP proviso.

question: Which ODI subscribers may be exempted from the additional disclosure requirement despite crossing the concentration or size thresholds, and what special condition applies to pooled investment vehicles seeking that exemption?
answer_summary: Exempted ODI subscribers include: government and government-related investors; public retail funds as defined under Regulation 22(4) of the FPI Regulations; ETFs with less than 50% exposure to India and India-related equities; pooled investment vehicles registered or regulated by a government/regulatory authority, subject to scheme-level caps on single-group equity ODI positions or Indian equity positions relative to global AUM; subscribers unable to liquidate due to statutory restrictions; and university funds/endowments eligible as Category I FPIs with Indian equity ODI positions below 25% of global AUM and global AUM above INR 10,000 crore equivalent. The April 2025 amendment changed only the size threshold, not these exemptions.
review_notes: Exemption categories are fully supported by chunks #5-#8. Second document is thin: only confirms the size threshold change did not affect exemptions.

question: What flexibility did the June 2024 circular create for NRI, OCI and resident-Indian participation in IFSC-based FPIs, and what additional CAF declarations did SEBI require in October 2024?
answer_summary: The June 27, 2024 circular, implementing the SEBI (FPI) Second Amendment Regulations 2024, allowed FPIs based in IFSCs and regulated by IFSCA to have up to 100% aggregate contribution by NRIs, OCIs and resident Indian individuals. Such FPIs must declare an intent to hold 50% or more aggregate NRI/OCI/RI contribution, submit PAN/economic-interest details, and treat changes as Type II material changes. The October 22, 2024 CAF modification added a Section B-II declaration confirming that no single NRI/OCI/RI (including a controlled investment manager) holds 25% or more and that aggregate contributions are intended to be or are above 50%, and it required Annexure-1 information/documents.
review_notes: Both cited docs support the IFSC FPI contribution flexibility, declaration/PAN/economic-interest conditions, Type-II change, and the October 2024 CAF Section B-II addition plus Annexure-1.

question: How does the periodicity of custodian KYC review differ for an ordinary FPI, a GS-FPI and a SWAGAT-FI FPI?
answer_summary: Under the May 2024 FPI Master Circular, ordinary Category I FPIs under Regulation 5(a)(i) are reviewed every three years during continuance, while other FPIs and high-risk cases are reviewed annually. For GS-FPIs, the custodian KYC review periodicity is harmonised with the applicable periodicity for the FPI's bank accounts as prescribed by RBI. For SWAGAT-FI FPIs, the periodicity is fixed at 10 years.
review_notes: Strong multi-document comparison: Master Circular Table 6 sets ordinary periodicity; GS-FPI circular harmonizes KYC with bank-account periodicity; SWAGAT-FI circular fixes 10-year review.

question: Where do an expired FPI's securities end up if still unsold after the extended disposal window, and how does that differ from the destination of shares when an FPI elects FDI reclassification?
answer_summary: If securities remain unsold after the post-expiry disposal period plus the additional 180-day period, they are deemed compulsorily written off by the FPI. The custodian must transfer those written-off securities to a separate escrow account operated by an exchange-empanelled broker, sell them at market price through the regular trading platform, and remit the net proceeds to the IPEF; post-write-off monetary corporate benefits are also credited to the IPEF. In contrast, when an FPI reclassifies its holding as FDI, the shares are transferred from its FPI demat account to its demat account maintained for FDI investments once RBI-prescribed reclassification reporting is complete.
review_notes: Chunks #14/#15 confirm written-off securities go to broker escrow and proceeds/monetary benefits go to IPEF; FDI reclassification chunk confirms transfer to FDI demat once RBI reporting is complete.

question: Under the proposed KRA framework, when must the KRA send prior intimation to all intermediaries that have fetched a client's record, and how does the separate NRI re-KYC circular manage GPS location evidence for NRI clients?
answer_summary: The KRA must send prior intimation when any of three triggers applies: (a) the KYC information has not been updated in the last five years, (b) the validity of the officially valid document in the KYC record has expired, or (c) the KYC pertains to a minor who has attained 18 years of age. Separately, for NRI re-KYC, the requirement that the client be physically located in India is relaxed; the app must instead ensure that the captured GPS latitude and longitude matches the country in the proof of address and must block spoofed IP connections.
review_notes: Supported by h74#38/39 (prior-intimation triggers) and kuc#0/1 (NRI GPS relaxation). New target within KRA/NRI pair: prior-intimation conditions are not covered by prior codex questions in this region.

question: How do the KRA proposal and the modified-nomination proposal use the investor's registered mobile number for opposite verification effects?
answer_summary: Under the KRA proposal, if the KRA tags a client's mobile number as seeded with Aadhaar and verified, intermediaries accessing the KYC record need not independently verify that mobile number. By contrast, under the modified-nomination proposal, one of the accepted online validation methods for a nomination is two-factor authentication in which one factor must be an OTP sent to the investor's registered mobile number and email address.
review_notes: Supported by h74#19/20 (Aadhaar-seeded mobile tag relieves intermediary verification) and q3hn#13 (nomination 2FA uses OTP to registered mobile/email). Plausible contrast question; no prior row pairs these two mobile-number uses.

question: What authentication methods are proposed for online and offline nominations under the modified norms, and why did SEBI first have to defer the original Phase III timeline?
answer_summary: Online nominations can be validated through a Digital Signature Certificate, Aadhaar-based e-sign or another e-sign facility recognised under the Information Technology Act, 2000, or two-factor authentication where one factor is an OTP sent to the investor's registered mobile and email. Offline nominations must carry the account-holder's wet signature and do not require a witness, unless the holder uses a thumb impression, which must be witnessed by two persons. SEBI deferred Phase III of the January 10, 2025 nomination circular from December 15, 2025 to a later notified date because depositories, depository participants and industry associations raised operational difficulties and sought more time for system and process changes.
review_notes: Supported by q3hn#13/14 (online/offline validation methods, wet-signature/witness rule) and hy97#0/1/3 (Phase III deferment rationale). Auth-method checklist is distinct from prior deferment questions and from codex q055's validation-plus-upload framing.

question: Why did SEBI remove references to transmission from the proposed modified-nomination circular, and what had happened to the original Phase III implementation deadline beforehand?
answer_summary: The modified-nomination consultation states that because norms for transmission in the securities market are being comprehensively reviewed for simplification, the references to transmission contained in the January 10, 2025 circular were removed from the proposed nomination circular so that transmission norms can be incorporated later. Before that, SEBI had already deferred Phase III of the January 10, 2025 circular from December 15, 2025 to a later date to be notified separately, following representations about operational difficulties and system-development needs.
review_notes: Supported by q3hn#8/9/10 (transmission-reference removal rationale) and hy97#0/1/3 (Phase III deferment). Strong version-delta + lineage question; no prior row focuses on the transmission-reference removal.

question: What must an investor acknowledge when opting out of nomination online, and how does the KRA proposal stop a closed account from continuing to receive stale updates?
answer_summary: When an investor opts out online, the regulated entity must display the Annexure B declaration and the investor must acknowledge it. The declaration warns that nomination helps quick identification and smoother transmission to legal heirs; without it, legal heirs may have to submit extra legal or court documents, causing delays; and if no claim is made for a prolonged period after death, the holdings may be treated as unclaimed assets and transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund. Separately, under the KRA proposal, the intermediary must inform the KRA within three working days of account closure, and the KRA must update or delink the relevant KYC record within two working days.
review_notes: Supported by q3hn#15/16/23 (online opt-out Annexure B acknowledgement) and h74#21/22 (3-day intermediary notice, 2-day KRA delinking). Two operational remedies paired thematically; distinct from codex q085 which pairs delinking with NRI relief.

question: How do the KRA and modified-nomination proposals differ on who publishes standardized forms and on how often investor records may be revised?
answer_summary: Under the KRA proposal, KRAs must, after consulting intermediaries, specify and publish a standardised format for capturing and storing the additional Part-II information on their websites. Under the modified-nomination proposal, the standardised nomination and opt-out forms are set out in Annexure A and Annexure B of the draft circular. KYC records trigger a KRA prior-intimation process if not updated in five years, if the officially valid document expires, or if a minor attains majority; nominations, by contrast, can be provided, changed or cancelled any number of times, with regulated entities giving an acknowledgement for every instance.
review_notes: Supported by h74#10/38/39 (KRAs publish Part-II format; KYC prior-intimation triggers) and q3hn#13/15/19/20/23 (draft circular defines Annexure A/B; nominations changeable any number of times). PublisheR and revision-frequency axes are new compared with codex q050's general paperwork-reduction question.

question: The January 30, 2025 KBCL sale confirmations cite a Notice of sale dated November 18, 2024 read with an Addendum dated December 16, 2024. Why was that Addendum issued and what change did it make to the process?
answer_summary: The Addendum was issued because interested bidders requested more time to submit the Earnest Money Deposit, as intimated by Quikr Realty Pvt. Ltd., the valuation agency. It extended the last date for submission of bids and remittance of EMD to December 19, 2024 (until 5:00 p.m.).
review_notes: Addendum reason and extended EMD deadline directly supported by public notice; confirmation order provides multi-doc link.

question: One KBCL one-property sale that was confirmed on January 30, 2025 was later withdrawn by the Recovery Officer. Which property was affected, what prompted the withdrawal, and what was the legal effect?
answer_summary: The Recovery Officer withdrew the confirmation for property Sr. No. 8 (Khasra No. 91, Pauri Village, Tehsil & District Mathura, area 0.3137 hectares), which had been knocked down to Atlaspac Ventures India Pvt. Ltd. The withdrawal (Order No. NRO/RO/1/2025 dated February 14, 2025) was made because of pending objection(s) received in respect of that property, and the confirmation stands withdrawn with immediate effect until further orders.
review_notes: Confirmation order and withdrawal order together identify Sr.No.8, the pending-objection trigger, and immediate-withdrawal effect.

question: Which KBCL one-property confirmation for the December 2024 e-auction drew five bidders, who bought the property, and how did the level of competition compare with property Serial No. 15?
answer_summary: Property Sr. No. 10 (Khasra No. 63, Pauri Village, area 0.4685 hectares) drew five bidders: Atlaspac Ventures India Pvt. Ltd., Shiv Kumar Agarwal, Meenakshi Khandelwal, Rajnish Kumar Tiwari, and Geeta Devi (Manoj Kumar). It was knocked down to Geeta Devi (Manoj Kumar) for Rs. 81,00,000. Property Sr. No. 15 (Khasra No. 315, Bhadaya Village) drew three bidders and was knocked down to Shatanshu Agrawal for Rs. 23,01,200.
review_notes: Bid counts, winners, and hammer prices for Sr.No.10 and Sr.No.15 match the two confirmation orders; clean comparison axis.

question: After the January 30, 2025 confirmations, SEBI issued Sale Certificates for KBCL properties Serial No. 9, 10 and 16. What legal provision supports those certificates, and what do they state about the status of the sales?
answer_summary: The Sale Certificates are issued under Section 28A(1)(c) of the SEBI Act, 1992 read with Rule 65 of the Second Schedule to the Income Tax Rules, 1961. Each certificate states that the full purchase consideration together with 1% poundage fee has been received, that the sale was confirmed on January 30, 2025, that the sale has become absolute, and the certificate is issued on February 19, 2025.
review_notes: Sale certificates for Sr.No.9, 10, and 16 state the Section 28A/Rule 65 basis and the full-payment/absolute-sale wording; confirmation orders add the January 30 date linkage.

question: Both KBCL Pauri village properties Serial No. 8 and Serial No. 9 were confirmed on January 30, 2025. What happened to each sale afterwards, and what accounts for the different treatment?
answer_summary: Property Sr. No. 8 (Khasra No. 91, area 0.3137 hectares, buyer Atlaspac Ventures India Pvt. Ltd.) had its confirmation withdrawn on February 14, 2025 because of pending objection(s), and the sale remains suspended until further orders. Property Sr. No. 9 (Khasra No. 235, area 0.3570 hectares, buyer Shatanshu Agrawal) proceeded to a Sale Certificate on February 19, 2025, which declared the sale absolute after full payment.
review_notes: Contrasting post-confirmation outcomes for adjacent Pauri properties (withdrawal vs. sale certificate) are supported across four cited documents.

question: For KBCL property Serial No. 10, what additional information does the February 19, 2025 Sale Certificate provide beyond what is recorded in the January 30, 2025 confirmation order?
answer_summary: The confirmation records that Geeta Devi (Manoj Kumar) knocked down the property at Sr. No. 10 for Rs. 81,00,000 and paid the full Rs. 81,81,000 including 1% poundage fee. The Sale Certificate adds that the certificate is issued under Section 28A(1)(c) of the SEBI Act, 1992 read with Rule 65 of the Second Schedule to the Income Tax Rules, 1961; states the purchaser's PAN and registered address; confirms receipt of the purchase consideration plus 1% poundage fee; and declares that the sale confirmed on January 30, 2025 has become absolute.
review_notes: Confirmation order supplies hammer price/payment; sale certificate adds legal provision, PAN, address, and absolute-sale declaration.

question: Anjani Portland Cement wants to merge its unlisted subsidiary into itself and has pointed out that the post-scheme allottees may have to be classified under the promoter-and-promoter-group category. If the company chooses to reclassify those allottees as public, what are the key milestones from board approval to shareholder approval under Regulation 31A?
answer_summary: SEBI says the company may resort to the Regulation 31A process for reclassification. Per the Shivalik guidance, after the board considers the reclassification request, the listed entity must apply to the recognized stock exchange for a no-objection within five days, and then place the request before shareholders in a general meeting within sixty days of receiving the no-objection letter. The reclassification must be approved by an ordinary resolution in which the promoters seeking reclassification and their related persons cannot vote; this GM requirement is dispensed with only if the reclassifying promoters and related persons together hold not more than one percent of the voting rights.
review_notes: Anjani establishes scheme-driven promoter-group classification; Shivalik chunks 10/11/16 directly support the 5-day/60-day timeline, ordinary resolution, related-person voting bar and 1% dispensation.

question: CMS Info Systems had six one-share nominee shareholders who were shown as holders of promoter shares only because they helped satisfy the minimum-member rule, while Anjani Portland Cement could end up classifying public shareholders of its unlisted subsidiary as promoter group after a scheme of amalgamation. What does SEBI say is the only way to remove those persons from the promoter category in each case?
answer_summary: In both letters SEBI ties the removal to the Regulation 31A reclassification process. CMS clarifies that a person falling within promoter/promoter group can be removed from that category only after completing the procedure under Regulation 31A; if the nominees genuinely do not meet the promoter-group definitions their holding can be explained only through theXBRL Notes functionality. Anjani similarly observes that post-scheme allottees may have to be classified as promoter and promoter group but the company may resort to Regulation 31A if it wants them treated as public.
review_notes: CMS 13/15 and Anjani 18 both point to Regulation 31A as the sole removal route; cross-case framing is a distinct memory target.

question: A listed entity argues that because its shareholding pattern consolidates holdings by PAN, each family member it reclassifies as public can skip the GM vote as long as that individual holds less than one percent. Using CMS and Shivalik together, why is that reasoning incorrect?
answer_summary: CMS says the shareholding of promoter and promoter group is consolidated on PAN/folio and that an individual or entity can appear in only one category, but this governs disclosure, not the shareholder-approval dispensation test. Under Shivalik, the one-percent dispensation applies only where the promoters seeking reclassification AND their related persons together do not hold more than one percent of the voting rights. Because Mrs. Tejinderjeet Kaur Ghumman, an immediate relative of two promoters seeking reclassification, herself held more than one percent in SBCL, the combined group crossed the threshold and the GM vote could not be dispensed with—even though the actual individuals being reclassified held much less.
review_notes: Well-supported threshold trap: CMS 12/13 covers PAN/folio disclosure consolidation, while Shivalik 10/16 imposes the combined promoters-plus-related-persons 1% dispensation test.

question: In CMS, the one-share nominee shareholders were not treated as promoters because they had no control, no influence over the board, and no written promoter agreement. If similar facts were presented in a Shivalik-style Regulation 31A reclassification request, which negative conditions besides lack of control would still have to be independently satisfied?
answer_summary: Lack of control alone is not enough. Shivalik's reproduction of Regulation 31A requires the promoter(s) seeking reclassification and their related persons not to: together hold more than ten percent of the total voting rights; exercise control over the listed entity's affairs; have special rights through formal or informal arrangements including shareholder agreements; be represented on the board or have a nominee director; act as key managerial personnel; be a wilful defaulter under RBI guidelines; or be a fugitive economic offender. If those conditions are satisfied, an ordinary resolution is also required unless the combined voting-rights dispensation applies.
review_notes: CMS chunk 4 supplies the no-control/no-influence/no-agreement facts; Shivalik 11/12 supplies the full negative-condition checklist under Regulation 31A.

question: Regulation 31A mentions both a 1% threshold for dispensing with shareholder approval and a 10% cap on post-reclassification voting rights. Using CMS and Shivalik, explain how related persons factor into each threshold and which threshold controls whether a GM vote is needed.
answer_summary: CMS says promoter-group holdings are consolidated by PAN/folio, so related persons who fall within the group are part of the same voting-rights pool for disclosure purposes. Shivalik applies this aggregate view to two different thresholds: the 1% test determines whether the GM ordinary-resolution requirement can be dispensed with—the promoters seeking reclassification and their related persons together must hold one percent or less to skip the vote; if they exceed that, a GM is mandatory. The 10% test is a residual post-reclassification condition: even after the GM, the reclassifying promoters and related persons must not together hold more than ten percent of the voting rights. The 1% test therefore controls the vote, while the 10% test acts as a ceiling for remaining eligible.
review_notes: CMS 12 anchors related-person aggregation via PAN/folio consolidation; Shivalik 10/12 cleanly distinguish the 1% vote-dispensation test and the 10% post-reclassification cap.

question: CMS suggested that if the nominee shareholders did not meet the promoter-group definitions, their status could be explained through the XBRL Notes functionality in the shareholding pattern. Does using the Notes functionality remove the need for a Regulation 31A reclassification, and what does Shivalik add?
answer_summary: No. CMS's Notes functionality is only a disclosure convenience for the period during which the shares are held by nominees and only if they do not meet the promoter-group definitions; it does not take the place of Regulation 31A. Shivalik reinforces that reclassification of any person falling within the promoter or promoter group must follow the formal Regulation 31A route—board approval, stock-exchange no-objection, shareholder approval subject to the voting restrictions, and all other conditions—even when the persons seeking reclassification hold no shares. There is no shortcut through shareholding-pattern notes.
review_notes: CMS 13/15 state Notes functionality applies only if nominees are outside promoter-group definitions and does not replace Regulation 31A; Shivalik 10/15 reinforces the mandatory formal route. The Shivalik letter also records that the reclassifying promoters held no shares, supporting the answer's framing.

question: The February 2026 capacity-planning circular and the March 2026 Core SGF coverage circular both set new numerical safety thresholds for commodity-derivatives market infrastructure institutions. For each circular, state the new numerical benchmark, what risk or capacity dimension it measures, and the old requirement it replaces.
answer_summary: Capacity circular: installed capacity must be at least 2 times (2x) the projected peak load for stock exchanges and clearing corporations in the commodity derivatives segment (up from the 1.5x benchmark in the December 10, 2024 general MII circular), and utilisation exceeding 75% of installed capacity now triggers immediate remedial action by the MII with SCOT oversight. Core SGF circular: credit exposure coverage must be calculated for simultaneous default of at least 3 clearing members (and their associates) causing the highest credit exposure, replacing the earlier requirement of default of at least 2 clearing members plus 50% of all clearing members.
review_notes: Supported by cited chunks: capacity circular sets 2x/75% thresholds and Core SGF circular raises stress default to 3 CMs; 1.5x baseline and old 2+50% rule are in the cited Dec 2024/Annexure-O chunks. Cross-doc threshold comparison adds a distinct memorisation target despite overlap with codex q093.

question: The March 27, 2026 press release extends trading suspensions for contracts on seven agricultural commodities. The February 2026 capacity-planning circular came out earlier. Does that circular cover only the stock exchanges mentioned in the press release, or does it also cover another category of market infrastructure institution?
answer_summary: The March 2026 press release is addressed to stock exchanges having a commodity derivatives segment. The February 2026 capacity-planning circular expressly applies to both stock exchanges and clearing corporations with a commodity derivatives segment. Both categories of MIIs must therefore prepare and submit the Capacity Planning and Real Time Performance Monitoring Policy, maintain installed capacity of at least 2x projected peak load, and act when utilisation crosses 75%.
review_notes: Supported: the March 2026 press release is addressed to stock exchanges, while the February 2026 capacity circular applies to both stock exchanges and clearing corporations in the commodity-derivatives segment. Actor-scope cross-reference is different from prior capacity/agriculture split questions.

question: Before the February 2026 circular, the December 10, 2024 capacity-planning guidelines deliberately excluded the Commodity Derivatives Segment of stock exchanges and clearing corporations. What process did SEBI use to close that gap, and when the provisions were applied to commodities, which paragraphs of the 2024 circular were modified?
answer_summary: SEBI closed the gap after receiving representations from commodity-derivatives stock exchanges and conducting a review in consultation with the Technical Advisory Committee (TAC) and through public consultation dated June 30, 2025. The February 2026 circular adopts most paragraphs of the December 10, 2024 circular mutatis mutandis for the Commodity Derivatives Segment but modifies paragraph 3.3 (installed capacity must be at least 2x, not 1.5x, projected peak load) and paragraph 3.13 (if utilisation exceeds 75%, the MII must take immediate action and SCOT oversees it, and the augmentation framework must be included in the MII's policy).
review_notes: Supported: Dec 2024 circular excluded the commodity-derivatives segment, and the Feb 2026 circular records the review/Consultation/TAC process plus the paragraph 3.3 and 3.13 modifications. Distinct structural-lineage target.

question: The May 2026 early-pay-in consultation relates to the same segment whose derivative contracts were kept suspended in the March 2026 press release. Which segment is it, what are the affected commodities, and under the draft circular which entity would provide the expanded early-pay-in facility?
answer_summary: Both documents concern the Agricultural Commodity Derivatives Segment. The March 2026 press release extends trading suspensions for derivative contracts in paddy (non-basmati), wheat, chana, mustard seeds and its derivatives (its complex), soya bean and its derivatives (its complex), crude palm oil, and moong until March 31, 2027. The May 2026 draft circular proposes that clearing corporations, rather than stock exchanges, provide the early-pay-in facility in respect of relevant derivatives contracts sold, extending the benefit from futures to options contracts.
review_notes: Supported: the press release lists the suspended agricultural commodities, and the early-pay-in draft identifies the Agricultural Commodity Derivatives Segment and assigns the expanded facility to clearing corporations. Adds a new cross-document linkage with the press release.

question: SEBI proposed in September 2024 to delete the Regulation 12 and Schedule I carve-outs that let listed entities issue 'payable-at-par' warrants or cheques when electronic payment of dividend, interest or redemption/repayment amounts was not possible. Was that proposal carried into the LODR Regulations as amended on December 16, 2025, and what exactly disappeared from Regulation 12?
answer_summary: Yes. The Fifth Amendment Regulations, 2025 (effective November 19, 2025) omitted the two provisos to Regulation 12. The consolidated LODR Regulations of December 16, 2025 therefore ends Regulation 12 after the list of payments (dividends, interest, redemption or repayment amounts) with a full stop, and no longer permits payable-at-par warrants or cheques, nor requires speed-post for dividend payments above Rs 1,500.
review_notes: Accepted. Both cited docs support the answer: the consultation proposed deleting the two Regulation 12 provisos, and the Dec 16 2025 consolidated LODR shows the Fifth Amendment (effective Nov 19 2025) omitted them. Distinct proposal-to-final textual memory target.

question: SEBI's October 2025 consultation proposed aligning Regulation 61A(3) with the Companies Act by transferring unclaimed amounts relating to listed non-convertible securities to IEPF or IPEF only after seven years from the maturity date, instead of after seven years in the escrow account. Was that proposal reflected in the LODR Regulations as amended on December 16, 2025?
answer_summary: No. The consolidated LODR Regulations dated December 16, 2025 still provide in Regulation 61A(3) that any amount transferred to the escrow account that remains unclaimed for seven years shall be transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund (for companies) or to SEBI's Investor Protection and Education Fund (for listed entities that are not companies). The seven-year clock still runs from the time the amount lies unclaimed in escrow; the October 2025 proposal to link the transfer to the maturity date had not been incorporated by then.
review_notes: Accepted. Cited Dec 16 2025 LODR Regulation 61A(3) still ties the seven-year transfer clock to time in escrow, while the consultation proposed linking it to maturity date. Clear fake-negative/absence-check target.

question: Before the LODR amendment that removed the payable-at-par exception for failed electronic payments, SEBI had already placed one class of securityholders on an electronic-only payment footing. Which class, under which instrument, and from what date? How did the September 2024 consultation and the December 16, 2025 regulation together make the rule uniform across holders?
answer_summary: Physical securityholders were first: SEBI Circular SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD_RTAMB/P/CIR/2021/655 dated November 3, 2021 mandated that any payment to investors holding securities in physical form be made only in electronic form, effective April 1, 2024 (now part of the Master Circular for RTAs dated May 7, 2024). The September 2024 consultation then proposed the same electronic-only requirement for demat account holders by deleting the Regulation 12 provisos. That change was carried into the LODR Regulations by the Fifth Amendment Regulations, 2025 effective November 19, 2025, and appears in the consolidated regulation of December 16, 2025. As a result, listed entities must make dividend, interest, redemption and repayment amounts electronically for both physical and demat holders, without reverting to payable-at-par warrants or cheques.
review_notes: Accepted. Supported: consultation cites Circular 2021/655 mandating electronic-only payments for physical securityholders from Apr 1 2024, and the Dec 16 2025 consolidated text shows the same rule extended to demat holders via the Fifth Amendment. Teaches a distinct staged-implementation target.

question: SEBI's October 2025 consultation proposed aligning Regulation 61A(3) with the Companies Act so that unclaimed amounts on listed non-convertible securities would be transferred to IEPF or IPEF only after seven years from the maturity date. Which LODR amendment eventually gave effect to that proposal, and how did it distinguish companies from non-company listed entities?
answer_summary: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) (Amendment) Regulations, 2026, notified on January 20, 2026 and effective from publication in the Official Gazette, substituted Regulation 61A(3). For companies, unclaimed amounts in the escrow account are to be transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund under section 125 of the Companies Act, 2013 and the rules made thereunder (which themselves require the seven-year period to run from maturity). For listed entities that are not companies, the amount must remain unclaimed and unpaid for seven years from the maturity date of the non-convertible securities before it is transferred to SEBI's Investor Protection and Education Fund under section 11 of the SEBI Act; such transferred amount does not bear any interest.
review_notes: Accepted. Cited Jan 2026 Amendment Regulations substituted Regulation 61A(3); companies go to IEPF under Companies Act section 125, non-companies to IPEF after seven years from maturity date under SEBI Act section 11 with no interest. Distinct amendment-identification and entity-distinction target.

question: The 2025 informal guidances for Century Plyboards, Welspun Corp and ISK Advisors each invoke a six-month period, but for three different PIT rules. What does each six-month test govern?
answer_summary: Each six-month period serves a distinct PIT purpose. In Century Plyboards, the six-month window is the contra-trade bar under Clause 3 read with Clause 10 of Schedule B: the donor attracts contra-trade restrictions if the gift occurs within six months of an opposite trade by the designated person and immediate relatives collectively. In Welspun Corp, the six-month gap between creation of a pledge and revocation of a pledge does not itself trigger contra-trade restrictions because beneficial ownership does not change until invocation, though the trade must be bona fide and pre-cleared. In ISK Advisors, the last-six-month lookback in Regulation 2(1)(d)(i) decides whether the merchant banker is still a connected person for bodies corporate whose public issues it managed; if more than six months have elapsed since listing/issue-management, the applicant is not automatically a connected person for those companies.
review_notes: Cited chunk text confirms three distinct six-month tests: Century contra-trade bar, Welspun pledge-revocation timing, ISK merchant-banker connected-person lookback. Extends earlier two-way comparisons by adding Welspun and changing answer shape to a rule map.

question: The Comprehensive FAQs on PIT Regulations say a compliance officer may relax contra-trade restrictions for reasons recorded in writing. Did SEBI grant that relaxation in the 2025 Century Plyboards guidance on the promoter-to-daughter gift, or what step did it leave to the company?
answer_summary: The Dec 2024 FAQs state that, under the code of conduct, the compliance officer may be empowered to grant relaxation from strict application of contra-trade restrictions for reasons recorded in writing provided the relaxation does not violate the PIT Regulations. In the 2025 Century Plyboards guidance, SEBI did not itself grant such a relaxation. It inferred that an inter-se promoter gift would attract contra-trade restrictions on the donor, and then expressly pointed the company's compliance officer to the company's own Code of Conduct to decide whether to grant Clause 10 relaxation while ensuring PIT compliance.
review_notes: Verified: Dec 2024 FAQs empower the compliance officer to record reasons for contra-trade relaxation; Century guidance did not grant the relaxation itself but left the company to apply its own Code of Conduct. Clear baseline-vs-application absence check.

question: A listed entity with listed non-convertible securities looks at Regulation 61A(3) of the SEBI LODR Regulations as consolidated on December 16, 2025 and sees that unclaimed amounts in its escrow account must be transferred to IEPF/IPEF after seven years in the account. It also sees that the SEBI Board approved aligning the transfer timeline with the Companies Act on December 17, 2025. If it wants to follow the post-Board rule, which amendment should it actually consult instead of the December 2025 consolidation, and what new trigger condition applies to the securities before the transfer to IEPF or IPEF?
answer_summary: It should consult the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) (Amendment) Regulations, 2026 (notification SEBI/NRO-GN/2026/295, January 20, 2026), not the December 16, 2025 consolidated LODR Regulations. The December 2025 consolidation still contained the old time-in-escrow rule. The amended Regulation 61A(3) ties the transfer to the maturity of the non-convertible securities: company listed entities must transfer to the IEPF under the Companies Act timeline, while non-company listed entities must wait until the amount has remained unclaimed and unpaid for seven years from the maturity date of the non-convertible securities before transferring it to the Investor Protection and Education Fund (with no interest accruing in the IPEF).
review_notes: Cited Board press release, Dec 16 2025 consolidated LODR, and Jan 2026 amendment support the answer. Teaches a distinct consolidation-vs-amendment timing trap / decoy-current-regulation target compared to kimi_run_000042_q02/q04.

question: An investor wants someone to be able to operate their single-holder demat account if they become physically incapacitated but still retain the capacity to contract. Can they achieve this through the nomination facility, and if not, what alternative does SEBI now propose?
answer_summary: Under the January 10, 2025 circular, a single-holder investor could authorise one nominee (excluding a minor nominee) to operate the account in such a situation, up to a specified percentage or absolute value of assets, and the nomination form included a specific clause allowing this authorisation. The March 2026 modified-nomination proposal drops this nominee-as-operator mechanism because of implementation costs, fraud/misuse risks, and legal ambiguity; it instead proposes that the existing Power of Attorney mechanism is sufficient for dealing with an incapacitated but contracting investor.
review_notes: Supported by Jan 2025 circular (para 3.5/form authorisation) and March 2026 proposal (Proposal 1 drops nominee-operator in favour of POA).

question: For a jointly held mutual fund folio, is nomination mandatory; and if the joint holders decide to nominate, whose consent or signatures are required? Trace how this changed from the June 2024 circular through the January 2025 circular to the March 2026 modified-nomination proposal.
answer_summary: The June 2024 circular exempts jointly held demat accounts and MF folios from the mandatory 'choice of nomination' requirement for new investors. The January 2025 circular retained survivorship rules and required the nomination form to be signed according to the mode of holding—_jointly_ held folios required all holders to sign. The March 2026 modified-nomination proposal explicitly makes nomination optional for jointly held accounts/folios and requires the consent of all joint-holders for providing or changing a nominee.
review_notes: Supported by June 2024 exemption for joint holdings, Jan 2025 signatory rules, and March 2026 optionality plus all-holders consent.

question: An NRI investor does not have an Indian PAN readily available to give as a nominee identifier. What was the original January 2025 requirement, what February 2025 amendment accommodated NRIs/OCI/PIO investors, and what does the March 2026 modified-nomination proposal require instead?
answer_summary: The January 2025 circular mandated that investors provide any one of PAN, driving licence number or the last four digits of Aadhaar as a personal identifier of the nominee. The February 28, 2025 amendment added that for NRI/OCI/PIO nominees, a passport number is acceptable. The March 2026 modified-nomination proposal removes this identifier requirement from the mandatory list: only the nominee's name and nature of relationship are mandatory, and all other details—including contact details, percentage share, KYC, personal identifier and guardian particulars—become optional.
review_notes: Jan 2025 mandates PAN/DL/Aadhaar identifier; Feb 2025 adds passport for NRI/OCI/PIO; March 2026 makes all nominee details except name/relationship optional.

question: An intermediary closes a client account and also accepts a change of nomination on the same day. What turnaround-time obligation applies to the KYC-record side, and what separate acknowledgement obligation applies to the nomination side?
answer_summary: Under the KRA consultation, the intermediary must inform the KRA within 3 working days of account closure, and the KRA must update or delink the relevant record within 2 working days of receiving that information. Under the modified-nomination proposal, the regulated entity must provide an acknowledgement to the investor for every instance of nomination, subsequent change, or cancellation, irrespective of the mode used.
review_notes: KRA proposal requires intermediary 3-wd closure notice and KRA 2-wd update; modified-nomination proposal requires acknowledgement for each nomination/change.

question: Under the modified-nomination proposal, what choice does an investor have about how their nomination information is shown in periodic statements, and what parallel duty does the KRA proposal place on intermediaries when they receive a KRA-disseminated client update?
answer_summary: The modified-nomination proposal requires regulated entities to print one of two things in periodic or holding statements as chosen by the investor: either the names of the nominee(s), or simply Yes/No to show whether nomination has been made. Separately, the KRA proposal inserts a new master-circular paragraph requiring intermediaries to update the KYC records of their clients as and when they receive an update from the KRA under Regulation 15(f) of the KRA Regulations.
review_notes: Modified-nomination proposal lets investor choose nominee names or Yes/No in statements; KRA proposal adds intermediary duty to update records on KRA dissemination.

question: An OCI card holder who actually lives in India and an NRI who lives outside India both want to complete KYC digitally. What specific location or address evidence must each produce, and why is the requirement of being physically in India not the same hurdle for both?
answer_summary: For the OCI card holder residing in India, the KRA proposal makes the overseas address proof optional provided the client submits proof of an Indian address showing residence of more than 182 days. For the NRI outside India, the separate December 2025 re-KYC circular relaxes the requirement that the client must be physically in India during digital onboarding; instead, the app must capture GPS latitude and longitude that match the country given in the proof of address, and must block spoofed IP addresses. The two relaxations differ because one applies to resident OCI/PIO clients and removes the need for overseas address evidence, while the other allows genuine NRIs abroad to complete re-KYC remotely by matching device geolocation to their declared address country.
review_notes: KRA proposal waives overseas address proof for OCI residents in India with >182-day Indian address; Dec 2025 circular relaxes physical-location-in-India for NRIs abroad via GPS and anti-spoofing.

question: How do the effective-date and transition rules differ between the KRA proposal's new supplementary-data obligations and the March 2026 modified-nomination proposal?
answer_summary: The KRA proposal takes effect from the circular issue date, gives intermediaries 6 months to upload Part-II supplementary information for existing KYC records, 3 months to update old closed accounts via the delinking process, and imposes the 3-working-day closure notice and 2-working-day KRA update immediately. The March 2026 modified-nomination circular leaves the exact effective date as 'xx xx, 20xx', makes default nomination apply only to single accounts opened on or after that date, and states that the new clauses apply _mutatis mutandis_ to existing accounts and folios as well.
review_notes: KRA proposal effective from circular issue with 6-month Part-II remediation, 3-month closed-account cleanup, and immediate closure timelines; modified-nomination leaves placeholder date and applies to existing accounts mutatis mutandis.

question: Both the KRA proposal and the modified-nomination proposal redefine what information is mandatory versus optional when onboarding a client. Which fields move to mandatory-only or optional-only buckets in each proposal?
answer_summary: In the KRA proposal, Part-II supplementary fields income range, place and country of birth, FATCA information, PEP status, occupation and the new identifiers (CKYC ID, DIGIPIN, OVD expiry date) are to be uploaded; net worth is explicitly optional and an alternate mobile number/email is optional. Source verification of all these is not a precondition—only selected fields may be validated if the KRA independently verifies them. In the modified-nomination proposal, only the nominee's name and nature of relationship are mandatory; date of birth is mandatory only if the nominee is a minor, and everything else—address, mobile, email, percentage share, nominee KYC, guardian details—is optional (with equal apportionment if percentages are not specified).
review_notes: KRA proposal uploads Part-II fields and keeps net worth/alternate contacts optional (source verification not a precondition); modified-nomination makes only name/relationship mandatory.

question: SEBI invited bids for KBCL properties through a June 11, 2024 public notice. A July 15, 2024 corrigendum and a July 31, 2024 addendum followed. What did each of those later notices address, and what change did each make?
answer_summary: The July 15, 2024 corrigendum responded to representations/objections: it kept properties Sr. No. 1, 2, 6, 9, 16 and 19 on hold until July 25, 2024 and tentatively rescheduled their auction to July 26, 2024; it also corrected the description of Sr. No. 17 by changing the word "Chormura" to "Bhadaya". The July 31, 2024 addendum then withdrew those same six properties from the auction list because investigation of the representations/objections was still pending.
review_notes: Cited corrigendum and addendum directly support the described hold/reschedule, typo correction, and withdrawal of Sr. No. 1/2/6/9/16/19. Truly multi-document and a distinct upstream notice-lineage target.

question: The KBCL auction notices were amended by an addendum on July 31, 2024 and again by an addendum on December 16, 2024. What issue prompted each addendum, and what concrete change to the auction process resulted?
answer_summary: The July 31, 2024 addendum responded to representations/objections received by SEBI; the six properties previously put on hold (Sr. No. 1, 2, 6, 9, 16 and 19) were withdrawn from that auction. The December 16, 2024 addendum was issued because interested bidders needed more time to submit the Earnest Money Deposit, as intimated by Quikr Realty Pvt. Ltd. (the valuation agency); it extended the last date for submission of bids and remittance of EMD to December 19, 2024 (until 5:00 p.m.).
review_notes: Both addenda are required to contrast the representation-driven July withdrawal with the EMD-extension reason in December. Partially overlaps the December addendum with kimi_run_000040_q01 but asks a new comparative intent.

question: The July 31, 2024 addendum withdrew six KBCL properties from the then-scheduled auction. Which of those properties later had separate one-property sale confirmation orders in the re-notified e-auction, and who bought each?
answer_summary: Of the six withdrawn properties, separate one-property sale confirmations were issued for Sr. No. 1, Sr. No. 2, Sr. No. 6, Sr. No. 9 and Sr. No. 16. Sr. No. 1 went to Sumant Yadav, Sr. No. 2 to Atlaspac Ventures India Pvt. Ltd., Sr. No. 6 to Atlaspac Ventures India Pvt. Ltd. (confirmation dated February 18, 2025), Sr. No. 9 to Shatanshu Agrawal, and Sr. No. 16 to Prashant Agarwal. No separate one-property confirmation for Sr. No. 19 was located in the reviewed corpus.
review_notes: The July 31 addendum sets the six-property cohort and the five one-property confirmations establish the downstream buyers; Sr. No. 19 negative is honestly flagged. New cross-reference target not covered by prior memory.

question: KBCL property Serial No. 3 appears in the seven-property confirmation order dated August 16, 2024 and again in a one-property confirmation order dated January 30, 2025. How did the buyer and the hammer price differ between the two rounds?
answer_summary: In the August 16, 2024 seven-property order, Serial No. 3 (Churmura village, described as Land No. 76) was knocked down to Hindustan Warehousing as part of a composite bid totalling Rs. 2,57,68,195; the amount attributable to Sr. No. 3 was Rs. 66,92,260. In the January 30, 2025 one-property order, the same serial (described as Khasra No. 235, Churmura village, area 0.8935 hectares) was knocked down to Mr. Ram Abtar for a bid of Rs. 45,74,000 (full payment including 1% poundage was Rs. 46,19,740).
review_notes: August 2024 seven-property order and January 2025 one-property order both required to compare buyer and hammer price for Sr. No. 3. Amounts and entities verified in cited chunks.

question: An existing PMS client already received the Most Important Terms and Conditions document by email in January 2025. In September 2025, the portfolio manager decides to update the risk-factor portion of its Disclosure Document. Must the client receive the whole Disclosure Document again, and what exactly has to be certified?
answer_summary: No. Under the September 9, 2025 circular on the Disclosure Document format, only the page(s) containing the change need to be sent and certified; each parameter of the Disclosure Document must begin on a fresh page, and only changed pages require certification by an independent Chartered Accountant and the Principal Officer. Those updated pages must be communicated to the client, updated on the portfolio manager’s website, and filed with SEBI within 7 working days of the change. The earlier MITC distribution to existing clients (required by January 1, 2025 under the May 2, 2024 circular) is a separate one-time exercise and does not alter the Disclosure Document update rule.
review_notes: Supported by both cited circulars: Sept 2025 circular (changed pages certified and communicated within 7 working days) and May 2024 circular (existing-client MITC by Jan 1, 2025). Distinct from prior PMS update vs fee-rollout comparisons because it pins the changed-page certification rule against the one-time MITC exercise.

question: A PMS client is on-boarded digitally in October 2024 and later receives an updated Disclosure Document in October 2025. Who must sign or certify the client-facing documents at each stage, and in what form?
answer_summary: For the digital on-boarding done on or after October 1, 2024, the new client must separately sign the fee annexure and add a note that she has understood the fee structure; if on-boarded digitally, this can be typed or written electronically with a finger or stylus, but if on-boarded physically it must be handwritten. For the updated September 2025 format Disclosure Document, the changed pages alone must be certified by an independent Chartered Accountant and the Principal Officer; the full document itself must close with the name and signature of at least two Directors or Designated Partners of the portfolio manager.
review_notes: Both cited circulars support the staged signature/certification rules (digital mode typed/electronic vs physical handwritten; changed pages certified by CA + Principal Officer; full document closes with two Directors/Designated Partners).

question: In a non-LVF AIF scheme using the April 2026 fast-track PPM route and in a PMS client account, respectively, who is responsible for ensuring that disclosures and client-account records are accurate?
answer_summary: For the AIF non-LVF scheme, the Merchant Banker and the Manager of the AIF are jointly responsible for ensuring the accuracy and completeness of all disclosures in the PPM and the declarations submitted to SEBI. For the PMS client account, the portfolio manager must maintain a separate portfolio record, keep books on a historical-cost basis, recognise purchases and sales on the trade date (not settlement date), and account for expenses and transaction costs as prescribed. So accuracy responsibility in the AIF context lies with the Manager plus the Merchant Banker, while in the PMS context it lies with the portfolio manager’s own accounting policies and record-keeping.
review_notes: AIF fast-track circular places accuracy responsibility on Manager + Merchant Banker; PMS Disclosure Document outlines portfolio manager's client accounting duties. Cross-regime 'respectively' shape genuinely requires both documents.

question: SEBI issued informal-guidance letters in 2025 for both Century Plyboards and Welspun Corp under the PIT Regulations, but in one of them it left some queries unanswered. What defect in the request caused SEBI to decline to answer, and how did the other request avoid that problem?
answer_summary: In Century Plyboards, Queries 4 and 5 were not answered because they rested on incomplete factual details and involved hypothetical or assumed facts. Paragraph 8 of the Informal Guidance Scheme, 2003 permits SEBI to decline requests that are general, do not completely describe the factual situation, or are hypothetical. In Welspun Corp, by contrast, the company gave concrete facts: dates of ESOP exercise, pledge creation, proposed revocation and sale, and confirmation that the MD was not in possession of UPSI and the trading window was open, so SEBI answered all four queries.
review_notes: Century Plyboards chunk #13 explicitly cites Para 8 of the Informal Guidance Scheme and states queries 4-5 were not answered due to incomplete/hypothetical facts. Welspun chunks establish the concrete factual predicates SEBI relied on.

question: Three 2025 informal guidances in the frontier region—Century Plyboards, Welspun Corp, and ISK Advisors—each contain a confidentiality clause tied to the Informal Guidance Scheme, 2003. What is the uniform blackout length, and from what date is it measured?
answer_summary: Each letter is not made public for 90 days from the date of issuance of that letter. The period runs from the date the SEBI response is issued, not from the date of the applicant’s original request or the date of the underlying transaction.
review_notes: Uniform 90-day confidentiality period verified in all three cited informal-guidance letters (Century #13, Welspun #12, ISK #12), measured from the date of issuance of each response.

question: Two promoter-group reorganisations both take an acquirer past the usual SAST open-offer trigger. In one, Kaygee Investments receives Ipca Laboratories shares from its wholly-owned subsidiary under a court/tribunal scheme; in the other, Empire Industries' promoters gift shares to their sons. Which SAST exemption applies to each, and what structural condition separates the two routes?
answer_summary: In the Ipca matter the exemption falls under Regulation 10(1)(d)(iii) of the Takeover Regulations: an acquisition pursuant to a scheme of arrangement that does not directly involve the target company as a transferor or transferee. For that exemption to apply, (i) the cash and cash-equivalent component in the consideration paid must be less than 25% of the total scheme consideration, and (ii) after the scheme, persons directly or indirectly holding at least 33% of the voting rights in the combined entity must be the same as those who held the entire voting rights before it. SEBI noted there was no cash component and the Premchand Godha family would retain 100% voting rights in KIPL. In Empire the inter-se family gift falls under Regulation 10(1)(a)(i), which exempts acquisitions among immediate relatives. There SEBI first tested the individual thresholds under Regulation 3(1) read with Regulation 3(3): Ranjit's shareholding would only rise from 16.14% to 18.58%, so no open offer arose and the exemption was unnecessary; Dileep's shareholding would move from 24.60% to 27.05%, crossing the 25% threshold, so the inter-se transfer exemption had to be invoked for him. The structural divide is that Ipca is a third-party corporate scheme routed through entities other than the target, while Empire is a direct transfer between natural-person immediate relatives.
review_notes: Cited Ipca chunks confirm the scheme is between KIPL and PCPL only, no cash component, and the Premchand Godha family retains 100% voting rights in KIPL. Empire chunks confirm the inter-se family gift and the donee-specific 25% threshold test (Ranjit 16.14%-18.58% ok; Dileep 24.60%-27.05% invokes 10(1)(a)(i)). Distinct scheme-vs-immediate-relative structural divide.

question: A shareholder proposes to move from below 25% to above 25% by acquiring target-company shares. Ipca Laboratories argued that its restructuring qualified for an exemption under Regulation 10(1)(d)(iii), while CHL Ltd. addressed the same risk through threshold and control analysis. Why could CHL not rely on Regulation 10(1)(d)(iii), and what did SEBI examine instead?
answer_summary: Regulation 10(1)(d)(iii) applies only when the acquisition is pursuant to a scheme of arrangement or reconstruction that does not directly involve the target company as a transferor or transferee. CHL's transaction was a preferential issue of compulsorily convertible preference shares and debentures by the target company itself, not a scheme between other entities, so that exemption was unavailable. SEBI instead tested whether an open offer was triggered under Regulations 3 and 4. On the numbers, the shareholding of the promoter and promoter group would actually fall by 0.96%, so Regulation 3(2) was not breached; none of the individual allottees would cross 25%, so Regulation 3(3) did not apply; and because the board would expand to 14 directors and no allottee would obtain the right to appoint a majority or control management/policy, there was no change in control under Regulation 4.
review_notes: Ipca chunks state Regulation 10(1)(d)(iii) applies to schemes not directly involving the target. CHL chunks show the transaction is a preferential issue of CCDs/CCPS by the target, promoter/PAC shareholding falls 0.96%, no individual crosses 25%, and board composition stays below control. Useful wrong-exemption-path memory target.

question: Ambo Agritec's promoter proposed to convert the remaining 38.5 lakh warrants, lifting his individual holding from 54.65% to 62.02% in one financial year. Empire Industries' donee Dileep Malhotra would rise only from 24.60% to 27.05% through a family gift. Both want to avoid an open offer. Why does Empire have a usable exemption while Ambo does not?
answer_summary: Ambo's increase is a fresh acquisition of shares by conversion of warrants. Since he already held more than 25%, the increase is tested under Regulation 3(2), and on a gross-acquisition basis the 7.37% rise in one financial year exceeds the 5% creeping limit. Regulation 3(3) is also engaged because the individual holding crosses thresholds. There is no SAST exemption available for a warrant conversion that breaches those limits, so an open offer is required. In Empire the acquisition is an off-market inter-se gift between immediate relatives, which qualifies for the exemption under Regulation 10(1)(a)(i). SEBI first identified which donee breached the threshold: Dileep would move above 25% so the exemption had to be invoked for him; Ranjit's holding would remain at 18.58% so no threshold was crossed and no exemption was needed. The presence of an express inter-se-relatives exemption is the decisive difference.
review_notes: Ambo chunks support 54.65%-62.02% / 7.37% gross acquisition breaching the 5% creeping limit. Empire chunks support the immediate-relative exemption and Dileep's 24.60%-27.05% threshold crossing. Overlaps prior Ambo/Empire threshold mapping but frames the comparison around exemption availability, which is a distinct practical target.

question: K.J. Joseph and Thomas John proposed to move 51.75% of Thejo Engineering into a family trust whose beneficiaries were promoters, their immediate relatives and lineal descendants, but one trustee would be a neutral third party. Empire Industries' promoters proposed to gift 4.90% to their sons. Both were trying to avoid an open offer. Why did the neutral trustee defeat the exemption in K.J. Joseph while Empire's gift to Dileep Malhotra was treated differently?
answer_summary: K.J. Joseph had to seek a discretionary exemption under Regulation 11(1) of the Takeover Regulations read with Chapter 8 of the SEBI Master Circular. Chapter 8 requires, among other things, that only individual promoters or their immediate relatives or lineal descendants act as trustees and beneficiaries. Because one of the five trustees was proposed to be a neutral trustee outside the promoter group, the trust structure did not satisfy that condition and SEBI concluded it would not be eligible for the exemption. Empire, however, relied on the self-operative inter-se transfer exemption under Regulation 10(1)(a)(i), which applies to direct transfers among immediate relatives and does not require a discretionary approval or a trustee structure. For Dileep Malhotra, the gift breached the 25% individual threshold under Regulation 3(1) read with Regulation 3(3), so the exemption was actually invoked; for Ranjit, no threshold was crossed and no exemption was necessary.
review_notes: K.J. Joseph chunks state the trust seeks Regulation 11(1)/Master Circular Chapter 8 relief and that the neutral trustee disqualifies it because trustees must be only promoters/immediate relatives/lineal descendants. Empire chunks support the self-operative 10(1)(a)(i) exemption and the Ranjit/Dileep split. The 51.75% figure is in chunk #2 of the K.J. Joseph document but is not listed in supporting_chunks; the answer itself does not depend on it.

question: Both Ipca Laboratories and K.J. Joseph/Thomas John proposed to rearrange promoter-linked shareholdings without an open offer. One route is treated as Regulation 10(1)(d)(iii); the other must go to SEBI under Regulation 11 read with Chapter 8 of the SAST Master Circular. What factual divide determines which procedural route applies?
answer_summary: The factual divide is whether the rearrangement fits an enumerated self-operative exemption or is a trust-based reorganisation that needs ad hoc SEBI approval. Ipca's transaction was a scheme of arrangement between Kaygee Investments and its wholly-owned subsidiary Paschim Chemicals, transferring Ipca shares indirectly; the target company was not a transferor or transferee, there was no cash component, and the same family group would continue to hold voting rights. That squarely meets the structural conditions of Regulation 10(1)(d)(iii), so no Board discretion is needed. Thejo Engineering's proposed family trust is not an inter-se transfer and is not a scheme falling under Regulation 10(1)(d)(iii); the applicants therefore had to seek a discretionary grant of exemption under Regulation 11(1) supported by Chapter 8 of the Master Circular, which lays down specific trustee/beneficiary composition conditions.
review_notes: Ipca chunks confirm the self-operative scheme exemption conditions. K.J. Joseph chunks confirm the trust must use discretionary Regulation 11(1) read with Master Circular Chapter 8. Clear procedural-route / exemption-categorization target.

question: Pritish Nandy's acquirer placed purchase orders in late March 2025 but the last tranche was credited to its demat account only on April 2, 2025. CHL Ltd.'s investors will convert CCDs and CCPS into equity on a single date. For SAST creeping-acquisition computations, which year controls in Pritish, and why is CHL not treated as a straddling acquisition across financial years?
answer_summary: In Pritish Nandy, SEBI treated acquisition as occurring in the financial year in which the purchase order was placed, not when demat credit occurred. Because "acquisition" includes "agreeing to acquire," and Regulation 13(2) requires a public announcement to precede the purchase order that would push voting rights beyond the threshold, the relevant moment is the placement of the order. Thus the 4.87% accretion counted against the financial-year 5% limit in FY 2024-25. In CHL, all preferential allottees were converting their CCDs and CCPS into equity on the same date, so there was no issue of deferred delivery or carry-over. The additional acquisition was measured as the difference between pre-allotment and post-allotment voting percentages on that single conversion date; since the promoter and promoter-group shareholding fell by 0.96%, no creeping limit was breached.
review_notes: Pritish chunks support purchase-order-year counting under Regulation 3(2) read with Regulation 13. CHL chunks support same-date conversion and the 0.96% promoter-group decrease. Distinct from prior Ambo/Pritish timing pair because it pins the date-trap against a simultaneous-conversion counterexample.

question: Both Ambo Agritec and Ipca Laboratories involve acquisitions that would otherwise trigger an open offer. Ambo argues that converting the remaining warrants within their tenure should be exempt; Ipca claims its share transfer is exempt under Regulation 10(1)(d)(iii). What factor about consideration and transaction structure makes only Ipca's claim sustainable?
answer_summary: The decisive factor is that Ipca's transfer was structured as a scheme between Kaygee Investments and its wholly-owned subsidiary Paschim Chemicals that did not directly involve the target, had no cash component, and preserved voting continuity for the Godha family. Those are the exact conditions of Regulation 10(1)(d)(iii). Ambo's proposed conversion was an acquisition of shares through the exercise of warrants, giving the promoter 7.37% more voting rights within a single financial year. It was not a scheme, carried value in the form of warrant/conversion consideration, and breached the 5% creeping-acquisition ceiling under Regulation 3(2) read with Regulation 3(3). No SAST exemption covers that warrant-conversion overrun, so an open offer was required.
review_notes: Ipca chunks support the cashless scheme/continuity conditions and Ambo chunks support the warrant-conversion creep. The question forces a structural/consideration comparison, which is adjacent to q01 and q03 but still teaches a distinct exemption-conditions memory target. Novelty is lower because the same documents are reused.

question: A bank holding funds for the RC 8446 defaulters receives the 30 January 2025 remittance order and then discovers that one of them opened a new savings account after the earlier attachment notices were served. Must the bank attach that new account before remitting, and where does the duty come from?
answer_summary: Yes, it must immediately attach the new account and intimate SEBI. The 30 December 2024 RC 8446 attachment notice (AP 13478) explicitly directs banks to "immediately attach any new account/s opened by the defaulter with your Bank post issuance of this notice of attachment and intimate the same". The 30 January 2025 remittance order does not repeat that forward-looking duty; it only directs banks and mutual funds to remit amounts already lying in attached accounts/folios.
review_notes: Supported: attachment notice directs banks to immediately attach new accounts opened post-notice, while the remittance order only deals with existing attached balances. Strong cross-document absence/contrast.

question: How does the instruction to banks and mutual funds change between the RC 8446 attachment notice and the general remittance order, both in the speed of compliance and in how they treat non-existent accounts?
answer_summary: The 30 December 2024 attachment notices require banks and mutual funds to provide account details, statements, and confirmation of attachment within 15 days of receipt; if no response is received within 15 days it will be presumed the defaulter has no account (and if there is no account, the same need not be reported). The 30 January 2025 remittance order replaces that slow-information phase with immediate action: banks/MFs must remit the attached amounts 'forthwith' by NEFT/RTGS, and if the defaulter has no account/folio with them they simply have nothing to remit and need not inform SEBI.
review_notes: Supported: attachment notice imposes 15-day reporting and presumes no account if no response, while remittance order demands forthwith remittance and only exempts notification for no account. Speed and treatment both require both documents.

question: Aromatic Tie Up failed to pay the RC 8309 demand. After SEBI issued the attachment notices to banks and depositories, can a bank still accept salary credits into the company's attached account, and why does the original demand notice not resolve this?
answer_summary: Yes, credits are allowed despite the freeze. The 15 January 2025 RC 8309 attachment notices state that no debit shall be made in the attached accounts/folios, but 'the credits, if any, into the account may be allowed.' The 13 November 2024 demand notice only restricts Aromatic Tie Up from transferring, mortgaging or otherwise dealing with its property after service; it does not set out any account-level freeze rules, so the attachment notices are needed to learn that debits are blocked while credits may pass through.
review_notes: Supported: attachment notices say no debit but credits may be allowed, whereas the demand notice only bars property transfers/mortgaging and gives no account-level freeze rule. Practical absence-style question requiring both docs.

question: A promoter-group relative with no access to unpublished price-sensitive information, and a merchant banker’s wholly-owned subsidiary, each plan to acquire shares of a listed company. In SEBI’s Century Plyboards and ISK Advisors informal guidances, what different test decides whether each person is treated as connected / covered by insider-trading restrictions, and which of the two statuses can be rebutted?
answer_summary: Under the Century Plyboards guidance, promoter-group members other than the promoter itself need not be classified as designated persons if they do not have access to UPSI; the test is the absence of UPSI access (Regulation 9(4)(iii) read with FAQ 51), and it operates as an exclusion. Under the ISK Advisors guidance, a subsidiary of a connected person is deemed to be a connected person unless the contrary is established; the test is corporate relationship (clause (b) of Regulation 2(1)(d)(ii) of the PIT Regulations), and the deemed-connection is rebuttable.
review_notes: Century Plyboards confirms promoter-group members without UPSI access need not be designated persons; ISK Advisors confirms clause (b) of Regulation 2(1)(d)(ii) makes a connected person's subsidiary deemed connected unless rebutted. Both tests and rebuttability distinction are directly supported.

question: In SEBI’s 2025 informal guidances for Century Plyboards and Welspun Corp, SEBI relied on specific answers in the Comprehensive FAQs on PIT Regulations to decide whether a non-sale transaction counted as ‘trading.’ Which FAQ conclusion did SEBI use in each guidance, and what additional company-level safeguard did it impose despite reaching that conclusion?
answer_summary: In Century Plyboards, SEBI cited FAQ 45, which treats a gift of shares as ‘dealing’ and therefore ‘trading,’ so the gift attracted contra-trade restrictions; however, SEBI noted the compliance officer could grant a relaxation for reasons recorded in writing. In Welspun Corp, SEBI cited the Comprehensive FAQ answer holding that creation, invocation and revocation of pledge all amount to trading; it nevertheless concluded that revocation of pledge within six months of creation would not trigger contra-trade restrictions because beneficial ownership does not change until invocation, provided the MD proves the transaction is bonafide and obtains pre-clearance from the compliance officer under Clause 6 of Schedule B read with Regulation 9(1).
review_notes: Century Plyboards cites FAQ 45 for gifts as trading and allows compliance-officer relaxation; Welspun Corp cites pledge creation/invocation/revocation as trading and exempts revocation-within-six-months subject to bonafide proof and pre-clearance. Cross-case mapping is supported.

question: Before April 2026, the AIF Master Circular required the first close of a scheme to be declared within 12 months from the date SEBI communicated that the PPM was taken on record. What did the April 2026 fast-track circular change for non-LVF schemes, and which category of schemes still follows the older Master Circular rule?
answer_summary: The April 2026 fast-track circular modifies para 2.3.1 of the Master Circular so that, for Angel Funds and non-LVF AIF schemes, the first close must be declared no later than 12 months from the date the AIF becomes eligible to launch the scheme (30 days after filing, or from the date of SEBI registration for the first scheme, whichever is later). Large Value Funds for Accredited Investors (LVF) schemes continue to follow the Master Circular rule of 12 months from the date of grant of AIF registration or filing of the PPM, whichever is later.
review_notes: Fast-track circular modifies para 2.3.1 of the AIF Master Circular for non-LVF/Angel schemes and sets first-close at 12 months from launch-eligibility; Master Circular preserves the older rule for LVF schemes. Supported.

question: A portfolio manager offers co-investment arrangements and also charges performance fees. Under the September 2025 PMS Disclosure Document format and the May 2024 digital onboarding circular, which performance-related disclosures must a discretionary portfolio manager give but a co-investment portfolio manager is exempt from?
answer_summary: The September 2025 format requires a discretionary portfolio manager to disclose portfolio management performance for the last three years, calculated using the Time Weighted Rate of Return method, but expressly provides that this sub-clause does not apply to a Co-investment Portfolio Manager. Both types of managers, however, must still comply with the May 2024 fee-transparency requirements: if performance fees are charged, the annexure to the PMS-client agreement must contain one-year and multi-year fee illustrations covering increase, decrease and unchanged scenarios and incorporating the high watermark principle, and a fee calculation tool must be shared with new clients onboarded on or after October 1, 2024.
review_notes: September 2025 format exempts co-investment portfolio managers from three-year TWRR performance disclosure while still requiring both types to comply with May 2024 fee-illustration and fee-tool requirements. Carve-out and continuing obligation supported.

question: An HUF and a body corporate are considering a PMS. Before signing the PMS agreement, what minimum financial eligibility thresholds must the portfolio manager disclose in the Disclosure Document for each of them, and what must each client separately acknowledge about fees under the digital onboarding circular?
answer_summary: The September 2025 PMS Disclosure Document format must disclose the accredited investor thresholds: for an individual, HUF, family trust or sole proprietorship, either annual income of at least ₹2 crore, or net worth of at least ₹7.5 crore (with at least ₹3.75 crore in financial assets), or annual income of at least ₹1 crore plus minimum net worth of ₹5 crore (with at least ₹2.5 crore in financial assets); for a body corporate or a trust other than a family trust, net worth of at least ₹50 crore; and for a partnership firm, each partner must independently meet the individual criteria.
