The May 2024 digital onboarding circular also requires that before taking up the assignment, the portfolio manager ensure the client has understood the fee structure; new clients onboarded on or after October 1, 2024 must separately sign the annexure on fees and charges and add a note that they have understood it (handwritten if physical, typed/electronic if digital).
review_notes: Disclosure Document format sets accredited-investor thresholds for HUF/body corporate/partnership firms; digital onboarding circular requires client acknowledgement of fee structure and signed fee annexure. Supported.

question: A bank receives the 30 January 2025 remittance order for RC 8446 and the 15 January 2025 bank attachment notice for RC 8309. In each case the named defaulter does not hold any account at the bank. Must the bank report that fact to SEBI, and why does the answer depend on which recovery certificate is involved?
answer_summary: Under the RC 8446 remittance order, the bank need not inform SEBI if the defaulter has no account or folio (para 6 of the order). Under the RC 8309 attachment notices, the bank/depository/mutual fund must inform SEBI by email to recoveryero@sebi.gov.in if the defaulter has no account, no folio or no balance (para 6 of AP 13644 and AP 13645). The two documents therefore impose opposite negative-response duties.
review_notes: Directly supported: RC 8446 remittance order (clf-blypzy4x7av0sam4cxz9tl55#4) says no account/folio need not be reported to SEBI, while RC 8309 attachment notices (clf-z184oghweflpj8uogkpi3y6l#3/#9) require reporting no account/balance to recoveryero@sebi.gov.in. Cross-RC contrast is materially different from prior intra-RC 8446 comparison.

question: Why does the RC 8309 attachment notice cite section 28A(1) and 11(2)(ia) of the SEBI Act read with section 226 of the Income-tax Act, while the RC 8446 remittance order cites section 28A read with sections 220 to 227, 228A, 229 and 232 of the Income-tax Act?
answer_summary: The RC 8309 attachment notices are conservatory: they invoke section 28A(1)/11(2)(ia) of the SEBI Act read with section 226 of the Income-tax Act to freeze accounts/folios so the defaulter cannot dispose of assets. The RC 8446 remittance order moves to collection: it invokes the wider certificate-proceeding provisions (sections 220–227, 228A, 229, 232 of the Income-tax Act) because it directs banks and mutual funds to remit the attached amounts to SEBI. The statutory spread tracks the procedural stage—freeze versus collect.
review_notes: Cited sections verified: RC 8309 attachment notices cite 28A(1)/11(2)(ia) r/w section 226 IT Act (clf-z184oghweflpj8uogkpi3y6l#4/#10); RC 8446 remittance order cites 28A r/w sections 220-227, 228A, 229, 232 IT Act (clf-blypzy4x7av0sam4cxz9tl55#5). Interpretation of conservatory freeze versus collection remittance is reasonable. Slightly abstract shape.

question: The demand notices for RC 8309 and RC 8446 were both issued in late 2024 and include interest on the underlying penalty. What interest rate applies to both, and how do the accrual periods explain why one demand is roughly fifteen times the other?
answer_summary: Both demand notices charge interest at 1% per month. For RC 8309, the penalty is Rs 5,00,000 and interest accrues from 21 September 2023 to 13 November 2024, producing Rs 75,000 in interest and a total demand of Rs 5,76,000. For RC 8446, the penalty is Rs 50,00,000 and interest accrues from December 2018 to December 2024, producing Rs 36,50,000 in interest, plus Rs 1,000 recovery costs, for a total demand of Rs 86,51,000. The larger demand therefore stems mainly from the bigger principal and the much longer interest accrual.
review_notes: Demand tables verified: RC 8309 penalty Rs 5,00,000 plus interest 21/09/2023-13/11/2024 at 1% p.m. equals Rs 75,000, total Rs 5,76,000 (clf-jjl8u1w34508ay7yfusr2bjb#1). RC 8446 penalty Rs 50,00,000 plus interest December 2018-December 2024 at 1% p.m. equals Rs 36,50,000, total Rs 86,51,000 (clf-usmhm3u65eul76yarb4tcutm#2/#3). Ratio ~15x holds; clean amount/date reconciliation across certificates.

question: A merchant banker's wholly-owned subsidiary wants to acquire shares of a listed company whose public issue the merchant banker managed nine months ago. The subsidiary argues that the PIT six-month connected-person window has closed and no unpublished price-sensitive information is involved. Is the acquisition free of SEBI reporting obligations, and what is the relevant deadline?
answer_summary: No. Under Regulation 27 of the SEBI (Merchant Bankers) Regulations 1992, a merchant banker must submit complete particulars of any acquisition of securities of a body corporate whose issue it managed within 15 days of the transaction. SEBI's August 2025 ISK Advisors guidance clarifies that while the PIT connected-person nexus from managing the public issue fades after six months, the acquisition-reporting duty under Regulation 27 still applies. A wholly-owned subsidiary of a connected person is also deemed connected unless the contrary is established, so it inherits the same restrictions and reporting obligations.
review_notes: ISK Advisors §3.2/3.3 confirms that, even after the six-month PIT connected-person window closes, an acquisition by a merchant banker (or its wholly-owned subsidiary deemed connected under Regulation 2(1)(d)(ii)) of securities of a body corporate whose issue it managed triggers the Regulation 27 15-day reporting duty in the MB Regulations.

question: The PMS Disclosure Document and the AIF fast-track Placement Memorandum both warn investors that SEBI has not approved the document. Despite that disclaimer, who bears legal responsibility for the accuracy of the information in each case, and what additional certificate must accompany the AIF document?
answer_summary: For the PMS Disclosure Document, the portfolio manager must prepare the document under Regulation 22 of the SEBI (Portfolio Managers) Regulations 2020, file it with SEBI, and certify any changed pages through an independent Chartered Accountant and the Principal Officer; the disclaimer merely notes that SEBI has not approved, disapproved or certified the contents. For the AIF fast-track PPM, the Manager and Merchant Banker are jointly responsible for ensuring that the PPM is true, accurate and compliant despite the same 'not approved by SEBI' warning, and the PPM must be filed with a signed Merchant Banker Due-Diligence Certificate.
review_notes: PMS Disclosure Document §1/§2.2 confirms the 'neither approved nor certified by SEBI' disclaimer and changed-page certification by an independent CA and Principal Officer; AIF fast-track circular §4.3/§5.1/§5.2 confirms that the Manager and Merchant Banker remain responsible and that a Merchant Banker Due-Diligence Certificate must accompany the PPM.

question: A promoter gifts shares to his daughter and a managing director revokes a pledge over ESOP shares. Both transactions are non-sales. In SEBI's Century Plyboards and Welspun Corp informal guidances, why is one treated as a contra trade while the other escapes contra-trade restrictions, and what precondition must each satisfy?
answer_summary: In Century Plyboards the gift is treated as 'dealing' in shares under FAQ 45 and therefore as 'trading'; because the gift is an off-market transfer that changes beneficial ownership between promoter-group parties, it attracts contra-trade restrictions for the donor, although the compliance officer may grant a recorded relaxation. In Welspun Corp, revocation of a pledge is also 'trading' because FAQs treat creation, invocation and revocation of pledge as dealing, but revocation is an opposite trade to creation that does not change beneficial ownership until invocation; hence it does not trigger contra-trade restrictions, and the subsequent sale also avoids them if bona fide. Both transactions still require pre-clearance from the compliance officer under Clause 6 of Schedule B read with Regulation 9(1) of the PIT Regulations.
review_notes: Century Plyboards §3.2 confirms FAQ 45 makes a gift 'trading' and that the donor attracts contra-trade restrictions with a possible compliance-officer relaxation; Welspun Corp §3.2/§3.3 confirms revocation of pledge is also 'trading' but, because beneficial ownership does not change until invocation, it escapes contra-trade restrictions subject to bona fide proof and pre-clearance. Distinct from prior FAQ/intent rows by focusing on the beneficial-ownership test.

question: The 2025 informal guidances for Century Plyboards, Welspun Corp and ISK Advisors each carry a confidentiality clause and a closing limitation. How long is each letter kept confidential, and what does the closing paragraph say about relying on the letter as a binding SEBI decision?
answer_summary: Each letter is not made public for 90 days from the date of issuance of that letter. The closing paragraphs further state that the position is based on the facts furnished in the request, different facts or conditions may lead to a different interpretation, and the letter does not express the decision of the Board on the queries; it also does not affect the applicability of any other law administered by SEBI or any other authority.
review_notes: All three cited informal-guidance letters (Century #13/#15, Welspun #12/#13, ISK #12) uniformly state a 90-day confidentiality period measured from the date of issuance and include the closing limitation that the letter is not a binding Board decision. Extends prior confidentiality-only rows by adding the non-binding limitation language.

question: An exchange is about to launch a brand-new single-stock futures contract and wants to fix its expiry day without asking SEBI first. Would this have been allowed under the March 27, 2025 consultation paper, and is it allowed under the May 26, 2025 final circular? What changed about the circumstances in which SEBI's prior approval is required?
answer_summary: Under the March 27, 2025 consultation paper (and its annexed draft circular), exchanges needed SEBI's prior approval for "launching or modifying any contract expiry or settlement day" (clf-ol9ubobnbwy1ix92dbdtigh5#4), so launching the new single-stock futures contract with its own expiry day would have required prior approval. Under the May 26, 2025 final circular (SEBI/HO/MRD/MRD-TPD-1/P/CIR/2025/76), the requirement was narrowed: exchanges need prior approval only for "modifying the settlement day of their derivatives contracts from the one which has been existing" (clf-fmjtd56s3n2metrhk3a79waq#2). Launching a new contract therefore does not, by itself, trigger the prior-approval requirement in the final rule; only changing an already-existing settlement day does.
review_notes: Cited chunks directly support the narrowing of the prior-approval trigger from 'launching or modifying any contract expiry or settlement day' to 'modifying the settlement day ... from the one which has been existing'. Strong two-document rule-delta; distinct memory target.

question: After the final circular on equity derivatives expiry days was issued on May 26, 2025, how long did stock exchanges have to submit their compliance proposals to SEBI? Why is this deadline absent from the March 2025 draft circular?
answer_summary: The May 26, 2025 circular directed stock exchanges to submit their proposals to SEBI by June 15, 2025 to operationalize the new expiry-day framework (clf-fmjtd56s3n2metrhk3a79waq#2). The March 27, 2025 consultation paper's annexed draft circular left the effective date as a literal placeholder '"DD-MM-YYYY"' because the rule was still under consultation and no operational start date had been fixed (clf-ol9ubobnbwy1ix92dbdtigh5#8).
review_notes: Chunk clf-fmjtd56s3n2metrhk3a79waq#2 supports the June 15, 2025 proposal deadline; chunk clf-ol9ubobnbwy1ix92dbdtigh5#8 supports the DD-MM-YYYY placeholder in the draft. Operational date/lineage target.

question: An exchange currently lists weekly expiry options on two different benchmark indices. After the May 26, 2025 circular on final settlement day, which of those weekly contracts can it keep, and what does the March 2025 consultation paper say was already proposed for that product category?
answer_summary: The exchange can keep only one weekly expiry option contract—on one of its benchmark indices. Both the March 27, 2025 consultation paper and the May 26, 2025 final circular retain the carve-out that "every exchange will continue to be allowed one weekly benchmark index options contract, on their chosen day (Tuesday or Thursday)" (clf-ol9ubobnbwy1ix92dbdtigh5#3/#4; clf-fmjtd56s3n2metrhk3a79waq#2). All other equity derivatives contracts, including the second benchmark index's weekly options, must have a minimum tenor of one month and expire on the last Tuesday or last Thursday of the month.
review_notes: Both cited docs support the single weekly benchmark index options carve-out. The March proposal question makes the final rule a continuation rather than a newly created exception. Product-scope exception target, distinct from q05.

question: Before SEBI finalized the May 26, 2025 circular on equity derivatives expiry days, what advisory body deliberated the comments received on the March 27, 2025 consultation paper, and by what date were those comments originally due?
answer_summary: The comments received on the March 27, 2025 consultation paper were examined by SEBI and further deliberated in the Secondary Market Advisory Committee (SMAC) before the final circular was issued (clf-fmjtd56s3n2metrhk3a79waq#1). The original deadline for submitting comments on the consultation paper was April 17, 2025 (clf-ol9ubobnbwy1ix92dbdtigh5#5).
review_notes: Chunk clf-fmjtd56s3n2metrhk3a79waq#1 confirms SMAC deliberation; chunk clf-ol9ubobnbwy1ix92dbdtigh5#5 confirms April 17, 2025 comment deadline. Clean procedural-timeline question.

question: A trader wants to trade a non-benchmark index options contract with a maturity shorter than one month. Under the final May 2025 expiry-day circular, is that possible, and where did the March 2025 consultation paper propose the same tenor and expiry-week treatment for such contracts?
answer_summary: No, that is not possible. Under the May 26, 2025 final circular, besides the single permitted weekly benchmark index options contract, all other equity derivatives contracts—including non-benchmark index futures/options and all single-stock futures/options—must have a minimum tenor of one month and expire in the last week of every month on the exchange's chosen day (last Tuesday or last Thursday) (clf-fmjtd56s3n2metrhk3a79waq#2). The March 27, 2025 consultation paper had already proposed the identical structure for these contracts (clf-ol9ubobnbwy1ix92dbdtigh5#3/#4). Thus a sub-one-month non-benchmark index option would not be permitted.
review_notes: Cited chunks support the one-month minimum tenor and last-week expiry for non-benchmark index options in both proposal and final. Applies the same rule as q03 but asks a distinct negative-permissibility / threshold memory target.

question: A high-net-worth investor signs a PMS agreement for ₹12 crore. A colleague tells her that only a "Large Value Fund for accredited investors" AIF can take similarly sized tickets and that this AIF category is therefore excluded from the April 2026 fast-track PPM route. What threshold in the PMS Disclosure Document makes her a Large Value Accredited Investor, and is the AIF category her colleague describes the one carved out of the fast-track mechanism?
answer_summary: Under the September 2025 PMS Disclosure Document format, a "Large Value Accredited Investor" is an Accredited Investor who has entered into an agreement with the portfolio manager for a minimum investment amount of ₹10 crore. Because her agreement is for ₹12 crore, she clears that PMS threshold. The April 2026 AIF fast-track circular carves out "Large Value Funds for accredited investors" (LVFs) from the fast-track route; the route applies to Angel Funds and non-LVF AIF schemes. So the AIF category her colleague names is indeed the one excluded.
review_notes: Chunk 14 defines Large Value Accredited Investor as ₹10 crore minimum; chunk 1 of AIF fast-track circular explicitly carves out LVFs from the fast-track route. Supported, distinct threshold-vs-regime-interaction target.

question: A merchant banker is about to sign the due diligence certificate for an AIF non-LVF PPM under the April 2026 fast-track circular. The same firm also plans to acquire shares of a listed company whose public issue it managed eight months ago, arguing that none of its teams now possess unpublished price-sensitive information. For each role, what must the merchant banker certify or disclose, and within what deadline?
answer_summary: For the AIF fast-track PPM, the merchant banker must sign a due diligence certificate stating that it independently exercised due diligence, that the PPM disclosures are true, fair and adequate for investors, and that the PPM complies with the SEBI (AIF) Regulations, 2012. For the planned share acquisition, the MB Regulations apply independently: Regulation 26 prohibits the merchant banker and its directors, partners, managers, principal officers, associates or relatives from trading in securities of managed bodies corporate on the basis of UPSI obtained during a professional assignment. The absence of UPSI does not remove the separate reporting duty under Regulation 27, which requires complete particulars of any acquisition of securities of a body corporate whose issue the merchant banker managed to be submitted to SEBI within 15 days. The quarterly-reporting proviso under Regulation 27 applies only to acquisitions made to meet underwriting or market-making obligations under the ICDR Regulations, 2018.
review_notes: AIF fast-track chunks confirm due-diligence certificate wording; MB Reg chunks 60-62 confirm Reg 26 UPSI prohibition and Reg 27 15-day acquisition reporting with narrow quarterly proviso. Human-shaped dual-role scenario; no same-intent duplicate in memory.

question: The 2025 ISK Advisors informal guidance says a wholly-owned subsidiary of a merchant banker is deemed a connected person unless the contrary is established. Does the same rebuttable presumption apply when the MB Regulations stop the merchant banker's directors, associates, or relatives from trading in securities of managed companies?
answer_summary: No. ISK Advisors relies on clause (b) of Regulation 2(1)(d)(ii) of the PIT Regulations, which creates a rebuttable presumption that a subsidiary of a connected person is also deemed connected. The MB Regulations use a different mechanism: Regulation 26 prohibits a merchant banker and any of its directors, partners, managers, principal officers, associates or relatives from entering into securities transactions of bodies corporate on the basis of unpublished price-sensitive information obtained during a professional assignment. That prohibition is conduct-based and applies to the listed categories of persons; it does not contain the same rebuttable-presumption carve-out for subsidiaries.
review_notes: ISK chunks 10-11 cite PIT Regulation 2(1)(d)(ii)(b) rebuttable-presumption rule; MB Reg chunks 60-61 show Reg 26 directly covers listed categories, not through the same deemed-connected mechanism. Clear distinct memorization target.

question: We are a bank-sponsored debenture trustee regulated by the Reserve Bank of India and already run a non-SEBI fee-based credit-information service. Reading the October 2025 amendment inserting Regulation 9C, the November 2025 terms-and-conditions circular and the April 2026 extension together, what is the final compliance deadline for segregation, website disclosures, stakeholder acknowledgements and the compliance report, and—because we are RBI-regulated—which activity must sit in the separate business unit?
answer_summary: The April 28, 2026 extension gives debenture trustees until October 27, 2026 to implement the October 27, 2025 amendment and the November 25, 2025 terms-and-conditions circular. For an RBI-regulated debenture trustee, the first proviso to Regulation 9C(1) of the amendment requires the debenture-trustee activity itself to be carried out through a separate business unit, and the November 2025 circular's conditions apply to that SBU.
review_notes: All three cited documents directly support the answer: extension circular fixes the October 27, 2026 implementation deadline, amendment's first proviso requires RBI-regulated DTs to carry the DT activity through a SBU, and the terms circular conditions apply to that SBU. Covers a distinct deadline/RBI special-rule memory target.

question: A debenture trustee proposes to cover an issuer's coupon shortfall by advancing funds and booking it as a fee, claiming it is a financial service outside SEBI's purview. Does Regulation 9C permit this activity?
answer_summary: No. Regulation 9C(1)(b) permits only activities that do not fall under SEBI or another financial-sector regulator and that are fee-based, non-fund based and pertain to the financial-services sector. Advancing funds is fund-based, so it is outside the permitted scope. The November 2025 terms-and-conditions circular also refers only to non-SEBI regulated fee-based, non-fund based financial services activities.
review_notes: Supported by both cited documents: Regulation 9C(1)(b) limits permitted activities to non-fund based, fee-based activities; the circular reproduces the same condition. Clear scope-exclusion trap with distinct practical target.

question: A debenture trustee regulated by IRDAI wants to use the same organisation to distribute insurance products. Under the October 2025 amendment and the November 2025 terms circular, (a) what makes this eligible for the trustee to carry on, (b) what must it disclose to clients and on its website about the insurance activity, and (c) which elements of IRDAI's regulatory framework still apply?
answer_summary: (a) The activity is eligible under Regulation 9C(1)(a) because it falls within the purview of another financial-sector regulator specified by SEBI—in this case IRDAI. (b) The trustee must list the activity on its website as non-SEBI regulated and state that no SEBI investor-protection mechanism is available; if the activity is regulated by another FSR, the name of that regulator (IRDAI) must also be disclosed. (c) The trustee must comply with IRDAI's regulatory framework for policy, eligibility criteria, risk management, investor grievance or dispute-handling mechanism, inspection, enforcement and claims to the extent specified by that regulator.
review_notes: Cited chunks corroborate each part of the answer: 9C(1)(a) and the amendment's FSR list cover IRDAI eligibility; paragraph 2.6/2.7 of the circular covers website/client disclosures and residual FSR-framework compliance. Slightly packing three sub-questions into one row, but still a distinct cross-regulator memory target.

question: After transferring its non-SEBI activities into a separate business unit, what continuing safeguards and governance must a debenture trustee maintain under Regulation 9C and the November 2025 terms circular?
answer_summary: The trustee must ensure that the net worth prescribed under the DT Regulations is ring-fenced from any adverse impact of the non-SEBI activities (Regulation 9C(2)). In its half-yearly compliance report it must submit an undertaking confirming compliance with Regulation 9C and the terms circular, and that undertaking must be reviewed and approved by its board of directors (November 2025 circular paragraph 2.11).
review_notes: Supported by amendment 9C(2) (net-worth ring-fencing) and circular paragraph 2.11 (board-reviewed undertaking in half-yearly compliance report). Distinct from the other rows; captures ongoing governance requirements.

question: Our debenture trustee currently shares IT servers, back-office staff and a common marketing brochure between its SEBI-regulated trustee function and a new non-SEBI fee-based advisory unit. Under the November 2025 terms circular read with Regulation 9C, which of these arrangements are allowed subject to conditions, and which are prohibited?
answer_summary: IT and other resources may be shared between SEBI-regulated and non-SEBI activities, but only subject to due procedures approved by the board of directors. Staff must be distinct; staff may cross the Chinese Wall only under board-approved due procedures, and the Chinese Wall does not apply to key managerial personnel. Marketing and advertising material, however, must be separate and distinct from SEBI-regulated activities.
review_notes: Circular paragraphs 2.4 (staff distinct), 2.5 (IT/resources shared under board procedures), and 2.8 (separate marketing material) directly support the allowed/prohibited split in the answer. Distinct operational-safeguard nuance target.

question: An index provider administers a benchmark that is tracked by several domestic mutual fund schemes. Does the SEBI (Index Providers) Regulations, 2024 automatically require it to register as an Index Provider? If not, what precise AUM test in the May 2026 circular decides whether the benchmark is a Significant Index, and what happens if the benchmark later falls below that threshold?
answer_summary: No automatic obligation. The 2024 Regulations apply only to Index Providers that administer Significant Indices consisting of Indian listed securities for use in the Indian market (Regulation 3(1)), and define Significant Indices broadly as those tracked by domestic mutual fund schemes whose cumulative AUM exceeds limits SEBI will specify (Regulation 2(1)(u)). The May 2026 circular operationalises the test: a benchmark/index is Significant only if the daily average cumulative AUM tracking it across mutual fund schemes exceeds Rs.20,000 crore for each of the past six months ending 30 June and 31 December every year. Importantly, once an index is placed in SEBI's list, it continues to be treated as a Significant Index unless its AUM stays below the threshold continuously for three years, i.e. six consecutive half-yearly reviews. So a temporary shortfall does not terminate the designation.
review_notes: Directly supported: Reg 3(1) scope and Reg 2(1)(u) definition are in the regulations; the Rs.20,000 crore daily-average AUM test and 3-year continuity rule are in the May 2026 circular chunks.

question: The January 2026 draft circular and the May 2026 final circular both use a Rs.20,000 crore AUM threshold to identify Significant Indices. Setting aside the updated list of indices, what two operational requirements did the final circular introduce that were absent from the January 2026 draft, and how did the RBI exemption change?
answer_summary: The January 2026 draft proposed the threshold, the six-month computation window ending 30 June/31 December, apportionment rules for multi-index schemes and indices of indices, a six-month registration window for providers of Significant Indices, and an exemption for indices that are RBI-regulated Significant Benchmarks under Section 45W of the RBI Act. The May 2026 final circular added two mechanisms not in the draft: first, a grandfathering/stability rule - an index remains in the Significant Indices list unless AUM stays below the threshold continuously for three years (six consecutive half-yearly reviews); second, a structural separation rule - SEBI-registered entities that provide Significant Indices departmentally must form a separate legal entity to carry out Index Provider activities within two years of the circular. The RBI exemption was also tightened/recast: it now covers indices notified as 'Significant Benchmarks' or classified as 'Authorized Benchmarks' under RBI directions issued under Section 45W.
review_notes: Compares draft and final circulars. The added continuity/grandfathering rule, separate-legal-entity requirement, and broadened RBI exemption (Significant + Authorized Benchmarks) are backed by cited chunks.

question: A stock exchange currently administers and licenses Significant Indices through its internal index division. It is registered with SEBI as a stock exchange, not as an Index Provider, and has not formed a separate entity for index activities. What deadlines and structural steps apply after the May 2026 Significant Indices circular, and which source imposes each?
answer_summary: Two distinct obligations arise. First, because the stock exchange is providing Significant Indices on the date of the May 2026 circular, it may continue that activity provided it submits an application for registration as an Index Provider within six months from the circular (May 2026 circular, para 7-8). Second, both the 2024 Regulations and the May 2026 circular require a SEBI-registered entity that carries out Index Provider activities departmentally to form a separate legal entity to conduct those activities: the Regulations give two years from the date of commencement of the regulations (Regulation 5(a) proviso), while the circular gives two years from the date of the circular (para 9). Therefore, regardless of which clock applies, the exchange must both apply for registration within six months and ring-fence the index business in a separate legal entity within two years.
review_notes: Supports both deadlines: 6-month registration window for existing providers in the final circular, and the 2-year separate-entity requirement from both Regulation 5(a) proviso and circular para 9.

question: A mutual fund subscribes to an RBI Authorized Benchmark that happens to track listed Indian securities, and it appears on SEBI's list of Significant Indices. The index provider is not registered with SEBI as an Index Provider because of the RBI exemption. If the mutual fund later disputes how a methodology change was applied, can it use the grievance redressal mechanism under the SEBI (Index Providers) Regulations, 2024?
answer_summary: No. Regulation 23 of the 2024 Regulations broadly says that any subscriber to an Index Provider has recourse to grievance redressal under the regulations. However, both the January 2026 draft circular and the May 2026 final circular clarify that the grievance redressal mechanism under Regulation 23 applies only to Significant Indices provided by Index Providers registered with SEBI. Because the index concerned is an RBI Authorized Benchmark (or RBI Significant Benchmark) under Section 45W of the RBI Act, it is excluded from the purview of the IP Regulations and the provider need not register with SEBI. Consequently, the mutual fund has no recourse under the IP Regulations grievance mechanism.
review_notes: Regulation 23 gives a broad subscriber grievance mechanism, but the final circular (and draft) restrict it to Significant Indices from SEBI-registered providers; RBI-exempt benchmarks fall outside, as cited.

question: A newly formed company plans to apply to SEBI for registration as an Index Provider, while a rival entity that has been administering an in-scope Significant Index unregistered since before the May 2026 circular wants to keep operating. What minimum net worth must the new applicant show, and what transition relief did the May 2026 circular give the existing provider?
answer_summary: The new applicant must satisfy Regulation 5 of the 2024 Regulations: among other things, it must have a minimum net worth of twenty-five crore rupees (or equivalent foreign-currency amount) at the time of application, separate legal-entity status, and fit-and-promoter/director fitness. For the existing provider, the May 2026 circular grants transition relief: an Index Provider providing Significant Indices as on the date of the circular may continue its activity provided it submits an application for registration to SEBI within six months from the date of the circular. This effectively gives existing providers a fresh window to come into compliance without ceasing operations, while new entrants must meet the eligibility thresholds upfront.
review_notes: Regulation 5(b) confirms the Rs.25 crore net-worth threshold; final circular paras 7-8 confirm the 6-month transition window for providers already offering Significant Indices.

question: An entity proposing to register as an Index Provider is collecting the supporting package required by the SEBI (Index Providers) Regulations, 2024. What independent assessment must accompany the application, and is the assessment required if the entity only administers an RBI 'Authorized Benchmark'?
answer_summary: Regulation 4(3) requires the applicant to file, with its Form A application, a compliance assessment report issued within the preceding twelve months by an independent external auditor confirming adherence to all IOSCO Principles for Financial Benchmarks. If the report cannot be submitted at the time of application, the applicant must give reasons and undertake to submit a detailed report within six months from the date of grant of the certificate. However, RBI-regulated benchmarks are carved out of the IP Regulations. Regulation 4(1) excludes 'Benchmarks' regulated by the Reserve Bank of India, including 'Significant Benchmarks' notified by RBI under Section 45W, from the purview of the regulations. The May 2026 circular clarifies that indices that are either RBI 'Significant Benchmarks' or 'Authorized Benchmarks' under Section 45W directions are excluded. Therefore, an entity whose only benchmark is an RBI Authorized Benchmark is outside the IP Regulations framework and need not submit the IOSCO assessment.
review_notes: Regulation 4(3) requires the IOSCO-principles auditor report (with the 6-month fallback), and Regulation 4(1) plus the final circular exclude RBI Significant/Authorized Benchmarks.

question: A domestic mutual fund scheme benchmarks 60% of its corpus to Nifty 50 and 40% to Nifty Midcap 150. For determining whether each of those indices crosses the Significant Indices threshold, how should the scheme's AUM be apportioned? Does the SEBI (Index Providers) Regulations, 2024 itself contain this AUM computation rule?
answer_summary: The 2024 Regulations do not contain the AUM computation rule. Regulation 2(1)(u) only defines Significant Indices as indices tracked by domestic mutual fund schemes whose cumulative AUM exceeds limits to be specified by SEBI from time to time, and Regulation 3(1) restricts the regulations' applicability accordingly. The detailed computational rule is supplied by the Significant Indices circulars. Both the January 2026 draft and the May 2026 final circular state that where a scheme tracks multiple indices or benchmarks, the cumulative AUM tracking each respective index or benchmark must be computed based on the portion of that scheme's AUM allocated to that index. Thus, 60% of the scheme's AUM is counted toward the Nifty 50 threshold and 40% toward the Nifty Midcap 150 threshold. For an index of indices, the AUM would be computed in proportion to the underlying weights.
review_notes: Apportionment rule is supported by consultation-paper chunk #3 and final-threshold language in circular chunk #2; Regulations themselves only define the framework.

question: The September 2025 consultation paper proposed excluding smaller stock brokers from the technical-glitch framework by requiring more than 10,000 registered clients. When the framework was finalised in January 2026, how did SEBI alter the way brokers must count those clients, and what numerical estimate had the consultation given?
answer_summary: The final January 9, 2026 circular changed the eligibility count by specifying that the registered-client threshold of more than 10,000 is calculated as on 31st March of the previous financial year excluding closed accounts (clf-cgy8nunw6tk7m92hd5k0eqn6#6). The September 22, 2025 consultation paper, which contained the draft circular, had estimated that around 457 smaller stock brokers would move out of the framework once the raised threshold applied (clf-sv5dd5bf29opbbtgcmbsed4r#4).
review_notes: Cited chunks directly support the final closed-account counting change and the consultation's 457-broker estimate. Both docs are necessary for the delta.

question: A broker's compliance team is updating its incident-response checklist using the September 2025 consultation draft and the January 2026 final circular. What is the key change in the unit of time for filing a Root Cause Analysis report, and does the trading-holiday adjustment apply to both the Preliminary Incident Report and the RCA?
answer_summary: The consultation paper's draft circular required the RCA to be submitted within 14 calendar days from the date of the incident (clf-sv5dd5bf29opbbtgcmbsed4r#13). The final January 9, 2026 circular changed this to 14 working days (clf-cgy8nunw6tk7m92hd5k0eqn6#7). In both documents, if the T+1 Preliminary Incident Report due date or the RCA due date falls on a trading holiday, the submission may be made on the next trading day (clf-sv5dd5bf29opbbtgcmbsed4r#12/#13; clf-cgy8nunw6tk7m92hd5k0eqn6#7).
review_notes: Draft RCA deadline is 14 calendar days; final is 14 working days; holiday adjustment applies to both PIR and RCA in both cited docs.

question: Compared with the September 2025 draft circular, the January 2026 final circular added one extra scenario to the list of technical issues that are not considered reportable technical glitches even if they otherwise look like broker-system malfunctions. What was the added scenario, and why was it excluded?
answer_summary: The final circular added 'or any technical issue causing widespread disruption' to the list of global issues outside the broker's control that are not treated as technical glitches (clf-cgy8nunw6tk7m92hd5k0eqn6#4). The September 2025 draft's carve-out covered only 'malfunction or technical disruption at the cloud service providers or any other global technology provider' (clf-sv5dd5bf29opbbtgcmbsed4r#9). It was excluded because SEBI's exemption covers glitches outside the stock broker's trading architecture and beyond the broker's control.
review_notes: Final circular expansion of global-issue carve-out to include 'any technical issue causing widespread disruption' is accurately traced to the cited chunks.

question: A stock broker relying on the draft annexed to the September 2025 consultation paper plans to implement the revised technical-glitch framework on November 1, 2025. What would be wrong with that plan, and when did the framework actually take effect?
answer_summary: The November 1, 2025 date appears only in the draft circular attached to the consultation paper; it was never adopted (clf-sv5dd5bf29opbbtgcmbsed4r#18). The actual final circular was issued on January 9, 2026 and came into effect from that same date (clf-cgy8nunw6tk7m92hd5k0eqn6#0/#12).
review_notes: Draft's November 1, 2025 effective date is contrasted with final circular's January 9, 2026 issuance and effective date as cited.

question: SEBI's January 9, 2026 press release said the revised technical-glitch framework would move about 60% of stock brokers out of the framework. Which earlier document gave an alternative numerical estimate, and which exact eligibility condition in the final circular produces that narrowing?
answer_summary: The January 9, 2026 press release stated that approximately 60% of stock brokers would move out of the framework (clf-eds09gwljh2r0d20ujryu16e#0). The September 22, 2025 consultation paper had earlier estimated that around 457 smaller stock brokers would move out (clf-sv5dd5bf29opbbtgcmbsed4r#4). The final January 9, 2026 circular sets the eligibility condition as stock brokers providing IBT/STWT trading platforms and having more than 10,000 registered clients excluding closed accounts, as on 31st March of the previous financial year (clf-cgy8nunw6tk7m92hd5k0eqn6#6).
review_notes: Press release 60% figure and consultation 457-broker estimate both supported; final eligibility condition is accurately cited. Distinct from Q1's counting-change focus.

question: Before the January 2026 circular was issued, SEBI proposed that a technical glitch affecting only one of a broker's two trading modes should not attract financial disincentive if the other mode worked properly. Did the final framework keep, modify, or drop that proposal, and what other scenario did it pair with it?
answer_summary: The final circular kept the proposal unchanged. It provides that financial disincentives are not applicable where (i) a technical glitch occurs in one of two trading modes while the other mode functions properly, or (ii) the glitch is minor in nature or has a minor impact on the broker's seamless operations (clf-sv5dd5bf29opbbtgcmbsed4r#10/#11; clf-cgy8nunw6tk7m92hd5k0eqn6#5).
review_notes: Both draft and final chunks confirm the one-mode-working and minor-impact financial-disincentive exemptions were retained unchanged.

question: Our firm only has the October 27, 2025 Debenture Trustees Amendment Regulations and the April 28, 2026 extension circular on file; the operational terms-and-conditions circular is missing. Can we still identify the missing circular's date, reference number and subject matter from the two documents we do have?
answer_summary: Yes. The April 28, 2026 extension circular records that the operational framework, including the terms and conditions governing activities outside SEBI's purview, was prescribed by SEBI circular HO/17/11/12(3)2025-DDHS-POD1/I/146/2025 dated November 25, 2025. Its subject matter is the specification of terms and conditions for Debenture Trustees carrying out non-SEBI activities under Regulation 9C of the SEBI (Debenture Trustees) Regulations, 1993.
review_notes: Supported. Extension circular records the missing terms circular reference number, date and subject; amendment supplies the Regulation 9C context.

question: Our company secretary says the six-month window for transferring non-SEBI activities under Regulation 9C expired on April 27, 2026, so we are now non-compliant. A colleague points to an April 2026 SEBI circular and says the deadline is actually October 27, 2026. Who is right?
answer_summary: The colleague is right. The October 27, 2025 amendment initially required existing debenture trustees to transfer their non-SEBI activities to separate business units within six months from Gazette notification, i.e., by April 27, 2026. The SEBI circular dated April 28, 2026, granted an additional six months, making the final implementation deadline October 27, 2026.
review_notes: Supported. Amendment states six months from notification; extension adds six months to October 27, 2026.

question: The April 2026 extension pushes the Regulation 9C implementation deadline to October 2026. Does that also relax the substantive conditions we must meet, such as the Chinese Wall, distinct staff, separate records, website disclosures and stakeholder acknowledgments?
answer_summary: No. Paragraph 4 of the April 28, 2026 extension expressly states that all other provisions of the November 25, 2025 terms circular remain unchanged. Only the final timeline is extended; the operational conditions—SBU segregation, Chinese Wall, distinct staff, separate records, separate advertising or marketing material, website disclosures and stakeholder acknowledgments—continue to apply as originally specified in that circular.
review_notes: Supported. Extension para 4 keeps all other terms-circular provisions unchanged; substantive conditions are listed in the terms circular.

question: We are entering into a new non-SEBI credit-information engagement with a client on May 15, 2026, after the April 2026 extension. Can we make the required disclosure about non-availability of SEBI investor protection and obtain the client's confirmation at any time up to October 27, 2026?
answer_summary: No. The April 2026 extension extends the overall implementation deadline to October 27, 2026 for existing and ongoing arrangements, but it does not remove the upfront timing requirement in the November 25, 2025 terms circular. For any new engagement entered into on or after May 15, 2026, the debenture trustee must make the written disclosure before undertaking the activity and obtain confirmation from the stakeholder at the time of engagement.
review_notes: Supported. Terms circular para 2.9 requires upfront disclosure and engagement-time confirmation for new activities; extension does not override this.

question: Our debenture trustee holds an IFSCA authorisation to provide corporate debt advisory services at GIFT City and also performs SEBI-regulated debenture trustee services. Which bucket under Regulation 9C does the IFSCA activity fall into, and what extra conditions apply because it is regulated by another financial sector regulator rather than being unregulated?
answer_summary: It falls under Regulation 9C(1)(a)—activities falling under the purview of another financial sector regulator—because IFSCA is named in the Explanation as a financial sector regulator. Paragraph 2.7 of the November 25, 2025 terms circular then requires the trustee to name IFSCA in its disclosures and comply with IFSCA's regulatory framework for policy, eligibility criteria, risk management, investor grievance handling, inspection, enforcement and claims, in addition to the generic SBU, Chinese Wall, distinct staff, separate records, separate marketing, website disclosure and stakeholder-confirmation requirements.
review_notes: Supported. Amendment Explanation names IFSCA as a financial sector regulator; terms circular para 2.7 specifies additional FSR conditions/disclosures.

question: The October 2025 amendment inserting Regulation 9C and the April 2026 extension circular are visibly different legal instruments. Under what statutory authority was each one issued?
answer_summary: The October 27, 2025 amendment was made in exercise of the powers conferred under section 30 of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992. The April 28, 2026 extension circular was issued in exercise of powers conferred under section 11(1) of the SEBI Act, 1992 and Regulation 2A of the SEBI (Debenture Trustees) Regulations, 1993.
review_notes: Supported. Amendment cites section 30 of the SEBI Act; extension circular cites section 11(1) of the SEBI Act and Regulation 2A of the DT Regulations.

question: A compliance team is onboarding an index provider that is currently a wholly-owned division of a stock exchange. Which fit-and-proper criteria apply to the promoters and directors of this provider, and what two related structural timelines govern its index-administration activities under the SEBI (Index Providers) Regulations, 2024 and the May 2026 Significant Indices circular?
answer_summary: For index providers whose promoter is a stock exchange, clearing corporation or depository, Regulation 6 of the 2024 Regulations directs SEBI to use the fit-and-proper criteria in the Securities Contracts (Regulation) (Stock Exchanges and Clearing Corporations) Regulations, 2018 and the SEBI (Depositories and Participants) Regulations, 2018, not the general Schedule II of the Intermediaries Regulations, 2008. Structurally, Regulation 5(a) already requires any stock exchange or regulated intermediary undertaking Index Provider activities departmentally to form a separate legal entity within two years from the commencement of the 2024 Regulations. The May 2026 Significant Indices circular reinforces this by requiring any entity already registered with SEBI in another capacity and providing Significant Indices departmentally to form a separate legal entity within two years from May 5, 2026.
review_notes: Reg 6 proviso and Reg 5(a) timeline are directly supported in the 2024 Regulations; May 2026 circular supplies the second structural deadline. Adds a distinct fit-and-proper memory target not covered by earlier memory.

question: An unregistered entity has been administering a Significant Index and obtained an external IOSCO-principles audit ten months before the May 2026 Significant Indices circular. It applies for SEBI registration before the six-month deadline. Can it file that same audit with its application, and when is the next required independent assessment after SEBI grants the certificate?
answer_summary: Yes, the same audit can be filed. Regulation 4(3) of the 2024 Regulations requires the application to be accompanied by an independent external auditor’s compliance-assessment report issued within the preceding twelve months. If it falls short, the applicant must give reasons and an undertaking to submit the report within six months of grant. For the recurring cycle, Regulation 24 normally requires the first assessment within one year of registration, but its second proviso says an existing entity that was assessed for IOSCO compliance within the past year need only undergo the next assessment within two years from the date of that last assessment. The report must also be published on the provider’s website.
review_notes: Reg 4(3)-(4) supports using a recent IOSCO audit; Reg 24 second proviso specifies the extended next-assessment cycle. The circular supplies the six-month registration window. Distinct from run_57's simpler assessment requirement.

question: A stock exchange that is already registered with SEBI plans to publish a widely tracked index calculated entirely from trades executed on its own cash and derivatives segments, and the index is likely to enter the May 2026 Significant Indices list. Is it required to publish a Code of Conduct for data submitters for that index, what methodology documents must still be made public, and what structural step does the May 2026 circular require because it will be a Significant Index?
answer_summary: No, the Code of Conduct for Data Submitters is not required for indices based on transaction data of regulated markets and stock exchanges. However, the exchange must still make its methodology documents publicly available so users can understand how the index is calculated and maintained, and must put in place guidelines covering the use of Expert Judgement. Because it is already registered with SEBI in another capacity and will provide the Significant Index departmentally, the May 2026 circular requires it to form a separate legal entity for Index Provider activities within two years from May 5, 2026.
review_notes: Reg 18(5) exemption and methodology/expert-judgment publication rules are directly cited; circular para 9 supplies the separate-legal-entity timeline for SEBI-registered entities. Adds a new checklist pairing.

question: During its compliance health-check, an index provider supplying Significant Indices wants to know the minimum retention period for its written records, audit trails, input-data records and oversight-committee minutes, and whether SEBI must be told where those records are kept. Does the May 2026 Significant Indices circular shorten either of these obligations?
answer_summary: Under Regulation 26 of the 2024 Regulations, these records must be maintained for a minimum period of eight years, and the index provider must intimate to the Board the place in India where its books of account, records and documents are kept. The May 2026 Significant Indices circular does not alter these record-keeping and storage-location requirements; it identifies the Significant Indices and sets the registration/structural conditions for providers of those indices, leaving Regulation 26 unchanged.
review_notes: Reg 26 gives the eight-year retention and intimation requirements; the circular is silent on record-keeping, so the negative conclusion is soundly grounded. Nice absence-check memory target.

question: Comparing the January 2026 draft circular’s Annexure-A with the May 2026 final circular’s Annexure-A (ignoring capitalization and minor wording changes), which broad BSE equity index was added, which Nifty duration-focused debt index was dropped, and how do the two lists treat RBI-regulated benchmarks?
answer_summary: The May 2026 final list adds BSE 200 as a Significant Index. The draft list contains NIFTY Medium Duration Debt A-III at No. 40, but that index is absent from the final list. Both annexures exclude RBI-regulated benchmarks from the purview of the SEBI (Index Provider) Regulations; the draft refers to RBI ‘Benchmarks’ including Significant Benchmarks notified under section 45W of the RBI Act, 1934, while the final expressly also includes indices classified by RBI as ‘Authorized Benchmarks’ under section 45W.
review_notes: Draft annexure is missing BSE 200 and contains NIFTY Medium Duration Debt A-III; final annexure adds BSE 200 and drops that debt index. RBI benchmark exclusion language differs as described. Strong version-diff question.

question: A Significant Index is included in the May 2026 Annexure-A, but its existing index provider informs SEBI that it does not intend to register as an Index Provider. How long do mutual-fund subscribers tracking that index have to migrate to a registered provider’s benchmark or stop tracking it, and which provisions decide what happens first?
answer_summary: First, the May 2026 circular gives an existing provider of a Significant Index only six months from May 5, 2026 to submit a registration application if it wishes to keep operating. Since this provider does not intend to register, that transition window closes. Second, the proviso to Regulation 20(3) of the 2024 Regulations requires subscribers registered with the Board, who track indices of existing providers that are not seeking registration or intend to cease publication, to shift to a new benchmark offered by a registered Index Provider or to stop tracking the index within three months of the notice of intent of cessation.
review_notes: Circular paras 7-8 set the six-month registration window; Reg 20(3) proviso sets the three-month subscriber migration/cessation period. Both provisions are needed to sequence the answer. Fresh subscriber-side memory target.

question: An ERP following a subscriber-pays model wants to withdraw an ESG rating because the rated company has stopped subscribing. A colleague argues that the February 2025 consultation draft only permits withdrawal when there are no active subscribers and adds no other exit route. Under SEBI's April 2025 final circular, what other circumstance now allows withdrawal for subscriber-pays ERPs, and what restriction applies to the withdrawn rating after that?
answer_summary: Under the April 29, 2025 final circular, a subscriber-pays ERP may also withdraw an ESG rating for an issuer where the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) is unavailable for that issuer or rated entity. Once a rating is withdrawn, the ERP must ensure that the withdrawn rating is not made available to any subscriber in the future. The February 13, 2025 consultation draft did not include either the BRSR unavailability ground or the post-withdrawal subscriber-access restriction; it only permitted withdrawal if there were no subscribers (subject to the rating-package exception) and required withdrawal to apply across all subscribers.
review_notes: Supported by clf-wtrsyjm7uuib4sv6uu2ocjss#7 (draft subscriber-pays withdrawal: no-subscribers/package-exception/all-subscribers) and clf-rfqmtdurntdu9o37suush0ra#2 (final adds BRSR-unavailability ground and post-withdrawal subscriber-access bar). Truly requires both docs; practical exception trap.

question: A listed company notices that its ESG rating is displayed differently on the ERP's website and on the stock exchange website. Under SEBI's April 2025 final circular on ERPs, which fields are required on an ERP's own website for subscriber-pays ratings, and which fields must stock exchanges display? Which of these elements did not appear in the February 2025 draft circular?
answer_summary: For subscriber-pays ERPs, the April 2025 circular requires the ERP's own website to disclose, for each rated issuer/security: name, sector, ESG rating and date of rating; this may be segregated year-wise, indicating the BRSR on which the rating is based. Stock exchanges must disclose under a separate tab: name of the rated issuer, symbol or ISIN as applicable, sector, ESG rating, date of rating, ERP name, business model of ERP (subscriber-pays or issuer-pays), and the ESG rating press release as a PDF attachment. The requirement to indicate the BRSR year on the ERP website and the detailed stock-exchange format fields (symbol/ISIN, ERP name, business model and press-release PDF) were absent from the February 2025 consultation draft, which only prescribed a four-field website disclosure and a simple prominent-disclosure obligation for exchanges.
review_notes: Draft chunk 8 confirms four-field subscriber-pays website disclosure; draft chunk 9 confirms only generic stock-exchange prominent-tab obligation. Final chunks 5 and 6 add BRSR-year indication and the seven-field exchange format (symbol/ISIN, ERP name, business model, press-release PDF). Multi-document scope/delta.

question: After receiving a detailed rating rationale from a subscriber-pays ERP, a rated entity intends to challenge the rating and request clarifications. Under SEBI's April 2025 final circular on ERPs, what standardized documents govern the rated entity's comments and the ERP's clarifications, and by when must the entity submit a single consolidated response? Was this two-way framework already present in the February 2025 draft circular?
answer_summary: The April 2025 circular introduces Annexure A (Standard Format for Rated Entity/Issuer's Comments on the Rating Report) and the attached Standards for Clarifications to be provided by the ERP. The rated entity must send a single consolidated response within two working days from the date of receipt of the rating rationale, to the email ID disclosed by the ERP on its website. The February 2025 consultation draft did not contain any format for rated-entity comments or any standards for ERP clarifications; those annexures and timelines were added only in the final circular.
review_notes: Final chunks 5, 12, and 17 establish Annexure A, Standards for Clarifications, and the two-working-day single-consolidated-response window via the ERP website email ID. Draft chunk 5 contains no analogous framework. Distinct procedural-timeline target.

question: A newly registered Category II ERP asks whether it must immediately set up an internal audit team and constitute a separate ESG Ratings Sub-Committee and Nomination and Remuneration Committee. How did the February 2025 draft circular and the April 2025 final circular address these transitional issues, and what additional qualification option did the final circular add for the internal audit team?
answer_summary: Both the February 2025 draft circular and the April 2025 final circular defer the internal-audit requirement and the ESG Ratings Sub-Committee/NRC requirements for Category II ERPs until two years from the date of issuance of the circular; until then, the board of the Category II ERP may handle those matters. In addition, the final circular expanded the internal audit team's qualification mix: Para 23.1.3 of the ERP Master Circular was modified so the team must have at least a Chartered Accountant (ACA/FCA) or a Cost Accountant (ACMA/FCMA), together with a CISA/DISA/DISSA-qualified systems auditor. The February draft did not introduce that cost-accountant or DISSA option; it only provided the Category-II deferral.
review_notes: Draft chunk 10 and final chunk 9 both state the two-year Category-II deferral for internal audit and ESG Ratings Sub-Committee/NRC. Final chunks 8 and 9 add the ACA/FCMA-or-ACMA/FCMA plus CISA/DISA/DISSA internal-audit qualification mix, absent from the draft. Distinct compliance-checklist target.

question: The January 2026 revision of the stock-broker technical-glitch framework explicitly supersedes an earlier SEBI circular. Which circular number and date does it replace, and where did SEBI first announce that the earlier framework was being reviewed?
answer_summary: The January 9, 2026 circular (HO/38/44/12(1)2026-MIRSD-TPD1) supersedes earlier SEBI circular no. SEBI/HO/MIRSD/TPD-1/P/CIR/2022/160 dated November 25, 2022. SEBI first flagged the review of that 2022 framework in the background of the September 22, 2025 consultation paper, which noted the earlier comprehensive framework and the representations received for its review.
review_notes: Final circular #12 states the superseded circular number/date; consultation paper #2 provides the background announcement that the 2022 framework was being reviewed.

question: SEBI's January 9, 2026 press release says the revised framework simplified reporting by extending the intimation window from one hour to two hours and moving from reporting to all exchanges to a single platform. Where are the two-hour intimation and the single reporting platform recorded in the final circular, and what name does the circular give the platform?
answer_summary: The final January 9, 2026 circular records the two-hour intimation to stock exchanges and clients in clause 7.1 and requires submission of the information/reports on ‘Samuhik Prativedan Manch,’ described as the common portal for submissions by stock brokers, in clause 7.5. This implements the press release's shift from the earlier one-hour window and multiple-exchange reporting to a single reporting platform.
review_notes: Press release #2 records the one-to-two-hour reporting extension and single-platform shift; final circular #6/#7 places the two-hour intimation in clause 7.1 and names the platform 'Samuhik Prativedan Manch' in clause 7.5.

question: When stock exchanges rationalise financial disincentives under the January 2026 circular, what three factors must they consider, and did the September 2025 draft already list those factors?
answer_summary: The final circular requires stock exchanges to rationalise and revise the financial disincentive structure considering (i) the applicable exemption for technical glitches, (ii) the type of glitches (major or minor), and (iii) the frequency of occurrences of the glitches. The September 2025 consultation draft only said exchanges should rationalise and revise the current disincentive structure; it did not enumerate those three factors.
review_notes: Final circular #11 lists the three factors for rationalising financial disincentives; consultation draft #17 only directs exchanges to rationalise/revise the structure without enumerating them.

question: The September 2025 consultation paper said the definition of a technical glitch would be tightened to exclude after-hours glitches and glitches outside the broker's control. How does the January 2026 final circular put that exclusion into practice?
answer_summary: The final circular confines a technical glitch to a malfunction in the broker's electronic system that occurs during a trading session of the stock exchange. It then lists six categories of technical issues that are not treated as technical glitches irrespective of when they occur and therefore need not be reported: global/cloud/provider disruptions (including widespread disruption), market-infrastructure-institution disruptions, KYC-process glitches, non-trading back-office issues, payment-gateway failures at banks/providers/aggregators, and decision-support-tool problems such as charts or back-office reports.
review_notes: Consultation #3 proposes excluding after-hours and out-of-control glitches; final circular #2 confines the definition to trading-session occurrence and #4 enumerates the six excluded categories.

question: The final January 2026 circular directs stock exchanges to issue detailed capacity-planning guidelines for brokers. What three matters must those guidelines cover, and what new qualifier appears in the final circular but not in the September 2025 draft?
answer_summary: Both documents require stock exchanges to issue detailed guidelines covering capacity planning, peak load, and new capacity required to tackle future load on the broker's trading system. The final circular adds that the extant guidelines shall be rationalised based on the size of the stock brokers and their technology dependency, a qualifier absent from the September 2025 draft.
review_notes: Both documents require guidelines on capacity planning, peak load, and new capacity; only final circular #8 adds the qualifier that extant guidelines be rationalised based on broker size and technology dependency.

question: The revised framework revisits business-continuity planning (BCP) and disaster-recovery site (DRS) requirements. Which category of stock brokers remains outside the BCP/DRS scope, and what determines how strictly the retained BCP/DR requirements apply to the remaining brokers?
answer_summary: Both the September 2025 draft and the January 2026 final circular keep BCP and DRS requirements from applying to small-size stock brokers. For the remaining brokers, stock exchanges must rationalise the existing BCP/DR guidelines based on the size of the stock brokers and their technology dependency, while still addressing matters such as DR sites in different seismic zones, the frequency of DR drills and trading from the DR site, RTO/RPO definitions, and coverage during system audits and ISO certifications.
review_notes: Both draft (#16/#17) and final (#10/#11) keep BCP/DR requirements from applying to small-size stock brokers; final circular frames rationalisation of those requirements for remaining brokers by size and technology dependency.

question: The January 2025 consultation paper on Safe and Efficient Transfers on UPI proposed '@payright' as the exclusive handle and listed four alternative handles it had considered. What handle did SEBI finally adopt in its June 2025 circular, and was the adopted handle one of the alternatives listed in the consultation paper?
answer_summary: SEBI adopted '@valid' (for example, abc.bkr@validhdfc). The final '@valid' handle was not among the four alternatives listed in the consultation paper; the draft had considered @validpay, @validinvest, @invest and @trustedpay.
review_notes: Draft @payright and alternatives verified in Annexure C; final @valid handle and examples verified. Clean proposal-vs-final rule.

question: The draft circular's Annexure B mapped twelve intermediary categories or entries (including Alternative Investment Funds and a separate entry for mobile applications used in public issues) to proposed username suffixes. How many categories does the final June 2025 circular map, and which two entries from the draft were left out?
answer_summary: The final circular's Annexure B maps ten categories and drops (i) Alternative Investment Funds including Venture Capital Funds (suffix 'aif') and (ii) the list of mobile applications for using UPI in Public Issues (suffix 'app').
review_notes: Draft Annexure B lists 12 entries including AIF and 'app'; final Annexure B lists 10 and drops both. Good version-delta count.

question: An intermediary understood from the January 2025 draft that it could link only one UPI ID to a business account 'to begin with.' Under the June 2025 circular, can it apply for '@valid' UPI IDs from multiple banks using a single SI Portal login, and what accounts must get a '@valid' UPI ID?
answer_summary: Yes. The draft's 'to begin with' one-UPI-ID-per-business-account restriction was removed. The final circular permits an intermediary to apply to multiple banks using the same SI Portal login, and it is expected to generate a '@valid' UPI ID for all accounts in which it receives funds from investors. It must add at least one account for each category-wise login.
review_notes: Draft 'to begin with' one-UPI-ID restriction and final removal verified; FAQ confirms multiple banks via one SI Portal login and account coverage rule.

question: SEBI's final June 2025 circular introduced an investor-facing verification functionality that had no analogue in the January 2025 draft. What is it called, how can an investor use it, and what bank-level details does it confirm?
answer_summary: It is called 'SEBI Check'. An investor can verify a UPI ID by scanning the QR code or by entering the UPI ID manually, and the tool also confirms the intermediary's bank account number and IFSC.
review_notes: Final circular introduces SEBI Check and usage modes; bank account/IFSC confirmation is documented in adjacent chunk not listed in supporting_chunks. Draft has no such feature, so two-doc framing holds.

question: The January 2025 draft said generating a QR code with the thumbs-up logo was 'advisable.' What is its status in the June 2025 circular, and what visual cue must appear both on the investor's confirmation screen and on the QR code?
answer_summary: It is mandatory under the final circular. The investor's confirmation screen and the QR code must display a white thumbs-up icon inside a green triangle.
review_notes: Draft FAQ calls QR generation 'advisable' (chunk 29, not listed); final FAQ makes it mandatory and retains the white thumbs-up/green triangle cue. Minor citation gap, docs support answer.

question: The draft circular left activity dates as 'DD-MM-YYYY' placeholders. Relative to T, the June 11, 2025 issuance date of the final circular, by when must intermediaries obtain '@valid' UPI IDs, by when must they stop using old UPI IDs, and from what fixed date were the new IDs available to investors?
answer_summary: Intermediaries must obtain '@valid' handles between T+90 days and T+105 days, stop using old UPI IDs by T+180 days (with the ongoing Mutual Fund SIP exception preserved by paragraph 6.1.3), and the new UPI IDs were available to investors from 1 October 2025.
review_notes: Draft placeholders vs final T-based timeline verified, including T+90-105 for obtaining handles, T+180 discontinuation (with MF SIP carve-out), and investor availability from 1 Oct 2025.

question: An Investment Adviser’s compliance officer prepared the first digital-accessibility action-taken report for submission to BSE Administration & Supervision Limited by 30 August 2025, relying on the July 31 SEBI circular. A colleague says a later circular moved both the deadline and the reporting authority. What is the revised due date for that initial list-of-platforms and action-taken report, and to whom should the IA now submit it?
answer_summary: The August 29, 2025 circular extends the initial 30-day submissions (the list of digital platforms and the compliance/action-taken report) by one month, making them due by 30 September 2025. It also changes the reporting authority for Investment Advisers from BSE Administration & Supervision Limited (BASL) to BSE Limited. The IA must therefore submit the report to BSE Limited by 30 September 2025.
review_notes: Initial 30-day list-of-platforms and action-taken report extended to 30 Sept 2025, and IA reporting authority moved from BASL to BSE Ltd, verified in the baseline circular and the 29 Aug extension circular.

question: A Research Analyst firm had understood that SEBI itself was the reporting authority for its digital-accessibility compliance under the July circular. It then saw the September compliance guidelines, which group IAs and RAs together under a different authority. To whom must the RA submit its compliance, and which intervening circular made the change?
answer_summary: The July 31 circular assigns Investment Advisers to BSE Administration & Supervision Limited and leaves the residual category of MIIs and other REs to SEBI. The August 29, 2025 circular expressly modifies the reporting authority for Investment Advisers and Research Analysts from BASL and SEBI respectively to BSE Limited for both. The September 25 guidelines restate this updated position in Table B, showing IAs/RAs reporting to BSE Ltd. Hence, a Research Analyst must submit its digital-accessibility compliance to BSE Limited.
review_notes: RA reporting authority changed from SEBI (implied by the residual category in the baseline circular) to BSE Ltd under the 29 Aug circular, with the updated table restated in the 25 Sept guidelines; solid but overlaps somewhat with q01.

question: By the end of 2025, the December clarification superseded one immediate deadline from the earlier extension. What interim deliverable now replaces the requirement to appoint an IAAP-certified accessibility auditor by 14 December 2025, and what is the specific email address for REs that report directly to SEBI?
answer_summary: The August 29 circular extended the auditor-appointment deadline to 14 December 2025. The December 8, 2025 clarification replaces that requirement with a status-of-readiness-and-compliance submission for each digital platform, due by 31 March 2026 to the specified reporting authorities. REs whose reporting authority is SEBI must send that status to digital_acc@sebi.gov.in.
review_notes: 8 Dec clarification replaces the 14 Dec 2025 auditor-appointment deadline with a status-of-readiness-and-compliance submission due 31 Mar 2026, and directs REs reporting to SEBI to use digital_acc@sebi.gov.in.

question: A venture capital fund sees in the July circular that ‘MIIs and the rest of the REs’ report to SEBI, but is unsure whether its digital-accessibility compliance goes through a stock exchange. Which document tells it whether it must report directly to SEBI, and which department should handle its submission?
answer_summary: The September 25 Compliance Guidelines, Part D/Table D, enumerate the REs that must submit their digital-accessibility compliance directly to SEBI and map each to a concerned department. A Venture Capital Fund is listed there as reporting directly to SEBI under the Alternative Investment Funds and Foreign Portfolio Investors Department (AFD), not through a stock exchange.
review_notes: VCF is listed in the 25 Sept guidelines Part D/Table D as reporting directly to SEBI under AFD, resolving the broader baseline statement that MIIs and the rest of the REs report to SEBI.

question: Under the December clarification, how may an investor escalate an accessibility problem with a regulated entity’s digital platform, and what existing internal requirement from the original circular does this build upon?
answer_summary: The December 8, 2025 clarification allows investors to lodge accessibility-related complaints against REs on SCORES; an ‘Accessibility’ complaint category is already provisioned, and the RE must remediate the issue for closure of the complaint. The original July 31 circular already required each RE to institutionalize an internal grievance redressal mechanism specifically for accessibility issues, with user-friendly channels and escalation to senior officers.
review_notes: 8 Dec clarification enables SCORES accessibility complaints, building on the baseline circular's internal grievance-redressal-mechanism requirement for accessibility issues.

question: An RE is preparing the consolidated final audit report that must be submitted after remediation. What PDF file-name format must it use, and which audit standard referenced in the original circular governs the underlying audit?
answer_summary: The September 25 Compliance Guidelines require the consolidated final audit report to be attached as [Department]_Table-C4_[SEBI Reg No.]_DDMMYYYY.pdf, where Department corresponds to the RE category in Part D and DDMMYYYY is the report date. The underlying audit must follow the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 or latest version, which the July 31 circular identifies as part of the baseline accessibility standards.
review_notes: Final audit report filename format [Department]_Table-C4_[SEBI Reg No.]_DDMMYYYY.pdf is grounded in the 25 Sept guidelines, and the governing WCAG 2.1 standard is grounded in the baseline circular.

question: Our managing director currently oversees the SEBI-regulated debenture trustee function and will also supervise the new non-SEBI SBU. Colleagues say Regulation 9C requires the two businesses to be walled off, so the MD cannot manage both. Are they right?
answer_summary: No. Regulation 9C requires non-SEBI activities to be undertaken through separate business units, and the terms circular generally requires the staff handling non-SEBI activities to be distinct from those handling SEBI-regulated activities. However, the terms circular expressly states that the Chinese Wall and staff-segregation requirement does not apply to key managerial personnel; ordinary staff may cross the wall only under board-approved procedures.
review_notes: Supported by Regulation 9C(1) (separate SBUs) and circular para 2.4 (Chinese Wall does not apply to key managerial personnel). Plausible compliance scenario and distinct from prior memory targets.

question: We have provided credit-information services to issuers since 2022. The November 2025 terms circular says that for existing and ongoing non-SEBI arrangements, disclosures, confirmations and a compliance report must be submitted within six months of that circular. The April 2026 extension gives us an additional six months for compliance. Is the May 2026 date still binding, or does October 27, 2026 now govern the existing-arrangement cleanup?
answer_summary: October 27, 2026 now governs the cleanup. The April 28, 2026 extension circular grants an additional six months for compliance with the amendment and the terms circular, stating that their provisions shall be implemented by debenture trustees by October 27, 2026. The extension effectively superseded the original six-month milestone for existing arrangements, even though it preserved all other substantive provisions of the terms circular.
review_notes: Supported by para 2.10 (six-month cleanup window for existing arrangements) and the April 2026 extension to October 27, 2026. Distinct deadline-interplay angle focusing on existing ongoing engagements.

question: An issuer argues that because the debenture trustee's non-SEBI credit-advisory SBU is housed in the same legal entity, investor grievances about the SBU can be escalated through the trustee's existing SEBI-regulated complaint channel. Is the issuer correct?
answer_summary: No. The terms circular requires the grievance redressal mechanism, including any escalation mechanism, for non-SEBI activities to be separate and distinct from that for SEBI-regulated activities and to be part of the SBU. Regulation 9C supplies the structural foundation by requiring non-SEBI activities to be undertaken through separate business units; the terms circular then adds the dedicated grievance-escalation requirement.
review_notes: Supported by Regulation 9C(1) (non-SEBI activities through SBUs) and circular para 2.2 (separate/dedicated grievance mechanism). No prior accepted row targets this operational safeguard.

question: We are a stockbroker permitted by SEBI to provide research analyst services. The marketing team wants to publish a webpage showing our desk's verified historical risk and return metrics, citing CARE Ratings' recognition as a PaRRVA. Does the October 2025 interim certified-past-performance circular already permit this webpage, and if not, what is the correct compliance route?
answer_summary: No. The October 2025 interim circular does not permit public advertising. It allows certified past performance only for the pre-operationalisation period, only on a client's specific request, on a one-to-one basis, and only when certified by an ICAI/ICMAI member. For claims of returns or performance the correct route is Chapter IIIC of the Intermediaries Regulations: such claims must be in the form of risk and return metrics verified by a credit rating agency recognized by SEBI as a Past Risk and Return Verification Agency.
