CARE Ratings was granted that recognition on April 29, 2026, and the CRA Regulations require the PaRRVA to engage a recognized stock exchange as a PaRRVA Data Centre (NSE is acting as the PDC). Regular PaRRVA services began on May 4, 2026.
review_notes: Cited chunks support answer. Interim circular restricts pre-PaRRVA data to one-to-one client-specific use; 16E/12A establish PaRRVA-verified route and PDC requirement; press release confirms CARE/NSE and service dates. Multi-doc and human-shaped.

question: A research analyst has been sharing certified past performance data with clients since February 2026 under the interim circular and assumes the concession stays alive until SEBI formally withdraws it. Is this assumption correct, and what operationalisation milestones govern the switch?
answer_summary: No. The interim concession is time-bound and mode-bound. It applies only to performance for the period before PaRRVA operationalisation; that data must be certified by an ICAI/ICMAI member, shared only on a client's specific request, on a one-to-one basis, and with a prescribed disclaimer. IAs/RAs using this relief must enroll with PaRRVA within three months of its operationalisation (announced on April 29, 2026). After two years from operationalisation, only PaRRVA-verified risk and return metrics may be communicated or displayed to clients. The pilot phase was launched on December 8, 2025 and regular services began on May 4, 2026.
review_notes: Circular paragraph 3(f) supplies the two-year sunset; paragraph 3(c) supplies the three-month enrollment deadline; press release gives operationalisation/pilot/regular-service dates; Intermediaries Reg 16E governs the post-switch standard. Supported and distinct from q01/q05.

question: When a credit rating agency is approved by SEBI to operate as a PaRRVA, what infrastructural arrangement must it put in place, and which two institutions held the PaRRVA and the PaRRVA Data Centre roles at operationalisation?
answer_summary: Regulation 12A(2) of the CRA Regulations requires an approved PaRRVA to engage a recognized stock exchange as a PaRRVA Data Centre, on the terms and conditions specified by SEBI. When PaRRVA was operationalised, CARE Ratings Limited held the PaRRVA role and the National Stock Exchange of India Limited was acting as the PaRRVA Data Centre (PDC).
review_notes: CRA Reg 12A(2) directly requires a recognised stock exchange as PaRRVA Data Centre; press release identifies CARE Ratings as PaRRVA and NSE as PDC. Both documents are required to answer.

question: A compliance manual states that an intermediary may display 'returns or performance' claims backed by any 'credit rating agency recognized by SEBI'. A colleague argues that the March 2025 amendments narrowed the permissible form of those claims and added another institutional condition. Which interpretation is correct and why?
answer_summary: The colleague is correct. The Intermediaries (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2025 inserted Chapter IIIC, which permits claims of returns or performance only when they are in the form of risk and return metrics verified by a credit rating agency recognized by SEBI specifically to carry out the activity of a Past Risk and Return Verification Agency. The CRA Regulations, in Chapter IIA Regulation 12A, further require that the credit rating agency may carry out PaRRVA activity only with the Board's approval and on such terms and conditions as may be specified, and that the PaRRVA must engage a recognized stock exchange as a PaRRVA Data Centre. Therefore, ordinary CRA recognition alone is insufficient.
review_notes: Intermediaries Reg 16E narrows permissible claims to PaRRVA-verified risk-return metrics; CRA Reg 12A adds Board-approval and PDC conditions. Plain CRA recognition is insufficient. Clear multi-doc scope trap.

question: We want to publish a five-year performance record that straddles the date PaRRVA became operational. What verification and timing rules apply to the pre-operationalisation and post-operationalisation portions, and when does the interim concession finally expire?
answer_summary: The pre-operationalisation portion may use certified past performance only if it is certified by an ICAI/ICMAI member, communicated only on a specific client request, on a one-to-one basis, with the prescribed disclaimer, and only for the period before PaRRVA operationalisation. To keep using this relief the IA/RA must enroll with PaRRVA within three months of operationalisation. After two years from operationalisation, only PaRRVA-verified risk and return metrics may be communicated or displayed in any client-facing material, so the pre-operationalisation certified segment may no longer be shown. The post-operationalisation portion must be in the form of risk and return metrics verified by a SEBI-recognized PaRRVA. CARE Ratings was recognized on April 29, 2026, and regular services began on May 4, 2026.
review_notes: Pre-operationalisation rules, three-month enrollment, two-year sunset, and post-operationalisation PaRRVA-verified requirement are all supported by cited chunks. Distinct transition-span target compared with q01/q02.

question: The February 2025 consultation paper proposed intraday monitoring of single-stock MWPL utilization. By the March 2025 interim circular and the September 2025 final framework, who was required to take the intraday snapshots, and what had the instrument coverage narrowed to?
answer_summary: The February 2025 consultation paper proposed that Clearing Corporations monitor single-stock MWPL utilization intraday through at least four random snapshots. The March 28, 2025 interim circular shifted the task to Stock Exchanges and covered equity index derivative contracts. The September 1, 2025 final framework kept Stock Exchanges as the monitoring authority but narrowed coverage to index options only.
review_notes: Cited chunks support the answer: the consultation paper assigns single-stock MWPL intraday snapshots to Clearing Corporations; the March 2025 interim circular shifts monitoring to Stock Exchanges and covers equity index derivative contracts; the September 2025 framework keeps Stock Exchanges and narrows coverage to index options only. Distinct policy-lineage target.

question: An exchange is drafting its intraday monitoring SOP for index derivatives. Under the March 2025 interim circular, how many intraday snapshots were required and what was the penalty position? What additional snapshot timing requirement and penalty rule did the September 2025 framework add?
answer_summary: The March 28, 2025 interim circular required a minimum of four random snapshots during pre-defined time windows but made it clear that there would be no penalty for intraday breaches of existing position limits and such breaches would not be treated as violations until further directions. The September 1, 2025 final framework also requires a minimum of four random snapshots but mandates that one snapshot be taken between 14:45 and 15:30 hours. It further provided that breaches on expiry days would additionally attract penalty or additional surveillance deposit, effective from December 6, 2025.
review_notes: All answer elements are supported: the March 2025 interim circular requires four random snapshots in pre-defined windows and grants no-penalty relief; the September 2025 framework adds one snapshot between 14:45-15:30 and expiry-day penalties effective December 6, 2025. Requires both circulars.

question: What intraday net and gross FutEq limits for index options were proposed in the February 2025 consultation paper, what limits did the September 2025 framework eventually set, and why did the March 2025 interim circular not simply adopt those new higher intraday limits?
answer_summary: The February 24, 2025 consultation paper proposed intraday index-options limits of Net FutEq ₹1,000 crore and Gross FutEq ₹2,500 crore. The September 1, 2025 framework set intraday limits of Net FutEq ₹5,000 crore and Gross FutEq ₹10,000 crore, against end-of-day limits of Net ₹1,500 crore and Gross ₹10,000 crore. The March 28, 2025 interim circular did not adopt the new FutEq intraday limits because industry associations (ANMI, BBF and CPAI) raised concerns about readiness of broker/client systems for existing notional limits and pointed out that systems built for current parameters would become obsolete once the FutEq proposals were finalized.
review_notes: Cited chunks verify the February 2025 consultation's proposed index-options intraday limits (Net FutEq ₹1,000 crore, Gross FutEq ₹2,500 crore), the September 2025 framework's final limits (Net ₹5,000 crore, Gross ₹10,000 crore), and the March 2025 interim circular's rationale (industry-systems readiness / obsolescence concern).

question: A market participant holds a large intraday position in index options that is fully backed by cash and cash equivalents. Was such a position intended to be exempt from the proposed index derivatives limits in the February 2025 consultation paper, and does the September 2025 intraday framework preserve that treatment?
answer_summary: Yes. The February 2025 consultation paper proposed that positions backed by cash or cash-like instruments be exempt from the stated index futures and index options limits. The September 1, 2025 framework preserves this treatment by allowing entities additional exposure against holdings of securities or cash/cash equivalents, in line with the May 29, 2025 circular.
review_notes: Both cited documents support the cash/cash-equivalent backed position exemption: the February 2025 consultation paper exempts cash/cash-like backed long positions from the stated limits, and the September 2025 framework preserves the treatment by allowing additional exposure against cash/cash equivalents.

question: Industry associations told SEBI in early 2025 that market participants were not ready to monitor existing notional limits intraday because the ecosystem was preparing for FutEq-based limits. How did SEBI accommodate that concern in the March 2025 interim circular, and what operational runway did it build into the September 2025 framework before the monitoring became effective?
answer_summary: In the March 28, 2025 interim circular SEBI accommodated the concern by implementing intraday monitoring from April 1, 2025, while providing that there would be no penalty for intraday breaches and such breaches would not be treated as violations until further directions. The September 1, 2025 framework built in operational runway by requiring exchanges and clearing corporations to prepare a joint SOP within 15 days of the circular and issue it to market participants before the framework became effective on October 1, 2025; the expiry-day penalty/additional surveillance deposit provision was deferred to December 6, 2025.
review_notes: Supported across both circulars: the March 2025 interim circular defers penalties and begins monitoring from April 1, 2025 due to readiness concerns; the September 2025 framework builds in a 15-day joint-SOP deadline and an October 1, 2025 effective date, with expiry-day provisions deferred to December 6, 2025.

question: The February 2025 consultation paper proposed at least four random intraday snapshots for single-stock MWPL utilization by Clearing Corporations. Did the March 2025 interim circular or the September 2025 final framework carry forward that specific single-stock MWPL intraday-monitoring proposal?
answer_summary: No. The March 28, 2025 interim circular implemented intraday monitoring only for equity index derivative contracts by Stock Exchanges. The September 1, 2025 final framework restricted intraday monitoring to index options only, again by Stock Exchanges. Neither circular retained the consultation paper's proposal for Clearing Corporations to monitor single-stock MWPL utilization intraday.
review_notes: Negative check is supported: the February 2025 consultation proposed single-stock MWPL intraday snapshots by Clearing Corporations; the March 2025 interim circular applies intraday monitoring to equity index derivatives by Stock Exchanges; and the September 2025 framework restricts it to index options only. Neither circular retained the single-stock MWPL proposal.

question: We have developed an in-house algorithmic-trading execution tool and want to publish back-tested risk-return metrics on our website as soon as PaRRVA services begin. The April 2026 press release lists algorithmic trading among the services PaRRVA will verify. Are we necessarily covered by the March 2025 verification requirement, and what single fact decides it?
answer_summary: Not necessarily. Regulation 16D of the SEBI (Intermediaries) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2025 applies the new Chapter IIIC only to Investment Advisers, Research Analysts, Algo Providers empaneled with a recognised stock exchange, and intermediaries permitted by the Board to provide those services. The Explanation to Regulation 16D defines an algo provider as a person empaneled with a recognised stock exchange for providing algorithmic trading services, in the manner specified by that exchange. A stand-alone proprietary tool that is not so empaneled is not an 'algo provider' for this purpose, even though the operationalisation press release says PaRRVA will eventually verify algorithmic-trading services. Only an entity falling within Regulation 16D must make claims in the form of PaRRVA-verified risk and return metrics under Regulation 16E.
review_notes: Chunk 10 of the Intermediaries Second Amendment clearly defines Reg 16D/Explanation 'algo provider' as empaneled with a recognised stock exchange; chunk 0 of the press release confirms algorithmic trading is a covered PaRRVA service. Good scope-boundary memory target.

question: After PaRRVA became operational, a research analyst posted unaudited 'annual return' figures on social media calling them merely informative. The head of compliance treats this as only a general advertising-code issue, while the legal head says SEBI now has a self-contained enforcement route under the March 2025 amendments. Whose view is stronger, and what does the October 2025 interim circular add on penalties?
answer_summary: The legal head's view is stronger. Regulation 16F of the SEBI (Intermediaries) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2025 expressly empowers the Board to take such action as it deems fit for a violation of Regulation 16E, including action under Chapter V of the Intermediaries Regulations. The October 30, 2025 interim circular reinforces this by warning that contravention will make an entity liable for enforcement actions, including summary proceedings under Regulation 30A(1)(c) of the SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations, 2008, which penalises claims of return or performance unless otherwise permitted by the Board. So the breach is not merely an advertising-code concern; it triggers a specific regulatory penalty framework.
review_notes: Reg 16F (chunk 11) authorises Board action including Chapter V; circular chunk 5 adds Reg 30A(1)(c) summary-proceedings warning. Multi-document enforcement/penalty target distinct from run 69.

question: An internal memo cites the October 2025 interim circular as the source of the restriction that past performance can be shown only in PaRRVA-verified risk-return metrics. What is the real source of that substantive restriction, and under what authority was the interim circular itself issued?
answer_summary: The memo confuses the temporary concession with the underlying prohibition. The substantive restriction comes from Regulation 16E(1) of the SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations, 2008, inserted by the March 21, 2025 Second Amendment, which permits returns or performance claims only in the form of risk and return metrics verified by a Board-recognised PaRRVA. The October 30, 2025 interim circular, which carved out a limited exception for the pre-operationalisation period, was issued under Section 11(1) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 and Regulation 30A of the SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations, 2008.
review_notes: Reg 16E(1) (chunk 10) is the substantive restriction; circular chunk 0/5 states issuance under Section 11(1) SEBI Act and Reg 30A. Source-authority confusion is a distinct memory target.

question: During the interim period an investment adviser emailed certified past performance to a few clients but omitted the prescribed disclaimer and used its own branded report template. The April 2026 press release confirmed the operationalisation date. What minimum corrections are required, and when will this certified pre-operationalisation route close entirely?
answer_summary: For pre-operationalisation claims, the October 30, 2025 circular requires: the data must be certified by a member of ICAI or ICMAI; it must be shared only on a client's specific request and on a one-to-one basis; it must not be made available to the public; and it must carry the disclaimer in paragraph 3(e) stating that the data are not verified by PaRRVA or any SEBI-recognised agency, may not be comparable with other IAs/RAs, computation may vary, users should apply due diligence, past performance is no guarantee, investment is subject to market risk, and SEBI/IAASB/RAASB registration is no assurance of future returns. IAASB/RAASB must specify the template, within one month of the circular, in consultation with Industry Standard Forums and SEBI. The IA/RA must also enrol with PaRRVA within three months of operationalisation (confirmed as April 29, 2026 by the press release). Finally, two years from that operationalisation date, only PaRRVA-verified risk-return metrics may be communicated; certified pre-operationalisation past performance may no longer be used.
review_notes: Interim circular chunks 0-5 support ICAI/ICMAI certifier, one-to-one mode, prescribed disclaimer, IAASB/RAASB template authority, 3-month enrolment, and 2-year sunset; press release chunk 0 fixes the operationalisation date. Adds checklist/template/enrolment details beyond run 69 questions.

question: Our firm is empaneled with NSE to provide algorithmic trading services, and we want to publish PaRRVA-verified metrics starting May 2, 2026. The press release announced PaRRVA operationalisation on April 29, 2026. Can we go live on May 2, and what document (besides the press release) confirms we are within the class of regulated persons affected?
answer_summary: No. Although PaRRVA was operationalised on April 29, 2026 and CARE Ratings was recognised as PaRRVA with NSE acting as PaRRVA Data Centre, the press release states that regular services begin only from May 4, 2026 (after a pilot phase launched on December 8, 2025). So May 2 is too early regardless of the operationalisation announcement. Whether the firm falls within the regime is confirmed by Regulation 16D of the Intermediaries (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2025, which applies Chapter IIIC to Algo Providers empaneled with a recognised stock exchange for providing algorithmic trading services. Being NSE-empaneled brings the firm within the scope of Regulation 16D, but publication must await regular services from May 4, 2026.
review_notes: Press release chunk 0 states regular services begin May 4, 2026 after a pilot; Intermediaries chunk 10 confirms an NSE-empaneled algo provider falls under Reg 16D. Clean date/scope trap.

question: The October 2024 draft circular on valuation of mutual-fund repo transactions said the new rule would apply within 30 days from the date of issuance, but carried a placeholder date of 'November XX, 2024'. What calendar effective date did SEBI set in the final circular, and why would a compliance team relying only on the draft language have been uncertain about the deadline?
answer_summary: SEBI set the effective date as January 01, 2025. The draft circular dated October 24, 2024 was not dated and only stated that the provisions would be applicable 'within 30 days from the date of issuance of this circular,' so a reader could not know the exact compliance date without the final circular, which was issued on November 26, 2024 and replaced the 30-day window with a fixed January 01, 2025 start date.
review_notes: Effective-date delta is supported by both circulars: the draft contains the placeholder and 30-day-from-issuance language, while the final circular fixes the date at Jan 01, 2025. Both documents are materially needed; the question teaches a distinct version-delta/date-trap target.

question: A mutual fund is self-valuing a 10-day tri-party repo (TREPS) backed by a corporate bond on a cost-plus-accrual basis as of late 2024. Comparing the October 2024 draft circular and the November 2024 final circular, will the fund still be allowed to do so after the rule takes effect, and which class of repos remains outside the new requirement to obtain prices from AMFI-empanelled valuation agencies?
answer_summary: No. Once the final circular became effective on January 01, 2025, repurchase (repo) transactions (including TREPS) with tenor of up to 30 days had to be valued on a mark-to-market basis rather than cost-plus-accrual. In addition, all repo transactions except overnight repos must obtain prices from AMFI-empanelled valuation agencies. Therefore the 10-day corporate-bond-backed TREPS must be marked to market using agency prices. Only overnight repos are exempt from the agency-pricing requirement.
review_notes: Applied-compliance scenario is supported by draft and final operative paragraphs: repo/TREPS up to 30 days move to mark-to-market; only overnight repos are exempt from agency pricing. The draft supplies the prior rule and comparison framing, while the final supplies the effective date and enacted rule. Distinct scope/exception memory target.

question: SEBI's October 2024 draft circular described the move to mark-to-market valuation for short-term mutual-fund repos as fixing an 'unintended regulatory arbitrage.' What concrete issuer-level mismatch did it identify, and which committee had recommended the change?
answer_summary: The mismatch was that an issuer's commercial paper would be valued on a mark-to-market basis while borrowing by the same issuer through repos on its corporate bonds, with tenor up to 30 days, could be valued on a cost-plus-accrual basis. This meant adverse news about the issuer would feed into the NAV via the commercial-paper position faster than via the repo position. The Mutual Fund Advisory Committee (MFAC) recommended the change. The final November 2024 circular adopted the rule but dropped the explanatory discussion.
review_notes: Policy-rationale claim is supported by the draft circular's discussion of the commercial-paper-vs-repo valuation asymmetry and the MFAC recommendation. The final circular enacts the rule without that explanation, confirming the proposal-to-final shift. Distinct rationale/actor memory target.

question: Our depository participant had marked April 1, 2025 as its CSCRF compliance deadline after the December 2024 clarification. After the March 28, 2025 extension circular, the head of operations insists DPs are still due on April 1 because the December circular specifically named them. Is she correct? What is the operative deadline for this DP and which circular governs?
answer_summary: No. The March 28, 2025 extension circular extends the CSCRF compliance timeline by three months till June 30, 2025 for all regulated entities except Market Infrastructure Institutions (MIIs), KYC Registration Agencies (KRAs) and Qualified Registrars to an Issue and Share Transfer Agents (QRTAs). Depository Participants are not excluded, so this DP's operative deadline is June 30, 2025.
review_notes: Supported by original, Dec 2024 and Mar 2025 circulars; DPs are not excluded from the March extension, so the operative deadline is 30 Jun 2025.

question: Under the original August 2024 CSCRF, KRAs were treated at par with MIIs. The December 2024 circular pushed KRA compliance to April 1, 2025, while the March 2025 extension excluded KRAs from the three-month extension. The April 2025 clarification then re-categorised KRAs from MIIs to Qualified REs. As of April 30, 2025, what is a KRA's compliance deadline and CSCRF category?
answer_summary: KRAs remain due on April 1, 2025 because the December 2024 extension was not displaced by the March 2025 extension, which expressly excludes KRAs. They are now classified as Qualified REs rather than MIIs under the April 2025 clarification.
review_notes: Original framework treats KRAs as MIIs, Dec 2024 extended KRA deadline to 1 Apr 2025, Mar 2025 expressly excludes KRAs, and Apr 2025 re-categorises KRAs as Qualified REs.

question: A registered investment adviser has been submitting its CSCRF cyber audit report to BASL under the original framework. Its compliance officer says a later circular moves IA reporting to BSE Ltd for five years from July 25, 2024. The chief compliance officer disagrees, arguing that IAs stayed with BASL and only research analysts moved. Who is right, and what happens to a research analyst registered only as an RA?
answer_summary: The compliance officer is right. The April 30, 2025 clarification changes the CSCRF reporting authority for both IAs and RAs from BASL and SEBI respectively to BSE Ltd for five years starting July 25, 2024. A research analyst that is not registered with SEBI in any other capacity is exempt from CSCRF altogether.
review_notes: Original table lists IAs reporting to BASL; Apr 2025 changes reporting authority for both IAs and RAs to BSE Ltd for five years from 25 Jul 2024, and standalone RAs are exempt.

question: A Portfolio Manager with AUM of Rs 2,500 crores and 80 clients classified itself as a small-size RE under the original CSCRF and believed it had to be onboarded to Market-SOC. Under the April 2025 clarification, which category applies, and is the Market-SOC requirement still mandatory for it?
answer_summary: Under the April 2025 clarification, a PM with AUM of Rs 3,000 crores or below is a self-certification RE, so this PM is self-certification rather than small-size. Because it has fewer than 100 clients, it is exempted from the mandatory Market-SOC requirement.
review_notes: Original PM table put AUM Rs 2,500 cr in small-size and mandated small/self-cert REs to Market-SOC; Apr 2025 makes AUM up to Rs 3,000 cr self-certification and exempts self-cert PMs with fewer than 100 clients from Market-SOC.

question: The original August 2024 CSCRF puts Merchant Bankers that are part of a conglomerate or SIFI group in the Qualified REs category. The April 2025 clarification revises MB categorisation. What is the highest CSCRF category a pure Merchant Banker can now reach, and what happened to the conglomerate/SIFI criterion?
answer_summary: The highest category a pure Merchant Banker can now reach is mid-size RE, which applies to MBs engaged in issue management activities. The conglomerate/SIFI criterion has been removed; all other MBs are treated as small-size REs.
review_notes: Original MB table placed conglomerate/SIFI-linked MBs in Qualified REs; Apr 2025 removes that criterion, making issue-management MBs mid-size and all other pure MBs small-size.

question: A listed RE is drafting its data-localisation programme because the August 2024 CSCRF requires Regulatory Data to be stored within the legal boundaries of India. Before it commits budget, its counsel says a later SEBI clarification has put the localisation requirement on hold. Is that correct?
answer_summary: Yes. The December 31, 2024 clarification keeps the data localisation guidelines and provisions (Data Security standard PR.DS.S2) in abeyance until further notification.
review_notes: Original framework requires Regulatory Data to be stored within India; Dec 2024 clarification keeps data-localisation provisions in abeyance until further notification.

question: A mid-size RE migrating to the cloud assumes it must buy a dedicated Hardware Security Module because CSCRF Annexure-J addresses cloud adoption and cryptography. What does the April 2025 clarification say about which categories must implement a dedicated HSM, and what option does a mid-size RE have?
answer_summary: The April 2025 clarification makes a dedicated HSM mandatory only for MIIs and Qualified REs. Mid-size, small-size and self-certification REs may implement any HSM alternative based on a risk assessment approved by their Board, Partners or Proprietor.
review_notes: Apr 2025 clarification makes dedicated HSM mandatory only for MIIs and Qualified REs and allows mid-size, small-size and self-certification REs to use HSM alternatives based on risk assessment approved by Board/Partners/Proprietor.

question: A stock broker has 800 total registered clients and an annual clientele trading volume of Rs 800 crores. Under the April 2025 clarification, is it covered by CSCRF at all?
answer_summary: No. Stock brokers with less than Rs 1,000 crores of annual clientele trading volume and less than 1,000 total registered clients are exempted from CSCRF under the April 2025 clarification. The original framework, by contrast, classified brokers by active-client thresholds without this blanket exemption.
review_notes: Apr 2025 clarification exempts stock brokers with less than Rs 1,000 cr annual clientele trading volume and fewer than 1,000 total registered clients from CSCRF, while the original framework used active-client thresholds without this blanket exemption.

question: SEBI circulated a draft framework on retail investor participation in algorithmic trading in December 2024. If a broker wanted to submit public comments on that draft, what was the deadline, and when did SEBI ultimately make the framework applicable?
answer_summary: Comments on the draft were due by January 03, 2025 (clf-bl07tqd8qr8sryzi6czr2gka#2). The final circular dated February 04, 2025 made the framework applicable from August 01, 2025 (clf-plxnfn0j4dtwc59evxw3y4h8#10).
review_notes: Mechanical check passed. Comment deadline Jan 03, 2025 is in clf-bl07tqd8qr8sryzi6czr2gka#2. Final circular applicability Aug 01, 2025 is in clf-plxnfn0j4dtwc59evxw3y4h8#10. True multi-doc timeline question.

question: Under the final February 2025 circular, when must a retail investor's self-developed algorithm be registered with the exchange, and how did that requirement differ from the December 2024 draft?
answer_summary: The final circular says a self-developed algo must be registered only if it crosses the specified order-per-second threshold to be evolved by the Brokers' Industry Standards Forum (clf-plxnfn0j4dtwc59evxw3y4h8#3). The December 2024 draft required self-developed algos to be registered without linking registration to an order-per-second threshold (clf-bl07tqd8qr8sryzi6czr2gka#7). Both documents allow the same registered algo to be used by the retail investor's family, defined as self, spouse, dependent children and dependent parents.
review_notes: Self-developed algo registration changed from unconditional (draft, chunk 7) to conditional on crossing the order-per-second threshold (final, chunk 3). Both documents also share the family-definition clause. Difficulty comes from the threshold/version-delta angle.

question: When entering into a revenue-sharing arrangement for a retail client's subscription charges and brokerage, what disclosure and governance condition does the February 2025 final circular impose on brokers and algo providers that had not been addressed in the December 2024 draft?
answer_summary: The final circular permits algo providers and brokers to share subscription charges and brokerage collected from the client, provided they make prominent and complete disclosure of all charges to the client and the broker ensures the arrangement does not create a conflict of interest (clf-plxnfn0j4dtwc59evxw3y4h8#6). The December 2024 draft only set out empanelment criteria and did not address revenue sharing, charge disclosure, or conflicts of interest (clf-bl07tqd8qr8sryzi6czr2gka#8).
review_notes: Revenue sharing and conflict-of-interest disclosure only appear in final circular chunk 6; draft chunk 8 stops at empanelment/eligibility. Strong negative/absence plus final-rule memory target.

question: Compared with the December 2024 draft circular, what new exchange-level safeguard for retail algorithmic strategies did the February 2025 final circular require stock exchanges to cover when issuing detailed operational modalities or FAQs?
answer_summary: The final circular requires exchanges to mandate measures to enhance the confidentiality of retail algo strategies, including confidentiality clauses, non-disclosure agreements, and encrypted submissions, as part of the detailed operational modalities or FAQs (clf-plxnfn0j4dtwc59evxw3y4h8#8). The December 2024 draft only contemplated detailed operational modalities on broker/algo-provider roles, risk management systems, and turnaround times, without imposing confidentiality/NDA/encryption safeguards (clf-bl07tqd8qr8sryzi6czr2gka#9).
review_notes: Confidentiality/NDA/encryption safeguard added in final circular chunk 8. Draft chunk 9 mentions operational modalities but not confidentiality. Distinct from revenue-sharing target in q03.

question: After issuing the February 2025 circular on safer retail algorithmic trading, SEBI set two deadlines: when the Brokers' Industry Standards Forum was to formulate implementation standards and when the circular's provisions would apply. What did SEBI change by its April 2025 extension circular?
answer_summary: The February 2025 circular required the Brokers' Industry Standards Forum to formulate implementation standards by April 01, 2025 and made the circular provisions applicable from August 01, 2025 (clf-plxnfn0j4dtwc59evxw3y4h8#10). The April 01, 2025 extension circular deferred the effective date of the implementation standards to May 01, 2025 while leaving the broader applicability of the framework unchanged at August 01, 2025 (clf-l073b3vijbb9yyr793zuyrpi#0).
review_notes: Feb circular sets ISF standards by Apr 01, 2025 and overall applicability from Aug 01, 2025. Apr extension circular defers implementation-standard effect to May 01, 2025 and confirms Aug 01, 2025 applicability. Minor wording gap between "formulate by" and "come into effect from" is acceptable as a timeline-extension reading; otherwise supported.

question: A broker wants to onboard retail clients for optional T+0 settlement in the first half of February 2025. Under the December 2024 enhancement circular, which scrips are actually available for optional T+0 trading and settlement at that point, and how does that differ from what the March 2024 beta circular originally permitted?
answer_summary: In February 2025 only the original 25 beta scrips plus the first bottom-100 batch of the new top-500 universe (as determined by market capitalisation as on December 31, 2024) are available. The March 21, 2024 circular launched a Beta version limited to 25 scrips with a limited number of brokers. The December 10, 2024 enhancement expands eligible scrips to the top 500 companies, phased in by adding the next bottom-100 companies each month starting January 31, 2025, until all top 500 are covered.
review_notes: Supported by both circulars: Dec 2024 enhancement stages bottom-100 batches monthly from 31 Jan 2025 on top of original 25 beta scrips; Mar 2024 circular established the 25-scrip beta set. Distinct effective-date/scoped-expansion target.

question: At the March 2024 launch of the Beta T+0 settlement cycle, which investors were effectively able to participate? How did the December 2024 enhancement change the participant base, and what did it require of custodians?
answer_summary: The March 2024 circular said all investors were eligible if they met MII timelines, process and risk requirements, but the mechanism was initially enabled only for non-custodian clients from March 28, 2024. The December 2024 enhancement removes that restriction and allows all stock brokers to participate, permits differential brokerage within regulatory limits, and requires MIIs and custodians to put in place systems for seamless institutional participation in optional T+0 settlement.
review_notes: Both docs needed: Mar 2024 circular made all investors eligible but enabled only non-custodian clients from 28 Mar 2024; Dec 2024 enhancement removes that restriction, opens to all brokers, permits differential brokerage, and imposes custodian/MII readiness. Distinct participant-base target.

question: A compliance officer treats the March 2024 T+0 circular as entirely unchanged after the December 2024 enhancement. Which specific paragraphs of the March 2024 circular are modified or rescinded by the enhancement, and from what dates do the major new provisions become effective?
answer_summary: With effect from January 31, 2025, paragraph 5 of the March 2024 circular stands modified and paragraphs 7, 8 and 9 of the March 2024 circular are rescinded. Provisions relating to the expanded top-500 scrips, all-stock-broker participation and reporting/FAQ dissemination apply from January 31, 2025, while provisions on Qualified Stock Brokers, custodians and the T+0 block-deal window apply from May 1, 2025. All other provisions of the March 2024 circular remain applicable.
review_notes: Directly grounded in Dec 2024 circular paras 6.1-6.4: para 5 modified, paras 7-9 rescinded from 31 Jan 2025; expanded scrips/all-broker/reporting provisions from 31 Jan 2025; QSB/custodian/block-deal provisions from 01 May 2025. Strong paragraph-level lineage target.

question: Under the beta T+0 circular, the T+0 segment ran a single continuous trading session. An institutional investor later asks whether a block deal executed at 2:10 p.m. in an eligible T+0 scrip can settle on T+0 basis after the December 2024 enhancement. What is possible, and how do the available block-deal windows compare between the T+0 and T+1 segments?
answer_summary: No. After the December 2024 enhancement, the T+0 block-deal window is available only in the morning session from 8:45 a.m. to 9:00 a.m.; trades in that window settle on T+0 basis. The T+1 segment retains two block-deal windows at 8:45-9:00 a.m. and 2:05-2:20 p.m. Therefore a 2:10 p.m. block deal cannot be settled on T+0 basis. Participation in the T+0 block window is optional.
review_notes: Dec circular establishes T+0 block window (8:45-9:00 a.m. only) and references continuing T+1 windows (8:45-9:00 a.m. and 2:05-2:20 p.m.); Mar circular supplies the beta baseline single continuous session. Practical exception/window-comparison target.

question: The March 2024 beta circular set a price band and rules for index calculation and settlement-price computation for the T+0 segment. Did the December 2024 enhancement alter those market-structure rules, and what is the continuing position?
answer_summary: The December 2024 enhancement did not alter those rules; it states that all other provisions of the March 21, 2024 circular remain applicable. Therefore the T+0 segment continues to operate with a price band of plus or minus 100 basis points around the underlying T+1 market price, recalibrated after every 50 basis points movement; T+0 prices are not considered in index calculation or settlement-price computation; and there is no separate close price for securities based on trading in the T+0 segment.
review_notes: Dec 2024 circular 6.4 keeps other Mar 2024 provisions applicable; cited Mar chunks hold the +/-100 bp price band, index/settlement exclusion and no-separate-close-price rules. Memory target is continuity/not-altered. Slightly lighter because answer omits netting.

question: How did the readiness obligation for brokers evolve from the March 2024 beta circular to the December 2024 enhancement, and what happens if a broker enters or exits the list of Qualified Stock Brokers after the enhanced framework takes effect?
answer_summary: The March 2024 circular launched the beta with a limited number of brokers and required MIIs to disseminate the list of participating brokers periodically. The December 2024 enhancement opens participation to all stock brokers and additionally requires Qualified Stock Brokers meeting the minimum-active-clients parameter as on December 31, 2024 to put in place systems and processes for seamless investor participation. If the QSB list changes, the exiting QSB must continue providing those systems and processes, while newly designated QSBs must implement them within three months from the date of updation of the list.
review_notes: Mar circular required periodic broker-list dissemination; Dec enhancement adds QSB readiness obligation and the enter/exit transition rule (exiters continue, new entrants get 3 months). Distinct procedural-transition target.

question: Can a stock broker charge a higher brokerage for trades that settle under the optional T+0 cycle than for trades settling under the existing T+1 cycle, and which circular governs or conditions that practice?
answer_summary: Yes. The December 10, 2024 enhancement explicitly permits stock brokers to charge differential brokerage for T+0 and T+1 settlement cycles, provided it remains within the regulatory limit. The March 21, 2024 beta circular did not provide for such differential brokerage.
review_notes: Dec circular para 3.2 explicitly permits differential brokerage within regulatory limits; Mar circular contained no such provision. Clean version-delta on cost allocation.

question: A charitable trust has registered only under the Indian Registration Act, 1908 because its State does not have a public-trust statute. Before SEBI's September 2025 review, could this trust register as a Not for Profit Organization on the Social Stock Exchange? Did the January 2025 consultation propose to change this, and what minimum validity must its registration certificate now have under the revised SSE circular?
answer_summary: Before the September 2025 review, such a trust could not register. The ICDR definition of Not for Profit Organization contained only a trust under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882 or a public-trust statute of the relevant State, a society under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, or a company incorporated under Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013. The January 2025 consultation pointed out the gap for trusts in States without a Trusts Act and proposed adding a trust registered under the Indian Registration Act, 1908. The September 9, 2025 ICDR Second Amendment inserted this in Regulation 292A(e)(iii), and the September 19, 2025 SSE circular replaced the registration-requirement table so that the NPO's registration certificate must be valid for at least the next 12 months at the time of seeking registration.
review_notes: Supported across consultation paper (gap + proposal), ICDR Second Amendment (Regulation 292A(e)(iii)), and SSE circular (table replacement + 12-month validity). Three-document, practical eligibility/threshold target.

question: A not-for-profit social impact assessment start-up has no three-year track record but employs two full-time social impact assessors, each with four years of experience, and wants to be empaneled with an SRO. Was this route available under SEBI's January 2025 consultation, and how did the September 2025 ICDR amendment encode the staffing alternative to a track record?
answer_summary: Yes. The January 2025 consultation proposed replacing 'Social Impact Assessment Firm' with 'Social Impact Assessment Organization' and allowing such an organization to be empaneled if it had at least two full-time social impact assessors each with a minimum three years of experience, in addition to the existing three-year track-record route. The September 9, 2025 ICDR Second Amendment codified this in Regulation 292A(g): a Social Impact Assessment Organization means an entity that has either (i) Social Impact Assessors with a minimum three-year track record, or (ii) at least two full-time Social Impact Assessors each with a minimum three years of experience, who must sign the social impact assessment report.
review_notes: Consultation paper proposes the two-full-time-assessor staffing route and amendment codifies it in Regulation 292A(g). Both docs materially needed; distinct professional-role threshold target.

question: An NPO working on wetland restoration targets natural ecosystems rather than underserved human populations and is concerned that it may not meet the 67% eligible-activity test. How did the September 2025 ICDR amendment change the target-segment and primacy-of-social-intent rules compared with the position described in the January 2025 consultation paper?
answer_summary: Previously, the target segment was limited to underserved or less privileged population segments or regions recording lower performance in the development priorities of the Central or State Governments, which implicitly excluded purely environmental entities. The January 2025 consultation proposed expanding the target segment to cover environmental and cultural ecosystem entities, adding Schedule VII CSR-aligned activities, and restricting the 67% activity primacy test. The September 9, 2025 ICDR Second Amendment replaced the target-segment clause to allow the Board to specify additional target segments, inserted an eligible activity covering Schedule VII of the Companies Act, 2013, and changed Regulation 292E(2)(c) so that the 67% primacy test applies only to a For Profit Social Enterprise. As a result, wetland-restoration NPOs can now qualify, and they are not subject to the 67% test.
review_notes: Consultation paper explains the prior target-segment limitation and 67% test concern; amendment expands target segments and narrows the 67% test to For Profit Social Enterprises. Both docs needed; clean scope-exception target.

question: The January 2025 consultation proposed adding (a) a Project/Programme Proposal and (b) disclosures of reimbursements and benefits to governing members to the minimum initial disclosures required before raising funds through Zero Coupon Zero Principal instruments. Which, if any, of these two proposals were introduced by SEBI's final Framework on Social Stock Exchange circular dated September 19, 2025?
answer_summary: Neither proposal was introduced by the September 19, 2025 circular. That circular only partially modifies paragraph 1, sub-paragraphs A (NPO registration requirements), C (annual disclosures under Regulation 91C), and D (Annual Impact Report under Regulation 91E) of the September 19, 2022 framework circular. It does not modify sub-paragraph B, which contains the minimum initial disclosure requirements for raising funds through ZCZP. Therefore, the Project/Programme Proposal and the expanded governing-member remuneration disclosures remained outside the final circular.
review_notes: Consultation paper proposes Project/Programme Proposal and reimbursement/benefit disclosures; final circular only modifies sub-paragraphs A, C, and D, leaving sub-paragraph B untouched. Distinct proposal-not-adopted target.

question: A Qualified Registrar to an Issue and Share Transfer Agent (QRTA) read the March 28, 2025 extension circular and concluded that its CSCRF compliance can be deferred until June 30, 2025. Is that conclusion correct?
answer_summary: No. The August 2024 CSCRF treats QRTAs at par with Market Infrastructure Institutions, grouping them together with stock exchanges, depositories, clearing corporations and KRAs. The March 28, 2025 extension expressly excludes MIIs, KRAs and QRTAs from the three-month extension to June 30, 2025. The QRTA's compliance timeline therefore remains tied to the original framework effective January 1, 2025, with only the December 31, 2024 regulatory forbearance until March 31, 2025 available if it can demonstrate meaningful progress.
review_notes: Supported: QRTAs are listed as REs under MIIs in the original framework (clf-so4bcc81xyajgilxai8engh5#69), and the March 2025 extension expressly excludes MIIs/KRAs/QRTAs from the June 30, 2025 deferral (clf-rhvvcmy0bagoog2b9420fpj6#2); the December 2024 forbearance supplies the March 31, 2025 qualifier (clf-txufrwkmu5acknluqmirv4z9#3). Distinct deadline/category trap.

question: An AIF manager handles an Alternative Investment Fund with corpus of Rs 5,000 crores and a Venture Capital Fund under the same manager with corpus of Rs 1,000 crores. Under the original August 2024 CSCRF each fund was categorised separately. What is the manager's CSCRF category under the April 30, 2025 clarification?
answer_summary: Small-size RE. The April 2025 clarification changes AIF and VCF categorisation from the fund level to the manager level and clubs their thresholds into a single table. It also directs that, where the same manager handles both AIFs and VCFs, the corpus of VCF schemes must be included for threshold computation. The combined corpus is Rs 6,000 crores, which falls in the band of more than Rs 3,000 crores and less than Rs 10,000 crores, giving the manager a small-size RE classification.
review_notes: Supported: original framework categorises AIFs and VCFs separately by fund/scheme corpus (clf-so4bcc81xyajgilxai8engh5#100/#112); April 2025 moves to manager-level aggregation including VCF corpus and clubs thresholds (clf-j21ykxpqm5v7pw4qcpyiptv9#8/#9). Combined Rs 6,000 crores correctly maps to small-size RE. Distinct from prior memory targets.

question: A stock broker has 8 lakh total registered clients and annual clientele trading volume of Rs 5,00,000 crores. Under the original August 2024 CSCRF, categorisation depended on active client base and IBT/algo trading status. How is it categorised under the April 30, 2025 clarification?
answer_summary: Qualified RE. The April 2025 clarification switches stock-broker categorisation to two independent parameters: number of total registered clients and annual clientele trading volume in crores. The client count of 8 lakhs would make the broker a mid-size RE, while a trading volume of Rs 5,00,000 crores makes it a qualified RE. Because the parameters are applied independently and the higher category applies when a broker falls into two different categories, it is classified as a qualified RE.
review_notes: Supported: original broker categorisation used active clients + IBT/algo (clf-so4bcc81xyajgilxai8engh5#102); April 2025 uses total registered clients and annual clientele trading volume independently, applying the higher category (clf-j21ykxpqm5v7pw4qcpyiptv9#3/#5). 8 lakh clients = mid-size; Rs 5,00,000 crores = qualified; higher-category rule gives qualified RE. Distinct from the low-threshold exemption question in memory.

question: A Depository Participant has only 80 clients. Does the April 30, 2025 clarification still require it to subscribe to SOC services or on-board to the Market SOC?
answer_summary: No. The original August 2024 CSCRF mandates SOC for all REs, with only client-based stock brokers having fewer than 100 clients exempt, and directs small-size and self-certification REs to be on-boarded on the Market SOC. The April 30, 2025 clarification adds a new carve-out for DPs: those with fewer than 100 clients are exempted from the requirement of SOC services or on-boarding to Market-SOC. The DP is therefore not required to subscribe to Market-SOC by virtue of its small client base.
review_notes: Supported: original framework mandates SOC for all REs except sub-100-client stock brokers and requires small/self-certification REs to board Market SOC (clf-so4bcc81xyajgilxai8engh5#37/#180); April 2025 adds a DP-specific carve-out for fewer than 100 clients (clf-j21ykxpqm5v7pw4qcpyiptv9#5). Clear exception trap and distinct target.

question: A corporate Investment Adviser registered only as an IA was classified as a small-size RE under the original August 2024 CSCRF. Under the April 30, 2025 clarification, is it still required to comply with CSCRF?
answer_summary: No. The original August 2024 CSCRF categorises non-individual Investment Advisers as small-size REs and exempts only individual IAs. The April 30, 2025 clarification overrides this for IAs that are not registered with SEBI in any other capacity, exempting them from CSCRF provisions. An IA that is also registered in another capacity must follow the highest category of that other registration.
review_notes: Supported: original framework categorises non-individual IAs as small-size REs (clf-so4bcc81xyajgilxai8engh5#106); April 2025 exempts IAs not registered in any other capacity and preserves highest-other-category rule for dual-registered IAs (clf-j21ykxpqm5v7pw4qcpyiptv9#6). Distinct from the RA/dual-registration reporting question in memory.

answer_summary: None of the four refinements was carried into the September 19, 2025 circular. The final circular partially modified paragraphs 1.A, 1.C and 1.D of the September 19, 2022 circular, but the paragraph 1.D (Annual Impact Report) changes only replaced the old 90-day deadline and the requirement that the AIR be 'audited' with a deadline of October 31 or the income-tax-return due date (whichever is later) and a requirement that the AIR be 'assessed by Social Impact Assessors.' It did not introduce mid-term/end-term reports, did not add cultural parameters, did not require a logic-model solution plan, and did not tie KPIs to the solution implementation plan. The annual-impact-report obligation otherwise remained as before, with listed-project AIR subject to external assessment and self-reporting continuing for NPOs registered without a listed security.
review_notes: Cited chunks confirm the four AIR refinements were proposed and that the final circular only modified para 1.D for deadline/assessor; all four refinements were dropped.

question: An NPO applying for registration on a Social Stock Exchange wants to use its stamped memorandum of association (rather than its registration certificate) to prove the three-year existence requirement, and points out that it holds a tax-exemption registration under section 10(23C) of the Income-tax Act instead of section 12A. Did SEBI's January 2025 consultation propose either of these relaxations, and were either of them accepted in the final Framework on Social Stock Exchange circular dated September 19, 2025?
answer_summary: The January 2025 consultation proposed both relaxations. The SSEAC recommended accepting a duly stamped MoA/AoA, trust deed or constitution, in addition to the registration certificate, for determining the age of the NPO, and expanding eligible tax-exemption registrations to include sections 10(23C) and 10(46) alongside 12A/12AA/12AB. Neither was accepted in the September 19, 2025 circular. That circular modified only the NPO-registration table to require registration certificate valid at least 12 months and to add trusts registered under the Indian Registration Act, 1908 as an eligible legal form. It did not add MoA/AoA/trust deed as an age-proof alternative, and it did not broaden the tax-exemption sections.
review_notes: Consultation chunks 47-48 propose MoA/AoA/trust-deed age proof and 10(23C)/10(46) tax exemption; final circular chunk 3 only updates certificate validity and legal forms, rejecting both relaxations.

question: A compliance officer assembling the Regulation 91C annual-disclosure package for an SSE-registered NPO has collected the Form 10B/10BB income-tax audit report, copies of the income-tax and FCRA returns, and the annual returns filed with the registering authority (Charity Commissioner/Registrar of Societies/Registrar of Companies). Did the January 2025 consultation propose adding any of these documents, and are they required under the post-amendment annual-disclosure list in SEBI's September 19, 2025 circular?
answer_summary: The January 2025 consultation proposed adding all of them to the financial-aspect annual disclosures, either as additional financial-statement items or by specifically requiring Form 10B/10BB, copies of income-tax and FCRA returns, and annual returns to the registering authority. SEBI's September 19, 2025 circular did not adopt any of these additions. The modified Regulation 91C list keeps financial-aspect disclosures limited to the financial statements (balance sheet, income statement and cash statement), programme-wise fund utilisation, and the auditor's report and auditor details.
review_notes: Chunks 57-58/60 show the proposed Form 10B/10BB, IT/FCRA returns and annual returns; final circular chunk 7 limits financial disclosures to statements, utilisation and auditor's report.

question: The January 2025 consultation suggested expanding Annexure I governance disclosures to include, for each governing-body member, details such as age, gender, occupation, relationship with other members, tenure, remuneration and reimbursements paid, passport details for foreign nationals, and third-party certifications such as GuideStar India. Did SEBI's Framework on Social Stock Exchange circular dated September 19, 2025 introduce any of these extra Annexure I fields?
answer_summary: No. The September 19, 2025 circular did not modify Annexure I. The governance disclosures it retained in paragraph 1, sub-paragraph C of the 2022 circular are the familiar list: ownership and legal form, governance structure, names of the governing body, executives with key responsibilities, meetings/attendance/performance review, organisation-level risks and mitigation, ethics/conflict mechanisms, remuneration policies, stakeholder grievance, and registration certificates/licenses. None of the Annexure-I enhancements proposed in the consultation became part of the final amendment.
review_notes: Chunks 70-72 confirm the proposed Annexure I enhancements; final circular chunks 5-6 leave the governance-disclosure list unchanged, so none were adopted.

question: An NPO preparing its minimum initial disclosures for a Zero Coupon Zero Principal instrument wants to include its GuideStar India certification and any third-party accreditations, arguing that the January 2025 consultation required such credentials to be disclosed. Was this requirement actually proposed in the consultation, and does the September 19, 2025 circular make these certifications part of the initial disclosure package?
answer_summary: The January 2025 consultation did propose adding certifications and accreditations (GuideStar India number and level, and other third-party accreditations) to the credibility items in the minimum initial disclosures for ZCZP issuance. The September 19, 2025 circular did not adopt this change; it only partially modified paragraphs 1.A, 1.C and 1.D of the 2022 circular and left the initial-disclosure requirements in paragraph 1.B unchanged. Therefore, GuideStar/third-party accreditations are not a required part of the ZCZP minimum initial disclosures under that final circular.
review_notes: Chunks 52-53 propose GuideStar/third-party accreditations for initial disclosures; final circular only partially modifies paras A, C and D, leaving para B unchanged.

question: The January 2025 consultation included detailed recommendations to change Annexure I (governance disclosures) and Annexure II (Annual Impact Report guidance, including mid-term/end-term reports) of the Social Stock Exchange framework. Which sub-paragraphs of the September 19, 2022 SSE circular did SEBI actually amend in its September 19, 2025 circular, and what does that mean for the status of Annexure I and Annexure II?
answer_summary: The September 19, 2025 circular partially modified only paragraph 1, sub-paragraphs A (minimum NPO registration requirements), C (annual disclosures under Regulation 91C) and D (Annual Impact Report under Regulation 91E) of the September 19, 2022 circular. Because the circular did not amend any Annexure, both Annexure I and Annexure II remained in their pre-existing form despite the consultation's Annexure-level proposals. Thus, Annexure I was not expanded with richer governing-body details and Annexure II was not expanded with mid-term/end-term reports or related guidance.
review_notes: Final circular chunk 2 states only paras 1.A, 1.C and 1.D were modified; consulted Annexure I/II proposals in chunks 70/73/80 therefore remain unamended.

question: A stock broker that qualified as a QSB as on December 31, 2024 is checking its mandatory systems-readiness deadline for the optional T+0 settlement cycle. What was the original deadline under the December 2024 circular? How did the April 2025 extension move it, and what does the October 2025 circular say now? Which substantive parts of the December 2024 framework continue unchanged despite the extensions?
answer_summary: The December 2024 enhancement originally required QSBs to put in place systems and processes for enabling seamless participation in optional T+0 settlement, with the QSB, custodian and block-deal provisions becoming effective from May 1, 2025 (clf-jrfnd7iyvrsgtbqy1evlsby5#2, #5). The April 29, 2025 circular extended only the QSB systems-readiness deadline to November 1, 2025, while keeping all other December 2024 provisions unchanged (clf-cixx7itd9cxq1hu5j3pdhet5#2). The October 30, 2025 circular further extended the QSB timeline and said further guidance would be intimated later, again leaving all other December 2024 provisions unchanged (clf-c6yffsfxjvvc0a3rsjeefigk#2). Therefore the expanded scrip universe (top 500), all-stock-broker participation, permission for differential brokerage, custodian participation, the morning-only T+0 block-deal window and the fortnightly reporting requirement all remain in force.
review_notes: Dec 2024 QSB/custodian/block-deal provisions were effective May 1, 2025; Apr 2025 extended QSB systems-readiness to Nov 1, 2025; Oct 2025 pushed QSB timeline further while leaving all other Dec 2024 provisions unchanged.

question: A service provider tells a compliance head that the April 2025 extension circular put the entire December 2024 optional T+0 enhancement on hold. Is the provider correct? What did the April 2025 and October 2025 circulars actually change, and what stayed in effect?
answer_summary: Incorrect. Neither extension suspended the broader optional T+0 settlement rollout. The December 2024 enhancement introduced a larger scrip universe (top 500), opened participation to all stock brokers, permitted differential brokerage, added custodian and block-deal mechanisms and retained fortnightly reporting (clf-jrfnd7iyvrsgtbqy1evlsby5#1, #2, #3, #4, #5). The April 29, 2025 circular extended only the QSB systems-readiness deadline from May 1, 2025 to November 1, 2025 and stated that all other provisions of the December 2024 circular remained unchanged (clf-cixx7itd9cxq1hu5j3pdhet5#2). The October 30, 2025 circular similarly delayed only the QSB readiness timeline, announcing that further guidance would be issued later, and reiterated that all other December 2024 provisions remained unchanged (clf-c6yffsfxjvvc0a3rsjeefigk#2).
review_notes: Negative-check is correctly rebutted: neither 2025 extension suspended the broader Dec 2024 rollout; both only deferred the QSB systems-readiness deadline and preserved other provisions.

question: An institutional investor wants to settle an equity cash-market trade on T+0, while also carrying a T+1 position in the same scrip. The broker says it can net the pay-in and pay-out obligations across the T+0 and T+1 segments to simplify settlement. Is it allowed, and what is the continuing rule?
answer_summary: No. The March 2024 beta circular expressly prohibits netting of pay-in and pay-out obligations between the T+1 and T+0 settlement cycles (clf-kdotyoyolu54966669w9mnbg#4). The December 2024 enhancement did not create any exception to this rule; paragraph 6.4 states that all other provisions of the March 21, 2024 circular remain applicable (clf-jrfnd7iyvrsgtbqy1evlsby5#6). Consequently, the T+0 and T+1 obligations must be settled separately.
review_notes: March 2024 beta circular explicitly prohibits netting between T+1 and T+0 pay-in/pay-out; Dec 2024 para 6.4 confirms all other March provisions remain applicable, so the no-netting rule continues.

question: The March 2024 beta circular, the December 2024 enhancement and both 2025 QSB extension circulars all cite the same statutory authority. What powers do they invoke, and under which specific Acts and SEBI regulations?
answer_summary: Each circular invokes powers under Section 11(1) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with Regulation 51 of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) (Stock Exchanges and Clearing Corporations) Regulations, 2018; Section 26(3) of the Depositories Act, 1996; and Regulation 97 of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Depositories and Participants) Regulations, 2018 (clf-kdotyoyolu54966669w9mnbg#5; clf-jrfnd7iyvrsgtbqy1evlsby5#6; clf-cixx7itd9cxq1hu5j3pdhet5#3; clf-c6yffsfxjvvc0a3rsjeefigk#3).
review_notes: All four circulars cite the same statutory authority (Section 11(1) SEBI Act 1992 read with Regulation 51 SCRR 2018; Section 26(3) Depositories Act 1996 read with Regulation 97 SEBI DP Regulations 2018).

question: Our CFO believes the March 28, 2025 extension circular also extended the December 31, 2024 regulatory forbearance, so no regulatory action can be taken through June 30, 2025 provided we show meaningful progress. Is that understanding correct?
answer_summary: No. The December 31, 2024 clarification granted regulatory forbearance only until March 31, 2025 for non-compliance with CSCRF requirements that became effective from January 1, 2025. The March 28, 2025 circular extends the compliance timeline by three months to June 30, 2025 for eligible REs, but it does not extend the forbearance. After March 31, 2025, the forbearance expires and SEBI may take regulatory action for non-compliance in the normal course.
review_notes: December 2024 forbearance ends March 31, 2025; March 2025 extension only defers the compliance deadline to June 30, 2025. Both cited docs are materially needed.

question: A stock broker that offers algorithmic trading was reclassified from mid-size to small-size under the April 30, 2025 clarification. Its head of compliance argues that, as a small-size RE, it now needs a cyber audit only once a year. Is that correct?
answer_summary: No. The original August 2024 CSCRF prescribes cyber-audit periodicity as follows: MIIs and Qualified REs at least twice a year; mid-size and small-size REs that provide IBT or algo trading at least twice a year; and all other REs at least once a year. The April 30, 2025 clarification revises the stock-broker categorisation thresholds and the way category is fixed for a financial year, but it does not amend this periodicity rule. Because the broker provides algorithmic trading, it remains subject to at least two cyber audits a year even after becoming small-size.
review_notes: August 2024 Table 21 keeps algo-trading small-size brokers on twice-yearly cyber audit; April 2025 reclassification does not amend that periodicity rule.

question: A firm holds both a Portfolio Manager registration and a Merchant Banker registration. Under the April 30, 2025 clarification, its portfolio-management business is self-certification while its merchant-banking activity falls in the mid-size category. Which CSCRF category's provisions govern the firm as a whole?
answer_summary: The firm is governed by the mid-size RE category. Paragraph 4 of the April 30, 2025 clarification states that if an RE is registered under more than one category, the provisions of the highest category under which it falls shall apply. Under the August 2024 framework the graded hierarchy is MIIs, Qualified REs, mid-size REs, small-size REs and self-certification REs. Since mid-size RE ranks higher than self-certification RE, the entire firm must comply with the mid-size obligations and cannot rely on the self-certification status of its PM arm.
review_notes: April 2025 paragraph 4 highest-category rule is grounded in the August 2024 graded hierarchy; distinct multi-registration target.

question: A Depository Participant is also registered as a stock broker with 4 lakh total registered clients and annual clientele trading volume of Rs 40,000 crores. Relying on its DP registration, it claims Qualified RE status under the April 30, 2025 clarification. Is that claim correct?
answer_summary: No. The April 30, 2025 clarification states that if a DP is also registered as a stock broker, it must be classified using the stock-broker criteria; only DPs "other than stock brokers" are treated as Qualified REs. Under the stock-broker table, 4 lakh total registered clients and Rs 40,000 crores annual clientele trading volume place the entity in the mid-size RE category. Therefore, the firm is a mid-size RE, not a Qualified RE.
review_notes: April 2025 DP/stock-broker override and stock-broker table are cross-read with the August 2024 category hierarchy; the two-parameter mid-size result is correct.

question: A stock broker has less than Rs 1,000 crores of annual clientele trading volume and fewer than 1,000 total registered clients, so it is exempt from CSCRF under the April 30, 2025 clarification. Is it still required to report cybersecurity incidents to SEBI through the CSCRF incident reporting portal within 24 hours?
answer_summary: No. The April 30, 2025 clarification exempts stock brokers that fall below both thresholds from CSCRF entirely. The original August 2024 CSCRF requires REs covered by the framework to notify SEBI of cybersecurity incidents within 6 hours by email and on the SEBI Incident Reporting Portal within 24 hours. Because the broker is outside the framework, those specific CSCRF incident-reporting timelines do not apply to it.
review_notes: April 2025 exempts sub-threshold stock brokers from CSCRF, so the August 2024 24-hour portal reporting requirement does not apply to them.

question: A KRA's HR head argues that because the April 30, 2025 clarification re-categorises KRAs from MIIs to Qualified REs, the requirement for its Chief Information Security Officer to report directly to the MD & CEO at a grade equivalent to CTO/CIO no longer applies. Is that correct?
answer_summary: No. The August 2024 CSCRF applies the direct CISO reporting and grade-equivalence requirement to both MIIs and Qualified REs. The April 30, 2025 clarification moves KRAs from the MII category to the Qualified RE category, but Qualified REs remain subject to the same CISO governance standard. Therefore, the reclassification does not relax the requirement that the CISO report directly to the MD & CEO and hold a grade at least equivalent to CTO/CIO.
review_notes: August 2024 CISO reporting/grade rule applies to MIIs and Qualified REs; April 2025 moves KRAs from MIIs to Qualified REs, leaving the rule unchanged.

question: A compliance officer says the December 2024 enhancement added extra surveillance restrictions to the optional T+0 segment. What surveillance treatment actually applies, and which circular controls it before and after the enhancement?
answer_summary: The March 2024 beta circular states that the surveillance measures applicable in the existing T+1 settlement cycle apply equally to scrips in the optional T+0 settlement cycle (paragraph 6(b)). The December 2024 enhancement did not introduce any additional surveillance restrictions; paragraph 6.4 of the enhancement circular provides that all other provisions of the March 21, 2024 circular remain applicable. Therefore, the T+0 segment continues to be governed by the same surveillance measures as the T+1 segment.
review_notes: Verified: March 2024 para 6(b) extends T+1 surveillance to T+0; Dec 2024 para 6.4 preserves all other March provisions. Distinct from the prior price-band/market-structure question (kimi_run_000077_q05) because this target is specifically surveillance treatment.

question: A broker hears that stock exchanges must submit quarterly progress reports on the optional T+0 settlement segment to SEBI. What reporting interval does SEBI actually require, and where does the obligation originate and survive after the enhancement?
answer_summary: SEBI requires Market Infrastructure Institutions to provide progress reports on a fortnightly basis, not quarterly. Paragraph 9 of the March 2024 beta circular directs MIIs to submit a fortnightly report on the progress of the Beta version of T+0 settlement until further direction. Paragraph 5 of the December 2024 enhancement circular preserves the same requirement, directing MIIs to provide a fortnightly report on activities under the optional T+0 settlement cycle until further direction.
review_notes: Verified: March 2024 para 9 and Dec 2024 para 5 both require fortnightly MII progress reports. Negative-check on quarterly cadence; both docs needed to show origin and survival.

question: Where must an investor find the official list of scrips available for optional T+0 trading and the operational guidelines for the segment, and does that publication duty apply only under the beta circular or continue after the enhancement?
answer_summary: The publication duty applies under both circulars. Under paragraph 7 of the March 2024 beta circular, MIIs must publish operational guidelines and FAQs along with the list of 25 scrips for the Beta version of T+0 settlement and disseminate the same on their websites. Paragraph 4 of the December 2024 enhancement circular imposes a corresponding obligation on MIIs to publish operational guidelines, FAQs, the list of eligible scrips and the list of Qualified Stock Brokers for the enhanced optional T+0 settlement cycle, and to disseminate these on their websites.
review_notes: Verified: March 2024 para 7 requires publication of guidelines/FAQs/list of 25 scrips; Dec 2024 para 4 requires guidelines/FAQs/eligible scrips/QSB list. Investor-facing disclosure duty across both circulars.

question: The beta circular of March 2024 introduces the optional T+0 cycle as the next step after an earlier settlement reform. What prior reform does it reference, what preconditions does it cite, and what new justification does the December 2024 enhancement add for widening the framework?
answer_summary: The March 2024 circular references SEBI's Circular No. SEBI/HO/MRD2/DCAP/P/CIR/2021/628 dated September 7, 2021 allowing the T+1 rolling settlement cycle, which was fully implemented by January 27, 2023. It cites the evolution of technology, architecture and capacity of Market Infrastructure Institutions; the depository ecosystem's ability to effect immediate transfer of securities through digital client-level holdings; and the real-time transfer capability of India's payments ecosystem as preconditions. It also notes expected benefits such as cost and time efficiency, transparency in charges, and strengthened risk management. The December 2024 enhancement adds that the scope was widened based on feedback received from stakeholders to increase the efficiency of the optional T+0 settlement cycle, with the approval of the SEBI Board.
review_notes: Verified: March 2024 references Circular 2021/628 T+1 reform and cites tech/depository/payments preconditions and efficiency benefits. Dec 2024 cites stakeholder feedback and Board approval for widening. Good lineage/rationale target.

question: After the December 2024 enhancement introduces a morning T+0 block-deal window, is participation in that window mandatory for eligible investors?
answer_summary: No, participation is optional for investors. Paragraph 3.5.2 of the December 2024 enhancement circular states that participation under the optional T+0 block-deal window shall be optional for investors. The March 2024 beta circular did not provide any block-deal window for the T+0 segment; it provided only one continuous trading session from 9:15 a.m. to 1:30 p.m.
review_notes: Verified: Dec 2024 para 3.5.2 says block-deal participation is optional; March 2024 had no block-deal window. Slightly weaker multi-doc necessity because Dec alone answers the mandatory question, but March is needed to describe the pre-enhancement regime.

question: Under the December 2024 enhancement, how does the optional T+0 scrip universe expand beyond the original 25 beta scrips, and when does that expansion begin?
answer_summary: With effect from January 31, 2025, the optional T+0 settlement cycle was made available to the top 500 scrips by market capitalization as on December 31, 2024. The expansion begins with the bottom 100 companies of that top-500 list, and the next bottom 100 companies are added every subsequent month until all top 500 companies are available. This larger list is in addition to the original 25 scrips made available under the March 2024 Beta version of the optional T+0 settlement cycle.
review_notes: Verified: March 2024 limited to 25 scrips; Dec 2024 expands to top 500 starting bottom-100-per-month from Jan 31, 2025, in addition to original 25. Rolls out schedule distinct from prior first-half-February eligible-set question.

question: A compliance team assumes every measure in the December 2024 enhancement circular takes effect on January 31, 2025. Which provisions apply from January 31, 2025, and which apply from May 1, 2025?
answer_summary: Paragraphs 3.1 (scrip expansion to the top 500), 3.2 (participation by all stock brokers and differential brokerage), 4 (MIIs' publication of operational guidelines, FAQs and lists) and 5 (fortnightly reporting) apply from January 31, 2025. Paragraphs 3.3 (Qualified Stock Broker readiness), 3.4 (custodian participation) and 3.5 (T+0 block-deal window) apply from May 1, 2025. Additionally, paragraph 5 of the March 2024 circular is modified and paragraphs 7, 8 and 9 of the March 2024 circular are rescinded with effect from January 31, 2025.
review_notes: Verified: Dec 2024 para 6 maps Jan 31 (3.1,3.2,4,5) vs May 1 (3.3,3.4,3.5) and modifies/rescinds March paras. March 2024 needed to ground the modified/rescinded paragraphs. Distinct granular applicability table.

question: A Credit Rating Agency’s compliance head points out that the August 2024 CSCRF applies to CRAs for the first time, and argues that the March 28, 2025 extension circular therefore gives CRAs a six-month runway until October 1, 2025. Is this correct? What is the operative compliance deadline for the CRA?
answer_summary: No. CRAs are among the REs covered by CSCRF for the first time, so the original framework made them compliant from April 1, 2025. The March 28, 2025 extension pushes that deadline out by three months to June 30, 2025 for all REs except Market Infrastructure Institutions, KYC Registration Agencies and Qualified Registrars to an Issue and Share Transfer Agents; CRAs are not excluded. The CRA must therefore comply by June 30, 2025.
review_notes: Original CSCRF sets April 1, 2025 for first-time REs; extension circular defers to June 30, 2025 excepting only MIIs/KRAs/QRTAs. CRA is not excluded.

question: A stock broker began FY 2025-26 as a Qualified RE because, as on March 31, 2025, it had more than 10 lakh total registered clients. By December 2025 its client base has fallen to 8 lakh. Can it reclassify itself as a mid-size RE for the remainder of FY 2025-26?
answer_summary: No. The April 30, 2025 clarification states that the category of a regulated entity shall be decided at the beginning of the financial year based on the data of the previous financial year, and once decided, the RE shall remain in the same category throughout the financial year irrespective of changes in the parameters during that year. Because it was a Qualified RE at the start of the year based on the previous financial year’s data, it remains a Qualified RE for the entire FY 2025-26.
