review_notes: Both original and April 2025 clarification source the same category-lock rule. Clear deadline/lineage target distinct from earlier reclassification questions.

question: A Registrar to an Issue and Share Transfer Agent services 75,000 folios and has 50 clients. Its compliance officer argues that the RTA is completely outside the scope of CSCRF because it has fewer than 100 clients. Is the RTA outside the framework, and is it required to subscribe to SOC services or on-board to Market-SOC?
answer_summary: No on both counts. The original August 2024 CSCRF excludes only RTAs servicing fewer than 10,000 folios from submission of compliance; this RTA is a small-size RE because it services between 10,000 and 1 crore folios. The April 30, 2025 clarification gives a further, narrower exemption: RTAs with fewer than 100 clients need not employ SOC services or on-board to Market-SOC, but they remain subject to the rest of CSCRF.
review_notes: Original RTA folio threshold keeps the 75k-folio RTA inside the framework; April 2025 narrows the <100-client exemption to SOC/M-SOC only. Well-supported two-doc distinction.

question: A Merchant Banker that handles public issues has been re-categorised as a mid-size RE under the April 30, 2025 clarification. Its legal counsel contends that mid-size REs are not required to constitute an IT Committee under CSCRF. Is that correct?
answer_summary: No. The original August 2024 CSCRF requires Market Infrastructure Institutions, Qualified REs and mid-size REs to constitute an IT Committee that mandatorily includes at least one external independent expert on cybersecurity. Because MBs engaged in issue-management activities are now mid-size REs under the April 2025 clarification, they must form an IT Committee. MBs that are not engaged in issue management are small-size REs, for which an IT Committee is desirable but Board or MD review is permitted if absent.
review_notes: Original framework requires MIIs/Qualified/mid-size REs to constitute IT Committee; April 2025 places issue-management MBs in mid-size category. Consequence-derived target.

question: A Designated Depository Participant has a non-institutional Depository Participant arm that would be a mid-size RE and a Custodian arm with assets under custody above Rs 10 lakh crores that is a Qualified RE. After seeing that the March 28, 2025 extension excludes MIIs, KRAs and QRTAs, the DDP believes its compliance deadline remains April 1, 2025. Is it correct?
answer_summary: No. The original CSCRF says DDP classification for submission of compliance shall be the highest category among its DP and Custodian registrations, so the DDP is a Qualified RE. The March 28, 2025 extension applies to all REs except MIIs, KRAs and QRTAs; it does not exclude Qualified REs. Because DDPs are first-time CSCRF entities with an original April 1, 2025 compliance date, the extended deadline is June 30, 2025.
review_notes: Highest-category rule for DDPs is supported in the original framework, and the March extension preserves the June 30, 2025 deadline for non-excluded REs.

question: Following the April 30, 2025 clarification, a compliance officer concludes that the original CSCRF rules on cyber-audit and VAPT periodicity no longer apply from financial year 2025-26 because so many entity categories were revised. Is that conclusion correct?
answer_summary: No. Paragraph 10 of the April 30, 2025 clarification states that cyber audits conducted from FY 2025-26 shall be conducted as per the original August 20, 2024 circular read with the clarifications issued. The category changes do not override the audit, VAPT or reporting cycles set out in the original framework.
review_notes: April 2025 confirmation that cyber audits from FY 2025-26 follow the original framework, and the original periodicity table is cited. Directly supported.

question: A Qualified RE reads the April 30, 2025 clarification and assumes that because compliance timelines were extended and categories were reworked, the one-year deadline to obtain ISO 27001 certification under the original framework has also been suspended. Is that assumption correct?
answer_summary: No. The original framework requires MIIs and Qualified REs to obtain ISO 27001 certification within one year of issuance of the CSCRF. The April 30, 2025 clarification preserves the original framework for cyber audits from FY 2025-26 and does not suspend the ISO 27001 certification requirement.
review_notes: Original framework imposes one-year ISO 27001 certification on MIIs and Qualified REs; April 2025 preserves original requirements and does not suspend it.

question: A Merchant Banker that is part of a conglomerate group was a Qualified RE under the original August 2024 CSCRF and appointed a Chief Information Security Officer reporting directly to its Managing Director. After the April 30, 2025 clarification removes the conglomerate/SIFI route and re-classifies the firm as a small-size RE because it is not engaged in issue management, must it continue to maintain a CISO directly reporting to the MD?
answer_summary: No. Under the original CSCRF, the CISO direct-reporting requirement applies only to Market Infrastructure Institutions and Qualified REs; mid-size, small-size and self-certification REs must designate a senior official or management personnel for cybersecurity. The April 2025 clarification removes the conglomerate/SIFI criterion for MBs and places non-issue-management MBs in the small-size category. Because it is no longer a Qualified RE, the firm is no longer required to maintain a CISO reporting directly to the MD.
review_notes: Original CISO direct reporting applies only to MIIs/Qualified REs while small-size uses a designated officer; April 2025 removes conglomerate/SIFI route and places such MBs in small-size. Distinct consequence.

question: A compliance head interprets the April 30, 2025 clarification to mean that all REs now submit their CSCRF compliance reports to BSE Ltd. because BSE Ltd. was named as the reporting authority for Investment Advisers and Research Analysts. Does the April clarification change the general reporting authority for other REs such as stock brokers or Market Infrastructure Institutions?
answer_summary: No. The original framework requires REs to submit compliance to their respective existing authorities: for example, MIIs to SEBI, stock brokers to stock exchanges and depository participants to depositories. The April 2025 clarification changes the reporting authority only for IAs and RAs, moving it to BSE Ltd. for five years starting July 25, 2024. Other REs continue to report to their pre-existing authorities.
review_notes: Original framework routes reporting to existing authorities; April 2025 modifies authority only for IAs/RAs. Supported and distinct from the narrower IA/RA reporting question.

question: In its August 2024 consultation paper SEBI floated two possible ways of mandating Qualified Stock Brokers to offer a blocked-amount facility for secondary-market trading. What were the two options, and which one did SEBI finally adopt in the November 2024 circular?
answer_summary: The consultation paper asked whether QSBs should be mandated (a) to provide the UPI block mechanism in the cash segment for their individual and HUF clients, with an appropriate glide path, or (b) to provide either that UPI block cash-segment facility or a 3-in-1 trading account facility covering cash and derivatives (clf-a9h4xho5bp14r6ywvsdcavag#0, #15, #16). The November 2024 circular adopted the either/or approach: QSBs must provide either the UPI block mechanism in the secondary-market cash segment or a 3-in-1 trading account facility, while clients may also continue the existing fund-transfer mode (clf-utpo2qxkorew2qj542iyrv1d#4, #5).
review_notes: Supported by both cited docs; distinct policy-evolution target comparing consultation options to the adopted either/or mandate.

question: A QSB compliance head recalls that the blocked-amount/3-in-1 requirement was first announced with an effective date in a September 2024 board-meeting press release, but wants to confirm whether the November 2024 circular kept or changed that date. What was the originally announced date, and does the circular preserve it?
answer_summary: The SEBI Board meeting press release dated September 30, 2024 stated that the requirement would take effect from February 1, 2025 (clf-eooq99utwgg01n1qmksqkp16#7). The November 2024 circular preserves the same date, providing that its provisions will come into effect from February 1, 2025 (clf-utpo2qxkorew2qj542iyrv1d#5).
review_notes: Board press-release date and circular preservation both directly supported; good effective-date continuity memory target.

question: Under the November 2024 circular, may a client of a QSB refuse both the UPI block mechanism and the 3-in-1 trading account and continue trading by transferring funds to the broker? Which earlier document first proposed the same either/or menu of facilities?
answer_summary: Yes. The circular expressly gives QSB clients the option to continue with the existing facility of trading by transferring funds to the trading member, or to opt for either the UPI block mechanism or the 3-in-1 trading account facility as provided by the QSB (clf-utpo2qxkorew2qj542iyrv1d#5). The August 2024 consultation paper had already framed the same either/or mandatory menu, asking whether QSBs should be required to provide either the UPI block mechanism in the cash segment or a 3-in-1 trading account facility (clf-a9h4xho5bp14r6ywvsdcavag#15, #16).
review_notes: Client opt-out right in circular and earlier either/or framing in consultation paper are both directly supported; distinct from q01/q06.

question: A QSB intends to rely exclusively on a 3-in-1 trading account to satisfy the new mandate. What minimum features must that account have under the November 2024 circular, and what important operational difference between the 3-in-1 facility and the UPI block mechanism was already flagged in the consultation paper?
answer_summary: The circular requires a 3-in-1 trading account to integrate the trading, demat and bank accounts; block funds for buy orders (releasing them if unexecuted); block securities for sell orders (releasing them if unexecuted); transmit the blocked pay-in post-market hours upstream to the clearing corporation; and let the client earn interest until pay-in (clf-utpo2qxkorew2qj542iyrv1d#2, #3, #5). The consultation paper noted that while 3-in-1 accounts could cover cash and derivatives without amount restrictions, the UPI block mechanism was then limited to the cash segment and faced restrictions on the number of daily blocks; it also observed that 3-in-1 offers lower client protection because pay-in and pay-out are routed through the trading member (clf-a9h4xho5bp14r6ywvsdcavag#15, #16).
review_notes: Circular's minimum 3-in-1 features and consultation's operational-difference notes are both directly supported; useful compliance checklist target.

question: The November 2024 circular says the mandate is meant to protect investors from the default of trading or clearing members. In the August 2024 consultation paper, what specific problems in the existing cash-collateral chain did SEBI identify as being addressed if client funds stayed blocked in the investor's own bank account?
answer_summary: The consultation paper listed four risks mitigated by the UPI block mechanism: reliance on members' reporting of client-wise collateral allocations, with members potentially reporting wrong amounts; misuse of client cash collateral retained by members and not passed on to the clearing corporation; wrongful withdrawal by members of client cash collateral from the clearing corporation; and non-settlement of payout by the trading member to clients (clf-a9h4xho5bp14r6ywvsdcavag#4). The November 2024 circular refers to the same protective purpose but does not restate these operational risks (clf-utpo2qxkorew2qj542iyrv1d#0).
review_notes: Consultation paper lists the four mitigated risks; circular states the protective purpose. Distinct risk-rationale memory target.

question: The August 2024 consultation paper described a key scope difference between the UPI block mechanism and a 3-in-1 trading account. How did the November 2024 circular preserve that difference when drafting the either/or mandate for QSBs?
answer_summary: The consultation paper said the UPI block mechanism would be available only for the cash segment and with restrictions on the number of daily blocks, whereas a 3-in-1 trading account could cover cash as well as derivatives without amount restrictions (clf-a9h4xho5bp14r6ywvsdcavag#15, #16). The November 2024 circular preserved this scope split by expressly limiting the UPI block option to the secondary-market cash segment while offering the 3-in-1 account as the alternative facility without imposing the same cash-segment qualifier (clf-utpo2qxkorew2qj542iyrv1d#4, #5).
review_notes: Directly supported scope split: UPI block limited to cash segment, 3-in-1 not constrained. Distinct exclusion/delta target.

question: A market commentary cites SEBI figures showing that a full shift of individual and HUF cash-segment clients to the UPI block mechanism would add only 0.67% to daily UPI transactions but 15.61% during the 8:00 pm-8:30 pm window. In which document did SEBI publish this capacity analysis, and why does the November 2024 implementing circular not reproduce it?
answer_summary: The capacity analysis appears in Table 1 of the August 2024 consultation paper, based on July 2024 transaction data, and it supported the conclusion that existing UPI capacity could absorb the additional pay-in load (clf-a9h4xho5bp14r6ywvsdcavag#7, #8, #9). The November 2024 circular does not repeat the statistical estimate; it records only that public consultation and stakeholder deliberations informed the decision and then proceeds directly to the QSB mandate (clf-utpo2qxkorew2qj542iyrv1d#2, #3, #5).
review_notes: Capacity-analysis figures and their source in the consultation are directly supported; circular rationale for not reproducing is inferred but consistent with cited text.

question: The October 2025 consultation paper on comprehensively rewriting the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations treated Capital Protection Oriented Schemes, Real Estate Mutual Fund schemes and Infrastructure Debt Fund schemes differently. How did the April 2026 SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026 ultimately handle each of these three scheme types — which were deleted outright, which were grandfathered, and why?
answer_summary: All three were removed as launchable categories, but IDF schemes were protected while CPOS and REMF schemes were not. Capital Protection Oriented Schemes were deleted entirely in the 2026 Regulations because mutual funds are pass-through vehicles and AMCs cannot assure capital protection. Real Estate Mutual Fund schemes were also deleted because SEBI already has a separate REIT regime and no such MF scheme had been launched under the 1996 Regulations. Infrastructure Debt Fund schemes were treated differently: the consultation noted that only two IDF schemes were registered and one was winding up, and Regulation 85(2)(d) of the 2026 Regulations preserves any IDF scheme launched before the notification date by providing that it shall continue to be governed by the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996.
review_notes: Verified: consultation docs describe CPOS/REMF deletions and the proposed grandfathering/no-new-IDF stance; Regulation 85(2)(d) of the notified 2026 Regulations locks in the IDF carve-out. Two documents are materially needed. Distinct scheme-category lineage target.

question: The October 2025 consultation proposed moving all detailed valuation guidelines into a single table in the Master Circular for Mutual Funds and keeping only broad valuation principles in the Regulations. Where do the actual investment-valuation norms reside in the notified SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026?
answer_summary: The consultation’s proposal was not adopted in that form. In the 2026 Regulations, detailed investment valuation norms remain in the Seventh Schedule to the Regulations itself. The NAV-computation regulation and the related scheme-management provision require AMCs to compute valuation in accordance with the investment valuation norms specified in the Seventh Schedule. The Seventh Schedule spells out detailed fair-valuation principles, methodologies for each security type, procedures for exceptional events and other implementation requirements.
review_notes: Verified: consultation proposed moving detailed valuation norms to the Master Circular; the notified 2026 Regulations keep them in the Seventh Schedule (Regulation referencing valuation norms + Seventh Schedule fair-valuation principles). Good proposal-not-adopted / fake-negative target.

question: An AMC board is updating its change-in-control and scheme-attribute-change playbook after the 2026 rewrite. Under the old 1996 framework, these events required newspaper advertisements. What did the October 2025 consultation propose, and what do the 2026 Regulations now require instead?
answer_summary: The consultation proposed replacing the newspaper-advertisement requirement for a change in control of the AMC and changes to fundamental attributes of schemes with alternative digital disclosure, citing that the 1996 newspaper requirement had become outdated. The 2026 Regulations adopted this approach. For a change in control of the AMC, Regulation 17 requires prior trustee and SEBI approval, written communication to unitholders including digital modes such as email/SMS, and display of prescribed details on the AMC’s website. For changes to fundamental attributes of a scheme, Regulation 29(c) similarly requires written communication to each unitholder (including email/SMS), disclosure on the AMC’s website, and an exit option at prevailing NAV without exit load.
review_notes: Verified: consultation explicitly pairs the old newspaper-ad requirement with change-in-control and fundamental-attribute changes; the 2026 Regulations carry the digital/web replacement plus exit option. Clean operational-mechanics change across two docs.

question: The March 20, 2026 Master Circular for Mutual Funds rescinds earlier circulars in its Appendix. How many circulars did it newly rescind, what date range do they cover, and how does its savings clause align with the repeal-and-saving clause in the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026?
answer_summary: The March 2026 Master Circular newly rescinded the 34 circulars listed at Sr. Nos. 1 to 34 in its Appendix, spanning from April 30, 2024 through March 13, 2026. This is in addition to the circulars already rescinded by the June 27, 2024 Master Circular. Its savings clause aligns closely with Regulation 85 of the 2026 Regulations: prior registrations, approvals, fees collected, inspections, enquiries, show-cause notices, pending applications, rights, obligations, liabilities and penalties under the rescinded circulars remain unaffected and are deemed to have been done under the corresponding provisions of the new Master Circular.
review_notes: Verified: Master Circular opens by rescinding Sr. Nos. 1-34 (April 30, 2024 through March 13, 2026 per Appendix) and contains a savings clause mirroring Regulation 85 of the 2026 Regulations. Good count + coordination target.

question: The consultation paper is dated October 28, 2025, the 2026 Regulations were notified on January 14, 2026, and the Master Circular is dated March 20, 2026. When did the 1996 MF Regulations and the listed circulars effectively give way to the new regime, and do prior actions survive?
answer_summary: Both documents carry April 1, 2026 as the switch-over point: the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996 were repealed from the date the 2026 Regulations came into force (April 1, 2026), not from the notification date of January 14, 2026; and the March 20, 2026 Master Circular updated the consolidated circular framework to include circulars up to that date, rescinding those listed in its Appendix from its issuance. Prior actions survive under both savings clauses. Regulation 85 of the 2026 Regulations protects registrations, approvals, fees, schemes, adjudications, investigations, rights and liabilities under the 1996 Regulations. The Master Circular’s savings clause protects the same categories of actions taken under the rescinded circulars, deeming them done under corresponding provisions of the new Master Circular.
review_notes: Partly verified: the 2026 Regulations clearly come into force April 1, 2026 and repeal the 1996 Regulations from that date (not Jan 14 notification). The Master Circular also carries April 1 as its force date; its rescission is phrased as 'stand rescinded' with savings clause. Rescission-from-issuance wording is interpretive but the core effective-date coordination is sound.

question: The August 2024 consultation paper compared the commercial arrangement for the UPI block mechanism with the ASBA facility used in primary-market issues. Who did it identify as the beneficiaries in the secondary market, and does the November 2024 implementing circular prescribe any fee that banks may charge clients for using the facility?
answer_summary: In the consultation paper, NPCI and banks receive compensation from issuers during primary-market ASBA issues because issuers are the beneficiaries there. In the secondary market, the investors executing trades would be the beneficiaries of the UPI block mechanism (paras 3.5-3.7). The consultation also noted that banks were free to design a fee structure but, at present, banks do not charge clients for UPI transactions (paras 3.11-3.12). The November 2024 circular does not prescribe any bank fee or commercial arrangement for the UPI block facility; it only mandates QSBs to offer either the UPI block mechanism or a 3-in-1 trading account.
review_notes: Supported by consultation paras 3.5-3.12 (beneficiaries, fee freedom, no current charges) and circular (silent on bank fees).

question: The November 2024 circular notes that clients using the blocked amount facility earn interest on available funds until pay-in. What estimate did the August 2024 consultation give for the annual interest that cash-segment clients could accrue if their balances remained in their own bank accounts, and what corresponding income would trading members stand to lose?
answer_summary: The consultation estimated that individual and HUF clients held an average daily cash balance of roughly Rs. 65,276 crore in the cash segment with their trading members (based on July 23-29, 2024 data). Assuming an average interest rate of 4%, the total annual interest accrued would amount to roughly Rs. 2,611 crore. Concomitantly, trading members would lose float income from those balances and may have to adjust brokerage rates (paras 3.8-3.11). The circular does not repeat the Rs. 2,611 crore figure but contains the operational design that keeps funds in the client's bank account earning interest.
review_notes: Circular confirms interest till pay-in; consultation gives Rs. 65,276 crore balance, 4%, Rs. 2,611 crore estimate and TM float loss.

question: The November 2024 circular instructs stock exchanges and clearing corporations to amend their bye-laws, rules and regulations and to disseminate the mandate to market participants. Beyond stock exchanges and clearing corporations, which other institutions did the August 2024 consultation identify as needing to make systems or process changes before the blocked-amount facility could be widely adopted?
answer_summary: The consultation recorded that SEBI held meetings with clearing corporations, NPCI, trading members and banks to identify bottlenecks and necessary steps. Notable developments included an NPCI circular dated July 31, 2024 enabling the UPI mandate feature of single block and multiple debits, and clearing corporations developing file formats required by trading members for back-office reconciliation (paras 2.9-2.10). The November 2024 circular's para 7 places the formal amendment and dissemination obligations only on stock exchanges and clearing corporations, but its mandate itself depends on the wider ecosystem changes noted in the consultation.
review_notes: Circular para 7 names SEs/CCs; consultation para 2.10 identifies NPCI, banks and TMs plus CC reconciliation formats.

question: The consultation proposed mandating the blocked-amount facility only for Qualified Stock Brokers rather than all stock brokers. What share of individual and HUF clients and what share of cash-segment gross trade value did it attribute to QSBs, and what did the November 2024 circular require QSBs to offer?
answer_summary: As of July 31, 2024, QSBs accounted for about 83% of unique individual and HUF clients and about 68% of the gross trade value in the cash segment (Table 2). Because of this scale, the consultation argued that QSBs were well placed to lead technological adoption (paras 4.1-4.5). The November 2024 circular translated this rationale into a mandate: QSBs must provide either trading supported by blocked amount in the secondary market (cash segment) using the UPI block mechanism, or a 3-in-1 trading account facility, while clients retain the option to continue transferring funds to the trading member.
review_notes: Consultation Table 2 gives 83% clients / 68% trade value; circular imposes either/or QSB mandate.

question: The August 2024 consultation invited public comments on mandating blocked-amount facilities for QSBs. By what date were comments due, and on what date did SEBI announce the Board's approval of the either/or mandate?
answer_summary: Comments on the consultation paper were to be submitted latest by September 12, 2024 (para 5.1). SEBI announced the Board's approval of the mandate in a press release dated September 30, 2024, following its 207th Board meeting. The same proposal was later formalised in the November 11, 2024 circular with effect from February 1, 2025.
review_notes: Consultation para 5.1 sets September 12, 2024 comment deadline; Board press release dated September 30, 2024 approves the mandate.

question: The November 2024 circular traces the UPI block mechanism to a provision of the October 2023 Master Circular on Stock Exchanges and Clearing Corporations. What was the status of that facility under the Master Circular, and what new obligation did the August 2024 consultation propose for QSBs?
answer_summary: Para 25.4.1.2 of Chapter 1 of the October 16, 2023 Master Circular introduced the UPI block mechanism as a non-mandatory facility to be provided by stock brokers. The August 2024 consultation paper then asked whether Qualified Stock Brokers should be mandated to offer either the UPI block mechanism in the cash segment or a 3-in-1 trading account facility, with an appropriate glide path (paras 4.6-4.7). The November 2024 circular adopted that either/or mandate.
review_notes: Circular para 2 cites Master Circular para 25.4.1.2 as non-mandatory; consultation paras 4.6-4.7 proposed QSB mandate.

question: Besides keeping funds in the client's own bank account, what structural change did the August 2024 consultation expect the UPI block mechanism to bring to settlement visibility? Did the November 2024 circular extend the mandatory UPI block facility to the derivatives segment too?
answer_summary: The consultation stated that the UPI block mechanism would provide client-level settlement visibility (both pay-in and pay-out) to clearing corporations by enabling direct settlement of funds and securities between the client and the clearing corporation, instead of routing them through the trading member (para 2.4.2). The November 2024 circular did not extend the UPI block mandate to derivatives; the either/or QSB mandate was for the cash segment only, although the 3-in-1 trading account alternative could be offered for both cash and derivatives.
review_notes: Consultation para 2.4.2 gives client-level settlement visibility; circular limits mandate to cash segment, not derivatives.

question: Both mandate options floated in the August 2024 consultation included an 'appropriate glide path for implementation.' Did the final rule keep a glide path, or did it set a single effective date?
answer_summary: Options 4.7.1(a) and 4.7.1(b) in the consultation paper proposed that QSBs be mandated either to offer the UPI block mechanism or to offer either facility, in both cases 'with an appropriate glide path for implementation.' The SEBI Board decision dated September 30, 2024 and the November 11, 2024 circular replaced that glide-path language with a fixed effective date of February 1, 2025.
review_notes: Consultation options 4.7.1(a)/(b) included glide-path language; Board and circular replaced it with a fixed February 1, 2025 effective date.

question: An existing Angel Fund has not yet disclosed an allocation methodology in its PPM. If it enters into an investment in January 2026, must the allocation follow a disclosed methodology, or did SEBI relax that requirement?
answer_summary: Yes, the allocation must follow a disclosed methodology. The September 10, 2025 circular originally required existing Angel Funds to disclose the methodology and made allocations from October 15, 2025 onward subject to it. SEBI relaxed only the timeline: by the October 15, 2025 circular, the deadline was extended to January 31, 2026. Allocations made after January 31, 2026 must be in accordance with the defined allocation methodology disclosed in the PPM.
review_notes: Both circulars are materially needed: the September 10 circular sets the original October 15, 2025 methodology deadline, and the October 15 circular extends it to January 31, 2026; clean deadline-relief question.

question: An Angel Fund proposes to invest INR 5 lakh in a startup after the AIF Regulations were amended on September 9, 2025. A colleague argues that the September 10, 2025 circular does not expressly lower the minimum investment, so the INR 25 lakh floor still applies. Is the colleague correct, and what is the actual permissible investment band?
answer_summary: The colleague is not correct. The November 2024 consultation paper proposed reducing the minimum investment to INR 10 lakh and raising the maximum to INR 25 crore. This change was carried into the AIF Regulations as amended on September 9, 2025, which now states that an Angel Fund's investment in any investee company must be not less than INR 10 lakh and not more than INR 25 crore. The September 10, 2025 circular implements the amended framework and therefore the lower INR 25 lakh floor no longer applies.
review_notes: Requires both the consultation paper (proposed INR 10 lakh-25 crore band) and the amended AIF Regulations (final 19F(2) rule) to defeat the INR 25 lakh floor argument; well-supported proposal-vs-final rule.

question: The November 2024 consultation paper proposed that every Angel Fund investment include contribution from at least three Accredited Investors, excluding the manager or sponsor. What is the post-September 9, 2025 rule, and where is it set out?
answer_summary: The post-September 9, 2025 rule is that each investment of an Angel Fund in an investee company must have contribution from at least two accredited investors (not three). This is set out in Regulation 19F(5) of the SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012 as substituted by the September 9, 2025 amendment. The proposal to require three investors did not make it into the final regulation.
review_notes: Clear proposal-vs-final contrast: consultation paper proposed three Accredited Investors per investment, while Regulation 19F(5) as substituted on September 9, 2025 requires at least two.

question: The November 2024 consultation proposed that an Angel Fund manager or sponsor keep a continuing interest of at least 0.5% of the investment amount or INR 1 lakh, whichever is higher, in each investment. What continuing-interest requirement applies after September 9, 2025?
answer_summary: After the September 9, 2025 amendment, the manager or sponsor must have a continuing interest in each investment of the Angel Fund of at least 0.5% of the amount invested or INR 50,000, whichever is higher. The final threshold is lower than the INR 1 lakh proposed in the consultation paper. The requirement is in Regulation 19G of the AIF Regulations as amended.
review_notes: Clear proposal-vs-final contrast: consultation proposed 0.5% or INR 1 lakh continuing interest, while Regulation 19G as amended requires 0.5% or INR 50,000 per investment.

question: A KYC Registration Agency (KRA) has been undergoing third-party Cyber Capability Index (CCI) assessments twice a year because it was treated as a Market Infrastructure Institution under the original August 2024 CSCRF. After the April 30, 2025 clarification, how often must it carry out a CCI assessment and who conducts it?
answer_summary: It must continue carrying out a Cyber Capability Index (CCI) assessment, but now on an annual basis and through self-assessment rather than third-party assessment. The original August 2024 CSCRF applies CCI only to Market Infrastructure Institutions (MIIs) and Qualified REs: MIIs must obtain third-party half-yearly assessments, while Qualified REs must conduct annual self-assessments. The April 30, 2025 clarification re-categorises KYC Registration Agencies (KRAs) from MIIs to Qualified REs, so the KRA moves from the half-yearly third-party regime to the annual self-assessment regime.
review_notes: Supported by baseline CCI rules (#16, #413) and April re-categorisation of KRAs (#7); traces a practical post-re-classification obligation.

question: A Merchant Banker that is not engaged in issue-management activity was a Qualified RE under the original August 2024 CSCRF because it was part of a conglomerate/SIFI group, and it has been running half-yearly red-team exercises. After the April 30, 2025 clarification, must it continue those exercises?
answer_summary: No, it may stop. The original August 2024 CSCRF makes red teaming mandatory only for Market Infrastructure Institutions and Qualified REs; it is not imposed on mid-size, small-size or self-certification REs. The April 30, 2025 clarification removes the conglomerate/SIFI route to Qualified RE status and places Merchant Bankers that are not engaged in issue management in the small-size RE category. Once this MB is small-size, the red-teaming obligation no longer applies.
review_notes: Red-teaming applies only to MIIs/Qualified REs (#319); April clarification places non-issue MBs in small-size (#10, #12), so obligation drops. Distinct memory target.

question: After the April 30, 2025 clarification reclassified its non-issue-management Merchant Banker as a small-size RE, the CFO proposes to appoint a cyber auditor who is not empanelled by CERT-In to reduce costs. Is this permissible?
answer_summary: No. The original August 2024 CSCRF states that only CERT-In empanelled IS auditing organisations shall be onboarded for external audit, including cyber audit, of regulated entities. The April 30, 2025 clarification revises entity categories but does not relax this auditor-em-panelment requirement; paragraph 10 expressly provides that cyber audits from financial year 2025-26 shall be conducted as per the original framework read with the clarifications issued. A small-size Merchant Banker must still use a CERT-In empanelled auditor for its external cyber audit.
review_notes: Baseline mandates CERT-In empanelled auditors for all RE external cyber audits (#174) and April clarification confirms original-framework read with clarifications still governs (#14).

question: A Merchant Banker that now falls in the "all other MBs" bucket under the April 30, 2025 clarification believes that, as a small-size RE, it can stop periodic employee phishing-awareness assessments. Was this assessment previously required, and does the April clarification remove that obligation?
answer_summary: No. The original August 2024 CSCRF requires all REs except small-size and self-certification REs to periodically assess employee cybersecurity awareness, for example through phishing-test success rates. Before the April 30, 2025 clarification, a Merchant Banker that was not engaged in issue management could still be a Qualified RE if it was part of a conglomerate/SIFI group, and so fell within this mandatory scope. The April clarification removes the conglomerate/SIFI route and reclassifies all non-issue-management MBs as small-size REs, so the awareness-testing requirement no longer applies to them.
review_notes: Baseline requires phishing/awareness testing for all REs except small-size/self-certification (#225-226); April clarification moves non-issue MBs to small-size (#10, #12).

question: A Merchant Banker maintained offsite 'golden images' of critical systems when it was a Qualified RE under the original August 2024 CSCRF. After the April 30, 2025 clarification reclassified it as a small-size RE, can it stop maintaining those golden images?
answer_summary: Yes. The original August 2024 CSCRF requires REs to maintain regularly updated offsite 'golden images' of critical systems only when they are Market Infrastructure Institutions or Qualified REs. The April 30, 2025 clarification removes the conglomerate/SIFI route to Qualified RE status and reclassifies a non-issue-management Merchant Banker as a small-size RE. Because it is no longer a Qualified RE, the specific golden-images obligation does not apply, although all REs remain subject to the general backup and recovery plan requirement.
review_notes: Golden-image backups are mandatory only for MIIs and Qualified REs (#337); April clarification removes the non-issue MB from Qualified status (#10, #12).

question: Our group runs both an investment adviser and a research analyst arm. Following SEBI's June 2025 investor charter updates, the compliance head wants one implementation note for obligations that apply identically to both arms. What must both charters now include on client communication, monthly complaint-data disclosure, grievance-resolution platforms, and the predecessor documents that are rescinded or amended?
answer_summary: Both arms must: (i) bring the updated Investor Charter to clients' notice by publishing it on their websites/mobile apps (if any), displaying it prominently in the office, and providing a copy as part of the onboarding kit / emails / letters; (ii) disclose monthly complaint data on their websites/apps by the 7th of the succeeding month in the Annexure B format; (iii) resolve investor complaints internally within 21 days and, if the investor is still dissatisfied, offer escalation through SCORES 2.0 (two-level review: IAASB for advisers / RAASB for analysts, then SEBI) and the SMARTODR platform for online conciliation/arbitration; physical complaints may be sent to SEBI's Office of Investor Assistance and Education. With the new circulars, the December 13, 2021 circulars (SEBI/HO/IMD/IMD-II CIS/P/CIR/2021/0686 for advisers and 2021/0685 for analysts) are rescinded, and Clause 8 of the May 21, 2024 Master Circular for Investment Advisers and Clause 5 of the May 21, 2024 Master Circular for Research Analysts stand amended accordingly. Both circulars took effect immediately on June 2, 2025.
review_notes: Cited chunks support the common communication/disclosure obligations, the 21-day/SCORES/SMARTODR escalation paths, and the rescission of the Dec 2021 circulars plus amendment of the May 2024 Master Circular clauses for both intermediaries. Broad checklist shape bundles several targets but is still a useful cross-arm implementation summary.

question: While reconciling the April 2025 draft with the June 2025 final version of the Investor Charter for Investment Advisers, the legal team spots two changes in the investors' rights section. What happened to the 'Right to Exit' and what 'Right to enforceability' wording present in the draft was left out of the final?
answer_summary: The Right to Exit was narrowed: the April 2025 draft stated simply 'Right to Exit from Financial product or service', while the June 2025 final added the qualifier 'in accordance with the terms of agreement with the investment adviser'. In addition, the April 2025 draft had an extra right — 'Right to enforceability and holding the Investment Adviser responsible for monitoring, enforcing investor rights' — that does not appear in the June 2025 final charter.
review_notes: Draft chunk #11 shows 'Right to Exit' without qualifier and the 'Right to enforceability' wording; final chunks #9/#10 show the added qualifier and the absence of the enforceability right. Clean draft-to-final diff.

question: An investor holds both an advisory account and a research subscription. Under the June 2025 charter updates, she is unhappy with how each intermediary first handled her complaints. What common next steps are available to her under both charters, and at which point does the SEBI-level escalation path first diverge?
answer_summary: Under both the Investment Adviser and Research Analyst charters, the intermediary must try to resolve the complaint immediately and in any case not later than 21 days from receipt. If she remains dissatisfied with the market participant's resolution, she may: (a) lodge the complaint on SCORES 2.0 with a two-level review (designated body, then SEBI) and/or email the designated body; (b) approach the SMARTODR platform for online conciliation or arbitration; and (c) send a physical complaint to SEBI's Office of Investor Assistance and Education in Mumbai. The first divergence is the designated body that conducts the first-level SCORES 2.0 review: the Investment Adviser Administration and Supervisory Body (IAASB) for investment advisers, and the Research Analyst Administration and Supervisory Body (RAASB) for research analysts.
review_notes: Both charters require redress within 21 days and offer SCORES 2.0, SMARTODR, email and physical escalation; the cited text clearly distinguishes IAASB from RAASB as the first divergence point.

question: Both the June 2025 Investment Adviser and Research Analyst charters contain an Annexure B note about impersonation-related complaints. What specific exception does the note create when the intermediary prepares its monthly complaint data, and by when must the disclosed data be published?
answer_summary: In both charters, Annexure B states that if an investment adviser or research analyst receives complaints due to impersonation by some other entity, it may adjust the number of such complaints from the total number of received/resolved complaints while preparing the table. The intermediary must close those impersonation-related complaints after following the due process specified by SEBI/IAASB (for advisers) or SEBI/RAASB (for analysts). Separately, the complaint data must be disclosed on the intermediary's website and mobile application, if any, by the 7th day of the succeeding month.
review_notes: Annexure B notes in IA chunks #14/#15 and RA chunks #13/#14 support the impersonation adjustment exception and SEBI/IAASB or SEBI/RAASB closure process; the 7th-of-succeeding-month deadline is supported by both circular bodies.

question: The head of compliance claims the June 2025 investor charters for investment advisers and research analysts are identical except for swapping IAASB/RAASB labels. Give two obligation or duty examples in each charter that have no true counterpart in the other, showing the charter is tailored to the regulated activity and not just the supervisory body.
answer_summary: Investment-adviser-specific items include: (i) the duty 'to do a proper and unbiased risk–profiling and suitability assessment of the client' and to provide advice on that basis; and (ii) the service-specific obligation 'not to access client's accounts or holdings for offering advice'. Research-analyst-specific items include: (i) the duty to 'publish research report based on the research activities of the RA' and to maintain confidentiality with respect to publication of the research report until it is made available in the public domain; and (ii) when distributing a third-party research report, the duty to disclose any material conflict of interest of that third-party provider or give a web address linking to the relevant disclosures. Investor-side differences also appear: for example, the research-analyst Do's tell investors to check research recommendations before investing, while the adviser Do's stress risk profiling and written terms-and-conditions. These divergences go beyond the name of the supervisory body.
review_notes: IA chunks #5/#6/#7 and RA chunks #5/#6 contain activity-specific duties (risk profiling/access limits vs. research-report publication/confidentiality/third-party COI) and the investor Do's differ along the same lines. The claim of template-swap is cleanly refuted.

question: A compliance officer at a domestic stock broker is reviewing the March 21, 2025 draft circular and the May 2, 2025 final circular on facilitating GIFT-IFSC operations. What was the last date for submitting public comments on the draft, and does the final circular's body explicitly acknowledge or cite that consultation exercise?
answer_summary: Public comments on the draft circular were due by April 11, 2025. The May 2, 2025 final circular (SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD-PoD/P/CIR/2025/61) does not explicitly acknowledge the consultation paper or mention the public-comment process anywhere in its body; the connection rests on identical subject matter, the matching SBU proposal, and the timing after the comment deadline.
review_notes: Verified: draft chunk 2 gives the April 11, 2025 public-comment deadline; final circular chunks 0-5 do not cite the consultation or public-comment process anywhere. Two distinct memory targets (deadline + absence of citation) in a clean lineage check.

question: Our firm already runs a GIFT-IFSC securities business through a separately incorporated subsidiary that was set up after getting SEBI's prior NOC. Reading the March 2025 draft circular and the May 2025 final circular together, what organisational forms are now permissible for GIFT-IFSC activities, and is the firm forced to dismantle its existing subsidiary?
answer_summary: The May 2, 2025 final circular permits a SEBI-registered stock broker to carry on GIFT-IFSC securities market activities through (i) a Separate Business Unit (SBU) of the stock broking entity itself, (ii) a branch that qualifies as an SBU, or (iii) the existing practice of a subsidiary or joint venture. The firm is not forced to dismantle its subsidiary; it only has an option to dismantle it at its discretion and move the business under an SBU. By contrast, the March 2025 draft had proposed the SBU route as the main alternative and provided for dismantling existing subsidiaries/JVs without expressly preserving the subsidiary option.
review_notes: Verified: final chunks 1 and 4 list SBU, branch-as-SBU and existing subsidiary/JV as allowable forms and state that existing subsidiaries/JVs may be dismantled only at the entity's discretion. The draft chunks 4/6 frame SBU as the main alternative without expressly preserving the subsidiary option, making the version delta real and materially requiring both docs.

question: An investor who dealt only with a stock broker's GIFT-IFSC SBU wants to lodge a complaint on SCORES and claim compensation from the stock exchange Investor Protection Fund. According to the March 2025 consultation-to-final circular lineage, what redress mechanisms are available to this investor and why?
answer_summary: Neither SCORES nor the stock exchange Grievance Redressal Mechanism or Investor Protection Fund (IPF) is available to investors who availed services of the GIFT-IFSC SBU. Both the draft and final circulars state that because the SBU's activities fall under the jurisdiction of the concerned regulatory authority (IFSCA) rather than SEBI / the domestic stock exchanges, the domestic exchange grievance and IPF framework does not apply.
review_notes: Verified: both draft chunk 6 and final chunk 4 state that SCORES, exchange grievance redressal and the Investor Protection Fund are unavailable to investors of the GIFT-IFSC SBU because those activities fall under another regulator's jurisdiction. Multi-doc necessity is weaker because both docs repeat the same clause, but the lineage framing preserves a distinct redress/investor-protection memory target.

question: The March 2025 draft requires the SBU's net worth to be segregated from the stock broker's Indian-market net worth and the broker's own net-worth criteria to be satisfied after excluding the SBU account. What additional net-worth condition did the May 2025 final circular introduce for the SBU itself?
answer_summary: The final circular added that the net worth for the purpose of the SBU shall be as per the regulatory framework issued by the concerned regulatory authority (IFSCA). The draft had only required segregation and exclusion from the domestic broker's net-worth calculation.
review_notes: Verified: draft chunk 6 only requires net-worth segregation and exclusion from the domestic broker's net-worth calculation; final chunk 4 adds that net worth for the SBU must be as per the regulatory framework issued by the concerned regulatory authority (IFSCA). The answer is supported by the contextual IFSCA references in the final circular.

question: The March 2025 draft proposed that the SBU be 'exclusively engaged in providing securities market related activities in GIFT-IFSC only'. How did the May 2025 final circular change the way it describes the permissible scope of SBU activities, and which regulator's permission does the final wording tie the activities to?
answer_summary: The final circular replaced the GIFT-IFSC-only geographic restriction with two references to IFSCA permission: the SBU must be exclusively engaged in securities market related activities as permitted by the IFSCA, and the activities carried out by the SBU shall be as permitted by the IFSCA. This shifts the decisive constraint from the location 'GIFT-IFSC only' to the regulatory framework of the International Financial Services Centres Authority.
review_notes: Verified: draft chunk 5 restricts the SBU to 'exclusively engaged in providing securities market related activities in GIFT-IFSC only'; final chunk 3 replaces the geographic restriction with 'as permitted by the IFSCA' in two places. The shift from location-based to regulator-permission scope is clearly supported.

question: An Angel Fund holds shares in a portfolio company that has ceased to qualify as a 'startup.' The fund wishes to exercise a pre-emptive right and make an additional investment in that company. A partner argues this is flatly prohibited because Angel Funds must invest only in startups. Is the partner right, and if not, what conditions govern such a follow-on investment?
answer_summary: No, the partner is not right. Regulation 19F(1) of the AIF Regulations, as amended on September 9, 2025, provides that Angel Funds shall invest only in startups, but it contains a proviso permitting 'additional investments' in existing investee companies that are no longer startups, subject to Board-specified conditions. The September 10, 2025 circular specifies those conditions: (i) the post-issue shareholding percentage of the Angel Fund in the investee company must not exceed the pre-issue shareholding percentage; (ii) the total investment in that company, including the follow-on, must not exceed INR 25 crore; and (iii) contribution must be accepted only from investors who had contributed to the existing investment, pro-rata to their contribution, with any renounced portion offered to the remaining such investors.
review_notes: Proviso in AIF Regulations and the Sep 10, 2025 circular's three follow-on conditions (shareholding cap, INR 25 crore ceiling, pro-rata contribution source) are directly supported by the cited chunks.

question: An Angel Fund's contribution agreements allow certain investors to share profits with the manager as 'carried interest.' Under the revised framework, does the requirement that investors' rights in distributions be pro-rata to their contribution still apply to the carried-interest portion?
answer_summary: No. Regulation 19G(6) preserves pro-rata rights for investors in distributions of proceeds, pro-rata to their contribution. However, the September 10, 2025 circular carves out an exception: the pro-rata requirement does not apply to the extent returns or profit on the investments are shared by an investor with the manager, sponsor, or employees/directors/partners of the manager as carried interest or additional return under a contribution agreement. Thus, the carried-interest slice is governed by the contribution agreement rather than by the pro-rata rule the consultation paper had framed.
review_notes: Sep 10, 2025 circular carves out a carried-interest exception to pro-rata distribution rights; consultation paper provides the version-delta context.

question: An Angel Fund intends to disclose in its PPM that the manager retains discretion to allocate each investment opportunity among consenting investors on a case-by-case basis. Does the revised Angel Fund framework permit this?
answer_summary: No. The September 10, 2025 circular requires the manager of an Angel Fund to strictly adhere to the allocation methodology disclosed in the PPM, and the methodology 'shall not provide any discretion to manager for allocation of investment on a case-to-case basis.' The consultation paper had stressed that allowing manager discretion could lead to unequal and preferential treatment among investors; the final framework therefore removes case-by-case discretion and requires a pre-defined, mechanical methodology.
review_notes: Circular explicitly bars case-by-case allocation discretion; consultation paper records the AIPAC/WG rationale for that prohibition.

question: A newly registered Angel Fund assumes that its 12-month first-close clock starts on the date it files its PPM with SEBI. Is this assumption consistent with the final September 2025 framework, and what happens if the first close is not declared within the applicable timeline?
answer_summary: No. The November 2024 consultation paper proposed that the first close occur within 12 months of the PPM being filed with SEBI. The September 10, 2025 circular ties the 12-month period instead to 'the date of SEBI communication for taking the PPM of the Angel Fund on record.' If the first close is not declared within that timeline, the Angel Fund must refile the PPM with SEBI as per applicable AIF Regulations and pay the requisite fee. The circular also requires onboarding at least five Accredited Investors before declaring first close.
review_notes: Clear delta between the consultation proposal (12 months from PPM filing) and the final framework (12 months from SEBI communication; refile + fee if missed).

question: The November 2024 consultation paper proposed that Angel Funds with total investments over INR 100 crore undergo a PPM audit. For an Angel Fund crossing that threshold in financial year 2025-26, what two ongoing compliance obligations does the final September 2025 framework impose beyond the consultation proposal?
answer_summary: The September 10, 2025 circular retains the PPM audit for Angel Funds whose total investments (at cost) exceed INR 100 crore, in line with the consultation proposal. In addition, from FY 2025-26 onwards, such Angel Funds must report necessary information, including investment-wise valuation and cash-flow data, to benchmarking agencies for performance benchmarking as per Chapter 16 of the AIF Master Circular, and must disclose the performance-versus-benchmark report whenever past performance is mentioned in the PPM or any marketing or promotional material.
review_notes: Final framework retains the >INR 100 crore PPM audit and adds benchmarking reporting plus past-performance-versus-benchmark disclosure from FY 2025-26.

question: The November 2024 consultation paper recorded that the Working Group recommended dispensing with the requirement for explicit investor approval before each Angel Fund investment, because requiring repeated approvals was repetitive and could delay decisions. Did SEBI adopt that recommendation in the final revised framework?
answer_summary: No. SEBI did not adopt the Working Group's recommendation. The consultation paper states that per-investment investor consent is an integral and distinguishing feature of the Angel Fund structure and must be retained, and investors who do not wish to make individual investment decisions can choose other AIF categories. The September 10, 2025 circular reflects this retained requirement in its allocation methodology provisions, which refer to allocating investments among angel investors 'who provide approval for such investment.'
review_notes: Consultation paper records the WG recommendation and SEBI's decision to retain per-investment consent; circular operationalizes it in allocation provisions.

question: A compliance officer is reconciling the June 2025 investor charter updates for the firm's investment adviser and research analyst subsidiaries. She expects the two circulars to have identical legal-effect paragraphs. Comparing the circulars, which predecessor circular number and date is rescinded in each case, which Master Circular clause is amended in each case, and which statutory regulation citation differs between the two despite both invoking Section 11(1) of the SEBI Act, 1992?
answer_summary: The Investment Adviser charter circular SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD-PoD/P/CIR/2025/80 rescinds SEBI Circular No. SEBI/HO/IMD/IMD-II CIS/P/CIR/2021/0686 dated December 13, 2021 and amends Clause 8 of the Master Circular for Investment Advisers dated May 21, 2024. It is issued under Section 11(1) of the SEBI Act, 1992 read with Regulation 15(15) of the SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, 2013. The Research Analyst charter circular SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD-PoD/P/CIR/2025/81 rescinds SEBI Circular No. SEBI/HO/IMD/IMD-II CIS/P/CIR/2021/0685 dated December 13, 2021 and amends Clause 5 of the Master Circular for Research Analysts dated May 21, 2024. It is issued under Section 11(1) of the SEBI Act, 1992 read with Regulation 24(9) of the SEBI (Research Analysts) Regulations, 2014. The differing citation is the subordinate regulation: Investment Advisers Regulations for IAs and Research Analysts Regulations for RAs.
review_notes: Cited chunks from both final circulars directly support the rescinded predecessor circular numbers, the amended Master Circular clauses, and the differing subordinate regulation citations (IA: 15(15); RA: 24(9)). Requires both documents to derive the distinguishing citation.

question: The research analyst compliance team is comparing the April 2025 draft of the Investor Charter for Research Analysts with the June 2025 final version. In the 'Rights of investors' section, what happened to the 'Right to enforceability and holding the Research Analyst responsible' language that appeared in the draft, and how was the wording of the 'Right to Exit' narrowed in the final?
answer_summary: In the April 2025 draft RA charter, the rights list included a separate 'Right to enforceability and holding the Research Analyst responsible for monitoring, enforcing investor rights'. The June 2025 final charter drops this enforceability right entirely. The draft also stated an unqualified 'Right to Exit from Financial product or service'; the final narrows this to 'Right to Exit from Financial product or service in accordance with the terms and conditions agreed with the research analyst'.
review_notes: Draft RA chunk #11 shows the unqualified Right to Exit and the separate enforceability wording; final RA chunks #9/#10 show the narrowed Right to Exit and the removed enforceability right. Same comparison shape as the prior IA draft-vs-final question, but on a different document, so it teaches a new memory target.

question: Both the June 2025 investor charters for investment advisers and research analysts introduce a duty to disclose the use of Artificial Intelligence. Within the 'Details of services provided to investors' section, how does the precise wording of the AI disclosure duty differ between the two intermediaries, and what does the difference reveal about the activity being regulated?
answer_summary: Both charters place the duty under 'C. Details of services provided to investors' / 'Disclosure to Clients'. The Investment Adviser charter requires disclosure of 'the extent of use of Artificial Intelligence tools in providing investment advisory services', while the Research Analyst charter requires disclosure of 'the extent of use of Artificial Intelligence tools in providing research services'. The wording is identical except for the activity description, reflecting that the IA duty is tied to investment advice and the RA duty is tied to research output.
review_notes: Both cited docs are needed to confirm the AI-disclosure phrase differs only by activity ('investment advisory services' versus 'research services'). The question captures a small but activity-calibrated compliance duty; difficulty is modest.

question: A financial educator wants a single investor-responsibilities slide for clients who receive both investment advice and research recommendations. Looking at the June 2025 charters, name at least one investor 'Do' that appears only under the Investment Adviser charter and at least one that appears only under the Research Analyst charter, and explain why each is specific to that service.
answer_summary: Investment-Adviser-specific Dos include: asking for risk profiling before accepting advice and insisting advice is based on that risk profiling; assessing the risk-return, liquidity and safety aspects before investing; and insisting on written terms and conditions regarding advisory fees and plans. These reflect the personalised suitability and agreement nature of advisory services. Research-Analyst-specific Dos include: paying attention to disclosures in research reports before investing; checking the research analyst's recommendation before buying/selling securities or applying in a public offer; and seeking clarifications on research recommendations, especially for complex/high-risk products. These reflect the report-driven, non-personalised nature of research services.
review_notes: IA chunks #11/#12 and RA chunks #10/#11 contain investor Do items that are activity-specific. The answer picks genuinely distinct responsibilities for advisers versus research analysts; not a template-swap question.

question: A listed entity earns most of its income from rental property, although it also makes long-term equity investments. Under the April 2024 consultation paper, can such an entity be treated as a listed Investment Company for the special call auction framework? And under the June 2024 circular, what should it look at to decide whether the framework applies to it?
answer_summary: The April 2024 consultation paper specifically excludes rental income from the Investment Company definition: an IC earns major revenue from interest or capital appreciation on investments, and rental income is classified under 'Diversified Commercial Services'. Therefore, an entity that mainly earns rental income does not fall within that definition. The June 2024 circular does not repeat the definition; it simply says ICs or IHCs shall be identified based on the uniform industry classifications provided by stock exchanges. So the entity must look at the exchange's uniform industry classification, but the consultation paper explains the underlying definitional boundary.
review_notes: Supported by both cited docs. Consultation footnote excludes rental income from IC definition; final circular delegates identification to exchange uniform industry classifications. Distinct scope-exclusion target.

question: Which book-value benchmark did SEBI ultimately pick to test whether an IC or IHC is trading at a deep-enough discount to qualify for the special call auction, and why is this narrower than one of the alternatives discussed in the April 2024 consultation?
answer_summary: The June 2024 circular requires the 6-month VWAP to be less than 50% of the book value per share based on the present value of the company's investments in shares of other listed companies. The April 2024 consultation, however, collected data and explicitly invited comments on two possible book-value bases: overall standalone book value (including all investments, including unlisted and non-investment assets) and book value calculated on a pro-rata basis using only investments in shares of other listed companies. By choosing the present value of listed-equity investments, the final rule disregards unlisted or non-investment assets that would otherwise inflate the benchmark and make the discount look larger.
review_notes: Supported. Consultation tested overall book value and pro-rata listed-investment book value; circular chose the narrower present-value-of-listed-investments benchmark. Strong proposal-vs-final lineage target.

question: A listed IHC is fully compliant with the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations and has submitted its audited financial results, but its scrip is currently suspended for trading. Would it qualify for the special call auction under the framework finally adopted in June 2024? Point to the specific change from the April 2024 proposal.
answer_summary: No. The April 2024 consultation said the scrip should have been listed and available for trading for at least one year and the company should have been compliant with all LODR Regulations, including submission of audited financial results. The June 2024 circular dropped the explicit LODR-compliance condition and instead added that the scrip must not be suspended for trading. Because this scrip is suspended, it is ineligible despite its LODR compliance.
review_notes: Supported. Consultation required full LODR compliance; final rule replaced that with a trading-suspension bar. Clear version-delta consequence.

question: A stock exchange intends to conduct a special call auction for an eligible IC and publishes the notice only seven days before the session, relying on the April 2024 consultation paper. Is this advance notice compliant? And by when was the first such special call auction required to be conducted?
answer_summary: Seven days' notice is not compliant. The April 2024 consultation had proposed a 7-day prior notice, but the June 2024 circular increased the advance notice to 14 days. The same circular directed that the first such special call auction be conducted in October 2024 by stock exchanges, based on the latest available audited financial statements of eligible companies.
review_notes: Supported. Consultation proposed 7-day notice; circular requires 14 days and fixes first auction in October 2024. Deadline/effective-date trap.

question: A company is listed on both NSE and BSE. It meets all eligibility criteria on NSE, but on BSE its 6-month VWAP is not low enough to satisfy the discount test. It argues that NSE should still run the auction and the discovered price should govern trading on BSE. What does the June 2024 circular say?
answer_summary: The June 2024 circular bars the scrip from the special call auction on any exchange if any eligibility criterion is not fulfilled at one exchange. So the company cannot hold the auction on NSE while falling short on BSE. At the same time, if the company were eligible and the auction succeeded on one exchange, the price discovered on that exchange would form the base for trading on the other exchanges.
review_notes: Supported. Circular bars auction if any criterion fails at one exchange and makes cross-exchange price common. Both docs needed to show coordination requirement and final rule.

question: On day one of a special call auction for an IHC, four unique PAN-based buyers and six unique PAN-based sellers participate, and no equilibrium price is discovered. The exchange declares the auction closed and refuses to reconvene. Is the exchange correct?
answer_summary: No. The auction is treated as successful only if price discovery is based on orders from at least five PAN-based unique buyers and at least five PAN-based unique sellers. With only four unique buyers, day one is not a success. However, if the auction is not successful on day one, it must continue on the next day and until a price is discovered. The exchange must reconvene; refusing is wrong.
review_notes: Supported. Circular formalises 5 PAN-based unique buyers/sellers and continuation until success; consultation stated the same threshold informally. Operational threshold target.

question: While explaining the basis for the special call auction framework, the June 2024 circular refers to 'public comments'. Does this mean the circular explicitly names the April 19, 2024 consultation paper by its title or date?
answer_summary: No. The June 2024 circular says the framework was decided after deliberations with stock exchanges, public comments, and the Secondary Market Advisory Committee, but it does not cite the April 19, 2024 consultation paper by title or date. The lineage has to be inferred from the matching subject and the two-month time gap between the documents.
review_notes: Supported. Circular mentions 'public comments' generically but does not cite the April 19 consultation by title or date; absence verified by direct read. Both docs needed.

question: SEBI introduced the special call auction with no price bands after some market participants complained that circuit filters were distorting price discovery for ICs and IHCs. Besides those representations, which groups or inputs did the June 2024 circular say SEBI relied on when finalising the framework?
answer_summary: The June 2024 circular states that the framework was decided after deliberations with stock exchanges, public comments, and recommendations of the Secondary Market Advisory Committee of SEBI. The April 2024 consultation paper also notes that SEBI held deliberations with stock exchanges and certain ICs or IHCs, and that it received representations from a market participant proposing free price discovery.
review_notes: Supported. Circular lists stock exchanges, public comments and Secondary Market Advisory Committee; consultation adds market-participant representations and IC/IHC deliberations. Actor-scope target.

question: The April 2024 consultation invited comments on the percentage threshold of assets invested in other listed companies, the percentage discount of 6-month VWAP to book value, and the lookback period for computing VWAP. What options were presented, and which combination did the June 2024 circular finally adopt?
answer_summary: The consultation paper offered four asset-threshold options (25%, 50%, 70% or 90%), three discount options (25%, 50% or 75%) and three VWAP lookback periods (1 year, 6 months or 3 months). The June 2024 circular settled on: at least 50% of total assets invested in scrips of other listed companies; 6-month VWAP less than 50% of the book value per share based on present value of investments in other listed companies; and if the scrip was not traded in the previous 6 months, the 6-month VWAP is treated as zero.
review_notes: Supported. Consultation offered multiple asset thresholds, discount levels and VWAP lookbacks; circular picked 50%/50%/6 months (with zero-VWAP fallback). Comprehensive option-selection target.

question: Before conducting a special call auction, stock exchanges must publish certain details for investors. What information had to be disclosed by the June 2024 circular, and which item was newly added compared with the disclosure package proposed in the April 2024 consultation?
answer_summary: Both documents require the exchange notice to include last traded price, the latest available overall book value, the book value based on investments in scrips of other listed companies, and the proportion of assets invested in other listed companies. The June 2024 circular adds one more item: the price of the latest buy-back or delisting, if any, offered by the company.
review_notes: Supported. Both documents require disclosure of last traded price, the overall and listed-investment book values, and the asset proportion; the final circular adds the latest buy-back or delisting price. Distinct disclosure-package delta.

question: A PSU board decided to voluntarily delist on August 10, 2025, published the initial public announcement on August 25, 2025, and is now completing the offer after September 3, 2025. The acquirer claims the new Part-F carve-out for PSU delisting should apply because the actual delisting is happening after the amendment came into force. Will Part-F apply, and which textual condition in the amending notification controls the answer?
answer_summary: No. Part-F was inserted by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Delisting of Equity Shares) (Amendment) Regulations, 2025, which came into force on the date of their publication in the Official Gazette (September 3, 2025). However, the notification contains a proviso that the provisions apply only to delisting offers where the initial public announcement has not been made. Because the initial public announcement was already made on August 25, 2025, the PSU cannot use the Part-F route and must follow the pre-existing voluntary delisting framework.
review_notes: citations verify the September 2025 amending notification’s commencement proviso: Part-F applies only where the initial public announcement had not been made.

question: The May 2025 consultation paper offered three options (A, B and C) for setting the exit price under the proposed PSU delisting carve-out. When Part-F was enacted in September 2025, which of those options did it adopt, and what happened to the 60-day volume-weighted average market-price parameter that Regulation 19A normally uses for frequently-traded shares?
answer_summary: Part-F adopted the valuer-based approach closest to Option B, not Option A or Option C. Under Regulation 38B(2)(d), the PSU delisting floor price must be at least the highest of: (i) the 52-week volume-weighted average acquisition price; (ii) the highest acquisition price paid in the 26 weeks before the reference date; and (iii) the price determined under a joint valuation report obtained from two independent registered valuers. The 60-day volume-weighted average market-price parameter that applies to frequently-traded companies under the general Regulation 19A floor-price computation does not appear in the Part-F formula. The pre-existing adjusted book-value carve-out for PSUs remains, but adjusted book value is folded into the two-valuer report rather than standing as a separate floor-price floor.
review_notes: Citations confirm Options A/B/C in the consultation and that Part-F replaced the 60-day VWAMP element of Regulation 19A with a two-independent-valuer floor-price approach.

question: A listed PSU was delisted under Part-F and now intends to apply for voluntary strike-off more than a year after delisting. Where does the consideration payable to public shareholders who did not tender have to go, and why is the September 2025 amendment to the Investor Protection and Education Fund Regulations relevant even though that amendment does not itself create the delisting procedure?
answer_summary: If the strike-off is effected after one year from the date of delisting but not later than thirty days from the expiry of that one-year period, the amount due to remaining public shareholders who did not tender must be transferred to a specified account of the designated stock exchange. The exchange must hold it for seven years, after which it is transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund established under the Companies Act, 2013. If it cannot be transferred there for any reason, it goes to SEBI's Investor Protection and Education Fund. The September 2025 IPEF Amendment Regulations matter because they add the monies transferred under Regulation 38B(3)(c) of the Delisting Regulations to the sources of the Investor Protection and Education Fund, harmonising the ultimate-fund leg of the waterfall.
review_notes: Citations verify the one-year-plus-thirty-days strike-off window and unclaimed-consideration waterfall, and the parallel IPEF amendment adds Regulation 38B(3)(c) monies as a fund source.

question: A listed public-sector insurance company in which the Central Government and another PSU together hold 93% of the equity wants to use the Part-F fixed-price delisting route introduced in September 2025. Leaving aside the general requirements, is the company an eligible PSU under the carve-out, and why does the answer not depend only on the 90% threshold?
answer_summary: The company is not eligible for the Part-F route. Although the 90% threshold is met (the aggregate shareholding of the acquirer along with other PSUs must equal or exceed 90% of the total issued shares of that class), Regulation 38B(1) expressly carves out banks, non-banking financial companies and insurance companies from the special PSU regime. Those categories must rely on the ordinary voluntary delisting provisions, not Part-F.
review_notes: Citations confirm the 90% threshold and the express exclusion of banks, NBFCs and insurance companies from Part-F eligibility.

question: The May 2025 consultation paper proposed that unclaimed consideration for remaining public shareholders in a PSU delisting be transferred from the escrow account to the designated stock exchange and held for seven years. Did the September 2025 Part-F provision carry that proposal forward exactly?
answer_summary: No. The final rule narrowed the proposal. The seven-year exchange-holding and IEPF/IPEF waterfall under Regulation 38B(3) applies only where the PSU undertakes voluntary strike-off after one year from the date of delisting but not later than thirty days from the expiry of that one-year period. It is not an automatic feature of every Part-F delisting, as the consultation paper had proposed.
review_notes: Citations confirm the consultation’s blanket escrow-to-exchange proposal became conditional in Part-F on the voluntary-strike-off timing window.

question: A small investment adviser has no website and no mobile app. Its proprietor says the May 2024 Master Circular still lets him email the Investor Charter once and the monthly complaint status to investors' registered email addresses, so nothing needs to change after the June 2025 charter update. Is he correct? Compare the May 2024 Master Circular with the June 2025 circular and the June 2025 Master Circular.
answer_summary: No. The May 2024 Master Circular (Clause 8.2) treated an IA without a website or mobile app as a special case, letting it send the Investor Charter as a one-time measure to investors' registered emails; Clause 8.3 similarly allowed such IAs to email the complaint-status monthly. The June 2025 update removes that carve-out. Both the June 2025 standalone circular and the June 2025 Master Circular (now Section 7.4) require disclosure on websites/mobile apps if the IA has them, but also impose unconditional access obligations in every case: making the charter available at prominent places in the office, providing a copy as part of the client onboarding process, and sending it through emails/letters.
