The complaint-data table must also be disclosed on websites/mobile apps (if any) by the 7th of the succeeding month. SCORES 2.0 and the ODR platform were the stated drivers for the update. Therefore a one-time email alone is no longer sufficient.
review_notes: Supported. The May 2024 Master Circular (Clause 8.2/8.3) gave IAs without websites/apps a one-time email fallback; the June 2025 standalone circular and June 2025 Master Circular remove that carve-out and add unconditional office/onboarding/email/letter obligations. SCORES 2.0/ODR are stated drivers.

question: Both the June 2025 Investment Adviser and Research Analyst standalone charters introduce a duty to disclose the extent of use of Artificial Intelligence tools, worded differently for advice and research services. When SEBI folded those updated charters into the June 2025 Master Circulars, did it preserve, alter, or drop that AI disclosure duty?
answer_summary: SEBI preserved the AI disclosure duties exactly as they appear in the standalone charters. The June 2025 Master Circular for Investment Advisers places the complete updated charter at Annexure F (including the duty to disclose 'the extent of use of Artificial Intelligence tools in providing investment advice'), and the June 2025 Master Circular for Research Analysts places the complete updated charter at Annexure D (including the duty to disclose 'the extent of use of Artificial Intelligence tools in providing research services'). Neither Master Circular deletes or narrows either disclosure; the wording difference between the two intermediaries remains intact because each annexure imports its respective standalone charter unchanged.
review_notes: Supported. Both standalone charters require AI-use disclosure, and the June 2025 Master Circulars place the full updated charters at Annexure F (IA) and Annexure D (RA) without deleting or narrowing that wording. Live search confirms the same AI-disclosure language appears inside the annexures.

question: In the Societe Generale front-running matter, SEBI settled two brokers that executed the Big Client's trades. What control failure did each broker's SCN allege, which one paid the higher monetary settlement, and was either broker also debarred from dealing in securities?
answer_summary: Antique Stock Broking was alleged to have allowed its dealer to use a mobile phone inside the dealing room and to have failed to maintain records of the Big Client's order placements; it settled for ₹22,44,000. Motilal Oswal Financial Services was alleged to have failed to retain evidence of the client's order instructions and to have tried to create supporting documents only after the orders were executed; it settled for ₹34,85,000. Neither broker settlement included a voluntary debarment term; only monetary settlement was imposed.
review_notes: Both broker SCN control failures and settlement amounts are directly supported by the cited Antique and Motilal Oswal chunks; neither order includes debarment.

question: Atul G. Chaturvedi settled separately from the rest of the Chaturvedi Group in the Societe Generale front-running matter. What linked his role at Antique to the group members' trading accounts, and how did his monetary settlement and disgorgement compare to the amounts payable by each of the four group applicants?
answer_summary: Atul was the Antique sales trader who handled Societe Generale's orders; he was privy to material non-public information about the impending trades and is alleged to have transmitted it to family members Rajni, Manish and Ashish Chaturvedi. Manish and Ashish are also directors of Indus Strategy Financial Advisors Private Limited. Atul settled for ₹96,00,000 plus disgorgement of ₹1,48,15,631. Each of the four group applicants paid a monetary settlement of ₹44,00,000; Rajni additionally disgorged ₹3,85,428 and Manish had a joint-and-several disgorgement of ₹15,65,136, while Ashish and Indus had no separate disgorgement term.
review_notes: Link between Atul's role at Antique and the group accounts is supported by the group order; Atul's settlement/disgorgement terms are supported by his individual order.

question: Across the four published settlement orders in the Chaturvedi/Societe Generale front-running cluster, which applicants or entities had to disgorge ill-gotten gains, what were the amounts, and which applicants settled with only a monetary payment? Did any entity escape debarment as well?
answer_summary: Disgorgement was imposed on Rajni Chaturvedi (₹3,85,428), Manish Chaturvedi (₹15,65,136 on a joint-and-several basis) and Atul G. Chaturvedi (₹1,48,15,631). Ashish Chaturvedi, Indus Strategy Financial Advisors Private Limited, Antique Stock Broking Limited and Motilal Oswal Financial Services Limited settled with monetary payments only. The two brokers escaped both disgorgement and the six-month voluntary debarment that applied to Atul and the four group applicants.
review_notes: Exhaustive disgorgement/debarment mapping across all four orders is supported by cited chunks; brokers indeed have neither disgorgement nor debarment.

question: Three of the four Chaturvedi/Societe Generale settlement applications had the same HPAC-meeting and Panel-approval dates, but the fourth did not. Match each applicant or applicant group to its Internal Committee meeting date and Panel approval date and identify the outlier.
answer_summary: Atul G. Chaturvedi, Antique Stock Broking and Motilal Oswal Financial Services all went before the HPAC on July 3, 2025 and were approved by the Panel of Whole Time Members on September 5, 2025. Their Internal Committee meetings differed: Atul and Motilal Oswal met SEBI on May 9, 2025; Antique's meeting was on June 6, 2025. The Chaturvedi Group (Manish, Ashish, Rajni and Indus Strategy) had an Internal Committee meeting on March 12, 2025, HPAC consideration on June 5, 2025 and Panel approval on August 18, 2025 — making it the outlier.
review_notes: Internal Committee, HPAC and Panel approval dates for each applicant group are directly supported by the cited chunks; the Chaturvedi group is the clear timeline outlier.

question: A compliance officer wants to know the total monetary recovery and the total disgorgement across the four Chaturvedi/Societe Generale settlement orders. What two aggregated figures should be reported, and which orders carry no disgorgement term?
answer_summary: Total monetary settlement across the four orders is ₹3,29,29,000: ₹44,00,000 each from four group applicants (₹1,76,00,000), ₹96,00,000 from Atul G. Chaturvedi, ₹22,44,000 from Antique Stock Broking and ₹34,85,000 from Motilal Oswal Financial Services. Total disgorgement is ₹1,67,66,195, coming from Rajni Chaturvedi (₹3,85,428), Manish Chaturvedi (₹15,65,136) and Atul G. Chaturvedi (₹1,48,15,631). No disgorgement appears in the settlement orders for Ashish Chaturvedi, Indus Strategy Financial Advisors, Antique Stock Broking or Motilal Oswal Financial Services.
review_notes: Aggregation figures are arithmetically correct and supported by the cited order chunks; the no-disgorgement list is consistent with q03.

question: Two unregistered advisers argue that their bank receipts are not advisory fees—one says they are payments for educational courses and stock-market workshops, while the other says they include astrology, property commission and website-development income. In the Baap of Chart and Madhav Tiwari / Divinecommodity.co final orders, how does SEBI justify treating the receipts as proceeds of unregistered investment-advisory activity, and what extra scrutiny did the Divinecommodity order apply because of the SAT remand?
answer_summary: In Baap of Chart, SEBI traced INR 12,42,86,704 transferred by the Bunch platform to accounts of Golden Syndicate Ventures Pvt. Ltd., Rahul Rao Padamati and Baap of Chart, INR 1,35,74,872 collected offline, and INR 3,42,15,040 received through UPI/IMPS with narrations such as "training", "Jackpot Algo" and "stock tips". Most of these amounts matched the prices of the courses/packages offered on websites/apps. SEBI concluded that the "educational courses" were merely a conduit for investment advice and directed refund of INR 17,20,76,616. In Madhav Tiwari / Divinecommodity.co, the SAT remand required SEBI to give the noticee an opportunity to explain every bank entry. The noticee produced digitally generated invoices and ledgers, but SEBI found them inconsistent and unreliable. SEBI therefore re-quantified using two corroborative filters: (i) entries whose narrations contained keywords indicating investment advisory activity, and (ii) recurring amounts that exactly matched the subscription-package prices advertised on the noticee's website. The combined amount of INR 10,77,060 and INR 6,71,615, i.e. INR 17,48,675, was directed to be refunded. The SAT remand therefore moved the case from a broad fee-based computation to an entry-by-entry scrutiny in which the noticee bore the burden of separating non-advisory receipts.
review_notes: Both cited orders support the fee-to-advice re-characterisation and the SAT-remand shift to entry-by-entry corroboration.

question: A colleague claims that SEBI uniformly bars unregistered investment advisers from accessing the securities market for a flat one year from the date of the final order. Is the claim consistent with the Baap of Chart, Chanchal Agrawal / Sharepati and Madhav Tiwari / Divinecommodity final orders? For each order, state the actual debarment length or trigger and any condition that can extend it.
answer_summary: The claim is not consistent. The three orders use different market-access formulas. In Baap of Chart, Mohammad Nasiruddin Ansari is debarred for one year and Noticee Nos. 2-7 are debarred for six months, both running from the date of the order. In Chanchal Agrawal / Sharepati, the debarment is for one year from the date of the order or one year from the date of completion of refunds to clients/investors, whichever is later; until refunds are completed, the clock does not start. In Madhav Tiwari / Divinecommodity.co, the debarment runs from the date of the order until the date on which the noticee files the chartered-accountant-certified repayment report; the market-access restraint is therefore tied to compliance rather than to a fixed calendar period.
review_notes: Debarment language in each cited order supports the three different formulas and conditions.

question: In the Chanchal Agrawal / Sharepati matter, SEBI imposed a monetary penalty of Rs. 1,00,000 under Section 15HB of the SEBI Act, whereas in the Madhav Tiwari / Divinecommodity matter it imposed Rs. 1,00,000 under Section 15EB (and Rs. 5,00,000 under Section 15HA). What fact about the timing of the alleged activity explains why Section 15HB was the correct provision for Agrawal but Section 15EB could be used for Tiwari?
answer_summary: Section 15EB of the SEBI Act, which creates a specific penalty for default by an investment adviser or research analyst, was not in force before 8 March 2019. Chanchal Agrawal's website was active from 2012 and the advisory activity covered by the SCN predated that date. Because no separate penalty provision existed for an investment adviser's default at the relevant time, SEBI resorted to the residual penalty under Section 15HB (contravention where no separate penalty is provided). Madhav Tiwari's activity, reflected in the FY 2020-21 to FY 2022-23 receipts, occurred after Section 15EB became effective, so SEBI could impose the specific penalty under Section 15EB for the IA Regulations violation, while the additional Section 15HA penalty related to the separate PFUTP/fraud finding.
review_notes: Cited orders support the pre-/post-March 2019 regime split and the corresponding penalty sections; the 15EB effective date is consistent but relies partly on statutory knowledge.

question: In the Safe Trading and Chanchal Agrawal / Sharepati matters, SEBI quantified unregistered advisory receipts partly by matching investor payments to the subscription-package prices shown to the public. Besides the archived website and bank-narration trail used in Sharepati, what channel-specific evidence did SEBI use in Safe Trading, and what additional conduct made Safe Trading a PFUTP violation rather than merely an unregistered-advisory violation?
answer_summary: In Chanchal Agrawal / Sharepati, SEBI used the archived website of www.sharepati.com because the live site was inactive, identified package-style tip services, and matched bank-account credits with narrations such as 'investment', 'trading' and 'INB deposit / investment' to attribute Rs. 54,35,707 in advisory fees. In Mohit Gupta / Safe Trading, SEBI relied on the Telegram channel 'SafeTrading Mohit Gupta' with 1,357 subscribers, a WhatsApp Business Account on the same mobile number, an Instagram handle '@safetrading.in' with 2,288 followers, and bank credits matching amounts such as Rs. 1,400 and Rs. 10,000 that corresponded to the advertised package prices. The conduct crossed into PFUTP because the noticee assured guaranteed accuracy of tips, offered an algo-trading service after asking investors to share their demat account IDs and passwords, and disseminated advice through digital media in a manner designed to influence investment decisions, thereby attracting Regulations 3(a)-(d) and 4(2)(k) and (s) of the PFUTP Regulations and a Section 15HA penalty.
review_notes: Channel and PFUTP findings are supported by Safe Trading and Sharepati cited chunks; the Section 15HA penalty is true but not inside the cited chunks.

question: An unregistered adviser routes investor payments through an education-tech platform and later argues the receipts are legitimate course fees, while another obtains AP/brokerage referral credits from a stock broker and argues the money is ordinary brokerage income. Comparing the Baap of Chart and Safe Trading final orders, how did SEBI reclassify those payments as unregistered advisory fees despite the involvement of apparently legitimate intermediaries?
answer_summary: In Baap of Chart, investor payments were routed through the Bunch platform into accounts of Golden Syndicate Ventures Pvt. Ltd., Rahul Rao Padamati and Baap of Chart, and Nasir Ansari also collected INR 1.35 crore offline. SEBI rejected the 'course fee' framing by noting that the videos/strategies contained specific buy/sell/hold recommendations, that purchasers were added to closed groups where tips were given, and that Nasir himself admitted regulatory complications because he had failed to register as a member. The platform was therefore treated as the collection channel, not the economic character of the transaction, and the entire INR 17,20,76,616 was directed to be refunded. In Safe Trading, RKSV told SEBI that its credits to Mohit Gupta were referral/brokerage credits in the normal course and that an authorised person cannot provide advisory or research services. SEBI accepted that explanation for the RKSV credits but found a separate stream of unregistered advisory income: credits matching the fixed subscription prices advertised on Gupta's Telegram/Instagram/WhatsApp channels and his offer of algo-trading after collecting demat credentials. The involvement of a registered broker did not sanitize the independent social-media advisory business, and SEBI directed refund of Rs. 23,94,574.50 collected from that activity.
review_notes: Baap of Chart and Safe Trading cited chunks support the reclassification of Bunch/broker-AP flows from nominal intermediaries to advisory proceeds.

question: Infosys featured in two separate Chairperson/Member final orders on alleged insider trading around mid-2020. One matter concerned the Vanguard strategic partnership and the other concerned Infosys’ quarterly financial results. For each order, state the head of UPSI under Regulation 2(1)(n) of the PIT Regulations and describe how the order fixed the start of the UPSI period.
answer_summary: In the January 31, 2025 final order, the UPSI was the strategic partnership with Vanguard, categorised under Regulation 2(1)(n)(iv) as information relating to acquisitions, disposals or expansion of business. The order held the UPSI period ran from June 29, 2020, when a Go-To-Market command-centre presentation shared with specific employees showed the announcement window as "2.5 weeks from announcement date (from 7/14 to 7/31)", establishing that the signing/announcement date of around July 14, 2020 had been finalised. In the September 9, 2024 final order, the UPSI was the quarterly financial results, categorised under Regulation 2(1)(n)(i). The UPSI periods were anchored to the first preparation of the internal "Flash" estimate for each quarter; for example, the June 30, 2020 quarter ran from June 29, 2020 to July 15, 2020 (public disclosure date) and the September 30, 2020 quarter ran from September 28, 2020 to October 14, 2020.
review_notes: Both cited orders support the UPSI-category split (Vanguard under expansion/business n(iv), results under n(i)) and the distinct period-fixation methods.

question: Two SEBI final orders examined suspected insider trading in the Infosys scrip during overlapping periods in 2020. The January 2025 order featured Keyur Maniar and Ramit Chaudhri, while the September 2024 order featured Pranshu Bhutra, Amit Bhutra, Bharath C. Jain and a cluster of entities such as Capital One Partners and Tesora Capital. Compare how the two orders described the composition of the alleged noticee ring and the type of securities traded in each matter.
answer_summary: The January 2025 order involved a small two-person ring: Ramit Chaudhri, an Infosys employee who was on internal email chains concerning the Vanguard deal and its July 14, 2020 announcement date, was treated as the source of UPSI, while Keyur Maniar, an external person, was the alleged trader. Keyur traded INFY futures and call options, building up an unusually concentrated and leveraged position, including strikes such as 880 CE where his open interest reached nearly 17% of the market on July 14, 2020. The September 2024 order involved a broader employee-connected-person-and-entity ring: Pranshu Bhutra, an Infosys legal/employment-law counsel, was alleged to have received UPSI from insiders Sunil Kumar Dhareshwar and Venkatasubramaniyam V.V. and passed it to his cousin Amit Bhutra; Amit acted as a hub who allegedly shared it with family members and partnership/AIF-type entities including Capital One Partners, Tesora Capital, New World Capital, Optimus Capital and Tattva Capital. Those entities traded in the cash/equity segment of INFY rather than in derivatives.
review_notes: Cited orders describe the two noticee-ring compositions and the Jan order confirms INFY F&O trading; the Sept order does not reference derivatives, supporting the equity/cash instrument contrast.

question: A compliance officer compares the two Infosys insider-trading final orders and sees that the January 2025 order imposed severe sanctions, whereas the September 2024 order exonerated all noticees and ordered release of impounded money. What evidentiary distinction did the two Whole-Time Members rely on to explain this opposite result?
answer_summary: The January 2025 order found direct evidence that Ramit Chaudhri had access to the precise Vanguard announcement date through internal emails and the GTM command-centre material, and that he made a 22-minute phone call to Keyur Maniar on July 8, 2020 that ended only seven minutes before Keyur began placing aggressive INFY futures and call-option orders, his first such trades in INFY since April 2020. The regulator treated this timing and pattern as sufficient to prove communication of UPSI and possession-based insider trading. By contrast, the September 2024 order held that the foundational allegation that Pranshu Bhutra had access to UPSI was not proved: he was neither a designated person under Regulation 9(4)/9A(2)(a) nor listed in Infosys’ Structured Digital Database as having access to UPSI, and mere regular communication with insiders did not establish access. In addition, the SAT had already quashed the interim order against Pranshu and Venkatasubramaniyam V.V. on April 25, 2022 because the prima-facie observations had been sufficiently explained. Because SEBI failed to prove that Pranshu received UPSI from Sunil or Venkat, it could not prove he passed UPSI to Amit, and the entire downstream tippee network therefore collapsed.
review_notes: Cited chunks support the opposing outcomes: direct Ramit->Keyur call/email trail in the Jan order versus the unproven Pranshu-access chain and the April 25, 2022 SAT quashing in the Sept order.

question: What remedial directions, if any, were issued in each of the two Infosys insider-trading final orders? Give the specific amount, interest calculation and market-access restriction from the January 2025 order and the treatment of impounded money in the September 2024 order.
answer_summary: In the January 31, 2025 order, WTM Ananth Narayan G. directed that noticees Keyur Maniar and Ramit Chaudhri be restrained from accessing the securities market and prohibited from buying, selling or dealing in securities, directly or indirectly, for one year from the date of the order; Keyur Maniar was directed to disgorge ₹2,60,70,624 along with simple interest at 12% per annum from July 17, 2020 (last sale date) until deposit into the escrow account, and to remit the amount to the Investor Protection and Education Fund within 45 days; and both noticees were directed to pay a penalty of ₹30 lakhs each under Section 15G of the SEBI Act. In the September 9, 2024 order, WTM Ashwani Bhatia issued no adverse directions at all: proceedings against Notices 1 to 16 were disposed of without any direction, the restraints imposed by the Interim and Confirmatory Orders on Notices 2 to 7 were vacated immediately, and any amounts impounded from those noticees and held in escrow, along with accrued interest, were ordered to be released to them.
review_notes: Direction/penalty details for the Jan order and the vacatur/release direction for the Sept order are directly supported by the cited chunks.

question: How did the September 2024 final order use the concepts of 'designated person' and the Structured Digital Database to evaluate Pranshu Bhutra’s access to UPSI, and why did that same formal-designation analysis not control the January 2025 order against Ramit Chaudhri?
answer_summary: The September 2024 order reasoned that Pranshu Bhutra was not among the designated persons identified by Infosys under Regulation 9(4) read with Regulation 9A(2)(a) of the PIT Regulations, and his name did not appear in the company’s Structured Digital Database as an employee with access to UPSI. Accordingly, mere regular communication with insiders or attendance at meetings was held insufficient to infer access. The January 2025 order did not rely on a formal-designation test because SEBI produced direct evidence that Ramit Chaudhrireceived internal emails in the first week of July 2020 identifying the Vanguard Master Service Agreement signing/announcement date as on or around July 14, 2020, and that he was part of the GTM command-centre material setting out the announcement window; that direct evidence established his access to UPSI independently of whether he was formally designated.
review_notes: Sept order reasoning on designated-person/SDD absence is supported by cited chunks; Jan order direct evidence for Ramit makes formal-designation analysis inapplicable.

question: SEBI passed confirmatory orders in March 2024 (LIC front-running), February 2026 (Patel Wealth Advisors) and March 2026 (Par Drugs) after earlier interim orders. What identical caveat appears in all three confirmatory orders about the status of the observations, and what instruction is given to the ongoing detailed investigation because of that caveat?
answer_summary: All three confirmatory orders state that their observations are tentative in nature and are made pending detailed investigation. Each order directs that the detailed investigation must be carried out without being influenced by any of the directions passed or any observations made either in the interim order or in the confirmatory order, and that appropriate further action will be taken based on the outcome.
review_notes: All three cited confirmatory-order chunks directly state the tentative-observations caveat and the instruction that the investigation proceed uninfluenced.

question: The confirmatory orders for Par Drugs, Patel Wealth Advisors and the LIC front-running matter each invoke powers under the SEBI Act. Which of these three orders invokes section 11D, and which one conspicuously does not? Answer by reference to the authorising provisions stated on the face of each order.
answer_summary: The Par Drugs confirmatory order (March 25, 2026) and the LIC front-running confirmatory order (March 19, 2024) both invoke section 11D: Par Drugs cites sections 11(1), 11(4), 11B and 11D; the LIC order cites sections 11(1), 11(4), 11B and 11D. The Patel Wealth Advisors confirmatory order (February 11, 2026) is issued under sub-sections (1) and (4) of sections 11 and 11B only and does not list section 11D on its face.
review_notes: Opening headings of the three orders support the 11D presence/absence pattern; distinct statutory-basis memory target.

question: Par Drugs asked SEBI to defer the confirmatory order until the NSE-appointed valuer produced a fresh valuation report and fairness opinion. How did SEBI dispose of that request, and how did the confirmatory order treat the interim directions restraining the slump sale and mandating the independent valuation?
answer_summary: SEBI rejected the request to keep the confirmatory order in abeyance. It noted that the confirmatory stage is only to confirm, modify or reverse the interim directions based on the material produced, and that the valuation report and other evidence would be examined by the Investigating Authority when passing the final order. Finding that Par Drugs had not rebutted the prima facie findings in the interim order, SEBI confirmed the interim directions under sections 11(1), 11(4), 11B and 11D; consequently, the restraints on the slump sale, the independent NSE valuation/fairness opinion and the cease-and-desist on alienation of the BTA assets continued.
review_notes: Confirmatory order disposes of the abeyance request and confirms interim directions; interim order documents the valuation/alienation restraints.

question: In the interim order against M/s Patel Wealth Advisors and its directors, SEBI restrained Noticees 2 to 5 from accessing the securities market and prohibited Noticee 1 from dealing in its proprietary account. What change, if any, did the February 2026 confirmatory order make to those restraints, and what interim obligation remained unchanged?
answer_summary: The confirmatory order confirmed the interim directions as a whole, but modified sub-paragraph II of paragraph 86 with respect to Noticees 2 to 5: their restraints from accessing the securities market and from buying, selling or dealing in securities were revoked. The restraints on Noticee 1 (the proprietary-account trading prohibition on PWAPL) and the impounding direction requiring deposit of INR 3,22,62,367.05 in a lien-marked fixed deposit remained in force.
review_notes: Both cited chunks support the partial revocation for Noticees 2-5 and the continued bar/impounding for Noticee 1.

question: Compare the procedural timelines in the Par Drugs and Patel Wealth Advisors matters: roughly how long after each interim order was the confirmatory order issued, and what common post-order process did the noticees receive before the confirmatory order was passed?
answer_summary: Par Drugs' interim order was dated September 15, 2025, and the confirmatory order was passed on March 25, 2026 — about six months later. Patel Wealth Advisors' interim order was dated April 28, 2025, and the confirmatory order was passed on February 11, 2026 — about nine and a half months later. In both matters, the noticees were allowed to inspect documents, file written submissions and were granted a personal hearing (Par Drugs on January 13, 2026; Patel Wealth Advisors on November 18, 2025).
review_notes: Confirmed time lags and shared document-inspection/reply/hearing process are directly stated in the cited background/hearing chunks.

question: How did SEBI's confirmatory orders finally dispose of the interim directions in the Par Drugs, Patel Wealth Advisors and LIC front-running matters: which sets of directions were left unchanged, and which were expressly modified or revoked? State how the treatment of the main noticee differed from the other noticees, if at all.
answer_summary: Par Drugs: every interim direction was confirmed unchanged. Patel Wealth Advisors: the directions as a whole were confirmed, but sub-paragraph II of paragraph 86 was modified to revoke the market-access restraints on Noticees 2 to 5; Noticee 1 (M/s Patel Wealth Advisors) remained barred from proprietary-account trading and the impounding of INR 3,22,62,367.05 continued. LIC front-running: all interim directions were confirmed subject only to the July 20, 2023 miscellaneous order that defreezed Kamlesh Agarwal's joint bank account; the trading restraint continued for all five noticees, so no individual noticee was released from the market-access bar.
review_notes: Synthesizes final disposition across three matters from confirmatory orders and underlying interim directions; each outcome is supported.

question: Two SEBI settlement orders dated September 16, 2025 allege insider trading in Adani group scrips by Ajay Bhatia and Supreet Singh Luthra. What was each applicant's approximate total monetary outgo (settlement amount plus disgorgement plus interest), which of them did SEBI describe as the source of the unpublished price-sensitive information, and what identical non-monetary undertaking applied to both?
answer_summary: Ajay Bhatia, described as the connected person/sub-subsidiary CEO who communicated the UPSI to Supreet Singh Luthra, paid a settlement amount of ₹1,04,87,903, disgorgement of ₹55,34,457 and interest of ₹9,58,902, for a total monetary outgo of ₹1,69,81,262. Supreet Singh Luthra, described as Bhatia's VAT consultant/connected person by association, paid a settlement amount of ₹40,00,000, disgorgement of ₹13,13,131 and interest of ₹2,92,702, for a total outgo of ₹56,05,833. Both applicants undertook voluntary debarment from the Indian securities market for six months from the date of the settlement order.
review_notes: Per-chunk totals, roles, and six-month debarment match both cited orders. Wording calls Bhatia the 'source' but the answer clarifies he communicated the UPSI received from insiders.

question: Both September 2025 Adani insider-trading settlements charge the applicant under Section 12A(d) and 12A(e) of the SEBI Act read with Regulation 4(1) of the PIT Regulations, but one applicant faces an additional charge under Regulation 3(1). Which applicant is it, and which conduct described in the orders accounts for the extra charge?
answer_summary: Ajay Bhatia faces the additional charge under Regulation 3(1) of the PIT Regulations for allegedly communicating unpublished price-sensitive information to Supreet Singh Luthra. Bhatia is said to have received the UPSI from insiders and then passed it on. Supreet Singh Luthra is charged only with trading while in possession of UPSI under Regulation 4(1), not with communicating it.
review_notes: Charge tables in paragraph 1 of each Adani order confirm Bhatia's extra Regulation 3(1) charge; the conduct is described accurately in the cited chunks.

question: The December 2024 SEBI settlement order in the HDFC Ltd./HDFC Bank insider-trading matter identifies two applicants and a family entity that actually traded on the merger UPSI. Does that order require disgorgement of the trading entity's profits or a market debarment, and how does that differ from the Ajay Bhatia settlement order?
answer_summary: The HDFC Ltd./HDFC Bank settlement order does not require disgorgement by the trading entity or a market debarment. The trading entity was Rupesh Dalal HUF (karta Rupesh Satish Dalal, the father of Applicant 2 Rahil Dalal), which earned profits of ₹5.67 lakh on HDFC Ltd. and ₹2.52 lakh on HDFC Bank from call-option contracts. Instead of disgorgement, the order settles with Applicant 1 Nimai Parekh (payment of ₹39 lakh) and Applicant 2 Rahil Dalal (payment of ₹35 lakh). By contrast, the Ajay Bhatia settlement order required both a disgorgement of ₹55,34,457 (computed from his own trades) and a six-month voluntary market debarment.
review_notes: The HDFC order contains HUF trading profits and settlement amounts but no disgorgement or debarment; contrast with Bhatia's disgorgement and six-month debarment is supported.

question: Two SEBI insider-trading settlements moved from revised settlement terms to a final order at very different speeds. In the HDFC Ltd./HDFC Bank matter, revised terms were submitted in August 2024 and the order was passed in December 2024. In the Ajay Bhatia matter, revised terms were submitted in June 2024. When was the Bhatia settlement order finally passed, what was the common interim approval step that preceded Whole Time Member approval in both cases, and on what date did the Whole Time Members approve each settlement?
answer_summary: The Ajay Bhatia settlement order was passed on September 16, 2025, more than a year after his revised settlement terms were submitted on June 24, 2024. Both cases followed the same procedural sequence in which the High Powered Advisory Committee recommended the settlement terms before a Panel of Whole Time Members approved the settlement. The Whole Time Members approved the Bhatia order on June 23, 2025, while they approved the HDFC Ltd./HDFC Bank order on November 6, 2024.
review_notes: Revised-term dates, HPAC recommendation, WTM approval dates, and final order dates are all present in the cited chunks of both orders.

question: The HDFC Ltd./HDFC Bank insider-trading settlement charged Applicant 1 under Section 12A(d) and Regulation 3(1), and Applicant 2 under Section 12A(d) and 12A(e) and Regulations 3(1) and 3(2). Why does the friend/receiver in the HDFC matter face the additional Regulation 3(2) allegation while Supreet Singh Luthra, the associate in the Adani matter, faces only Regulation 4(1)?
answer_summary: In the HDFC matter, Rahil Dalal (Applicant 2) was alleged to have procured the UPSI from Nimai Parekh and then shared it with his father and Rupesh Dalal HUF, who traded on it. That communication of UPSI to another person who traded triggered the Regulation 3(2) charge. In the Adani matter, Supreet Singh Luthra was alleged only to be in frequent telephonic contact with Ajay Bhatia and to have traded while in possession of the UPSI; he was not alleged to have passed the information on to anyone else who traded, so he is charged under Regulation 4(1) only.
review_notes: The HDFC order alleges Applicant 2 shared UPSI with his father/HUF who traded, supporting the Regulation 3(2) charge; Luthra is alleged only to have traded while in possession.

question: Three SEBI Adjudicating Officer orders issued in 2025 under the 'insider trading' label cover Refex Industries, Swan Energy and Mastek. What monetary penalty was imposed in each matter, under which section(s) of the SEBI Act, and what category of noticee bore the liability?
answer_summary: Refex Industries: Anil Jain (Chairman and Managing Director / promoter group insider) was fined Rs. 10,00,000 and Kamlesh Jain / Jain Family Trust were jointly and severally fined Rs. 25,00,000 under section 15G of the SEBI Act (PIT Regulations 3(1) and 4(1)). Swan Energy: Mr. Rahul Sharma (a designated person / employee of the company) was fined Rs. 1,00,000 under section 15HB (Regulation 9(1) read with clause 6 of Schedule B) and another Rs. 1,00,000 under section 15A(b) (Regulation 7(2)(a)). Mastek Ltd.: Integrated Master Securities Private Limited (stockbroker / trading member) was fined Rs. 1,00,000 under section 15A(a) for furnishing false information during investigation, while the alleged record-keeping / Brokers Regulations violations were given the benefit of doubt.
review_notes: Penalty amounts, penalty provisions and noticee categories are supported by the cited ORDER paragraphs in all three AOs; cross-scrip comparison truly needs all three documents.

question: All three 2025 orders are titled as insider-trading adjudications, but only one actually penalises communicating or trading on unpublished price-sensitive information. Which one is it, and what misconduct did the other two orders punish instead?
answer_summary: The Refex order is the one that penalises UPSI-related conduct: it holds the CMD, Anil Jain, communicated UPSI about the March 2023 quarterly financial results to Kamlesh Jain, who then traded through the Jain Family Trust. The Swan Energy order penalises code-of-conduct breaches by a designated person—entering contra trades, failing to obtain pre-clearance and failing to disclose trades exceeding Rs. 10 lakh—without concluding the trades were motivated by possession of UPSI. The Mastek order penalises the stockbroker for furnishing false information during SEBI's investigation by recreating call recordings, not for trading on UPSI; alleged call-recording / Brokers Regulations breaches were left unpunished.
review_notes: Refex chunks confirm UPSI communication/trading allegations; Swan and Mastek chunks confirm the proceedings instead punished code-of-conduct/pre-clearance/disclosure breaches and false information during investigation respectively.

question: In the Swan Energy order the noticee had already disgorged his alleged gains (Rs. 30,25,133) and argued that SEBI should not impose an additional penalty. Was that argument accepted, and how does the treatment of disgorgement there compare with the penalty basis in the Refex and Mastek orders?
answer_summary: The argument was accepted only in part. For the contra-trade violation under clause 10 of Schedule B, the AO agreed that the unlawful gains had already been disgorged and, following the SAT in Uday Agarwal v. SEBI, imposed no separate penalty under section 15HB. However, the AO rejected the argument for the pre-clearance and disclosure violations, imposing Rs. 1,00,000 under section 15HB (Regulation 9(1) read with clause 6) and Rs. 1,00,000 under section 15A(b) (Regulation 7(2)(a)). In Refex there was no prior disgorgement before the AO; penalties totaling Rs. 35,00,000 were imposed directly under section 15G for communicating / trading on UPSI. In Mastek the penalty of Rs. 1,00,000 under section 15A(a) was for providing false information during the investigation, not for insider-trading gains or disgorgement.
review_notes: Swan chunks show the contra-trade disgorgement argument succeeded under Uday Agarwal but pre-clearance/disclosure penalties remained; contrast with Refex direct 15G penalties and Mastek false-information 15A(a) penalty is well supported.

question: Each order considered the section 15J penalty factors (disproportionate gain, loss to investors, repetitive nature). In which of the three matters did the AO rely on the noticee's prior regulatory history to support the quantum, and why did the absence of quantified investor loss not preclude a penalty in the other two?
answer_summary: Refex: The AO expressly noted Noticee 2's prior SEBI penalties (Richa Industries, B C Power Controls, Le Waterina Resorts) while determining the penalty under section 15G, even though no specific investor loss was proved. Swan Energy: The AO treated the disclosure and pre-clearance obligations as absolute and imposed nominal penalties totalling Rs. 2,00,000 despite the absence of investor complaints and despite the profits being disgorged. Mastek: No quantified gain or loss was shown, but the AO imposed Rs. 1,00,000 under section 15A(a) because prior disciplinary directions against the stockbroker were treated as an aggravating circumstance for the false-information violation.
review_notes: Refex chunks cite Noticee 2's prior penalties and Mastek chunks cite prior disciplinary directions; Swan chunk confirms absolute-obligation rationale despite no quantified loss or investor complaints.

question: Gretex Corporate Services Limited faces three SEBI enforcement outcomes in the same cluster: the listed-company adjudication order dated June 27, 2025; the corporate-services adjudication order dated January 13, 2026; and the merchant-banker enquiry order dated October 30, 2025. Which order carries the largest monetary penalty, and which order imposes a non-monetary operating restriction on the same entity?
answer_summary: The largest monetary penalty is in the listed-company adjudication order of June 27, 2025, which fines Gretex Rs. 20,00,000/- under Section 15HB. The non-monetary operating restriction is imposed by the October 30, 2025 merchant-banker enquiry order, which prohibits Gretex from taking up any new assignment or contract as a SEBI-registered merchant banker for 21 days. The January 13, 2026 corporate-services adjudication order imposes only monetary penalties totalling Rs. 15,00,000/- (Rs. 10 lakh under Section 15HB and Rs. 5 lakh under Section 15A(b)).
review_notes: Cited chunks confirm listed-company AO imposes Rs. 20,00,000 under Section 15HB, corporate-services AO imposes Rs. 15,00,000 total under Sections 15HB/15A(b), and the merchant-banker enquiry imposes a 21-day operating ban.

question: In the October 30, 2025 enquiry order against Gretex Corporate Services Limited as merchant banker, one issuer accounted for roughly 40% of the IPO proceeds earmarked as a security deposit for renting office space. Name that issuer and determine whether it is one of the four IPOs reviewed in the January 13, 2026 corporate-services adjudication order.
answer_summary: The issuer is Jayant Infratech Limited, whose prospectus dated June 24, 2022 proposed deploying about 40% of the IPO proceeds as a security deposit for renting office space under a MoU with BRV Leasing Andheri LLP. It is not one of the four IPOs examined in the January 13, 2026 corporate-services adjudication order, which reviewed Sudarshan Pharma Industries Limited, Akme Fintrade (India) Limited, Owais Metal and Mineral Processing Limited, and Interiors & More Limited.
review_notes: Enquiry chunks identify Jayant Infratech as the issuer for the 40% office-space object; corporate-services AO chunk lists the four IPOs reviewed and Jayant is absent. Both docs are needed for the membership determination.

question: Three SEBI proceedings address the same underlying conduct of Gretex Corporate Services Limited but use different legal routes. Contrast the enabling provisions: (a) the June 27, 2025 listed-company adjudication, (b) the January 13, 2026 corporate-services adjudication, and (c) the October 30, 2025 enquiry order. Why could the enquiry order impose an operating ban while the two adjudication orders could only impose monetary penalties?
answer_summary: (a) The listed-company adjudication is exercised under Section 15-I of the SEBI Act read with the Adjudication Rules; it finds violations of LODR Regulation 32, LODR Regulation 30 read with the September 9, 2015 circular, and ICDR Regulation 245 read with Schedule VI, and imposes a Section 15HB penalty. (b) The corporate-services adjudication is also under Section 15-I of the SEBI Act; it finds violations across ICDR Regulations 245(2)(b), 245(3), 25(5), 25(9)(b), MB Regulations 9A(1)(e), 9A(1)(f), Regulation 13 read with Schedule III clauses, and Regulation 27, and imposes Sections 15HB and 15A(b) penalties. (c) The enquiry order is under Section 12(3) of the SEBI Act read with Regulations 23 and 27 of the SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations, 2008 and Regulation 35 of the SEBI (Merchant Bankers) Regulations, 1992; it finds violation of Regulation 7 (net worth) and Regulation 13 read with Schedule III (due diligence) and therefore the competent authority could recommend action under Regulation 26 of the Intermediaries Regulations, resulting in a direction prohibiting new assignments. The adjudication route is capped at monetary penalty, whereas the intermediary-enquiry route can impose business restrictions.
review_notes: Legal-route summary matches cited provisions: listed-company and corporate-services AOs are under Section 15-I and cap out at monetary penalties, while the enquiry is under Section 12(3)/Intermediaries Regs/MB Regs and can reach a business restriction under Regulation 26/27.

question: Gretex raised an overlapping-inspection / parallel-proceedings objection in two of the three orders. Explain how the October 30, 2025 enquiry order and the January 13, 2026 corporate-services adjudication order each responded to that objection.
answer_summary: In the October 30, 2025 enquiry order, the Chief General Manager rejected the parallel-proceedings objection by noting that the ongoing adjudication and the enquiry concerned completely different violations and were distinct in nature and scope: adjudication is for monetary penalty, whereas the enquiry is under the Intermediaries Regulations and could lead to action under Regulation 26. In the January 13, 2026 corporate-services adjudication order, the Adjudicating Officer acknowledged that the inspection period overlapped with a prior inspection (April 1, 2021 to January 31, 2023) that gave rise to the pending enquiry, but held that the allegations in the two proceedings were different, so the objection was not tenable.
review_notes: Directly supported by enquiry chunk #14 (distinct nature/scope and monetary-vs-intermediary action) and corporate-services chunk #80 (overlapping inspection period but different allegations).

question: Both the June 27, 2025 listed-company order and the October 30, 2025 merchant-banker enquiry order involve an offering object described as renting office space through a security deposit. In which role was Gretex acting in each proceeding, and what different factual misuse or due-diligence failure connected to that object did SEBI identify?
answer_summary: In the June 27, 2025 listed-company order, Gretex was the issuer; it raised Rs. 2.55 crore for a security deposit to rent office space, then terminated the lease, routed funds through a subsidiary (Sunview Nirman Pvt Ltd), and eventually invested in a residential flat in Parel, diverting the IPO proceeds into real-estate contrary to the prospectus statement. In the October 30, 2025 merchant-banker enquiry order, Gretex was the lead manager for Jayant Infratech Limited; it failed to verify that the office-space property representing about 40% of the IPO proceeds was under construction at the relevant time and failed to disclose that material risk adequately to investors.
review_notes: Listed-company AO chunks show Gretex as issuer diverting the 2.55 Cr office-space deposit through Sunview; enquiry chunks show Gretex as lead manager for Jayant Infratech failing to verify the under-construction office property.

question: Three 2026 SEBI settlement orders for listed companies—Indiabulls Real Estate, Markolines Pavement Technologies, and Mangalam Global Enterprise—were all disposed of under the Settlement Regulations, but the settlement applicants are different. Who filed the settlement applications in each matter, and what does the difference show about where SEBI located the alleged misconduct?
answer_summary: In Indiabulls Real Estate, the four applicants are promoter-connected private limited entities (Agnes Developers, Everlast Projects, Lincoln Developers and Deneb Developers) alleged to have acted as conduits for diversion of funds from a subsidiary to promoter-connected entities; the listed company itself is not a settlement applicant. In Markolines Pavement Technologies, the applicant is the listed company itself, for failing to file the half-yearly statements of deviation/no deviation/no variance in utilisation of IPO proceeds. In Mangalam Global Enterprise, the applicants are individuals—six independent directors and two compliance officers—for failing to act diligently or discharge their disclosure duties. The pattern shows that a settlement for a listed company can be brought by the issuer, its KMPs/officers, or promoter-connected entities, depending on whom SEBI alleged committed the violation.
review_notes: Supported by the three settlement orders: promoter-connected conduit entities for Indiabulls, the listed issuer for Markolines, and independent directors/compliance officers for Mangalam. Multi-document comparison is essential to map applicants to violation location.

question: Each of the three 2026 listed-company settlement orders for Indiabulls Real Estate, Markolines Pavement Technologies and Mangalam Global Enterprise says the adjudication proceedings are disposed of under section 15JB of the SEBI Act. Which two orders also expressly invoke section 19 of the SEBI Act and the formula 'Regulations 23 read with Regulation 28' of the Settlement Regulations, and which uses the shorter 'regulation 23(1)' wording?
answer_summary: The Indiabulls Real Estate and Mangalam Global Enterprise orders dispose of the proceedings 'in exercise of the powers conferred under Section 15JB read with Section 19 of the SEBI Act and in terms of Regulations 23 read with Regulation 28' of the Settlement Regulations. The Markolines Pavement Technologies order uses the shorter formulation: the proceedings are disposed of 'in terms of section 15JB of the SEBI Act read with regulation 23(1)' of the Settlement Regulations. All three nevertheless preserve SEBI's right under Regulation 28 to revive or initiate proceedings for untrue representations or breach of undertakings.
review_notes: Directly supported by operative paragraphs: Indiabulls and Mangalam use Section 15JB read with Section 19 plus Regulations 23 read with 28; Markolines uses section 15JB read with regulation 23(1). All three also preserve Regulation 28 revival rights.

question: Compare the settlement timelines for the listed-company matters of Indiabulls Real Estate, Mangalam Global Enterprise and Markolines Pavement Technologies. Which matter had the longest interval between the Show Cause Notice and the remittance of the settlement amount, and what feature of the case explains the delay?
answer_summary: Indiabulls Real Estate had the longest SCN-to-remittance interval. Its SCN was dated November 01, 2023, its Internal Committee meetings occurred in December 2025, the Whole Time Members approved settlement on March 12, 2026, and the money was remitted on April 13, 2026—a gap of roughly two-and-a-half years. By contrast, Mangalam Global Enterprise moved from SCN on February 10, 2025 to remittance on March 06, 2026, and Markolines Pavement Technologies moved from SCN on May 22, 2025 to remittance on April 15, 2026. The Indiabulls delay reflects the older subject matter (alleged fund diversion from FY 2009-10 to 2016-17) and the time between the 2023 SCN and the 2025-26 settlement-stage meetings.
review_notes: Timelines verified from SCN dates and remittance records across all three orders; Indiabulls has the longest interval (Nov 2023 SCN to Apr 2026 remittance), explained by older fund-diversion subject matter and elapsed procedural time.

question: In the listed-company settlements for Markolines Pavement Technologies, Indiabulls Real Estate and Mangalam Global Enterprise, only one of the three records a concrete post-SCN compliance step taken by the applicant before payment. Which matter is it, what filing was made, and why is it absent from the other two?
answer_summary: Markolines Pavement Technologies records that after the SCN was issued, the company confirmed it had filed the overdue half-yearly statements of deviation/no deviation/no variance in utilisation of IPO proceeds with BSE and submitted copies to SEBI on July 16, 2025. This was part of the settlement discussion because the original violation itself was a continuous-disclosure default under LODR Regulation 32. The other two matters rest on different allegations—Indiabulls concerns alleged diversion of funds through promoter-connected conduit entities and does not describe a corrective disclosure, while Mangalam concerns alleged corporate-governance failures by independent directors and compliance officers, where the settlement is by individuals rather than a corrective issuer-level filing.
review_notes: Markolines records post-SCN filing of deviation/no-deviation statements and submission to SEBI on July 16, 2025. The other two matters concern fund diversion and officer-level governance duties, so no issuer-level corrective filing is described.

question: In the BKS/RKS Family Trust and Arjun Discretionary Trust front-running matter, SEBI passed two 2024 settlement orders—one against Angel One Limited and another against Jitendra Kewalramani and related individuals. On what four axes do the two settlement orders materially differ: (i) date and legal basis of the SCN, (ii) the underlying violation alleged, (iii) the monetary amount and any disgorgement, and (iv) non-monetary market-restraint terms?
answer_summary: Axes of difference: (i) SCN dates and scope – Angel One received a separate SCN dated April 24, 2024, while the Kewalramani group was covered by a common SCN dated January 24, 2024. (ii) Underlying violation – Angel One was charged with broker-level omissions: failure to maintain voice-recording/order-instruction records under SEBI/HO/MIRSD/DOP1/CIR/P/2018/54 and supervisory/responsibility failures under the SEBI circular on market access through authorised persons, read with stock-broker Code of Conduct. The individuals were alleged to have front-run the Big Clients’ orders directly in the equity cash segment, violating Sections 12A(a)-(e) of the SEBI Act and Regulations 3(a)-(d), 4(1) and 4(2)(q) of the PFUTP Regulations, 2003. (iii) Money terms – Angel One paid only a settlement amount of ₹21,64,500; the individuals paid settlement amounts ranging from ₹55,90,000 to ₹64,29,371, plus disgorgement of ₹50,00,000 to ₹1,06,25,679.95 along with simple interest at 12% p.a. from the impugned transaction to the filing of the settlement application. (iv) Non-monetary terms – Angel One undertook only corrective measures with no debarment; the individuals undertook a six-month debarment/restraint from the securities market and association with listed entities/intermediaries.
review_notes: Both cited settlement orders support the four-way comparison: SCN dates/violation bases, money terms, and restraint/disgorgement outcomes. Teaches a distinct broker-vs-individual memory target.

question: Two groups applied to settle the same BKS front-running investigation in early 2024. Why did Angel One’s settlement close in September while the Kewalramani group’s settlement was not approved until November/December? Map the key procedural milestones (settlement-application filing, IC meeting, HPAC meeting, Whole-Time Member acceptance, and remittance) for each side.
answer_summary: Angel One filed a single settlement application (No. 7823/2024) on May 15, 2024. Its IC meeting took place on July 29, 2024, the HPAC considered it on August 14, 2024, the Panel of Whole Time Members accepted the settlement on September 12, 2024, and remittance was confirmed on September 23, 2024. The Kewalramani individuals filed four separate applications between March 18 and March 28, 2024, had IC meetings on July 16 and August 14, 2024, were placed before the HPAC on September 30, 2024, were accepted by the Panel on November 12, 2024, and completed payments/undertakings between November 26 and December 9, 2024 before the December 19 order. The individuals’ settlement took longer because it bundled six applicants with different settlement amounts and disgorgement figures, requiring coordinated HPAC consideration and separate undertakings, whereas Angel One was a single broker-level application with a modest settlement amount and no debarment undertakings.
review_notes: Procedural timeline and reasons for delay are directly supported by both settlement orders; genuinely multi-document because the closing rhythm differs across the two files.

question: Angel One Limited paid only a settlement amount of ₹21.64 lakh and faced neither disgorgement nor debarment. For the individual applicants settled on December 19, 2024, which applicants had both a settlement amount and a disgorgement component, which applicant’s disgorgement exceeded its settlement amount, and which individuals paid only a settlement amount plus debarment?
answer_summary: Applicants required to pay both a settlement amount and disgorgement were: Samir Kothari (settlement ₹57,20,000; disgorgement ₹50,00,000 plus 12% simple interest); Kuntal Goel (settlement ₹55,90,000; disgorgement ₹1,06,25,679.95 plus 12% simple interest); and Jitendra N. Kewalramani (settlement ₹64,29,371; disgorgement ₹50,00,000 plus 12% simple interest). Kuntal Goel’s disgorgement exceeded his settlement amount. Applicants paying only a settlement amount plus a six-month debarment undertaking were Jitendra N. Kewalramani HUF, Dipika J. Kewalramani and Pallavi Shailesh Nayak (each ₹57,20,000). Angel One, by contrast, paid ₹21,64,500 only and was not debarred.
review_notes: The individual settlement table lists amounts/debarment undertakings exactly as the answer states; Angel One doc supplies the contrasting baseline. Clear conditional extraction target.

question: In the October 2025 final order against the remaining family-trust front-running noticees, several argued that the charges should collapse because SEBI had already settled with the alleged main perpetrators (December 19, 2024) and with the broker Angel One (September 27, 2024). How did the quasi-judicial authority distinguish the two settlement orders, and why did it still impose penalties/restraint despite the disgorgement already paid?
answer_summary: The QJA noted that the December 19, 2024 settlement disposed of Noticee Nos. 1–5 and 25 (the main front-runners/info carrier and related parties) without admission/denial. It held that settlement of those named noticees does not automatically extinguish allegations against the remaining noticees, distinguishing Atlantaa Ltd. because the present case rested on individual acts rather than vicarious director liability. It further held that the Angel One broker settlement (September 27, 2024) was irrelevant to the personal liability of these remaining noticees. Because the alleged wrongful gains had already been disgorged through the December 19 settlement, the authority treated further disgorgement as infructuous, but it still imposed market restraints and monetary penalties on Noticee Nos. 6, 7, 8, 10, 12, 14, 15, 17, 19, 20, 21, 27 and 29 under Sections 11/11B of the SEBI Act and Section 15HA read with PFUTP Regulations.
review_notes: The October 2025 final order explicitly distinguishes the Dec 19 settlement and holds that the Angel One settlement has no relevance to the remaining noticees' individual liability; cites Atlantaa vicarious-liability distinction.

question: A VCF's real-estate scheme ultimately winds up about four years after its tenure expired, while a Category II AIF temporarily parks uninvested proceeds in a savings mutual fund instead of a liquid mutual fund and omits the lapse from its FY 2023-24 CTR. Both choose to settle without admitting SEBI's findings. What provisions did SEBI cite in each settlement order, and what were the settlement amounts?
answer_summary: SEBI cited Regulation 23(1)(a) read with Regulations 23(3) and 24(2) of the SEBI (Venture Capital Funds) Regulations, 1996 against ICICI Prudential Venture Capital Fund (and its investment manager and trustee), and the settlement amount was ₹14,35,500. For Unicorn India Ventures Debt Fund–I / Fund III, SEBI cited Regulation 15(1)(f), 20(1), 20(2) and 20(5) of the SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012, read with clauses 2(a) and 2(c) of the Code of Conduct in Schedule IV and Regulation 28 read with paragraph 15.2 of the Master Circular for AIFs dated May 7, 2024 (for the fund and manager; the key managerial personnel were cited for Regulation 15(1)(f), 20(1) and Code of Conduct clauses 2(a) and 2(c)), and the settlement amount was ₹25,50,000.
review_notes: Supported by both cited settlement orders. Distinct cross-regime comparison of a delayed VCF wind-up (Reg 23/24 VCF Regulations 1996; ₹14,35,500) and a Category II AIF's non-liquid temporary investment (Reg 15/20 AIF Regulations 2012 plus Code/Master Circular; ₹25,50,000). Each document is materially needed for the provisions and amounts.

question: SBICAP Trustee Company settled with SEBI twice: in June 2024 and again in March 2026. In tabular form, contrast the nature of the alleged breaches, the specific debenture-trustee provisions and circulars invoked, and the settlement amounts.
answer_summary: | Aspect | June 2024 settlement | March 2026 settlement | |---|---|---| | Core breach | Website/disclosure deficiencies: improper disclosure on Recovery Expense Fund, interest/redemption calendar, and asset-cover certificates. | Failure to create encumbrance on security receipts through the depository system for two NCD issuances of JM Financial Asset Reconstruction Company Limited; only a deed of hypothecation was executed and no holding statement was obtained from the depository participant. | | Provisions invoked | Regulation 16 read with Clauses 4 and 15 of Schedule III of the SEBI (Debenture Trustees) Regulations, 1993; circulars dated November 3, 2020, May 27, 2019 and November 12, 2020; Regulations 15(1)(b), 15(1)(s) and 16 read with Schedule III. | Regulation 16 of the SEBI (Debenture Trustees) Regulations, 1993 read with Clauses 1 and 4 of the Code of Conduct in Schedule III; Clause 2.1(g) and Clause 2.4 of the Master Circular for Debenture Trustees. | | Settlement amount | ₹25,08,000 | ₹23,45,000 |
review_notes: Supported by both cited SBICAP Trustee settlement orders. Clear same-entity temporal comparison: 2024 website-disclosure deficiencies (₹25,08,000) versus 2026 security-receipt encumbrance failure (₹23,45,000). Provisions and circulars align with the cited chunks.

question: Two SEBI-registered AIFs, a Category II debt fund and a Category III trust, each settled enforcement proceedings in April–May 2026. One allegedly retained penal exit loads from defaulting investors for the investment manager rather than crediting them to the scheme; the other temporarily invested un-invested proceeds in a savings mutual fund and failed to report it. Which AIF was accused of which conduct, what AIF Regulations provisions were invoked in each case, and what was the settlement amount?
answer_summary: The Category II AIF, Unicorn India Ventures Debt Fund–I / Unicorn India Ventures Fund III, was accused of deploying un-invested proceeds from May 15–24, 2023 in Aditya Birla Sun Life Savings Fund Regular Growth Plan (not a liquid mutual fund) and failing to disclose the breach in the FY 2023-24 Compliance Test Report. SEBI cited Regulation 15(1)(f), 20(1), 20(2) and 20(5) of the AIF Regulations read with Code of Conduct clauses and Regulation 28 read with the Master Circular for AIFs dated May 7, 2024; the settlement amount was ₹25,50,000. The Category III AIF, Motilal Oswal Alternative Investment Trust, was accused of retaining penal exit loads from 109 defaulting investors (₹8.69 crores, including taxes) instead of crediting them to the scheme, wrongly liquidating an investor's portfolio, lacking a distributor code-of-conduct framework, and not acting on distributor defaults/mis-selling. SEBI cited Regulations 20(1), 20(2), 20(3) and 24(a) of the AIF Regulations read with clauses 1(b), 2(a) and 2(d) of the Code of Conduct; the settlement amount was ₹38,76,000.
review_notes: Supported by the Unicorn India Ventures and Motilal Oswal settlement orders. Useful Category II vs Category III AIF conduct/provision/amount mapping. Though it overlaps Q01's Unicorn details, the memory target—category-specific misconduct and penalty amounts—is distinct.

question: In the SBICAP Trustee March 2026 settlement, SEBI's Internal Committee required the applicant to submit an action-taken report against officers-in-default. Before accepting the Unicorn India Ventures AIF summary settlement, what corrective step did SEBI note the AIF had already taken, and how did the nature of that step differ from the trustee's remedy?
answer_summary: In the SBICAP Trustee 2026 settlement, the Internal Committee specifically asked the applicant to submit an action-taken report against officers-in-default, and recommended settlement partly because the applicant had taken action against them. In contrast, the Unicorn India Ventures AIF itself rectified the incorrect deployment by reallocating the temporary investment from the savings mutual fund to a liquid mutual fund scheme, and SEBI noted that rectification in the order. The trustee's remedy was personnel-level disciplinary action, while the AIF's remedy was operational reallocation of the non-compliant deployment.
review_notes: Supported by the SBICAP Trustee 2026 order and the Unicorn India Ventures order. Teaches a distinct remedial-shape contrast: personnel-level action-taken report against officers-in-default versus operational reallocation from savings mutual fund to liquid mutual fund.

question: The same NFRA order against Aravind Maiya triggered both a settlement order against Embassy Office Parks Management Services in November 2025 and an adjudication order against Axis Trustee Services in April 2026. What facts formed the common basis of the two proceedings, and how did the final outcomes differ?
answer_summary: Both proceedings arose from the NFRA order dated August 19, 2024 finding Aravind Maiya guilty of professional misconduct, and the ensuing delays by the Embassy Office Parks REIT manager in disclosing the NFRA order and SEBI's assessment of Maiya's fitness to act as CEO to stock exchanges and unitholders. The Embassy manager resolved the matter through a settlement order dated November 17, 2025, paying Rs.18,39,825 without admitting or denying the alleged violations under Regulation 7(d) read with clauses 1, 2, 7 and 8 of Schedule VI and Regulation 10(14) of the REIT Regulations. Axis Trustee, as the REIT trustee, was adjudicated separately: SEBI held it failed in its independent oversight duties, including immediate disclosure/information to SEBI and an independent fit-and-proper assessment of Maiya, and imposed a monetary penalty of Rs.10,00,000 under Section 15HB of the SEBI Act.
review_notes: Supported by both cited orders: common NFRA-order nucleus, manager settlement for Rs.18,39,825 and trustee penalty of Rs.10,00,000. Strong parallel-case comparison.

question: A REIT trustee learns that the manager's CEO has been debarred from audit practice by the NFRA. Based on the SEBI orders in the Embassy Office Parks matter, what must the trustee do itself, and why does merely relying on the manager's own legal advice about the CEO's 'fit and proper' status amount to a breach?
answer_summary: The trustee must exercise independent and continuous oversight over the manager, ensure prompt compliance and disclosure to unitholders and stock exchanges, and independently assess the CEO against the fit-and-proper criteria in Schedule II of the SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations, 2008. In the Axis Trustee adjudication, SEBI rejected the argument that it could substitute the manager's legal opinions for its own assessment, observing that the trustee held meetings on October 15-16, 2024, nearly two months after the NFRA order, and failed to carry out an independent assessment despite SEBI's August 20, 2024 direction. The settlement order shows the manager itself had obtained legal opinions arguing fit-and-proper criteria did not apply and delayed disclosure of those opinions and of SEBI's October 8, 2024 letter stating Maiya was no longer fit and proper; the trustee's reliance on the manager's position duplicated that materially delayed approach rather than fulfilling its separate fiduciary duty.
review_notes: Cited chunks support the trustee's independent oversight duty and SEBI's rejection of substituting the manager's legal opinions. Distinct applied-compliance memory target.

question: Before the November 2025 settlement with Embassy Office Parks Management Services, SEBI passed an interim order in the same matter. What interim directions were given to the manager, and how did the later settlement and adjudication orders show whether the manager and trustee had independently addressed the fit-and-proper issue before SEBI intervened?
answer_summary: The interim order dated November 4, 2024 directed EOPMSPL to suspend Mr. Aravind Maiya from acting as its CEO and appoint an interim CEO with immediate effect, in compliance with applicable laws including fit-and-proper criteria, until further directions or until the NFRA Order was stayed/set aside, whichever was earlier; it also directed the manager to ensure compliance with fit-and-proper criteria generally. SEBI noted that, despite the August 20, 2024 communication and the manager's contrary legal opinions, more than a month had passed without compliance. The November 2025 settlement order disposed of the manager's proceedings on payment of Rs.18,39,825 under a settlement without admission/denial, implying the issue was ultimately not resolved through the manager's own assessment but through settlement. The April 2026 adjudication order separately found Axis Trustee had failed to carry out its own independent fit-and-proper assessment and disclosure obligations, confirming that both the manager and trustee had left the regulatory duty unresolved until SEBI stepped in.
review_notes: Interim order directions (suspend CEO, appoint interim CEO, ensure fit-and-proper) verified. Later settlement and adjudication orders confirm the issue was not resolved by the manager/trustee before SEBI intervened. Good lineage question.

question: SEBI issued ex-parte interim orders within months of each other against (i) unregistered online bond platforms, (ii) the Trafiksol ITS Technologies IPO, and (iii) Suumaya Industries and its promoters. Looking only at the interim orders, which one required an exchange to keep issue proceeds in an interest-bearing escrow account, and which two imposed either a simple cease-and-desist/market-access ban or an officer disqualification?
answer_summary: Only the Trafiksol IPO interim order directed BSE to keep the IPO proceeds in an interest-bearing escrow account and to deny Trafiksol and its affiliates access to the funds until further orders; it also blocked listing. The unregistered online bond platform order did not freeze escrowed proceeds but instead directed altGraaf, Tap Invest and Stable Investments to forthwith cease and desist from offering securities for public subscription and to preserve all records and communications since inception for inspection. The Suumaya interim order did neither: it restrained Ushik Gala from holding the position of director or KMP in any listed company or SEBI-registered intermediary, and restrained Noticee Nos. 2 to 5 from buying, selling or dealing in securities or accessing the capital market directly or indirectly until further orders.
review_notes: Verified: Trafiksol escrow/no access (chunks 14-15), OBPP cease/desist + record preservation (chunk 40), Suumaya director/KMP restraint and market-access ban (chunk 117). Three-way direction-type comparison is multi-document and distinct.

question: Both the unregistered online bond platform interim order and the Suumaya Industries interim order become effective immediately and give the notices 21 days to submit replies or seek a personal hearing. However, the Suumaya order is styled as an 'interim order cum show cause notice.' What extra show-cause burden is placed on the Suumaya noticees that is absent from the unregistered online bond platform order?
answer_summary: In addition to replying to the interim directions, Noticee Nos. 2 to 12 in the Suumaya matter are directed to show cause why suitable directions or prohibitions under sections 11(1), 11(4) and 11B(1) of the SEBI Act—including directions to bring back funds allegedly siphoned off and restraints on accessing the securities market or associating with listed companies and intermediaries—should not be issued against them. They must also show cause why an inquiry should not be held under rule 4 of the SEBI (Procedure for Holding Inquiry and Imposing Penalties) Rules, 1995 and why penalties should not be imposed under sections 11(4A) and 11B(2) of the SEBI Act. The unregistered online bond platform order is a plain interim ex-parte order: the notices may file reply/objections and ask for a hearing, but they are not simultaneously called upon to show cause against further directions or penalties.
review_notes: Verified: Suumaya 'interim order cum SCN' adds show-cause against further directions/penalties and rule 4 inquiry (chunks 117-120); OBPP is plain interim with reply/hearing only (chunks 40-41). Clear procedural-escalation contrast.

question: After the Trafiksol IPO interim order blocked the listing and locked the IPO proceeds in an interest-bearing escrow account, SEBI passed a later order to deal with the fact that investors' funds had been locked in for months. What sequence of steps did that later order prescribe for refunding investors and handling the shares already allotted to them?
answer_summary: The later order directed Trafiksol to refund the money paid by investors who had been allotted shares in the IPO. BSE, in coordination with the bankers to the issue, was to oversee the refund and ensure it was completed within one week. The interest earned on the issue proceeds under the interim order was to be refunded proportionately to investors. Once the money was credited to the applicants' bank accounts, the depositories were directed to transfer the IPO-allotted shares to a separate demat account opened in the Company's name, and the Company was directed to take appropriate steps to cancel those shares.
review_notes: Verified: interim escrow (chunks 14-15) plus final-order refund/cancellation sequence (chunks 40-41). Procedural-chain question across the two Trafiksol orders; distinct from other rows.

question: The frontier hint flags asset restraint, cessation and appointment of an independent auditor or monitoring agency as typical ex-parte interim directions. In the three orders against unregistered online bond platforms, Trafiksol and Suumaya, which matter involved a forensic accountant appointed during the investigation, which recorded a voluntary offer to appoint a monitoring agency, and which simply directed preservation of records for inspection?
answer_summary: The Suumaya matter involved the appointment of a Forensic Accountant and Investigator (FAI) by SEBI during the investigation; the FAI's report informed the interim order, but the appointment was not part of the interim directions. The Trafiksol interim order recorded that the company had consented to the appointment of a Monitoring Agency suggested by BSE to oversee the software procurement process, but this was a voluntary undertaking rather than a direction in the order itself. The unregistered online bond platform order contained neither an FAI nor a monitoring-agency appointment; it simply directed the platforms to preserve all records and communications from inception.
review_notes: Verified: Suumaya FAI appointment (chunk 9), Trafiksol voluntary Monitoring Agency consent (chunk 7), OBPP simple records preservation (chunk 40). Cross-document role/status mapping is distinct.

question: A compliance officer is reviewing two stock-broker adjudication orders that both arose from inspections and imposed penalties under section 15HB of the SEBI Act: Anand Rathi Shares and Stock Brokers Limited (March 2026) and Abhipra Capital Limited (March 2025). The former carried a penalty of ₹10 lakh, the latter a composite penalty of ₹8 lakh. In both orders the AO could not quantify a disproportionate gain or investor loss. What explains the higher penalty in the Anand Rathi order?
answer_summary: In the Anand Rathi order, the AO explicitly treated the broker’s status as a Qualified Stock Broker (QSB), the fact that it had been penalised earlier by SEBI, and the repetitive nature of some of the inspected violations as aggravating factors; these moved the calibrated penalty upward even though no quantifiable gain or loss could be shown under section 15J. In contrast, the Abhipra AO accepted that the violations were first-time/non-repetitive, noted the broker’s argument (and the existence) of earlier exchange fines for overlapping observations as a mitigating factor, and therefore moderated the composite penalty to ₹8 lakh split across three separate provisions (₹5 lakh under 15HB, ₹1 lakh under 15A(c), ₹2 lakh under section 23D of the SCRA).
review_notes: Penalty-quantum factors directly supported: Anand Rathi AO cites QSB status, prior SEBI penalty and repetitive violations (clf-rou8wpyfvbj7f0fvoxm8oh63#106-107); Abhipra AO treats exchange fines as mitigating, finds no repetition and splits ₹8 lakh across 15HB/15A(c)/23D (clf-tlivzagtesp1k13wldl81srk#172,#180,#182).

question: A junior associate notices that the Abhipra Capital adjudication order imposed separate penalties under section 23D of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act and section 15A(c) of the SEBI Act, while the Anand Rathi and Fourdegreewater stock-broker orders were penalised only under section 15HB. Which concrete deficiency drove the section 23D charge, and why did the other two orders not need it?
answer_summary: Section 23D punishes a stock broker’s failure to segregate securities or moneys of a client, or use of a client’s securities/moneys for itself or another client. In Abhipra, the AO established that the broker failed to segregate client funds from own funds, transferred funds 212 times between the client/settlement bank account and its own bank account without daily reconciliation to justify the purpose, and failed to do actual settlement for inactive clients. Because this was a client-money/segregation failure, section 23D was directly attracted. The Anand Rathi order concerned cyber-resilience, capacity planning, BCP/DR, DLP, incident-reporting and API-segregation failures; none of those findings involved misuse or non-segregation of client money, so section 15HB was sufficient. Likewise, the Fourdegreewater order dealt with an OBPP routing trades outside the RFQ platform and failing to comply with the stock-broker code of conduct, again not a client-fund segregation issue, so only section 15HB applied.
review_notes: Section 23D charge is grounded in Abhipra's client-fund segregation failure and 212 un-reconciled transfers (clf-tlivzagtesp1k13wldl81srk#32,#113,#176); Anand Rathi and Fourdegreewater orders concerned cyber/API/VAPT and RFQ/OBPP routing respectively, so only 15HB applied.

question: A broker receives a thematic inspection report alleging procedural lapses in client and authorised-person onboarding, and wants to know whether every inspection finding ends in a monetary penalty. The Jainam Broking and Ortem Securities adjudication orders both followed stock-broker inspections, yet Jainam was discharged without penalty while Ortem was fined ₹3 lakh. What materially separates the two outcomes?
