answer_summary: Jainam’s lapses were held to be largely procedural: it initially submitted excess and inaccurate client-onboarding data but corrected it promptly, and it placed the administrative warning before its Board but erroneously forwarded the Board resolution to BSE rather than SEBI. Because the data discrepancy was resolved and no malafide intent was found, the AO disposed of the SCN without penalty. Ortem’s authorised-person inspection, by contrast, revealed substantive governance failures: an AP’s terminals were operated by employees of an unapproved entity (Twinkle Stock Consultants) with whom the registered AP had no agreement; the broker had not inspected that AP for three years; pre-order trade confirmations were not maintained; and the AP’s notice board displayed misleading information. Since the Master Circular makes the stock broker responsible for acts and omissions of its authorised persons, these core control breaches warranted a ₹3 lakh penalty.
review_notes: Jainam's data errors and BSE-forwarded Board resolution are treated as procedural and no malafide is found (clf-u44t9631ofkc7co45oq6e1xm#21,#24,#27). Ortem's AP-terminal misuse by Twinkle employees, missed AP inspections, missing pre-order confirmations and misleading notice Board are substantive control breaches warranting ₹3 lakh (clf-bn3tkoeh6eto4mklig8b8rdb#13,#17,#20,#23,#25,#29).

question: A compliance head wants to know when an individual director or officer, rather than only the broker company, will be personally penalised for an inspection finding. Comparing the Fourdegreewater OBPP order and the Ortem Securities authorised-person order, what principle governs personal liability for inspection lapses?
answer_summary: The two orders show that personal liability in an inspection-based AO is not automatic; it requires evidence of the individual’s active involvement in the violation. In Fourdegreewater, noticees 2-5 (directors/officers) were proceeded against but ultimately discharged because the AO found no evidence linking them actively to the non-RFQ routing, relying on SAT precedent that mere directorship does not make a person liable. In Ortem, the AO proceeded only against the company, not against individuals, but still grounded corporate liability on Clause 32.7.1 of the SEBI Master Circular for Stock Brokers, which makes the broker responsible for the acts and omissions of its authorised persons. The combined reading is: the broker entity is accountable for the conduct of its APs and platform operations, while directors/officers attract personal AO penalties only when they are shown to have played an active role in the breach, not merely by virtue of their position.
review_notes: Fourdegreewater directors were discharged for lack of active involvement in non-RFQ routing, citing SAT precedent that mere directorship is insufficient (clf-s4sicfmu7od06hem41nkv22v#72,#74); Ortem's corporate liability rests on Master Circular clause 32.7.1 making the broker responsible for AP acts/omissions (clf-bn3tkoeh6eto4mklig8b8rdb#25,#29).

question: Both the Anand Rathi (January 2025 cyber thematic) and Abhipra Capital (joint 2022) inspections faulted data-security and cyber-resilience controls. What control or evidence gap was common to both orders, and what made the Anand Rathi situation materially worse than Abhipra’s?
answer_summary: Both orders found that the broker lacked adequate data loss prevention (DLP) arrangements and could not prove effective data-security controls during the inspection period: Anand Rathi could not establish that a live DLP solution existed during the inspection period; Abhipra had no documented DLP policy/procedure and lacked evident encryption for data at rest, among other cyber-resilience deficiencies. What made Anand Rathi graver was that the same porous boundary allowed an API meant for stockbroking KYC to be used for the mutual-fund distribution vertical without VAPT coverage. That cross-vertical reuse of the API facilitated an unauthorised access/data-breach incident in late September 2024; the broker also delayed reporting the incident to exchanges beyond six hours, failed to segregate stockbroking activities from other activities, and relied on post-inspection corrective evidence. The AO therefore treated the case as involving not merely missing documentation but an exploited control gap affecting investor data.
review_notes: Both orders fault DLP absence: Anand Rathi could not show a live DLP during inspection (clf-rou8wpyfvbj7f0fvoxm8oh63#48,#51) and Abhipra lacked documented DLP policy/procedure and evident encryption (clf-tlivzagtesp1k13wldl81srk#164). Anand Rathi's cross-use of a stockbroking KYC API for MFD without VAPT coverage, the September 2024 breach and delayed >6-hour reporting to exchanges are supported by clf-rou8wpyfvbj7f0fvoxm8oh63#80-81,#85,#89-92.

question: In the Shares Bazaar AIF matter, what directions did SEBI impose in its February 2024 interim ex parte order, and which of those directions were preserved in the October 2024 confirmatory order?
answer_summary: The interim ex parte order dated February 1, 2024 restrained Shares Bazaar AIF from taking fresh commitments or investments, from drawing down funds already committed, and required it to immediately inform existing and prospective investors about the directions. It also directed custodian Orbis Financial Corporation not to permit debit or credit transactions in the AIF’s trading, demat and bank accounts (clf-kxl3s94aoscqd8haeals0uf0#31, #32). The confirmatory order dated October 30, 2024 confirmed all these directions of the interim order without modification and kept them in force pending further investigation (clf-h28j24d8azke4fehf09zie6n#43, #44).
review_notes: Interim directions and their confirmatory preservation are directly supported by the cited chunks; solid multi-document lineage question.

question: Shares Bazaar AIF argued that the investigation report underlying the interim directions only recommended action against SBPL and not against the AIF. How did SEBI justify continuing the directions against the AIF itself?
answer_summary: SEBI distinguished between the examination report, which was a fact-finding exercise into SBPL’s unauthorised money mobilisation as a research analyst, and the interim proceedings against Shares Bazaar AIF for procuring registration through misrepresentation and against SBPL as the AIF’s manager-cum-sponsor (clf-h28j24d8azke4fehf09zie6n#25, #26). Because the AIF’s registration was obtained by concealing SBPL’s BSE expulsion and submitting a false declaration, allowing the AIF to keep mobilising funds would harm investors and market integrity. The need to prevent that harm justified the directions against the AIF (clf-kxl3s94aoscqd8haeals0uf0#29, #30).
review_notes: Confirmatory order distinguishes the SBPL examination report from the AIF misrepresentation proceedings; interim order supports the investor-harm rationale.

question: SBPL told SEBI that the money it collected was from subscriptions to compulsorily convertible debentures rather than an assured-return PMS scheme. What evidence across the interim and confirmatory orders led SEBI to reject that explanation?
answer_summary: The interim order pointed to SBPL’s ICICI Bank account 7777XXX9202, which contained narrations such as "PMS", "Referral" and "Dividend" and showed funds being used either to pay off earlier investors in the MMFF scheme or to finance sister company Kisaan Parivar Private Limited, prompting SEBI to refer the matter to the Economic Offences Wing as a suspected Ponzi/multi-level marketing scheme (clf-kxl3s94aoscqd8haeals0uf0#7, #29). The confirmatory order added that the CCD board resolution was dated October 6, 2023 while the debenture certificate was issued December 20, 2022; that funds were collected from March 2021 to October 2022, long before the claimed CCD issuance; that a July 2022 service agreement carried a SBPL director’s signature after the ex-CEO’s removal; and that none of the investors SEBI contacted spoke of CCD subscriptions (clf-h28j24d8azke4fehf09zie6n#33, #34, #36, #37).
review_notes: CCD-subscription defence is refuted by date mismatches, bank narrations, and investor evidence across the interim and confirmatory orders.

question: While the interim and confirmatory orders were restraining Shares Bazaar AIF, what penalties did the Adjudicating Officer impose on Beacon Trusteeship and SKI Capital in November 2024, and how did those penalties complement the earlier directions?
answer_summary: The Adjudication order dated November 28, 2024 imposed a total penalty of ₹5,00,000 on Beacon Trusteeship — ₹2,00,000 under Section 15EA and ₹3,00,000 under Section 15HB of the SEBI Act — and ₹3,00,000 on SKI Capital under Section 15HB of the SEBI Act (clf-h6mqoskluijw5n8m36bcb81g#62). Beacon, the trustee, was penalised for failing to independently verify SBPL’s disciplinary history and for issuing a fit-and-proper undertaking that pre-dated SKI’s due diligence certificate; SKI, the merchant banker, was penalised for failing to independently exercise due diligence over the PPM disclosures (clf-h6mqoskluijw5n8m36bcb81g#34, #35, #60). These monetary penalties complemented, rather than replaced, the ongoing operational freeze on the AIF ordered earlier by the Whole-Time Member (clf-h28j24d8azke4fehf09zie6n#44).
review_notes: AO penalty amounts and statutory mapping are confirmed by the cited penalty table; Beacon/SKI due-diligence findings are supported elsewhere in the AO.

question: Beacon Trusteeship defended itself by saying it had relied on SKI Capital’s due diligence certificate and performed KYC, audit and constitution-document checks when declaring SBPL fit and proper. How did the Adjudicating Officer reject that argument?
answer_summary: The AO noted a timing defect: Beacon’s fit-and-proper undertaking was dated March 15, 2023, while SKI’s revised due diligence certificate was dated March 27, 2023, so Beacon could not have relied on the revised certificate (clf-h6mqoskluijw5n8m36bcb81g#34, #35). It also held that a trustee has an independent statutory duty under Clause 3(b) of Schedule IV of the AIF Regulations and Clause 13.2.2(ii) of the SEBI Master Circular read with Regulations 20(1) and 20(2) to exercise independent due diligence and professional judgment, and cannot discharge that duty by relying on the fund manager or merchant banker (clf-h6mqoskluijw5n8m36bcb81g#36, #60). The confirmatory order had earlier clarified that due diligence lapses by the trustee and merchant banker would not cure SBPL’s unfitness, but SEBI reserved the right to proceed against every entity involved in the misrepresentation (clf-h28j24d8azke4fehf09zie6n#41).
review_notes: Timing defect and independent statutory-duty rejection are directly supported; confirmatory order preserves action against all involved entities.

question: SBPL was expelled by BSE as a trading member in December 2022. Trace the distinct regulatory consequences that flowed from that single expulsion for SBPL and for Shares Bazaar AIF through to November 2024.
answer_summary: The BSE expulsion of SBPL on December 30, 2022 produced two linked enforcement tracks. First, because a stock broker must hold stock-exchange membership, SEBI cancelled SBPL’s stock-broker registration on July 31, 2024 under Section 12(3) of the SEBI Act read with Regulation 30A of the Intermediaries Regulations (clf-da1ew6zdc3oqbh0foscj8oi6#10, #11). Second, SBPL concealed that expulsion when acting as sponsor/manager of Shares Bazaar AIF. The AIF obtained SEBI registration in April 2023, but after the truth surfaced SEBI issued an interim ex parte order on February 1, 2024 freezing new commitments, drawdowns and custodian account movements, confirmed those directions on October 30, 2024 (clf-kxl3s94aoscqd8haeals0uf0#31, #32; clf-h28j24d8azke4fehf09zie6n#43, #44). Finally, on November 28, 2024, the AO penalised Beacon Trusteeship and SKI Capital for deficient due diligence in the same registration (clf-h6mqoskluijw5n8m36bcb81g#62).
review_notes: Two linked enforcement tracks from the BSE expulsion are traced across all four cited documents; AIF registration date is accurate but sourced from a non-cited chunk.

question: SEBI took enforcement action against two AMCs for distinct control failures. In the L&T Mutual Fund matter, SEBI issued a Chairperson/Member order imposing a monetary penalty; in the Axis Asset Management matter, SEBI accepted a suo motu settlement. What was the key procedural difference in how the L&T case reached the final order compared with the Axis case, and which document type did SEBI rely on in the Axis case that had no equivalent in the L&T case?
answer_summary: In the L&T matter, the final Chairperson/Member order was passed under subsection (3) of section 15-I of the SEBI Act as a revision of an exonerating Adjudicating Officer order dated August 23, 2023, and it was not a settlement. In the Axis matter, the applicants filed suo motu settlement applications under the SEBI (Settlement Proceedings) Regulations, 2018, neither admitting nor denying the findings. SEBI relied on forensic reports by Alvarez & Marshal India, Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu India and BDO India, and on an ad interim ex-parte order dated February 28, 2023, in the Axis case; no forensic report or interim order is referenced in the L&T inspection order.
review_notes: Both cited chunks support: L&T Chairperson order was passed under s.15-I(3) revising the AO's exonerating order and imposed penalty under s.15HB; Axis was a suo motu settlement, neither-admit-nor-deny, relying on forensic reports and an ad interim ex-parte order absent from the L&T file.

question: Axis Asset Management Company appeared in two SEBI settlement orders within five months: one in November 2024 for charging TER to AMC books, and another in March 2025 for dealing-room and front-running allegations. How did the two settlements differ in (a) the number and composition of applicants, (b) the settlement amount, and (c) the source of evidence?
answer_summary: (a) The November 2024 TER settlement had two corporate applicants—Axis AMC and Axis Mutual Fund Trustee—and was settled for Rs. 16,57,500. The March 2025 settlement had six applicants—the AMC, trustee and four named individuals (Chandresh Kumar Nigam, Darshan Kapadia, Jinesh Gopani and Pawan Jhangiani)—and was settled for Rs. 6,27,30,000 jointly and severally. (b) The March 2025 amount was roughly 37.9 times the November 2024 amount. (c) The March 2025 order explicitly cites forensic reports by Alvarez & Marshal, Deloitte and BDO and an ad interim ex-parte order dated February 28, 2023; the November 2024 TER settlement refers to a show cause notice dated March 22, 2024 and pending adjudication proceedings under section 15E/15HB.
review_notes: Intra-AMC contrast supported: Nov-2024 TER settlement had 2 corporate applicants and Rs.16,57,500 tied to SCN dated Mar 22, 2024 / pending adjudication; Mar-2025 dealing-room settlement had 6 applicants (AMC, trustee, 4 individuals), Rs.6,27,30,000 jointly and severally, with forensic reports and interim order as evidence sources.

question: Three AMCs—Groww, Navi and Nippon Life India—faced SEBI action over mutual-fund expenses booked to the AMC rather than to the scheme. Which of these matters ended by adjudication rather than settlement, and which settlement involved expenses that had breached the 2-basis-point-of-AUM Grey-list cap?
answer_summary: The Nippon Life India matter ended by adjudication: the Adjudicating Officer imposed Rs. 2 lakh on the AMC under section 15E and Rs. 1 lakh on the trustee under section 15HB of the SEBI Act. The Groww and Navi matters ended by settlement. Of those, the Navi settlement specifically involved scheme-related expenses that exceeded the permissible limit of 2 basis points of the respective scheme's AUM for FY 2024-25 under Regulation 52(1) read with para 10.1.12 of the SEBI Master Circular. Groww's settlement concerned scheme expenses paid by the AMC instead of from the scheme during April 2020 to March 2022, but did not invoke the 2 bps Grey-list cap.
review_notes: Three-way expense cluster verified: Nippon ended by adjudication (Rs.2 lakh on AMC under s.15E and Rs.1 lakh on trustee under s.15HB); Groww and Navi ended by settlement; Navi specifically concerned expenses exceeding the 2-bps-of-AUM Grey-list cap under Reg.52(1) read with the Master Circular.

question: If an AMC does not pay the monetary outcome imposed in the L&T Mutual Fund Chairperson/Member order on time, what can SEBI do? If, instead, the representations made by the applicants in the Axis March 2025 settlement are later found to be untrue, what can SEBI do?
answer_summary: Under the L&T Chairperson/Member order, if the Rs. 5 lakh penalty is not paid within 45 days of receipt, SEBI may initiate consequential proceedings, including recovery proceedings under section 28A of the SEBI Act, for realisation of the penalty with interest, by attachment and sale of movable and immovable properties. Under the Axis March 2025 settlement, if any representation made by the applicants is later found untrue, or if they breach undertakings/waivers, or if there was a discrepancy in computing the settlement terms, SEBI may initiate appropriate action under Regulations 28 and 31 of the Settlement Regulations; this allows enforcement action to be revived despite the settlement.
review_notes: L&T order para 59 confirms recovery proceedings under s.28A if the Rs.5 lakh penalty is not paid within 45 days; Axis settlement clause confirms revival action under Regulations 28 and 31 if representations are untrue or undertakings breached.

question: The Navi, Groww and Axis March 2025 settlements all resolved potential enforcement proceedings on a 'neither admit nor deny' basis. Beyond paying money, what identical protective clause did SEBI retain in each order, and how did the Axis settlement differ structurally in the number of parties bound?
answer_summary: Each settlement order reserved SEBI's right to initiate appropriate action if any representation was later found untrue, if undertakings or waivers were breached, or if there was a discrepancy in computing the settlement terms (under Regulations 28 and, where cited, 31 of the Settlement Regulations). Structurally, the Axis March 2025 settlement bound six applicants—the AMC, trustee and four named individuals—jointly and severally, whereas the Navi and Groww settlements each bound only two corporate applicants (AMC and trustee) jointly and severally.
review_notes: Identical protective clause verified in all three settlement orders (SEBI may act if representations untrue, undertakings/waivers breached, or discrepancy in settlement computation). Axis bound six applicants jointly and severally; Navi and Groww each bound two corporate applicants.

question: What statutory provisions powered the final order in the L&T Mutual Fund inspection matter, and how did that differ from the statutory basis of the Axis March 2025 settlement and the Nippon TER adjudication?
answer_summary: In the L&T matter, the Chairperson/Member passed the final order under subsection (3) of section 15-I of the SEBI Act, 1992 (review of the Adjudicating Officer's exonerating order) and imposed the monetary penalty under section 15HB. In the Axis March 2025 matter, the settlement was passed under section 15JB read with section 19 of the SEBI Act and in terms of Regulation 23 of the SEBI (Settlement Proceedings) Regulations, 2018. In the Nippon matter, the Adjudicating Officer imposed penalty under section 15E of the SEBI Act on the AMC and under section 15HB on the trustee, following an inquiry under section 15-I read with Rule 5 of the Adjudication Rules, 1995.
review_notes: Statutory bases verified: L&T final order under s.15-I(3) with penalty under s.15HB; Axis settlement under s.15JB read with s.19 and Reg.23 of the Settlement Regulations; Nippon inquiry under s.15-I read with Rule 5, penalties under s.15E (AMC) and s.15HB (trustee).

question: A compliance officer at Orbis Financial asks why SEBI settled with the custodian for deficiencies found in the FY 2021-22 inspection but pursued a full adjudication against AIRD Investment Commercial LLC over the same period. What common deficiency linked the two matters, and how did the final outcomes differ in amount, form and continuing obligations?
answer_summary: Both matters originated from SEBI’s FY 2021-22 inspection of Orbis Financial, which found, among other things, that Orbis failed to monitor FPI investments in debt instruments and made incorrect submissions. SEBI separately examined AIRD and held that it held short-term G-Secs above the 30% RBI limit for 562 days. Orbis settled the custodian-inspection proceeding for ₹1,59,25,000 under Section 15JB read with Regulation 23 of the Settlement Regulations, submitted a process note/undertaking on monitoring debt limits under Regulation 25(2)(b) of the FPI Regulations read with Clause 9 of Part C of the Operational Guidelines and RBI Circular RBI/2017-18/199, and the order is without prejudice to SEBI action for untrue disclosures or breach. AIRD was adjudicated to pay ₹20,00,000 under Section 15HB of the SEBI Act, with 45 days to pay or face recovery under Section 28A.
review_notes: Common Orbis FY 2021-22 deficiency in monitoring FPI debt investments is cited in both docs; Orbis settled for INR 1,59,25,000 under Section 15JB/Regulation 23 with a corrective process note and undertaking, while AIRD was adjudicated INR 20,00,000 under Section 15HB with 45 days to pay.

question: On the same day, SEBI passed adjudication orders against AIRD Investment Commercial LLC and Aviator Global Investment Fund for breaching the RBI short-term debt-investment limit for FPIs. Aviator argued its case differed materially from AIRD’s. What was that argument, why did the Adjudicating Officer reject it, and how did the penalties reflect the factual difference?
answer_summary: Aviator contended that SEBI had overlooked its non-dematerialised debt holdings and that, once those were included, its short-term exposure would have been below 30%. It also argued the investments were long-term when made and became "short term" only as redemption approached. The AO rejected the argument because, even after accepting Aviator’s revised holdings, the non-compliance persisted for 373 days, and the RBI circular’s residual-maturity test looks at maturity at the relevant date, not intent at purchase. AIRD did not dispute the calculation, simply pleaded oversight, and was non-compliant for 562 days. The penalty on AIRD was ₹20,00,000; on Aviator, ₹10,00,000—reflecting the shorter duration and Aviator’s partially successful factual challenge.
review_notes: Aviator's non-dematerialised-holdings and long-term-intent defenses, the AO's residual-maturity rejection, the 373-day vs 562-day durations, and the INR 10,00,000 vs INR 20,00,000 penalties are all supported by the cited chunks.

question: A fund-of-funds manager compares the ACACIA Group settlement with the DDP eligibility-criteria settlement. Leaving aside that one involves FPIs and the other their DDPs, how do the underlying compliance failures and the duration of the breaches differ?
answer_summary: The ACACIA settlement involved six related FPIs that failed to disclose Conifer Capital Management and Gregory Alexander as the beneficial-owner-by-control, submitted revised BO declarations only in August 2023, and thereby breached the 10% equity-limit in McDowell Holdings from 17 October 2014 until the holding fell below 10% on 22 August 2024—more than nine years. The DDP settlement involved Deutsche Bank, HSBC, HDFC Bank and Citi Bank granting registration, renewal, or transaction permission to FPIs that were ineligible under the FPI Regulations, violating Regulations 4(d), 4(e) and 4(f); the order frames this as intermediary due-diligence failures rather than a continuing single-stock breach.
review_notes: ACACIA involved undisclosed Conifer/Gregory Alexander BO-by-control and a roughly nine-year 10% McDowell equity-limit breach; the DDP settlement involved banks registering or transacting ineligible FPIs under Regulations 4(d)-(f), framed as intermediary due-diligence failures.

question: An analyst predicts that penalties for letting ineligible FPIs register and for breaching the short-term debt limit are imposed under entirely different SEBI Act provisions. Is the analyst right? Which statutory provision appears in both enforcement streams, and which FPI-Regulation provisions are specific to each?
answer_summary: The analyst is wrong. Both streams reference Section 15HB of the SEBI Act as the penalty provision: the DDP proceedings were initiated under Section 15HB (and disposed of through settlement under Section 15JB read with Regulation 23 of the Settlement Regulations), and AIRD was adjudged to pay ₹20,00,000 under Section 15HB. The FPI-Regulation provision specific to the DDP eligibility case is Regulations 4(d), 4(e) and 4(f). The provision specific to AIRD’s debt breach is Regulation 20(5) read with Clause 9 of Part C of the Master Circular for FPIs and DDPs dated December 19, 2022 and RBI Circular RBI/2017-18/199 dated June 15, 2018.
review_notes: Both enforcement streams reference Section 15HB (DDP settlement disposed under Section 15JB/Regulation 23 after 15HB initiation, AIRD adjudged under 15HB). Stream-specific provisions (Regulation 4(d)-(f) for DDPs; Regulation 20(5) read with Master Circular Clause 9 Part C and RBI circular for AIRD) are supported.

question: After publishing the adjudication order against AIRD Investment Commercial LLC, SEBI issued a one-page corrigendum. What did it correct, and why must the order be read together with the corrigendum?
answer_summary: The corrigendum corrected the noticee’s PAN. The adjudication order had stated the PAN as "AAOC A8357P"; the corrigendum clarified it should read "AASCA9404H". It expressly states that the adjudication order "shall always be read with this Corrigendum" and that the rest of the order remains unchanged, so the enforceable identity of the noticee is only accurate from both documents together.
review_notes: Corrigendum corrects the noticee PAN from AAOC A8357P to AASCA9404H and states the AIRD order must be read with it.

question: An FPI believes that because its custodian tracks holdings, any breach of the 30% short-term G-Sec cap is primarily the custodian’s fault. Using the AIRD adjudication and the Orbis custodian settlement, explain where SEBI places responsibility for the limit and whether the custodian can still face separate action.
answer_summary: The AIRD adjudication holds that Regulation 20 of the FPI Regulations places the onus on the FPI itself to adhere to debt-investment norms; AIRD’s plea that it relied on Orbis to monitor limits was rejected because the FPI is the registered intermediary. Separately, the Orbis custodian settlement shows a custodian can be punished for its own failure to monitor FPI debt investments: Orbis settled for ₹1,59,25,000 and submitted a process note and undertaking setting out how it would monitor compliance with Regulation 25(2)(b) read with Clause 9 of Part C and RBI Circular RBI/2017-18/199. Thus, the FPI is primarily liable for respecting the limit, while the custodian has a distinct monitoring duty and can be separately sanctioned.
review_notes: AIRD order puts statutory onus on the FPI under Regulation 20 and rejects reliance on the custodian; the separate Orbis settlement confirms a custodian can be sanctioned for failing to monitor FPI debt investments.

question: A regulatory analyst is comparing how SEBI resolved recent enforcement actions against three market infrastructure institutions: National Stock Exchange of India Limited (NSEIL), Multi Commodity Exchange Clearing Corporation Limited (MXCCL), and NSE Clearing Corporation Limited. For each settlement, what was the inspection/examination period, the core alleged deficiency, the final settlement amount, and whether SEBI imposed additional non-monetary or corrective conditions?
answer_summary: The three settlements can be compared as follows: 1. NSEIL — Inspection period February 01, 2021 to March 31, 2022. The order lists seven operational/surveillance deficiencies, including outsourcing of media-tape storage without a contract, waiver of MCSGFC penalties by an internal committee, sharing confidential/price-sensitive information with NSE Data & Analytics Limited for onward distribution, permitting client-code modifications without due diligence, lacking a policy on frequent broker modifiers, failing to review error trades, and failing to verify genuineness of client-code changes. Settlement amount: ₹40,35,00,000. SEBI also required a system audit report, a compliance report on corrective measures, and an internal review to identify officers-in-default and take performance-appraisal measures (originally six months, extended by six months). 2. MXCCL — Annual inspection period December 01, 2022 to October 31, 2023. The alleged violation was that MXCCL blocked the highest margin shortfall instead of the cumulative margin shortfall over the previous 30 days when calculating the Margin Shortfall Block Amount, contrary to SEBI Circular dated September 01, 2016 read with the Master Circular dated August 04, 2023 and Regulation 7(4)(b) of the SECC Regulations, 2018. Settlement amount: ₹2,70,00,000. The order records only the standard settlement-payment and without-prejudice terms, not additional non-monetary corrective conditions. 3. NSE Clearing Corporation — Examination of interoperability-framework compliance. The alleged violations were failure to maintain sufficient Inter-CCP collateral from Indian Clearing Corporation Limited and failure to comply with provisions of the Inter-CCP agreement. Settlement amount: ₹27,13,10,000, split as ₹23,75,00,000 for the collateral shortfall and ₹3,38,10,000 for the agreement-compliance failure. The applicant reported subsequent corrective/remedial measures, but the order does not prescribe the kind of officer-default review imposed on NSEIL.
review_notes: Full three-way table supported by all three settlement orders (NSEIL chunks 0-7, MXCCL chunks 0-5, NSE Clearing chunks 0-5). Teaches distinct corpus-wide comparator target.

question: Only one of these three MII settlement orders — NSEIL, MXCCL, or NSE Clearing Corporation — imposed a specific post-settlement personnel-accountability condition beyond the ordinary settlement payment and without-prejudice terms. Which entity was it, what was the condition, and how long did SEBI allow to complete it?
answer_summary: NSEIL. The High Powered Advisory Committee recommended, and the Panel of Whole Time Members approved, that NSEIL be advised to conduct an internal review to identify the officers-in-default and take appropriate measures in their performance appraisals. This review was to be completed within six months; SEBI later extended this by another six months. NSEIL's Internal Disciplinary Committee eventually concluded that the decisions were taken at the organisational/Board level and no specific individual was found accountable, a finding approved by the Nomination and Remuneration Committee and the Board. MXCCL's order and NSE Clearing Corporation's order do not contain comparable officer-specific personnel terms.
review_notes: Negative check verified: only NSEIL order imposes the officer-in-default review/performance-appraisal condition (chunks 7-8 of NSEIL); MXCCL and NSE Clearing lack comparable personnel terms.

question: Both MXCCL and NSE Clearing Corporation settled alleged risk-management failures. One order states a single consolidated settlement amount; the other breaks the settlement amount into two line items tied to specific violations. Which clearing corporation is which, and what are the two line-item amounts in the split settlement?
answer_summary: MXCCL's settlement records a single consolidated amount of ₹2,70,00,000. NSE Clearing Corporation's settlement splits the amount: ₹23,75,00,000 for failure to maintain sufficient Inter-CCP collateral from Indian Clearing Corporation Limited, and ₹3,38,10,000 for failure to comply with various provisions of the Inter-CCP agreement, totaling ₹27,13,10,000.
review_notes: Amount-reconciliation target supported by MXCCL (single ₹2.70cr, chunk 3) and NSE Clearing (split ₹23.75cr/₹3.38cr, chunk 4). Both documents materially needed to contrast.

question: Two of the three settlements involve clearing corporations, but only one cites Indian Clearing Corporation Limited (ICCL) and the Inter-CCP agreement dated June 01, 2019. Which settlement is it, and alongside that agreement, which SEBI circular lays down the interoperability framework for the alleged violation?
answer_summary: NSE Clearing Corporation Limited's settlement cites ICCL and the Inter-CCP agreement dated June 01, 2019. The cited SEBI circular laying down the interoperability framework is the circular dated November 27, 2018. MXCCL, the commodity clearing corporation, instead bases its alleged violation on the SEBI Circular on 'Additional risk management norms for National Commodity Derivatives Exchanges' dated September 01, 2016 read with the Master Circular dated August 04, 2023.
review_notes: Entity/statutory-citation disambiguation matched: NSE Clearing cites ICCL, Inter-CCP agreement 01-Jun-2019 and SEBI circular 27-Nov-2018 (chunks 0-1); MXCCL uses commodity margin circular 01-Sep-2016 (chunks 0-1).

question: The NSEIL and MXCCL settlements arose from SEBI inspections covering specific periods, while the NSE Clearing Corporation settlement arose from an examination framed differently. State the inspection/examination label and period for each of the three settlements, and identify which specific external entity (other than the applicant) appears in the NSE Clearing Corporation allegations.
answer_summary: NSEIL: Inspection of NSEIL for the period February 01, 2021 to March 31, 2022. MXCCL: Annual inspection for the period December 01, 2022 to October 31, 2023. NSE Clearing Corporation: Examination to check whether NSE Clearing Corporation Limited was ensuring compliance with SEBI norms and the provisions of the Interoperability Agreement; the period of alleged deficiency is not expressed as a bounded inspection window in the settlement order. The external entity named in the NSE Clearing Corporation allegations is Indian Clearing Corporation Limited (ICCL), from which the applicant allegedly failed to maintain sufficient Inter-CCP collateral.
review_notes: Inspection/examination origins confirmed across all three orders (NSEIL chunk 0, MXCCL chunks 0-1, NSE Clearing chunk 0) and external entity ICCL identified for NSE Clearing.

question: A compliance officer is preparing a note showing which of these MII settlements were preceded by a formal Show Cause Notice. Among NSEIL, MXCCL and NSE Clearing Corporation, which one had a Show Cause Notice served before settlement, and what was its date?
answer_summary: Only NSE Clearing Corporation had a formal Show Cause Notice served before settlement — SCN dated November 21, 2023. The NSEIL and MXCCL settlement orders describe the applicants filing suo-motu settlement applications before any enforcement proceedings were initiated, and neither order records a prior Show Cause Notice.
review_notes: Absence/procedural-timeline check supported: NSE Clearing SCN dated 21-Nov-2023 (chunk 0-2); NSEIL and MXCCL orders describe suo-motu settlement applications without prior SCN.

question: Three SEBI settlement orders in 2025-26 involved JP Morgan Chase Bank N.A., Fino Payments Bank Limited and Citicorp Investment Bank (Singapore) Limited – ODI. Which applicant paid the smallest settlement amount, which paid the largest, and how did the regulatory regime underpinning the Fino charges differ from that of the other two?
answer_summary: Fino Payments Bank paid the smallest amount, ₹5,88,921.45, while Citicorp Investment Bank (Singapore) Limited – ODI paid the largest, ₹36,00,000. JP Morgan Chase Bank N.A. settled for ₹34,42,500. Fino’s charges arose under the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, specifically for failing to make timely and complete disclosure of frauds perpetrated by its employees, whereas JP Morgan and Citicorp were charged under the SEBI (Foreign Portfolio Investors) Regulations, 2019, for DDP and ODI-issuer conduct respectively.
review_notes: Settlement amounts and underlying regimes are directly supported by the cited chunks across all three orders; tight three-way comparison with a clean memory target.

question: SEBI settled FPI-infrastructure charges against JP Morgan Chase Bank N.A. and Citicorp Investment Bank (Singapore) Limited – ODI in 2025-26. What was the DDP-side lapse in the JP Morgan matter, what was the ODI-issuer-side lapse in the Citicorp matter, and which settlement was approved by the Panel of Whole Time Members first?
answer_summary: JP Morgan, acting as a DDP, granted Category II licences to four UK FPIs that were not on the UK-FCA register, re-categorised them as Category I without verifying their lack of FCA regulation, and delayed blocking fresh purchases for 38 days after a Type I material change of an FPI merger (64 purchase transactions occurred in that window). Citicorp, as an ODI issuer, issued an ODI to Symmetry Master Fund Limited on December 19, 2023 without completing fresh KYC and delayed remitting the $800 regulatory fee for 69 days. Citicorp’s settlement was approved by the Panel of Whole Time Members on January 27, 2025, while JP Morgan’s Panel approval came on January 21, 2026, so Citicorp’s approval was earlier.
review_notes: DDP lapse and ODI-issuer lapse are supported by the cited chunks; Panel approval dates (Jan 21, 2026 vs Jan 27, 2025) are directly in the orders.

question: Both JP Morgan Chase Bank N.A. and Fino Payments Bank Limited ended their SEBI matters through settlement under the 2018 Settlement Regulations, but the gateway into settlement was different. Which applicant entered settlement suo-motu and which did so while an adjudication proceeding and SCN were already pending, and what wording in the Fino order confirms the latter procedural posture?
answer_summary: JP Morgan filed a suo-motu settlement application under Chapter II of the SEBI (Settlement Proceedings) Regulations, 2018, before any adjudication or SCN was issued. Fino, by contrast, had an adjudication proceeding initiated against it under Section 15-I of the SEBI Act, 1992, and received SCN No. SEBI/HO/EAD/EAD5/P/OW/2024/31639/1 dated October 08, 2024; it then filed Settlement Application No. 8256/2024 while the adjudication was pending. The Fino order disposes of the ‘instant Adjudication Proceedings initiated against Fino Payments Bank Limited vide SCN No. ... dated October 08, 2024,’ confirming the proceeding was already live.
review_notes: Suo-motu entry (JP Morgan #0) and pending-adjudication/SCN path (Fino #8/#11) are both explicit; the quoted disposal wording is accurate.

question: Fino Payments Bank and Citicorp Investment Bank (Singapore) Limited – ODI each settled charges where a failure to act within the expected timeframe worsened the breach. What was the critical deadline or expected action in each case, approximately how long was the delay, and how did the settlement amounts reflect the difference in scale?
answer_summary: Fino received KPMG’s investigation report on November 08, 2023 regarding employee-fraud complaints, but it failed to make the required disclosure by the next day, i.e., November 09, 2023, and did not issue subsequent updates. Its settlement amount was ₹5,88,921.45. Citicorp issued an ODI to Symmetry Master Fund Limited on December 19, 2023 before completing fresh KYC, with KYC checks eventually completed only on January 10, 2024, and deposited a regulatory fee of USD 800 on February 26, 2024, i.e., 69 days after issuance. Citicorp’s settlement amount was ₹36,00,000, significantly higher than Fino’s, reflecting the FPI-infrastructure nature of the breach.
review_notes: Fino disclosure deadline and Citicorp ODI KYC/fee-delay facts are supported; both settlement amounts match the cited chunks; distinct deadline-delay target.

question: A merchant banker is told that a settlement under the SEBI Settlement Proceedings Regulations will finally put an end to pending adjudication. Two merchant-banker enforcement files show that this is not automatic. Compare the ICICI Securities inspection settlement with AFCO Capital's rejected settlement and explain when SEBI can still revive a settled merchant-banker proceeding.
answer_summary: ICICI Securities' settlement order (SO/NH/RJ/2024-25/7414) disposed of the SCN under Section 15JB of the SEBI Act read with Regulation 23(1) of the Settlement Regulations after it paid Rs. 69,82,500/- and issued caution letters to officers-in-default. But the order expressly preserves SEBI's right under Regulation 28 to restore or initiate proceedings if any settlement representation is later found untrue, any undertaking or waiver is breached, or there was a discrepancy in computing the settlement terms. AFCO Capital, by contrast, applied to settle the adjudication for its Standard Shoe Sole & Mould open-offer violations but its settlement application was rejected by SEBI's letter dated September 10, 2025; the AO then imposed a total penalty of Rs. 2,00,000/- (Rs. 1,00,000 under Section 15HB and Rs. 1,00,000 under Section 15A(a)). Settlement therefore neither extinguishes SEBI's remedies nor is it guaranteed.
review_notes: Supported by cited settlement order (SO/NH/RJ/2024-25/7414) and AFCO AO. Both documents needed: ICICI shows conditional Regulation 28 reservation, AFCO shows a rejected settlement resulting in AO penalty. Clear applied-compliance contrast.

question: In the enforcement cluster around AFCO Capital's open offer for Standard Shoe Sole & Mould, SEBI examined both the merchant banker and its advisor SSRK Mohan Babu over document-signing. Why did the company end up paying Rs. 2 lakhs while the advisor received the benefit of doubt?
answer_summary: The advisor's adjudication order records that the only place SSRK Mohan Babu appeared as a 'Director' was in the pre-printed Escrow Agreement, while IndusInd Bank's email clarified that he was merely nominated to authorise escrow operations and was not captured as a director. Given this ambiguity, the AO held the PFUTP allegation was not clearly established and discharged him without penalty. The company's order concerned different, admitted procedural breaches: AFCO failed to open a separate BSE acquisition window, delayed half-yearly reports, left the compliance-officer post vacant for 411 days, and delayed intimating SEBI. Those were separately established, attracting Rs. 1,00,000 under Section 15HB and Rs. 1,00,000 under Section 15A(a). The same open offer supplied the facts, but the charges and evidence thresholds were different.
review_notes: Company AO establishes Rs. 2 lakh penalty for acquisition-window, half-yearly-report, compliance-officer and intimation lapses. Advisor AO shows the PFUTP/signing-as-director charge was not proved because IndusInd Bank clarified he was merely an advisor/escrow nominee. Both AOs required for the divergence.

question: After AFCO Capital paid the adjudication penalty of Rs. 2 lakhs, SEBI passed a further order on March 30, 2026. What non-monetary direction followed, under what power, and how did SEBI answer AFCO's claim that it had already been punished?
answer_summary: Under Section 12(3) of the SEBI Act read with Regulation 27 of the Intermediaries Regulations, SEBI prohibited AFCO from soliciting and accepting any new client for its merchant-banking activity for one month from receipt of the order. The Quasi-Judicial Authority reduced the Designated Authority's recommended two months to one. AFCO's objection was overruled by distinguishing the November 24, 2025 AO penalty (failure to open the acquisition window, delayed half-yearly reports, 411-day absence of a compliance officer, and delayed intimation) from the September 13, 2024 warning letter (website disclosure/NISM-KMP issues). The 12(3) direction addressed the more serious finding that AFCO had failed to exercise independent professional judgment and effectively outsourced core activities; a monetary penalty alone was not enough.
review_notes: March 30, 2026 order is reproduced in cited chunks: Section 12(3) read with Regulation 27 of Intermediaries Regulations, one-month new-client prohibition, reduction from DA-recommended two months, and the double-jeopardy/earlier-warning-letter distinction. Company AO supplies the prior penalty and violation basis.

question: Neither of the two merchant-banker resolutions relied on money alone. What non-monetary obligations did SEBI impose in the ICICI Securities settlement and in the March 2026 AFCO Capital order, and where was each merchant banker required to demonstrate compliance?
answer_summary: ICICI Securities was required to take appropriate action against the officers-in-default for the inspection violations and inform SEBI; it later emailed that it had issued caution letters. The March 2026 order against AFCO Capital directed it to refrain from soliciting or accepting any new merchant-banking client for one month, and to submit to SEBI a copy of the NISM Series-IIIA certificate, photo evidence of displaying the investor-grievance mechanism at its office premises, and intimation through the SEBI Intermediary portal. While ICICI demonstrated compliance by email and the action was noted by the WTM panel, AFCO's submission was to be made to SEBI and its contents recorded in the order's finding.
review_notes: ICICI settlement order confirms caution-letter/officer action and SEBI notification via email/WTM panel. March 2026 AFCO order confirms one-month new-client ban plus NISM Series-III-A, investor-grievance-display evidence and SI-portal intimation. Cross-case checklist is a distinct memory target.

question: Two AIF concentration-limit settlements follow very different procedural tracks. In the Abans AIF-1 settlement, what numerical mistake converted the 25% cap into an apparent over-investment? In the Finideas Growth Fund (IRFC) settlement, how did SEBI’s Notice of Summary Settlement determine the settlement amount and compliance route instead of the ordinary Internal Committee / High Powered Advisory Committee path?
answer_summary: In the Abans AIF-1 order, the manager treated the Scheme’s initial corpus of ₹65.99 crores plus the ₹8.24 crore net gain from liquidating investments as the new investible funds (₹74.23 crores), making the 25% cap appear to be ₹18.55 crores. Because Regulation 2(1)(p) and 2(1)(h) define corpus as the total funds committed by investors and exclude gains/losses from liquidation, the concentration limit was overstated and the manager allegedly exceeded it. The matter went through the standard settlement route: Internal Committee meeting on July 29, 2025, revised terms on August 6, 2025, HPAC recommendation on September 15, 2025, Panel approval on October 14, 2025, and remittance in December 2025 for ₹8,70,000. By contrast, the Finideas Growth Fund order involved a Category III 10% concentration-limit breach in Indian Railway Finance Corporation from May 31, 2023 to July 31, 2023 under Regulation 15(1)(d). SEBI issued a Notice of Summary Settlement under Regulation 16 of the Settlement Regulations on December 2, 2024 (followed by an email on January 30, 2025) offering settlement at a fixed amount of ₹12,75,000 to be paid jointly and severally within 30 days. The applicants accepted and paid, so the matter did not involve revised proposals or full HPAC deliberation in the manner seen in Abans.
review_notes: Strong two-document procedural comparison; the Abans calculation error and the Finideas/IRFC Notice of Summary Settlement route are directly supported by the cited chunks. The answer's 'Category III' descriptor for the IRFC AIF was not found in the cited chunks.

question: The Indiabulls AIF settlement and the Motilal Oswal Alternative Investment Trust settlement both involve non-concentration compliance defaults by AIFs, yet the underlying misconduct differs. What scheme-asset and investor-reporting issues are specific to Indiabulls, and what investor-facing defaults involving exit loads and distributor controls appear in Motilal Oswal? What amount settled each matter, and which order includes an express statement that corrective steps had been taken?
answer_summary: Indiabulls AIF: The alleged defaults included pledging IBDARA scheme assets for a loan taken by an investee company; failing to draw down equal percentages of commitment across unit classes for the IBDARA Scheme; breaching concentration limits in an investee company for both IBREF and IBDARA; failing to ensure proper valuation frequency for both schemes; and misrepresenting or disclosing inaccurate financial information regarding IBDARA valuations to investors. The applicants also allegedly failed to comply with a May 12, 2017 deficiency letter requiring bi-annual valuation, and filed inaccurate information in CTRs with the trustee. The approved settlement amount was ₹1,43,32,500. Motilal Oswal Alternative Investment Trust: The allegations centred on investor-facing defaults. Of the ₹35.17 crores paid by 109 defaulting investors against a ₹115 crore commitment, the AIF retained ₹8.69 crores (about 25% of the paid amount) as penal exit load, with the investment manager appropriating the amount instead of crediting it to the scheme for the benefit of non-defaulting investors. One investor’s portfolio was wrongfully liquidated because of poor coordination between distributor, customer-service and operations teams. The AIF also lacked any documented distributor process, code of conduct, or framework for action against distributors, and took no action for investor defaults or alleged mis-selling. The applicants expressly stated in a June 6, 2025 letter that they had implemented corrective measures. The approved settlement amount was ₹38,76,000.
review_notes: Distinct violation-profile contrast between Indiabulls (scheme-asset/reporting defaults) and Motilal Oswal (exit-load retention, wrongful liquidation, distributor-control gaps); amounts and the corrective-steps statement are supported.

question: Settlement timing affects reserve planning. Map the full sequence from Internal Committee meeting to revised settlement terms, HPAC recommendation, Panel approval, Notice of Demand and final remittance in the Abans and Motilal Oswal AIF settlement orders. Which application had the longer overall gap between the first Internal Committee meeting and confirmed remittance, and by roughly how many months?
answer_summary: Abans AIF-1: Internal Committee meeting on July 29, 2025; revised settlement terms by email on August 6, 2025 (proposing ₹8,70,000); HPAC recommendation on September 15, 2025; Panel of Whole Time Members approval on October 14, 2025; Notice of Demand on November 26, 2025; remittance confirmed on December 11, 2025. The gap from IC meeting to remittance is about four-and-a-half months. Motilal Oswal Alternative Investment Trust: Internal Committee meetings on May 27, 2025 and September 25, 2025; revised terms by email on October 3, 2025 (proposing ₹38,76,000); HPAC recommendation on November 28, 2025; Panel approval on January 20, 2026; Notice of Demand on January 30, 2026; remittance confirmed on February 27, 2026. The applicants had separately stated in a June 6, 2025 letter that corrective measures had been taken. The overall gap from the first IC meeting to remittance is about nine months. Thus, the Motilal Oswal settlement took roughly five months longer from first IC meeting to remittance than the Abans settlement.
review_notes: Timeline mapping from Internal Committee meeting through demand and remittance is directly supported for both Abans and Motilal Oswal; the gap calculation is arithmetically sound.

question: On 30 April 2026, SEBI passed an order against seven noticees in the matter of front running by Prijesh Kurani and others. A later document corrected that order, and on the same 30 April 2026 the Bombay High Court disposed of M.D. Abubakar's writ petition against SEBI. What is the procedural outcome of each of those two later documents—one correcting the SEBI order and the other disposing of the writ?
answer_summary: The 4 May 2026 corrigendum corrects a typographical error in para 61(vi) of the April 30 front-running order: the addressee for forwarding payment details is changed from 'The Division Chief, CFID' to 'The Division Chief, IVD' (same SEBI Bhavan-II address and email tad@sebi.gov.in), and it states that the original order must always be read with the corrigendum. The Bombay High Court, in Md. Abubakar v. SEBI (Writ Petition (L) No. 5671 of 2026) dated 30 April 2026, disposed of the writ petition as withdrawn, granting liberty to the petitioner to avail of the statutory appellate remedy under Section 15Z of the SEBI Act, 1992 before the Hon'ble Supreme Court.
review_notes: Supported by cited chunks: corrigendum fixes para 61(vi) and says original order must be read with it; High Court order disposes writ as withdrawn with Section 15Z liberty. Strong cross-document procedural contrast.

question: The 4 May 2026 corrigendum to the Prijesh Kurani front-running order claims to fix a single typographical error. Which sub-paragraph of para 61 is corrected, which two noticees are directly affected by it, and what specific wording differs between the original order and the corrected text?
answer_summary: Para 61(vi) is corrected. It applies to Noticee 1 (Prijesh Kurani) and Noticee 7 (Pranav Vora). The only wording difference visible in the address line is the division name: the original order directed proof-of-payment details to 'The Division Chief, CFID', while the corrigendum revises this to 'The Division Chief, IVD' at the same SEBI Bhavan-II address and the same email id tad@sebi.gov.in.
review_notes: Supported by corrigendum and original order: para 61(vi) affects Notices 1 and 7, and the division abbreviation changes from CFID to IVD. Precise multi-document textual-delta target.

question: In Md. Abubakar v. SEBI, the Bombay High Court disposed of Writ Petition (L) No. 5671 of 2026 as withdrawn on 30 April 2026. What statutory appellate remedy did the court identify, and how does the relief route in that court order differ from SEBI's own correction mechanism used for the Prijesh Kurani order issued the same day?
answer_summary: The court identified the appellate remedy available under Section 15Z of the SEBI Act, 1992. It allowed the petitioner to withdraw the writ petition with liberty to avail that appellate remedy before the Hon'ble Supreme Court. The difference is procedural: the court order reflects a judicial refusal to hear a constitutional writ because a statutory appeal channel exists, whereas the Prijesh Kurani corrigendum is an administrative self-correction by SEBI to fix a clerical error in the original order with which it must be read together.
review_notes: Court order explicitly cites Section 15Z appellate remedy and grants liberty to approach Supreme Court; corrigendum demonstrates SEBI's administrative self-correction. Clear procedural comparison.

question: The April 30, 2026 front-running order imposed a monetary penalty on Notices 1 and 7 and required them to remit it online within a fixed period. What was the penalty amount for each noticee, how long do they have to pay it, and how did the May 4 corrigendum alter the instruction about where to send proof of payment?
answer_summary: Both Noticee 1 (Prijesh Kurani) and Noticee 7 (Pranav Vora) were penalised Rs. 10 lakh each. The amount must be paid within 45 days of receipt of the order through SEBI's online 'PAY NOW' facility. The corrigendum revised para 61(vi) so that the forwarding address is 'The Division Chief, IVD' rather than 'The Division Chief, CFID'; the SEBI Bhavan-II address and email tad@sebi.gov.in remained unchanged.
review_notes: Original order chunk confirms Rs. 10 lakh penalty for Noticees 1 and 7 and 45-day online payment window; corrigendum chunk revises forwarding division from CFID to IVD. Good penalty-plus-version-delta target.

question: In two May 2026 first appeals under the RTI Act, SEBI's Appellate Authority upheld the CPIO's refusal but on different legal grounds. What is the distinct RTI Act basis for each refusal, and which judicial or administrative precedent did the authority cite?
answer_summary: Kamla Rani Yadav sought her late husband's share purchase/sale, nominee, bank and demat account details. The CPIO replied that SEBI does not maintain that information in the normal course of regulating the securities market, and the Appellate Authority agreed, citing the Supreme Court in Central Board of Secondary Education & Anr. v. Aditya Bandopadhyay (9 August 2011) that the RTI Act does not oblige a public authority to collect or collate information it does not hold. Her appeal was dismissed. Saurabhi Bharat Rele asked several 'why' and 'how much' questions about SEBI Circular CIR/IMD/DF/21/2012 (direct/regular plan treatment of pre-2013 corpus). The CPIO replied that the queries sought clarification or opinion, not 'information' as defined in section 2(f) of the RTI Act, and the authority agreed, citing the Central Information Commission in Azad Singh v. CPIO, Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. (23 March 2021) that a CPIO cannot create, interpret or compile information and is only a communicator of records already held. His appeal was also dismissed.
review_notes: Both cited RTI appeal orders support the distinct legal bases and cited precedents; directly multi-document and teaches a statutory-basis comparison.

question: Both RTI appeals decided on 7 May 2026 refer to filing dates and CPIO replies, but only one was dismissed as time-barred. Which appeal was late, why did it miss the 30-day window, and why was the other appellant not caught by the same objection?
answer_summary: Saurabhi Bharat Rele's appeal in Appeal No. 6830 of 2026 was time-barred. The CPIO reply was dated 20 January 2026, so a first appeal under section 19(1) of the RTI Act had to be filed within 30 days from receipt of that reply. The appeal was received by the Appellate Authority only on 9 April 2026, and the appellant neither asked for condonation of delay nor gave any reason for the delay. Kamla Rani Yadav's appeal in Appeal No. 6831 of 2026 was filed on 9 April 2026 against a reply dated 2 April 2026, so it was within the 30-day window and the authority did not raise limitation.
review_notes: Filing/receipt dates and limitation reasoning are supported by both cited RTI orders; contrasting the two appeals is necessary.

question: Three SEBI orders issued in the first week of May 2026 decide requests of very different kinds. What did each requester seek, which statute or regulation supplied the decision-making framework, and what relief was ultimately granted or refused?
answer_summary: (1) Kamla Rani Yadav: asked under the RTI Act for her deceased husband's shareholder, sale/purchase, nominee and account details. The authority agreed with the CPIO that the information was not maintained by SEBI and dismissed the appeal. (2) Saurabhi Bharat Rele: asked under the RTI Act for clarification/opinion on SEBI Circular CIR/IMD/DF/21/2012 and investor losses. The authority held the queries were not 'information' under section 2(f) and dismissed the appeal. (3) Six Muthoot family trusts: applied under Section 11 of the SEBI Act, 1992 read with Regulation 11(5) of the SAST Regulations, 2011, for exemption from making an open offer over an indirect promoter-family reorganisation. The Whole Time Member, acting on the Takeover Panel's recommendation, granted the exemption subject to conditions such as completing the acquisition and filing a report within 21 days; the exemption is valid for one year.
review_notes: All three cited orders verify the request subjects, decision-making statutes/regulations, and relief granted/refused; captures the cross-statute Muthoot exemption conditions.

question: In its May 2026 RTI appeal orders, SEBI directed the losing applicants to other avenues in one case but not the other. What alternative guidance did SEBI give in each appeal, and why did the character of each request make the guidance different?
answer_summary: In Kamla Rani Yadav's appeal, SEBI pointed the applicant to the listed company and/or its registrar and transfer agent, the websites and helpdesks of the depositories, and the investor service centres of the stock exchanges, because the information, though not with SEBI, could exist with those third parties. In Saurabhi Bharat Rele's appeal, the queries asked for opinions, reasons and calculations about a SEBI circular (CIR/IMD/DF/21/2012), so there was no external factual source SEBI could refer the appellant to; the authority simply upheld the position that the RTI Act did not compel SEBI to create or interpret such information.
review_notes: Differential guidance across the two RTI appeals is supported; distinct from q01/q02 in targeting practical onward-direction rather than legal basis.

question: In early 2024 two unrelated SEBI proceedings—a settlement under the SEBI Settlement Scheme, 2022 and an adjudication against Arjun Sharma for unregistered investment advisory—both ended with an order involving about ₹1,00,000. Beyond the amount, how do the legal effects of the two orders differ, and which one expressly preserves SEBI's power to restart enforcement later?
answer_summary: The settlement order dated January 3, 2024 disposed of the PFUTP/reversal-trade proceedings against Indira Mondal and Techno Road-Link under Regulation 26 of the SEBI (Settlement Proceedings) Regulations, 2018: SEBI will not initiate or continue enforcement action for the said defaults, but the order is expressly without prejudice to SEBI's right under Regulation 28 to resume proceedings if any representation is later found untrue or an undertaking/condition is breached. The Arjun Sharma order dated February 14, 2024 is a final adjudication for unregistered investment advisory that imposes a ₹1,00,000 penalty under Section 15EB, directs refund of ₹12,47,848 to investors, asset restrictions and a one-year market debarment, and warns of recovery/prosecution for non-compliance; it does not reserve a right to reopen the same determination.
review_notes: Both cited docs materially needed: settlement order shows Reg 26/28 finality and restart right, Arjun Sharma order shows final adjudication with penalty/debarment. Chunks directly support the comparison.

question: Three early-2024 SEBI orders each concern money moving between a party and SEBI or investors: a January 2024 settlement order reversing a BSE options adjudication for two applicants, the January 2024 order against Saurabh Verma for unregistered investment advisory, and the February 2024 order against Arjun Sharma for unregistered investment advisory. Who is required to pay whom in each order, and what is the character of each payment?
answer_summary: In the settlement order dated January 3, 2024, Indira Mondal and Techno Road-Link each paid ₹1,00,000 to SEBI as a settlement amount under the SEBI Settlement Scheme, 2022 to dispose of the PFUTP/reversal-trade proceedings; there is no direction to refund investors. In the Saurabh Verma order dated January 31, 2024, the noticee must refund the entire ₹1,67,24,995 collected as unregistered advisory fees to investors/complainants and must separately pay ₹1,00,000 each as penalties under Sections 15HB and 15EB to SEBI. In the Arjun Sharma order dated February 14, 2024, the noticee must refund ₹12,47,848 collected as advisory fees to investors and separately pay a ₹1,00,000 penalty under Section 15EB to SEBI.
review_notes: Requires all three cited documents to tabulate payment flows and characters (settlement amount to SEBI vs investor refunds plus penalties). Cited chunks support the stated amounts and payees.

question: Two orders passed within six weeks in early 2024—the January 3 settlement order for Indira Mondal and Techno Road-Link and the February 14 unregistered investment advisory order against Arjun Sharma—both dispose of enforcement proceedings but impose very different restrictions on future market activity. What market-access restriction does each impose, if any, and what explains the difference?
answer_summary: The January 3, 2024 settlement order imposes no market-access bar on the applicants; it simply terminates the pending PFUTP/reversal-trade proceedings under Regulation 26 subject to the Regulation 28 caveat. The February 14, 2024 Arjun Sharma order debars him from accessing the securities market, directly or indirectly, for one year from the date of the order or until he files the refund-completion report, whichever is later, and forever prohibits him from undertaking investment advisory activities without SEBI registration. The difference reflects the distinction between a negotiated settlement that conclusively closes the dispute (subject to honesty and compliance conditions) and a final adjudication that finds an unregistered advisory violation and imposes protective and punitive directions.
review_notes: Comparison of market-access restrictions is directly supported: settlement order has no bar, Arjun Sharma order imposes one-year debarment and forever bans unregistered IA. Distinct from q01.

question: The January 3, 2024 settlement order and the January 31, 2024 unregistered investment advisory order against Saurabh Verma each leave a door open after the order is pronounced, but the door serves a different party. What future right does each order reserve, and for whose benefit?
answer_summary: The settlement order reserves SEBI's right under Regulation 28 of the Settlement Regulations to restart or continue enforcement against the applicants if any representation made during settlement is later found untrue or if they breach any undertaking or condition; this safeguards SEBI, not investors. The Saurabh Verma order reserves investors'/complainants' right to pursue other legal remedies before any appropriate forum for refund of money or deficiency in service despite SEBI's refund direction, and also reserves SEBI's right to recover the refund amount under Section 28A of the SEBI Act if the noticee fails to comply; thus it protects both investor remedies and SEBI enforcement.
review_notes: Directly supported by cited chunks: Reg 28 settlement reservation serves SEBI, while Saurabh Verma order reserves investors' remedy rights and SEBI Section 28A recovery. Teaches a distinct post-order rights target.

question: A compliance head is reviewing three mid-2024 SEBI outcomes against listed firms and their insiders: Reliance Home Finance, PTC India Financial Services and Eco Hotels (Aditya Dalmia). In each case, what was the primary provision of the SEBI Act that framed the final action, who ultimately bore the liability, and which of the three was resolved through the settlement route rather than a penalty or restraint order?
answer_summary: Reliance Home Finance: a penalty of ₹8,00,000 was imposed on the listed company itself under Section 15A(b) of the SEBI Act for LODR disclosure defaults. PTC India Financial Services: SEBI passed directions including market restraints and monetary penalties totalling ₹35,00,000 against individuals Pawan Singh (₹25,00,000 and a 2-year restraint) and Rajib Kumar Mishra (₹10,00,000 and a 6-month restraint), exercising powers under Sections 11/11B read with Section 15HB of the SEBI Act. Eco Hotels/Aditya Dalmia: the matter was resolved through a Summary Settlement Order against promoter Aditya Dalmia and his HUF, framed under Section 15JB read with Section 19 of the SEBI Act and the Settlement Regulations, 2018; they remitted ₹8,99,000 and SEBI agreed not to initiate enforcement action for the disclosed violations.
review_notes: Supported by all three cited docs. Clean statutory-provision / liability-bearer framing; settlement route is clearly Eco Hotels/Aditya Dalmia under Section 15JB/Settlement Regulations.

question: In 2024 SEBI found material corporate-governance lapses in both PTC India Financial Services and Reliance Home Finance. Why did PTC's order impose individual restraints and penalties on its MD-CEO and Non-Executive Chairman while Reliance's order penalised only the listed company?
answer_summary: The PTC violations went beyond simple disclosure delay: Pawan Singh, as MD-CEO, was found to have entrenched control over the board, blocked the appointed Director-Finance from joining, delayed placement of the Forensic Audit Report on the suspected related-party NSL loan account before the board, and did not co-operate with the forensic auditor. Rajib Kumar Mishra, as Non-Executive Chairman, had the authority to correct course but instead acted as a silent spectator and collaborator. These individual roles justified Section 15HB penalties and market restraints under Sections 11/11B. Reliance Home Finance, by contrast, concerned delayed or missing disclosures of the NCLT order of June 21, 2021, the EoI bid of July 29, 2020 and the resolution-plan approval of June 19, 2021 by the entity; the SCN and final order were directed at the company, which was fined ₹8,00,000 under Section 15A(b).
review_notes: Supported by PTC and Reliance orders. Contrasts active individual misconduct/governance obstruction with entity-level disclosure delay; distinct from q01 and q05.

question: Both Reliance Home Finance and Aditya Dalmia in the Eco Hotels matter were penalised/settled for delayed disclosure. What was the length of each delay, what event triggered the duty, and how did that translate into the final financial consequence?
answer_summary: Reliance Home Finance invited expression-of-interest bids on July 29, 2020 but disclosed them on July 31, 2020 (one-day delay), and approved a resolution plan on June 19, 2021 but disclosed it on June 21, 2021 (one-day delay); it also never disclosed the NCLT order of June 21, 2021 and the subsequent appeals. The Adjudicating Officer imposed a consolidated penalty of ₹8,00,000 on the company. Aditya Dalmia and his HUF acquired shares of Eco Hotels on March 1, 2015, crossing the 5% threshold and triggering Regulation 29(2) read with Regulation 29(3) of the Takeover Regulations, but disclosed the acquisition only on December 28, 2023—a delay of 3,223 days. Because the promoters accepted summary settlement, they paid ₹8,99,000 as a settlement amount rather than an adjudicated penalty.
review_notes: Supported by Reliance and Eco Hotels orders. Dates/delays verified from chunks (EoI Jul 29 disclosed Jul 31; RP Jun 19 disclosed Jun 21; Eco threshold crossing Mar 1 2015 disclosed Dec 28 2023, 3,223 days).

question: Reliance Home Finance was told to pay ₹8,00,000 and Aditya Dalmia/HUF paid ₹8,99,000 around the same time, yet one was a penalty and the other a settlement. What practical difference did SEBI draw between the two outcomes, and what ongoing enforcement risk survived in each case?
answer_summary: Reliance Home Finance's ₹8,00,000 was a non-consensual penalty under Section 15A(b); the company had to pay within 45 days, failing which SEBI could start recovery under Section 28A including attachment and sale of movable and immovable properties. Aditya Dalmia/HUF's ₹8,99,000 was a settlement amount paid under Section 15JB read with Section 19 and the Settlement Regulations, 2018; SEBI agreed not to initiate enforcement action for the disclosed violations, but expressly reserved the right under Regulation 28 to reopen proceedings if any representation was untrue, any undertaking condition was breached, or there was a discrepancy in calculating the settlement terms.
review_notes: Supported by both cited docs. Good procedural distinction: Reliance penalty under Section 15A(b) with Section 28A recovery risk; Dalmia settlement under Section 15JB/Settlement Regulations with Regulation 28 reopening right.

question: Both PTC India Financial Services and Eco Hotels/Aditya Dalmia involved consequences for individuals connected to the issuer, but one pair faced Section 15HB restraints and penalties while the other settled. How did the individuals' roles and the nature of their defaults explain the different routes?
answer_summary: In PTC, Pawan Singh and Rajib Kumar Mishra were serving MD-CEO and Non-Executive Chairman respectively of a listed NBFC. Their conduct concerned active obstruction of board processes, concealment of a forensic audit pointing to suspected related-party fund diversion in the NSL/NNPIPL account, and failure to maintain arm's-length governance, supporting fraud-like liability under Section 15HB and personal market restraints under Sections 11 and 11B. Aditya Dalmia and his HUF were erstwhile promoters of Eco Hotels (not directors at the relevant time) who simply failed to disclose crossing the 5% shareholding threshold under Regulation 29 of the Takeover Regulations. SEBI treated this as a technical but serious promoter-disclosure default and, because the applicants accepted summary settlement, disposed of it under Section 15JB read with Section 19 and the Settlement Regulations, 2018.
review_notes: Supported by PTC and Eco Hotels orders. Focuses on role/conduct difference for individuals (directors/active obstruction vs erstwhile-promoter threshold disclosure default); distinct from q02.

question: Blackstone Capital Partners (Singapore) VI FVCI Pte. Ltd. appears in an unserved show-cause notice dated 31 December 2024 and then in an unserved hearing notice dated 17 January 2025. Read together, what is it being asked to do, by whom, and by when; and what is the consequence if it ignores both notices?
answer_summary: The show-cause notice asks Blackstone to show cause why its FVCI registration should not be cancelled, following a 29 November 2024 Designated Authority report that recommended cancellation of the registrations of 19 defunct FVCIs. The reply is due within 21 days of receipt, by e-mail to bhagwand@sebi.gov.in and pivushkumarm@sebi.gov.in; if no reply is received, it is presumed that the noticee has nothing to submit and SEBI will proceed on the material available on record. The subsequent hearing notice grants a personal hearing before Mr. G Ramar, CGM & QJA, on 11 February 2025 at 11:30 AM at SEBI Bhavan II, G Block, BKC; an online (Zoom) hearing may be requested by e-mailing piyushkumarm@sebi.gov.in. Attendance must be confirmed by 7 February 2025. If the noticee fails to appear, it is again presumed that it has nothing more to say and the matter will proceed on the material available.
review_notes: Both the Blackstone SCN and hearing notice support the deadlines, presiding authority, online/hearing mode, confirmation date and default presumption.

question: After speed-post and e-mail service failed, SEBI served the unserved show-cause notices for Blackstone Capital Partners (Singapore) VI FVCI and Amrapali Aadya Trading and Investment Pvt. Ltd. through different substituted-service channels. What channel did SEBI use for each notice, and what factual trigger explains the choice?
answer_summary: For Blackstone, SEBI published the SCN on the SEBI website under the 'Unserved Notices/Summons' section on 13 November 2024. The trigger was that hard-copy SPAD service to the 19 FVCIs could not be completed: Singapore notices returned with 'Addressee no longer with the Company'; Mauritius notices were returned undelivered without remark because the post office said there was no speed-post service to the addresses; Blue Dart needed the addressee's telephone number, which SEBI did not have on record. For Amrapali Aadya, SEBI published both the SCN and a Hearing Notice dated 6 September 2024 in the Hindustan (New Delhi edition) and Times of India (New Delhi edition) newspapers on 14 September 2024, following Rule 7(3) of the Adjudication Rules. The trigger was that SPAD delivery to the noticee's last known address returned with the comment 'Left without address', and subsequent attempts to serve through a Market Infrastructure Institution (BSE) also failed.
review_notes: Cited chunks support both publication channels (SEBI website vs Rule 7(3) newspapers) and the distinct SPAD/MII failure triggers for each noticee.

question: Two hearing notices published under SEBI's 'Unserved summons/Notices' section—one for Blackstone Capital Partners (Singapore) VI FVCI and one for Amrapali Aadya Trading and Investment Pvt. Ltd.—look structurally similar but differ in practical details. If counsel reads both files, what three things other than the case name must they note before diarising the hearing?
answer_summary: First, the presiding authority differs: Blackstone is to be heard by Mr. G Ramar, CGM & QJA, whereas Amrapali is to be heard by Mr. Ananth Narayan G, Whole Time Member. Second, the date, time and default consequence differ: Blackstone's hearing is on 11 February 2025 at 11:30 AM and Amrapali's on 4 February 2025 at 2:30 PM; in both, non-appearance creates a presumption that the noticee has nothing more to say and the matter proceeds on record. Third, the mode and confirmation mechanics differ: Blackstone's notice expressly allows a Zoom hearing and requires attendance confirmation by 7 February 2025 by e-mail to piyushkumarm@sebi.gov.in; Amrapali's notice requires confirmation by e-mail to bhagwand@sebi.gov.in and piyushkumarm@sebi.gov.in (with participant details) and does not offer an online option in the notice itself. The venues also differ in building/plot: Blackstone at PN C/7, G Block BKC, and Amrapali at Plot No. C4-A, G Block BKC.
review_notes: Both hearing notices support the authority, date/time, mode, confirmation mechanics and venue differences.

question: Two post-enquiry show-cause notices under Regulation 27(1) of the SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations, 2008—one for Blackstone Capital Partners (Singapore) VI FVCI and one for Amrapali Aadya Trading and Investment Pvt. Ltd.—were both preceded by a Designated Authority's enquiry report. What did each report recommend cancelling, and what was the report date?
answer_summary: In the Blackstone matter, the Designated Authority's Enquiry Report dated 29 November 2024 recommended cancellation of the certificate of registration of 19 defunct FVCIs. The 31 December 2024 SCN asks Blackstone to show cause why its FVCI registration should not be cancelled or why any other fit action under the Intermediaries Regulations should not be taken. In the Amrapali matter, the Designated Authority's Enquiry Report dated 2 December 2024 recommended cancellation of Amrapali Aadya Trading and Investment Pvt. Ltd.'s Portfolio Manager registration (INP000004862). The 24 December 2024 SCN asks Amrapali to show cause why that recommended action or any other permitted action should not be taken.
review_notes: Both post-enquiry SCNs directly support the respective DA report dates and the recommended cancellation actions (19 FVCIs vs Amrapali PM registration).

question: The April 2026 sale certificates cite one rule of the Second Schedule to the Income-tax Act, 1961, while the order confirming those sales cites a different rule in the same schedule. What does each rule govern, and why are both cited across the two documents?
answer_summary: The sale certificates are issued 'Under Section 28A of SEBI Act, 1992 read with Rule 65 of the Second Schedule to the Income-tax Act, 1961.'
