question: The BG6 sale certificate refers to 'the following properties' and lists two sale deeds, while the other three April 2026 sale certificates list one deed each. Does the BG6 entry represent two separate parcels, or a single lot? Justify using the auction notice and confirmation order.
answer_summary: It represents a single lot. The February 2026 public notice and the April 2026 confirmation order describe the same physical parcel — vacant land at Banerjee Para Road, Mouza-Mulajore, Ward No. 24, Holding No. 129, Bhatpara, North 24 Parganas, total area 19.57 decimal — but the conveyance is supported by two sale deeds, I-3593/2012 and I-7407/2012.
review_notes: Single-lot conclusion is solid: sale certificate, notice and confirmation order all describe one parcel with two sale deeds. Minor descriptive wording differs from cited text.

question: What condition in the Second Schedule to the Income-tax Act had to be satisfied before the Recovery Officer could confirm the April 2026 e-auction sales, and how many days elapsed between the last scheduled auction date and the confirmation order?
answer_summary: The condition was that no application had been made under Rule 60 of the Second Schedule to set aside the sale and the successful bidders had deposited the full bid amount plus 1% poundage fee. Once that was satisfied, Rule 63(1) obliged the Recovery Officer to confirm the sale, making it absolute. The last auction date was March 11, 2026 (for G1 and MBK2; BG6 and BG8 were on March 9), and the confirmation order is dated April 20, 2026, so 40 days elapsed.
review_notes: Rule 60 absence and full payment are stated in the confirmation order; auction dates in the public notice and 40-day gap to April 20 confirmation are correct.

question: The sale certificates name only the corporate defaulters, while the confirmation order also lists individuals. Who are the additional individuals and how are they linked to the three defaulter groups?
answer_summary: The confirmation order identifies the directors/promoters of each company as defaulters along with the companies. For Bishal Group of Companies, they include Madhab Chandra Purkait, Gautam Kumar Halder, Mohd Kalimullah Baidya, Tushar Kanti Nandi, Santosh Kumar Paul, Swapan Kumar Bose, Ram Kumar Sinha, Sushant Kumar, Sachin Kumar Thakur, Chandan Shah, Kuntal Bhattacharjee, Benukar Banerjee, Priti Rani Chowdhury, Ratan Chowdhury and Shima Chowdhury. For GSHP Realtech Limited, they include Sanjay Kumar Srivastava, Arun Kumar Singh, Dharampal Kumar Rawat, Mahesh Kumar Singh and Raj Kumar Mondal. For MBK Business Development (India) Limited, they include Prafulla Kumar Kundu, Saikat Roy, Anshuman Ghosh, Tanmoy Kundu, Saikat Brahmachari and Sadhan Chandra Brahmachari. These individuals are named as directors/promoters and are covered by the relevant recovery certificates.
review_notes: Directors/promoters listed in the confirmation order match the answer; sale certificates only reference the generic 'Directors/Promoters' phrase.

question: Two February 2024 SEBI orders examine suspected market misconduct: one against M/s NIFM Equity and Commodity Research for unregistered investment advisory activity, the other against Tushar Gupta for front-running trades linked to Tata Absolute Return Fund. Both proceedings looked serious at first. Why did one end in penalties and directions while the other was disposed of without any direction?
answer_summary: The NIFM order found direct evidence that the noticees had held themselves out as an investment advisory company since 2012, offered packaged tips through SMS, WhatsApp, email and Yahoo Messenger, and received Rs. 25,20,474.26 in their bank account after the IA Regulations came into force. With that admission and banking evidence, SEBI held they had acted as an investment adviser without registration in violation of Section 12(1) of the SEBI Act read with Regulation 3(1) of the SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, 2013, and imposed refund directions plus Rs. 2 lakh penalty under Section 15HB and Rs. 2 lakh under Section 15EB. In the Tushar Gupta order, although the trading pattern was statistically striking—about Rs. 560 crore gross traded value in roughly 2.5 months, 144 alleged front-run instances and a high overlap with the Big Client’s scrip days—SEBI found no documentary evidence that Tushar Gupta possessed non-public information about the Big Client’s impending orders or that he was connected to the Big Client, its dealers or other suspected entities. Because the essential ingredient of front-running (use of non-public information) was not proved beyond reasonable doubt, the SCN was disposed of without any direction under Sections 11 and 15HA read with the PFUTP Regulations.
review_notes: Supported by both cited orders; contrasts evidentiary proof (admissions/bank receipts in NIFM) with unproven information channel in Tushar Gupta.

question: A compliance officer is mapping the statutory hooks used in the February 2024 NIFM unregistered IA order and the Tushar Gupta front-running order. Which SEBI Act provisions and subordinate regulations does each order rely on, and how do the penal routes differ?
answer_summary: NIFM: Section 12(1) of the SEBI Act, 1992 read with Regulation 3(1) of the SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, 2013 (mandatory registration); directions and remedial powers under Sections 11(4), 11(4A), 11B(1), 11B(2) and Section 19; penalties under Section 15EB (default by an investment adviser/research analyst) and Section 15HB (residual contravention penalty). Tushar Gupta: alleged violations under Section 12A(a)-(c) and penalty under Section 15HA of the SEBI Act read with Regulation 3(b)-(d) and Regulation 4(2)(q) of the SEBI (Prohibition of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices) Regulations, 2015, which specifically captures placing orders while in possession of non-public information regarding a substantial impending transaction. The key difference is that the IA route punishes operating without registration and violating IA Regulations, while the front-running route punishes manipulative/fraudulent trading practices tied to misuse of non-public information.
review_notes: Statutory citations match cited chunks for both orders; penal-route distinction is a distinct memory target.

question: Both the NIFM and Tushar Gupta orders were issued by CGM-level officers in late February 2024. One imposes a refund mechanism plus monetary penalty; the other imposes none. Contrast the NIFM directions with the Tushar Gupta conclusion and explain what produces the divergence.
answer_summary: The NIFM order dated February 29, 2024 directed the noticees to refund all money collected as advisory fees (Rs. 25,20,474.26) within three months, issue a public notice in two national dailies and one vernacular newspaper within 15 days, make repayments through banking channels with audit trails, refrain from selling assets except for refunds, deposit any remaining balance in an escrow account for one year and then transfer surplus to the Investors Protection and Education Fund, debar access to the securities market for two years, and pay Rs. 2 lakh under Section 15HB plus Rs. 2 lakh under Section 15EB within 45 days. The Tushar Gupta order dated February 27, 2024 concluded that the front-running allegation was unsubstantiated because SEBI could not establish that Tushar Gupta had non-public information about, or any connection with, the Big Client or its dealers, despite a suspicious trading pattern. Therefore it disposed of the SCN without any direction or monetary penalty.
review_notes: Detailed directions and amounts in NIFM order are supported; outcome contrast adds a separate memorization target from q01.

question: The NIFM order debars the noticees from accessing the securities market for two years. Did the Tushar Gupta order contain any comparable debarment or direction, and if not, what finding in that order explains the absence?
answer_summary: No comparable debarment or direction appears in the Tushar Gupta order. The order disposed of the SCN against Tushar Gupta without any direction because SEBI found no cogent material on record showing that he possessed non-public information about the impending trades of the Big Client, or that he had any connection with the Big Client, its dealers or other suspected entities identified in the wider front-running network. Without proof of the information channel that defines front-running under Regulation 4(2)(q) of the PFUTP Regulations, the violation was not substantiated, so no debarment, penalty or remedial direction followed.
review_notes: Absence of debarment/direction in Tushar Gupta order is verified in cited concluding chunks; narrow negative check.

question: Arun Panchariya was originally asked to pay over Rs. 87 crore under Recovery Certificate 7816, but SEBI released his attached accounts after he paid only Rs. 20 lakhs. What legal development produced that reduction, and which finding from the original order remained untouched?
answer_summary: The original demand arose from WTM Order No. WTM/AB/IVD/ID4/14459/2021-22 dated December 15, 2021, which imposed a penalty of Rs. 67 crore on Arun Panchariya in the Winsome Textile Industries GDR matter. RC 7816 of 2024 demanded Rs. 87,77,01,000 including interest. He appealed to SAT (Appeal No. 21 of 2023), and SAT by order dated October 15, 2025 allowed the appeal only on penalty quantum, remanding it to SEBI. SAT held that the Rs. 67 crore penalty was disproportionate since SEBI had imposed Rs. 20 lakh in larger GDR cases, and set aside the finding that Arun Panchariya was involved in the second leg of the fraud. The first-leg fraud finding was upheld. SEBI passed a fresh final order on February 5, 2026 reducing the penalty to Rs. 20 lakh. After payment, SEBI's release order dated May 5, 2026 directed release of attached accounts.
review_notes: Supported by Final Order, Notice of Demand and Release Order. SAT Appeal 21/2023 produced the fresh Feb 5 2026 order reducing the penalty, while the first-leg fraud finding remained untouched.

question: In Arun Panchariya's RC 7816, the demand notice, the remittance order, and the release order each cite a different figure. What are the three amounts, and what produced the gap between the sums demanded and the sum finally paid?
answer_summary: The Notice of Demand dated June 10, 2024 certified Rs. 87,77,01,000 (Rs. 67 crore WTM penalty plus interest from December 2021 to June 2024 at 1% p.m.). The General Remittance Order dated August 2, 2024 stated the current dues as Rs. 89,11,01,000 (the original demand plus further accrued interest/costs). The Release Order dated May 5, 2026 records that recovery was completed after payment of only Rs. 20,00,000. The gap was produced by SAT Appeal No. 21 of 2023: SAT by order dated October 15, 2025 allowed the appeal on penalty quantum, and SEBI's fresh Final Order dated February 5, 2026 reduced the penalty from Rs. 67 crore to Rs. 20 lakh. Once the reduced penalty was paid, the larger accrued interest demand fell away and the accounts were released.
review_notes: Demand Rs.87,77,01,000, remittance Rs.89,11,01,000 and final payment of Rs.20,00,000 are all directly cited; the gap is explained by the SAT remand and fresh final order.

question: SEBI attached Arun Panchariya's bank and demat accounts under RC 7816 in July 2024 and directed banks to remit the attached amount in August 2024. Trace the procedural steps and dates from that attachment to the May 2026 release, and identify what made the earlier remittance direction unnecessary.
answer_summary: Step 1: July 1, 2024 – SEBI issued notices of attachment (Attachment Proceeding Nos. 12279 and 12280) attaching Arun Panchariya's bank accounts/lockers, demat accounts and mutual fund folios under RC 7816 of 2024. Step 2: August 2, 2024 – SEBI issued a General Remittance Order directing banks and mutual funds to remit Rs. 89,11,01,000 to SEBI's account. Step 3: October 15, 2025 – SAT allowed Arun Panchariya's Appeal No. 21 of 2023 and remanded only the quantum of penalty to SEBI. Step 4: February 5, 2026 – SEBI passed a fresh Final Order reducing the penalty from Rs. 67 crore to Rs. 20 lakh. Step 5: May 5, 2026 – SEBI issued the release order directing release of attached accounts because the recovery proceedings were completed after payment of the reduced penalty. The August 2024 remittance direction became unnecessary because the underlying penalty was drastically reduced by the SAT-driven fresh order.
review_notes: Attachment/remittance timeline supported by the attachment and remittance notices; SAT intervention and the reduced penalty made the earlier remittance direction unnecessary.

question: Shamo Devi (Appeal No. 6828) and Manas Pal (Appeal No. 6827) each asked SEBI for details connected to an ongoing investor recovery or refund process. Both appeals were dismissed. What different legal reasons did the Appellate Authority accept for refusing disclosure, and in which case did it identify the true information-holder as outside SEBI?
answer_summary: Shamo Devi asked about her PACL refund calculation and status. The Authority held that SEBI did not possess the detailed refund information, citing Pattipati Rama Murthy v. CPIO, SEBI (July 8, 2013), and noted that the Justice (Retd.) R.M. Lodha Committee--not SEBI--handles PACL repayments; it also cited M Shanmugam v. CPIO, PACL to observe that the Lodha Committee is not a public authority under section 2(h) of the RTI Act. Manas Pal asked about sale deeds, mutation, stay orders, third-party objections and the effect of a Sale Certificate in the MBK recovery. The Authority accepted SEBI's claim that the sale-deed details were fiduciary/confidential/personal and exempt under sections 8(1)(d), (e), (g) and (j), that queries 2-4 and 6 were clarifications or opinions not 'information' under section 2(f), and that query 5 had become moot once the property was withdrawn from the auction.
review_notes: Supported by both cited orders: Shamo Devi rests on non-availability/Pattipati Rama Murthy and Lodha Committee not a public authority, while Manas Pal turns on section 2(f) clarifications/opinions and the section 8(1)(d)/(e)/(g)/(j) exemption cluster. Teaches a distinct comparison of recovery-related disclosure refusals.

question: An RTI applicant who disagrees with SEBI's reply asks the Appellate Authority to (i) direct SEBI to obtain details from another body and (ii) consider new arguments raised for the first time in the appeal. How did the April 30, 2026 orders in Shamo Devi (Appeal No. 6828) and Santosh Kumar (Appeal No. 6826) decide those two requests?
answer_summary: (i) In Shamo Devi, the Authority refused to order SEBI to obtain the PACL refund information from the Justice Lodha Committee, holding that the Committee is not a public authority under section 2(h) of the RTI Act and that SEBI cannot be required to create or procure information it does not hold. (ii) In Santosh Kumar, the Authority refused to consider submissions raised for the first time at appeal, citing Harish Prasad Divedi v. Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited to reiterate that an information seeker cannot expand the scope of an RTI enquiry at the appeal stage.
review_notes: Both cited orders directly answer the two requests: Shamo Devi refuses to compel SEBI to obtain PACL refund details from another body and holds the Lodha Committee is not a public authority; Santosh Kumar rejects new submissions raised first time at appeal, citing Harish Prasad Divedi. Clear multi-document pairing.

question: Based on the three Appellate Authority orders dated April 30, 2026 in Appeal Nos. 6826, 6827 and 6828, what are three distinct ways an RTI appeal can fail even if the CPIO's reply appears short?
answer_summary: First, the original application may contain no actual information request, so there is nothing for SEBI to disclose (Santosh Kumar, Appeal 6826). Second, the request may ask for clarifications, opinions or confirmations instead of 'information' as defined in section 2(f), or it may seek exempt material (Manas Pal, Appeal 6827). Third, the request may concern information held by a non-SEBI body or information that SEBI does not hold, so SEBI cannot be compelled to obtain or create it (Shamo Devi, Appeal 6828). All three appeals were dismissed.
review_notes: Checklist question that uses all three orders to enumerate independent failure modes: no intelligible request (Santosh), clarification/opinion/exempt material (Manas), and information held by a non-SEBI/non-public-authority entity (Shamo Devi). Supported by the cited chunks and adds a different memorization target from the pairwise questions.

question: How many of the RTI appeals numbered 6826, 6827 and 6828 were allowed or remanded by the Appellate Authority in its orders dated April 30, 2026, and what was the outcome in each?
answer_summary: None were allowed or remanded; all three were dismissed. Appeal No. 6826 (Santosh Kumar) was dismissed because no intelligible information was asked in the application and new points raised in the appeal could not be entertained. Appeal No. 6827 (Manas Pal) was dismissed because the requested information was either exempt, fell outside the definition of 'information', or had become moot after the property was withdrawn. Appeal No. 6828 (Shamo Devi) was dismissed because the detailed PACL refund information was not with SEBI and the Justice Lodha Committee was not a public authority under the RTI Act.
review_notes: Simple but valid exhaustive-count question across the three orders: none were allowed or remanded, all dismissed. Although the outcome is derivable from q04, the count/outcome framing is a distinct memory target and is directly supported by each order.

question: Three recovery demand notices—RC 7511, RC 7556 and RC 7600—were issued by SEBI's Western Regional Office within weeks in early 2024. Two arise from penalties imposed in earlier SEBI orders, while the third follows a direction to refund. Identify the refund-based notice, the original order it refers to, and explain why the phrase "Jointly & Severally" appears only in that one.
answer_summary: The refund-based notice is RC 7511 dated January 17, 2024 against Cash Cow Broking & Advisory Solutions (and its partners). It traces back to a Whole Time Member order dated January 18, 2022 directing refund of Rs.1,03,74,093, plus accrued interest and recovery costs. The certificate says the amount is due "Jointly & Severally" because the notice lists both the partnership firm and its three partners as co-defaulters, making each partner personally liable for the full amount. In contrast, RC 7556 (Jalaj Agrawal) and RC 7600 (Sharda Sharma) are issued to single individuals: RC 7556 follows an Adjudicating Officer penalty order dated January 18, 2023 in the Panafic Industrials matter, and RC 7600 follows an Adjudicating Officer penalty order dated September 18, 2023 in the Capri Global Capital matter.
review_notes: Supported by all three notices; identifies refund-based RC 7511, its WTM origin, and the firm-with-partners 'Jointly & Severally' phrasing that distinguishes it from the AO-penalty notices.

question: Each of the RC 7511, RC 7556 and RC 7600 demand notices cites Explanation 1 to section 28A of the SEBI Act and warns that transfers of property or bank-account money to a spouse, minor child, son's wife or son's minor child are treated as the defaulter's property if made after a particular date. What are the three trigger dates, and why is the earliest one tied to a refund direction rather than a penalty order?
answer_summary: RC 7511 (Cash Cow Broking) uses January 18, 2022, the date of the Whole Time Member refund direction. RC 7556 (Jalaj Agrawal) uses January 18, 2023, the date of the Adjudicating Officer penalty order in the Panafic Industrials matter. RC 7600 (Sharda Sharma) uses September 18, 2023, the date of the Adjudicating Officer penalty order in the Capri Global Capital matter. The earliest date belongs to the refund-based notice because the underlying liability—the direction to return money—was created in January 2022, before the penalty orders that gave rise to the two individual certificates.
review_notes: Explanation 1 trigger dates (18-Jan-2022, 18-Jan-2023, 18-Sep-2023) match the cited chunks, and the reason the refund-direction date is earliest is directly supported by RC 7511 chunk #6.

question: Despite very different scales, all three demand notices include the same fixed cost component. What is it, and how do the principal-plus-interest compositions explain why RC 7511's total is so much larger than RC 7556's and RC 7600's totals?
answer_summary: All three notices include a recovery cost of Rs.1,000. RC 7511 totals Rs.1,29,68,616: a Rs.1,03,74,093 refund direction plus Rs.25,93,523 interest from January 2022 to January 2024 (about 25 months at 1% per month). RC 7556 totals Rs.16,96,000: a Rs.15,00,000 penalty plus Rs.1,95,000 interest for roughly thirteen months. RC 7600 totals Rs.5,31,000: a Rs.5,00,000 penalty plus Rs.30,000 interest for about five months. The far larger RC 7511 total is therefore driven both by a larger original liability and by a much longer interest accrual period.
review_notes: Fixed Rs. 1,000 recovery cost and principal-plus-interest breakdowns are supported across all three cited notices; the long 25-month accrual explains the oversized RC 7511 total.

question: Three SEBI orders issued in early 2024 dealt with Prashant Gole, four entities in Jump Network Limited, and IIFCL Mutual Fund. Which of the three was resolved through a settlement under Section 15JB of the SEBI Act, and what condition did SEBI secure so that investors in the schemes would not ultimately fund the settlement amount?
answer_summary: The IIFCL Mutual Fund matter was resolved through a settlement order under Section 15JB of the SEBI Act, 1992 read with Regulation 23(1) of the SEBI (Settlement Proceedings) Regulations, 2018. The settlement amount of INR 1,02,37,500 was payable jointly and severally by the five applicants. SEBI secured an undertaking from IIFCL Asset Management Company Limited that the settlement amount would not be recovered from or borne by unit holders of the schemes. The Prashant Gole matter resulted in cancellation of the investment adviser registration, while the Jump Network matter resulted in adjudication penalties.
review_notes: Settled. IIFCL chunk 7/10/11 confirms Section 15JB+Regulation 23(1) settlement amount and unit-holder safeguard. Gole chunk 31 and Jump chunk 11 confirm the non-settlement routes.

question: After receiving the common show-cause notice in the Jump Network adjudication, Noticee Nos 3 and 4 expressed a desire to settle under the Settlement Proceedings Regulations, much as the IIFCL Mutual Fund applicants did. Why did that option close off for them, and what route did the matter consequently take?
answer_summary: Noticee Nos 3 and 4 in the Jump Network matter submitted their reply to the SCN and expressed an intention to opt for settlement, but they failed to apply for settlement within the stipulated timeframe. The Adjudicating Officer therefore proceeded to impose individual penalties of INR 4,00,000 on each of the four noticees under Section 15A(b) of the SEBI Act for SAST disclosure violations. By contrast, the IIFCL applicants filed settlement applications while adjudication was pending and successfully completed settlement under Section 15JB read with Regulation 23(1) of the Settlement Proceedings Regulations, 2018.
review_notes: Settled. Jump chunk 11 records Noticee Nos 3 & 4's settlement intention and failure to apply within time; IIFCL chunk 7/10 supplies the alternative successful settlement route.

question: A compliance officer is reviewing the financial consequences in three 2024 orders: the Prashant Gole investment-adviser cancellation order, the IIFCL Mutual Fund settlement, and the Jump Network adjudication. Map the aggregate monetary consequence and the governing SEBI Act section or settlement mechanism for each matter.
answer_summary: Prashant Gole: an ex-parte adjudication had earlier imposed INR 1,00,000 under Section 15C of the SEBI Act for failing to resolve investor grievances and INR 5,00,000 under Section 15HA for fraudulently dealing with clients, totalling INR 6,00,000; the March 2024 enquiry order cancelled his investment adviser registration. IIFCL Mutual Fund: the five applicants settled for a single jointly-and-severally amount of INR 1,02,37,500 under Section 15JB of the SEBI Act read with Regulation 23(1) of the Settlement Proceedings Regulations, 2018. Jump Network: each of the four noticees was penalised INR 4,00,000 (aggregate INR 16,00,000) under Section 15A(b) of the SEBI Act for SAST disclosure violations.
review_notes: Settled. Gole chunk 3 gives 15C/15HA penalties; IIFCL chunk 7/10 gives 15JB/Regulation 23(1) settlement amount; Jump chunk 49 gives four 15A(b) penalties. Full cross-matter reconciliation required.

question: Both IIFCL Mutual Fund and Jump Network involved multiple noticees, but the financial liability was structured very differently. Contrast the liability structure in the two matters and explain what formal choice produced the difference.
answer_summary: In IIFCL Mutual Fund, the five applicants (IIFCL AMC and four individuals) were jointly and severally liable for a single consolidated settlement amount of INR 1,02,37,500. The amount was recommended by the Internal Committee under Schedule II read with Regulation 10 of the Settlement Proceedings Regulations, 2018 and accepted by all applicants together. In Jump Network, each of the four noticees was independently liable for a separate penalty of INR 4,00,000 under Section 15A(b) of the SEBI Act, aggregating INR 16,00,000, because the matter proceeded to full adjudication rather than settlement. The difference flowed from whether the parties took the collective settlement route under the Settlement Proceedings Regulations or contested/proceeded via adjudication under the Adjudication Rules.
review_notes: Settled. IIFCL chunk 7/8 establishes joint-and-several consolidated settlement amount; Jump chunk 48/49 establishes four separate 15A(b) penalties. The formal-route contrast is material.

question: In the Jump Network and Prashant Gole matters respectively, noticees raised defences based on elapsed time and suspension of business. How did SEBI respond to each defence at the stage of deciding whether liability should still attach?
answer_summary: In Jump Network, Noticee Nos 3 and 4 argued that the SCN was issued about four years after the earliest transaction and was therefore invalid. The Adjudicating Officer rejected this holding that the SEBI Act prescribes no limitation period for taking cognizance of breaches, Section 11C permits SEBI to investigate at any time, and the interval was explained by the time needed to analyse multiple transactions. In Prashant Gole, the noticee claimed he had stopped operating as an investment adviser from March 2020 and was unaware of the requirement to obtain BASL-IAASB membership. The Enquiry Officer accepted that he may not have been aware but ruled that the obligation under SEBI Circulars SEBI/HO/IMD/IMD-I/DOF1/P/CIR/2021/579 and 622 was clear, that he remained a registered intermediary, and that the violation warranted cancellation of his IA registration.
review_notes: Settled. Jump chunk 23/25 reject the limitation-period defence; Gole chunks 18/27/28/30 accept non-awareness but hold circulars 579 and 622 binding and cancel registration.

question: Three related BSE illiquid-stock-options adjudication orders from November 2024 — against Aditi Agrawal, Khushi Merchandise Pvt Ltd, and Pritamkumar Nenmal Shah — each impose a ₹5 lakh penalty under Section 15HA of the SEBI Act for PFUTP violations. What distinguishes the underlying trades in the three orders, and why does that not change the penalty amount?
answer_summary:
Although the statutory violation and penalty are the same, the fact patterns differ:

- Aditi Agrawal (individual, PAN BMRPA6208C): two non-genuine reversal trades on 30 March 2015 in the contract VOLT15APR310.00CE with counterparty Merfin Consultants Pvt Ltd, generating 200,000 units of artificial volume (50% of the market volume in that contract). Adjudication Order No. Order/BM/DS/2024-25/30978 dated 14 November 2024.

- Khushi Merchandise Pvt Ltd (private company, PAN AADCK8520D): two non-genuine reversal trades on 17 March 2015 in the contract PFCL15MAR260.00CE with counterparty Radhey Shyam Manchanda, generating 270,000 units of artificial volume (100% of the market volume in that contract). Adjudication Order No. Order/BM/GN/2024-25/30973 dated 14 November 2024.

- Pritamkumar Nenmal Shah (individual, PAN AEJPS4582E): four non-genuine reversal trades in two contracts (AMBC15APR220.00CEW3 and AMTK15APR130.00CEW3) on 23 March 2015 with the same counterparty Neel Naresh Shah, generating 32,000 units of artificial volume (100% of the market volume in each contract). Adjudication Order No. Order/BM/GN/2024-25/30955 dated 6 November 2024.

The penalty stays at the uniform ₹5 lakh floor because in each case SEBI found the same PFUTP breach (Regulations 3(a)-(d), 4(1) and 4(2)(a)), the same absence of quantifiable disproportionate gain or investor loss under Section 15J, and the same Adjudicating Officer (Barnali Mukherjee) applying the minimum monetary penalty prescribed by Section 15HA.
review_notes: Supported by all three AO orders. Cross-entity comparison of contracts, counterparties, volume percentages, and 15J-based reasoning for the identical ₹5 lakh minimum penalty is a distinct memory target.

question: Aditi Agarwal, Khushi Merchandise, and Pritamkumar Shah each received a recovery demand tied to the same underlying ₹5 lakh AO penalty in the BSE illiquid stock options matter, but the stated totals were ₹5,26,000, ₹5,21,000, and ₹5,16,000 respectively. What causes the totals to differ?
answer_summary:
The difference comes entirely from the interest accrued between the adjudication order date and the recovery demand date; the principal penalty (₹5,00,000) and the recovery cost (₹1,000) are the same for all three:

- Aditi Agarwal: AO order dated 14 November 2024; demand dated 27 March 2025. Interest at 1% per month for about 5 months = ₹25,000. Total = ₹5,00,000 + ₹25,000 + ₹1,000 = ₹5,26,000 (Recovery Certificate No. 8691 of 2025).

- Khushi Merchandise Pvt Ltd: AO order dated 14 November 2024; demand dated 12 February 2025. Interest at 1% per month for 4 months = ₹20,000. Total = ₹5,00,000 + ₹20,000 + ₹1,000 = ₹5,21,000 (Recovery Certificate No. 8620 of 2025).

- Pritamkumar Nenmal Shah: AO order dated 6 November 2024; demand dated 9 January 2025. Interest at 1% per month for 3 months = ₹15,000. Total = ₹5,00,000 + ₹15,000 + ₹1,000 = ₹5,16,000 (Recovery Certificate No. 8517 of 2025).
review_notes: Supported by the AO dates and the three Notices of Demand (RC 8691/8620/8517). Interest-accrued date-trap cleanly explains the total gaps; distinct from the trade-pattern target of q01.

question: Pritamkumar Nenmal Shah's ₹5 lakh AO penalty was imposed on 6 November 2024, and the corresponding Recovery Certificate was completed on 11 February 2025. What sequence of SEBI documents traces the debt from the adjudication order to completion?
answer_summary:
The recovery chain for Pritamkumar Nenmal Shah proceeds through four linked documents:

1. Adjudication Order No. Order/BM/GN/2024-25/30955 dated 6 November 2024 imposed a ₹5 lakh penalty under Section 15HA and gave 45 days to pay, warning of recovery under Section 28A on default.

2. Notice of Demand dated 9 January 2025 drew Recovery Certificate No. RC 8517 of 2025 for ₹5,16,000 (penalty ₹5,00,000 + three months' interest ₹15,000 + recovery cost ₹1,000), required payment within 15 days, and listed recovery modes including attachment and arrest.

3. Notices of Attachment dated 27 January 2025 (Attachment Proceeding No. 13855 for bank/post-office accounts and No. 13856 for demat and mutual-fund folios) froze relevant accounts to the extent of the dues.

4. Completion Order dated 11 February 2025 recorded that the outstanding amount had been paid and formally completed RC 8517 of 2025.
review_notes: Supported by AO, Notice of Demand, attachment notices (AP 13855/13856), and completion order. Recovery-chain procedural question teaches a different facet than q01/q02.

question: On 28 April 2026 the Appellate Authority disposed of three separate RTI appeals filed by Shyam Prakash Sharma, Suram Singh and Shamshad Kouser. The grounds for dismissal differ materially. Classify the three appeals by the Authority's reasoning: which were dismissed because SEBI simply did not hold the requested information, and which one was dismissed relying on statutory exemptions or the 'not information' doctrine? For each class, state the RTI Act provisions or precedents the Authority relied upon.
answer_summary: Shamshad Kouser (Appeal Nos. 6819 & 6820 of 2026) and Suram Singh (Appeal No. 6818 of 2026) were dismissed because SEBI said the requested information was not available with it. The Authority cited the Central Information Commission's decision in Sh. Pattipati Rama Murthy vs. CPIO, SEBI (8 July 2013) that if SEBI does not possess information, it cannot invent it. It also noted that disposal of PACL assets and repayment to investors is entrusted to the Justice (Retd.) R.M. Lodha Committee, constituted under the Supreme Court order dated 2 February 2016, and directed the appellants to the PACL public notices, press releases, status reports and FAQs on the SEBI website. Shyam Prakash Sharma (Appeal No. 6817 of 2026) was dismissed on different statutory grounds: queries about the internal DRHP review checklist/SOP were exempt under Section 8(1)(a) as strategic/internal-functioning information; the query seeking SEBI's power to detain/cancel an IPO based on complaints was rejected as not being 'information' under Section 2(f); and queries seeking the names, designations and contact details of individual officers were exempt under Sections 8(1)(g) and 8(1)(j) as personal information whose disclosure could endanger safety and invade privacy.
review_notes: Verified across all three appeal orders and the cited PACL press release. Correctly contrasted the 'information not available' dismissals (Kouser/Suram) with the statutory-exemption dismissal (Shyam) and named the right RTI Act sections/precedents.

question: Two of the 28 April 2026 RTI appeals—by Shamshad Kouser and Suram Singh—concerned PACL refund records, and the Authority rejected both saying the information was not with SEBI. Who actually has responsibility for disposing of PACL assets and repaying investors, under what Supreme Court authorisation, and what aggregate refund figure did SEBI's February 2024 status update report for small eligible claims?
answer_summary: Responsibility for disposing of PACL assets and repaying investors lies with the Justice (Retd.) R.M. Lodha Committee in the matter of PACL Ltd., constituted pursuant to the Supreme Court order dated 2 February 2016. The Authority directed the appellants to the PACL public notices, press releases, status reports and FAQs already available on the SEBI website. SEBI's press release dated 15 February 2024 stated that the Committee had effected refunds for 20,84,635 eligible applications with outstanding principal of up to ₹19,000, aggregating ₹1,021.84 crore.
review_notes: Verified in Shamshad Kouser/Suram Singh orders and the 15 Feb 2024 PACL refund press release. Lodha Committee mandate, Supreme Court authorisation date and aggregate refund figure (Rs.1021.84 crore for 20,84,635 claims up to Rs.19,000) are all directly supported.

question: All three 28 April 2026 RTI appeals were dismissed, but only two of the appellants—Shamshad Kouser and Suram Singh—were pointed toward the Justice (Retd.) R.M. Lodha Committee and PACL public materials. Which appellant was treated differently and what distinctive RTI Act grounds did the Authority use to refuse his requests?
answer_summary: Shyam Prakash Sharma (Appeal No. 6817 of 2026) was the appellant not linked to PACL. His requests were refused on distinctive RTI Act grounds: the requests for SEBI's internal DRHP review checklist/standard operating procedure (queries 1 and 2) were exempt under Section 8(1)(a) because they were strategic/internal-functioning information; the request asking which regulations empower SEBI to detain or cancel an IPO based on complaints (query 3) was held not to be 'information' under Section 2(f); and the requests for officers' names, designations and contact details (queries 4 and 5) were exempt under Sections 8(1)(g) and 8(1)(j) as personal information.
review_notes: Verified in all three appeal orders. Correctly singles out Shyam Prakash Sharma as the non-PACL appellant and accurately captures the distinct Section 8(1)(a), 2(f), 8(1)(g) and 8(1)(j) grounds used by the Authority.

question: The High-Powered Sale Committee published four Sai Prasad Group e-auction notices between August 2025 and March 2026. How many properties were offered in each notice and in which states were they located? What Supreme Court background explains why the pool spans several states?
answer_summary: August 2025: 16 properties (14 in Chhattisgarh – Bilaspur, Korba, Kanker, Raipur, Raigarh – and 2 in North Goa). October 2025: 57 properties in Madhya Pradesh, including 45 in Agar Malwa. December 2025: 9 properties in Maharashtra (8 in Solapur, 1 in Raigarh). March 2026: 47 properties, of which 46 are in Maharashtra (1 in Mumbai, 2 in Nashik, 35 in Osmanabad/Dharashiv, 6 in Pune, 2 in Thane) and 1 is in Jharkhand (Ranchi). The Supreme Court constituted the High-Powered Sale Committee by its July 15, 2024 order in Writ Petition (Crl.) No. 546 of 2023 to liquidate all movable and immovable assets of Sai Prasad Properties Ltd., Sai Prasad Foods Ltd., Sai Prasad Corporation Ltd. and their directors; those assets were attached by Maharashtra under the MPID Act and by SEBI under section 28A of the SEBI Act, so the sale pool reflects the states where the attached assets are situated.
review_notes: Supported across all four Sai Prasad notices and the caution notice; property counts, state/district breakdowns, and Supreme Court liquidation background verified.

question: How did the Sai Prasad HPSC notices sequence the RFP publication, bid-due, and e-auction dates from August 2025 to March 2026, and which round applied staggered deadlines for different property clusters?
answer_summary: August 2025: RFP published 13 August, bid due 19 September, e-auction 30 September 2025. October 2025: RFP published 30 October; the Agar Malwa RFP closed on 28 November with auction on 15 December, while the rest had a bid due date of 20 November and auction on 8 December 2025. December 2025: RFP published 24 December, bid due 14 January 2026, e-auction 23 January 2026. March 2026: RFP published 25 March, bid due 15 April 2026, e-auction 30 April 2026. Only the October 2025 round split the schedule by property cluster.
review_notes: RFP publication, bid-due and e-auction dates verified in each notice; the Agar Malwa staggered deadline confirmed in the October 2025 notice.

question: Why are the Sai Prasad Group immovable properties sold through the High-Powered Sale Committee rather than by the companies or their directors, and what warning did SEBI issue to discourage the public from acquiring those assets through other channels?
answer_summary: The Supreme Court constituted the HPSC by its July 15, 2024 order in Writ Petition (Crl.) No. 546 of 2023 to liquidate all movable and immovable assets of Sai Prasad Properties Ltd., Sai Prasad Foods Ltd., Sai Prasad Corporation Ltd. and their directors. Those assets had already been attached by Maharashtra under the MPID Act (notifications dated 23.03.2016 and 28.06.2016) and by SEBI under section 28A of the SEBI Act (prohibitory orders dated 10.03.2017 and 12.02.2020), and the Supreme Court directed that no court or authority could create third-party interests in them. SEBI cautioned the public that any purchase or dealing in those assets outside the HPSC process would be at the person's own risk and could attract legal action, because the HPSC has the exclusive power to sell the attached assets.
review_notes: Caution notice and Sai notice together support the SC HPSC constitution, MPID/SEBI attachment history, and public warning against unauthorised dealings.

question: A bidder wants to know the reserve price before bidding in the Sai Prasad HPSC e-auction. Is the reserve price set out in the public notice, and how does this compare with the Hina Vijaykumar Vora recovery auction notice?
answer_summary: The Sai Prasad HPSC public notices do not state a fixed reserve price. They direct bidders to the Request for Proposals published on the designated portals for property details and participation terms, so any reserve price is part of the RFP package. In contrast, the Hina Vijaykumar Vora notice explicitly states that the property will not be sold below the reserve price fixed and instructs bidders to enter their bids accordingly.
review_notes: Sai notice refers bidders to the RFP and does not publish a reserve price; Hina Vora notice explicitly states the property will not be sold below the fixed reserve price.

question: What do the Sai Prasad HPSC notices tell a bidder about withdrawing a bid before the e-auction, or about SEBI/HPSC cancelling a sale after the highest bid is knocked down? How does this compare with the Hina Vijaykumar Vora notice under RC No. 2619/2019?
answer_summary: The Sai Prasad HPSC public notices do not specify a withdrawal or post-sale cancellation procedure; those details are left to the RFP. The notices only place the risk on the purchaser through the 'as is, where is, whatever there is' sale basis and disclaim responsibility for title discrepancies. In the Hina Vijaykumar Vora notice, a bidder may withdraw before the revised last date for submission of bids by informing SEBI and the agency and can seek refund of the EMD. The Hina notice also states that a SEBI stay may defer or cancel the auction with no damages payable, and that failure to pay 25% of the bid amount or the balance purchase price plus 1% poundage fee within the stipulated time will lead to cancellation of the sale to the successful bidder and forfeiture of the EMD and other deposits.
review_notes: Sai notice applicable-conditions chunks do not address withdrawal or cancellation; Hina Vora notice sets out withdrawal, stay/deferral, and default/forfeiture rules.

question: Anita Devi Chokhani and Ravi Himmatramka and Sons HUF were both penalised by the same Adjudicating Officer in SEBI's BSE illiquid stock options enforcement drive. As of 6 May 2026, how far had recovery progressed for each noticee, and what was the last recovery document issued in each case?
answer_summary: For Anita Devi Chokhani the recovery lifecycle had run its full course by 6 May 2026: the Adjudicating Officer imposed a Rs.5 lakh penalty on 27 November 2025 (Order/JS/VC/2025-26/31809), a demand notice under RC 9052 of 2026 was issued on 26 February 2026 for Rs.5,21,000, bank/demat/MF accounts were attached vide Attachment Proceeding Nos.15241 and 15242 of 2026 on 17 March 2026, and on 6 May 2026 SEBI issued both a completion certificate and a release order after recovering the entire amount. For Ravi Himmatramka and Sons HUF, recovery was still at the demand stage on 6 May 2026: the AO imposed a Rs.5 lakh penalty on 5 March 2026 (Order/JS/DP/2025-26/32175) and the demand notice under RC 9103 of 2026 was issued on 6 May 2026 for Rs.5,16,000; no attachment, completion or release order for this noticee had appeared by that date.
review_notes: Verified against all cited chunks: Anita's full recovery lifecycle (AO order 27 Nov 2025, demand 26 Feb 2026 for Rs.5,21,000, attachment 17 Mar 2026 AP 15241/15242, completion and release 6 May 2026) and Ravi's demand-stage status (AO 5 Mar 2026, demand 6 May 2026 for Rs.5,16,000). Truly multi-document across two noticees.

question: Both Anita Devi Chokhani and Ravi Himmatramka and Sons HUF were fined Rs.5 lakh in the BSE illiquid stock options adjudication. When SEBI drew up their respective recovery certificates, why did Anita's demand exceed Ravi's by Rs.5,000?
answer_summary: Both recovery certificates carry the same Rs.5 lakh base penalty and Rs.1,000 recovery cost. The difference comes from interest. Anita Devi Chokhani's AO order was dated 27 November 2025 and her RC 9052 demand notice was dated 26 February 2026; interest was charged at 1% per month from 27/11/2025 to 26/02/2026 (about three months), producing Rs.20,000. Ravi Himmatramka's AO order was dated 5 March 2026 and his RC 9103 demand notice was dated 6 May 2026; interest ran from 5/03/2026 to 6/05/2026 (about two months), producing Rs.15,000. Hence Anita's total demand was Rs.5,21,000 while Ravi's was Rs.5,16,000.
review_notes: Amount reconciliation supported by the two adjudication orders and two demand notices: identical Rs.5 lakh base + Rs.1,000 cost, with interest gaps (Anita 27/11/2025 to 26/02/2026 = Rs.20,000; Ravi 05/03/2026 to 06/05/2026 = Rs.15,000). Both noticee records are required.

question: A bank holding Anita Devi Chokhani's account receives first the Notice of Attachment dated 17 March 2026 (AP 15241 & 15242 of 2026) and then the release order dated 6 May 2026 for RC 9052. What did the first document require, what fact changed by the second, and what must the bank do once the second arrives?
answer_summary: The March attachment notice ordered the bank to attach all accounts and lockers of Anita Devi Chokhani to the extent of Rs.5,21,000, to prohibit debits (while allowing credits), and to furnish account details, statements, and confirmation of attachment. The May release order states that SEBI has recovered the entire amount including interest and costs, marking full and final settlement of the RC 9052 demand. Upon receiving the release order, the bank must release any attached bank accounts/lockers, demat accounts and mutual fund folios of the defaulter.
review_notes: Attachment notice requires attaching accounts/lockers, prohibiting debits while allowing credits, and furnishing details; release order confirms full recovery and directs release of attached bank/locker/demat/MF accounts. Both cited documents are essential to the compliance action.

question: Anita Devi Chokhani was directed to pay a Rs.5 lakh penalty within 45 days of the Adjudicating Officer's order. Trace the subsequent recovery milestones from that order through to the release of her accounts, identifying the document that marks each milestone.
answer_summary: (1) 27 November 2025 - Adjudication Order (Order/JS/VC/2025-26/31809) imposing Rs.5 lakh penalty and warning of recovery under section 28A if unpaid within 45 days. (2) 26 February 2026 - Notice of Demand under RC 9052 of 2026 for Rs.5,21,000 (penalty Rs.5,00,000 + interest Rs.20,000 + recovery cost Rs.1,000). (3) 17 March 2026 - Attachment notices AP 15241 & 15242 of 2026 attaching bank accounts/lockers, demat accounts and mutual fund folios. (4) 6 May 2026 - Completion order declaring recovery completed after receipt of the entire amount, and release order directing banks/NSDL/CDSL/mutual funds to release the attached accounts/folios.
review_notes: End-to-end procedural timeline for Anita Devi Chokhani supported across five cited documents (AO order, demand, attachment, completion, release). Adds a distinct enumeration target from the parallel comparison in q01.

question: Three SEBI orders issued in September 2024 deal with a listed company’s promoter group, a 23-entity trading ring, and an unregistered investment adviser. Which provision of the SEBI Act, 1992 links all three matters, and which regulation appears in the Premier Synthetics and Madhav Tiwari orders but not in the Alka India order?
answer_summary: Section 12A of the SEBI Act, 1992 is the common thread. In Alka India, the promoter/PAC group violated Section 12A(f) read with Regulations 10 and 14(1) of the SAST Regulations, 1997 by failing to make an open offer. In Premier Synthetics, the 23 entities violated Section 12A(a), (b), (c) read with the PFUTP Regulations for circular trading and price manipulation. In Madhav Tiwari, the noticee violated Section 12A(a), (b), (c) read with the PFUTP Regulations for misleading advisory promises. The PFUTP Regulations therefore appear in the Premier Synthetics and Madhav Tiwari orders, but not in the Alka India order, which rests on the SAST Regulations.
review_notes: Supported: Section 12A(f) in Alka (#4/#47/#97), 12A(a)-(c)+PFUTP in Premier (#5/#143) and Madhav (#1/#10); PFUTP only in latter two. Truly three-way statutory/regulatory delta.

question: A compliance associate is comparing the September 2024 Alka India, Premier Synthetics and Madhav Tiwari orders to train staff on penalty ranges. Which order turns on a penalty provision whose statutory maximum is capped at five lakh rupees, and which two orders invoke a provision whose floor is five lakh rupees and whose ceiling is twenty-five crore rupees or three times the profits?
answer_summary: The Alka India order uses Section 15H(ii) of the SEBI Act, which imposes a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees for failure to make the public announcement/open offer required under the SAST Regulations. The Premier Synthetics and Madhav Tiwari orders both rely on Section 15HA of the SEBI Act, which prescribes a minimum penalty of five lakh rupees and a maximum of twenty-five crore rupees or three times the profits made out of fraudulent and unfair trade practices, whichever is higher.
review_notes: Supported: Section 15H(ii) cap of Rs 5 lakh in Alka (#100); Section 15HA floor Rs 5 lakh / ceiling Rs 25 crore or 3x profits in Premier (#251) and Madhav (#45/#54). Clean penalty-range comparison.

question: In the September 2024 Alka India and Premier Synthetics adjudications, several noticees never responded to the show-cause notice or attended hearings. Besides deciding those matters on the material on record, what additional consequence did the Premier Synthetics adjudicator impose for non-cooperation that the Alka India adjudicator did not?
answer_summary: In Alka India, the Adjudicating Officer proceeded ex-parte against Noticee 9 (Cavalier Securities Ltd.) and presumed admission of the charges, but imposed no separate penalty for non-cooperation. In Premier Synthetics, the Officer found Notices 2 to 19 and 21 to 23 in violation of Sections 11C(3) and 11C(5) of the SEBI Act for failing to comply with summons and, in addition to the Section 15HA penalty for PFUTP violations, imposed a separate Section 15A(a) penalty on each of those noticees.
review_notes: Supported: Alka ex-parte against Noticee 9 with no added penalty (#21-#24); Premier finds 11C(3)/(5) breach for 2-19/21-23 and imposes separate Section 15A(a) penalty (#239-#241, #250, #267-#284). Distinct procedural-escalation target.

question: The Alka India and Premier Synthetics orders end with monetary penalties and recovery warnings, while the Madhav Tiwari order adds detailed non-monetary directions. What is the key factual distinction in the Madhav Tiwari matter that justifies a refund direction, a two-year market debarment and an escrow mechanism rather than only a monetary penalty?
answer_summary: Madhav Tiwari operated as an unregistered investment adviser, collected advisory fees from investors, and disseminated guaranteed-return claims through Divinecommodity.co. The order records Rs. 1,70,12,615 credited to his Axis Bank and ICICI Bank accounts as advisory fees, treating the sums as proceeds of an illegal activity. Because investors had paid money for unlawful advisory services, SEBI directed refund of those amounts, publication of public notices, maintenance of residual sums in escrow for investor claims, a two-year debarment from the securities market, and a bar on carrying on investment-advisory activity without registration. The Alka India and Premier Synthetics matters concerned open-offer/disclosure breaches and market-manipulative trading, not the holding of investor money as advisory fees.
review_notes: Supported: Madhav collected Rs 1,70,12,615 advisory fees (#48/#49), directed refund/escrow/debarment (#50/#51/#53); Alka (#107) and Premier (#285) are monetary-penalty/recovery orders. Sharp regime-interaction question.

question: Of the three September 2024 orders, two had to handle parties who failed to participate in the proceedings, while one did not. Which order avoided any ex-parte or non-cooperation finding, and what fact in its procedural history explains why?
answer_summary: The Madhav Tiwari order avoided any ex-parte or non-cooperation finding because the noticee submitted his reply to the show-cause notice dated March 22, 2024 on May 8, 2024 and participated in the proceedings. In contrast, the Alka India adjudicator proceeded ex-parte against Noticee 9 (Cavalier Securities Ltd.) after it failed to reply or attend the hearing, and the Premier Synthetics adjudicator found Notices 2 to 19 and 21 to 23 in violation of Sections 11C(3) and 11C(5) of the SEBI Act for failing to comply with summons.
review_notes: Supported: Madhav replied to SCN and participated (#12); Alka Noticee 9 ex-parte (#21/#24); Premier notices 2-19/21-23 failed summons (#239/#241). Different answer shape from q03 (absence across three orders vs consequence).

question: The Alka India order treats the penalty as jointly and severally payable by seven noticees, while the Premier Synthetics and Madhav Tiwari orders impose separate amounts on each party. What explains the different liability structures?
answer_summary: Alka India’s penalty under Section 15H(ii) arose from a common breach: the promoter/PAC group collectively crossed the 15% voting-rights threshold after the June 30, 2004 conversion of NCRPS and failed to make a single open offer. Because the obligation ran against the group, the Adjudicating Officer made the seven noticees jointly and severally liable. In Premier Synthetics and Madhav Tiwari the misconduct was individualised — specific trading contributions, specific advisory fees and specific misleading statements — so the penalties were separately assessed against each noticee under Sections 15HA/15A(a) and Sections 15HA/15EB respectively.
review_notes: Supported: Alka penalty jointly & severally (#104); Premier per-noticeee 15HA + 15A(a) amounts (#267-#284); Madhav single noticee penalties under 15HA and 15EB (#54). Distinct responsibility-allocation target.

question: Why was the Madhav Tiwari matter passed by an ED/CGM under Sections 11(1), 11(4), 11B(1) and 11B(2) of the SEBI Act, whereas the Alka India and Premier Synthetics matters were decided by an Adjudicating Officer under Section 15-I?
answer_summary: Madhav Tiwari’s case required directional and injunctive relief — refund to investors, public notice, asset restraint, debarment from the securities market, and directions to banks, depositories, stock exchanges and others — which is rooted in SEBI’s general powers under Section 11 and its power to issue directions under Section 11B, exercised by the ED/CGM. Penalties under Sections 11(4A) and 11B(2) read with Sections 15EB and 15HA were ancillary to those directions. The Alka India and Premier Synthetics cases were pure penalty proceedings for identified violations, so they were adjudicated by an Adjudicating Officer under Section 15-I read with Rule 5 of the SEBI Adjudication Rules.
review_notes: Supported: Alka and Premier are Section 15-I AO orders (#0/#5, #0); Madhav invokes Sections 11/11B/11(4A)/11B(2) for directions (#0/#11). Approval-authority distinction is a clean memory target.

question: Each of the three September 2024 orders reached enforcement through a different entry point. Match the Alka India, Premier Synthetics and Madhav Tiwari matters to the originating trigger and explain why the channel matters for how the case was framed.
answer_summary: Madhav Tiwari originated from a Multi Commodity Exchange of India Ltd. reference email dated August 17, 2021 about the Divinecommodity.co website offering guaranteed-return tips, framing the case as unregistered investment advisory. Alka India originated from a SEBI examination of the listed company’s shareholding pattern and promoter demat compliance, prompted by a complaint dated January 13, 2022 about non-allotment of shares after the Jenice Textiles amalgamation, framing it as a disclosure/takeover issue. Premier Synthetics originated from SEBI’s market investigation into abnormal price and volume spikes in the scrip during November 2017–October 2018, framing it as market manipulation. The different channels explain why one became an ED/CGM direction order, while the other two remained adjudication-office penalty orders.
review_notes: Supported: Madhav from MCX email Aug 17, 2021 (#0); Alka from BSE examination triggered by complaint Jan 13, 2022 (#2/#53); Premier from investigation into PSL trading based on complaints/SMS (#0/#4/#5/#253). Source-resolution comparison.

question: Both of Ravi Prakashkumar Shah's April 2026 RTI first appeals—Appeal Nos. 6803 and 6815—were decided against him, but one was dismissed and the other disposed of as infructuous. What was the decisive difference in the facts and reasoning that produced each outcome, and which member of SEBI's Appellate Authority decided each appeal?
answer_summary: Appeal No. 6803 (April 10, 2026, order by Maninder Cheema) was disposed of as infructuous: the appellant's only grievance was that the CPIO's reply uploaded on March 18, 2026 was not opening in the RTI MIS portal. The Appellate Authority noted a portal glitch on March 17-18, 2026, found the reply was now viewable, enclosed a copy with the order, and held that nothing survived. Appeal No. 6815 (April 23, 2026, order by Ruchi Chojer) was dismissed on merits: the appellant had appealed against queries 3, 4, 7 and 10, which asked broadly whether SEBI had sought reports, directed examinations, or tracked foreign/HFT participation in MCX Gold Futures. The authority held those queries were vague, generic and sought clarification/confirmation rather than recorded "information" as defined in Section 2(f) of the RTI Act, relying on CIC decisions in T. V. Sundaresan v. CPIO, SEBI and Azad Singh v. CPIO, Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd.
review_notes: Verified by both cited orders: Appeal 6803 disposed as infructuous (portal glitch, Maninder Cheema) and Appeal 6815 dismissed on Section 2(f) vagueness (Ruchi Chojer). Strong parallel comparison of disposition/reasoning/member.

question: Ravi Prakashkumar Shah filed two RTI first appeals against SEBI that were decided in April 2026. Match each appeal number with the date of the underlying RTI application, the date of the CPIO reply, and the appeal registration number, and explain which procedural event made the March 18, 2026 reply different from the March 27, 2026 reply.
answer_summary: Appeal No. 6803 corresponds to an RTI application dated February 20, 2026, a CPIO reply dated March 18, 2026, and appeal registration SEBIH/A/E/26/00109. Appeal No. 6815 corresponds to an RTI application dated February 26, 2026, a CPIO reply dated March 27, 2026, and appeal registration SEBIH/A/E/26/00120. The March 18 reply was uploaded to the RTI MIS portal but was temporarily inaccessible to the appellant because of a portal technical issue on March 17-18, 2026; the March 27 reply was accessed and challenged on its substance as incomplete or misleading.
review_notes: Dates and registration numbers verified in both orders; March 18 portal accessibility issue confirmed in Appeal 6803. Operational pairing is distinct from the other questions.

question: Ravi Prakashkumar Shah's two April 2026 RTI appeals challenged SEBI replies, but only one resulted in a reasoned dismissal on the scope of the RTI Act. What statutory provision and case law were invoked in Appeal No. 6815 but not in Appeal No. 6803, and why was the same reasoning unnecessary in the earlier appeal?
answer_summary: Appeal No. 6815 invoked Section 2(f) of the RTI Act and Central Information Commission precedents in T. V. Sundaresan v. CPIO, SEBI (November 24, 2021) and Azad Singh v. CPIO, Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. (March 23, 2021), holding that broad, confirmation-seeking queries are not recorded "information" under the Act. That reasoning was unnecessary in Appeal No. 6803 because the appellant there complained only of an RTI MIS portal access problem on March 17-18, 2026; once a copy of the CPIO reply was enclosed and the reply was found to have been provided within time, the authority disposed of the appeal as infructuous without reaching the merits of the information request.
review_notes: Section 2(f) and CIC precedents (T.V. Sundaresan, Azad Singh) verified in Appeal 6815 chunks; Appeal 6803 reasoning limited to portal issue. Clean negative/absence check.

question: Comparing the two April 2026 Appellate Authority orders involving Ravi Prakashkumar Shah, one describes the specific information requested (MCX Gold Futures surveillance, FPI/HFT participation, etc.), whereas the other does not even state the subject of the RTI request. Why did absence of the substantive request not stop the authority from disposing of the second appeal, and what was the practical result?
answer_summary: The absence of the substantive request did not prevent disposal because the appellant's grievance in Appeal No. 6803 was limited to the RTI MIS portal's accessibility: the CPIO reply had been uploaded on March 18, 2026 but was temporarily unavailable due to a portal glitch on March 17-18. The Appellate Authority verified the reply was now viewable and enclosed a copy with its order, so the appeal became infructuous. By contrast, Appeal No. 6815 reached the merits precisely because the appellant challenged the reply itself, and the authority then scrutinised the vague MCX Gold Futures queries under Section 2(f) of the RTI Act.
review_notes: Record-completeness delta verified: 6815 lists MCX Gold Futures queries, 6803 omits substantive request because the only grievance was portal access. Result disposed as infructuous.

question: Two women investors, Pramita Devi and Umarawati Devi, filed RTI appeals on the same day disputing PACL land-allotment entries that were blocking their refund claims. In what different ways did each appellant frame her information request—one asking how to correct the entry and reopen the refund claim, the other asking for certified records of the alleged allotment—and what common RTI Act reasoning led the Appellate Authority to dismiss both appeals?
answer_summary: Pramita Devi (Appeal No. 6814 of 2026) asked: (i) the basis on which her PACL certificate showed "Land Allotted YES"; (ii) details of any land or property allotted, including location and date; (iii) the procedure to correct the incorrect entry and reopen her refund claim; (iv) whether the certificates could still be considered for refund now; and (v) the present status of her PACL refund eligibility under the Justice (Retd.) R.M. Lodha Committee process. Umarawati Devi (Appeal No. 6813 of 2026) asked for certified/evidentiary records: documents relied on to record that land had been allotted, copies of land allotment letters or allocation records, specific land details including state, district, survey number and size, the date on which land was recorded as allotted, verification or inspection reports showing possession, and any SEBI or Lodha Committee circulars, guidelines or procedures for correcting incorrect PACL land-allotment data. In both cases the CPIO had replied that the information sought was not available with SEBI. The Appellate Authority dismissed both appeals on the same reasoning: under the RTI Act SEBI cannot invent information it does not hold, citing the Central Information Commission decision in Sh. Pattipati Rama Murthy v. CPIO, SEBI (July 8, 2013). It added that disposal of PACL properties and repayment to investors rests with the Justice (Retd.) R.M. Lodha Committee constituted by the Supreme Court's February 2, 2016 order, and pointed both appellants to PACL public notices, press releases, status reports and FAQs already on the SEBI website.
review_notes: Both cited orders verified. Compares the two appellants' query framings against the shared CPIO reply and CIC Rama Murthy non-invention rationale, plus Lodha Committee redirection. Distinct paired-comparison memory target.

question: A PACL investor believes that the April 23, 2026 RTI appeals by Pramita Devi and Umarawati Devi show that SEBI will correct a wrong land-allotment entry or obtain the missing documents if the request shows the entry is blocking a refund. Is that correct? What did the Appellate Authority actually direct SEBI to do in each case, and what alternative guidance, if any, did it offer?
answer_summary: No, that is not correct. The Appellate Authority did not direct SEBI to correct any land-allotment record, obtain missing documents from PACL or the Lodha Committee, or grant any individualized refund relief to either Pramita Devi or Umarawati Devi. In both appeals it upheld the CPIO's response that the requested information was not available with SEBI and dismissed the appeals. The only guidance it offered was that the responsibility for disposal of PACL properties and repayment to investors lies with the Justice (Retd.) R.M. Lodha Committee (constituted pursuant to the Supreme Court's February 2, 2016 order), and that both investors could consult PACL-related public notices, press releases, status reports and FAQs already published on the SEBI website.
review_notes: Absence claim verified: Authority did not order SEBI to correct records, obtain documents, or grant individualized refund relief. Alternative guidance correctly points to the Lodha Committee and public PACL materials. Useful misbelief intercept.

question: Two RTI appeals, Appeal Nos. 6813 and 6814 of 2026, were decided on the same day by the same Appellate Authority. What was the procedural history common to both appeals, which Central Information Commission decision did the Authority rely on in dismissing each, and how did the two appellants' factual grievances differ even though both concerned the same underlying PACL refund problem?
answer_summary: Both Pramita Devi (Appeal No. 6814) and Umarawati Devi (Appeal No. 6813) filed RTI applications on March 16, 2026 (received through the RTI MIS portal), received responses from the CPIO on March 24, 2026, and filed first appeals on March 26, 2026 (registration numbers SEBIH/A/E/26/00119 and SEBIH/A/E/26/00118 respectively). The Appellate Authority (Ruchi Chojer) disposed of both appeals on April 23, 2026, dismissing each. In both orders it cited the Central Information Commission decision in Sh. Pattipati Rama Murthy v. CPIO, SEBI (July 8, 2013), for the proposition that SEBI cannot create information it does not hold. Despite this common track and outcome, the grievances differed. Umarawati Devi disputed the portal's assertion that land had been allotted against her PACL certificates and stated she never received possession; she sought the evidentiary basis and verification records. Pramita Devi's application concerned a PACL investment held in her name; the certificates had been deposited at a PACL Varanasi office in 2014 for a loan that was never disbursed, and the application focused on correcting the "Land Allotted YES" entry and reopening the refund claim.
review_notes: Procedural timeline (applications/replies/appeals/dates/registration numbers) and common CIC precedent verified across both orders. Contrasts factual grievances between the two appellants. Distinct from q01/q02.

question: Two first appeals under the RTI Act decided on April 16, 2026—Appeal No. 6810 by Rohit Aggarwal and Appeal No. 6811 by Vivek Tripathi—were both remitted to the CPIO for de novo consideration. In each appeal, which RTI Act exemption did SEBI rely on when denying the information, and why did the Appellate Authority find the exemption claim unpersuasive?
answer_summary: In Rohit Aggarwal's Appeal No. 6810, SEBI refused the request for copies of circulars, clarifications, advisory notes, file notings or regulatory communications defining or interpreting 'new business' and post-death distributor transactions under AMFI Circular CIR ARN 15/12/13, invoking Section 8(1)(a) of the RTI Act (internal functioning / strategic decision-making). The Appellate Authority held that the CPIO had not given sufficient justification for invoking that section and remitted the application for de novo reconsideration within 15 working days from receipt of the order. In Vivek Tripathi's Appeal No. 6811, SEBI denied certified ROC correspondence and director replies in the Helios Plantation & Developers matter under Section 8(1)(h), claiming ongoing prosecution proceedings, but the Authority held the CPIO failed to show how disclosure would actually impede investigation or prosecution (citing the Delhi High Court in Amit Kumar Shrivastava v. Central Information Commission) and remitted query nos. 1 and 3 for a fresh reply within 15 working days.
review_notes: Both cited orders support the exemption sections and the de-novo remand reasoning; distinct comparison of the two remanded appeals.

question: In deciding Vivek Tripathi's Appeal No. 6811, the Appellate Authority cites a Delhi High Court ruling on Section 8(1)(h). In Ajay Basudev Bose's Appeal No. 6809, it cites Central Information Commission and Karnataka High Court rulings for Sections 8(1)(g) and 8(1)(j). What common test do these precedents impose on a public authority that withholds information, and why did the Authority grant relief in one appeal but dismiss the other?
answer_summary: All the cited decisions require the public authority to give cogent, case-specific reasons for withholding: Section 8(1)(h) cannot be invoked with a bare claim of ongoing prosecution—the authority must demonstrate how disclosure would actually impede investigation or prosecution (Delhi High Court, Amit Kumar Shrivastava v. CIC). Likewise, Sections 8(1)(g) and 8(1)(j) Personal information can be withheld only if disclosure has no public-interest relationship and would cause unwarranted privacy invasion or endangerment (Central Information Commission, Prerit Misra v. CPIO, SEBI; Karnataka High Court, H.E. Rajashekarappa v. State PIO). In Tripathi's case the CPIO offered no such justification for the Section 8(1)(h) claim regarding Helios prosecution documents, so the Authority remitted query nos. 1 and 3 for a fresh reasoned reply. In Bose's case the Authority accepted that SEBI officer names/designations satisfied the personal-information test and that ED/PMLA/SFIO/Finance Ministry material did not pertain to SEBI, so the appeal was dismissed.
review_notes: Precedent-compulsion angle is supported by both orders; note that Bose’s query 1 also relied on Section 8(1)(h), but the question’s stated 8(1)(g)/8(1)(j) focus is accurate.

question: In Vivek Tripathi's appeal about Helios Plantation & Developers, several queries were rejected as seeking clarification or opinion rather than 'information' as defined in Section 2(f) of the RTI Act. Rohit Aggarwal's appeal about the AMFI circular also asked SEBI to define or interpret a term. Why did the Authority nonetheless remand Aggarwal's request for a de novo reply instead of treating it as non-information?
answer_summary: Tripathi's queries nos. 11, 14 and 23 sought confirmations, reasons, opinions or clarification that would require the CPIO to create or infer information rather than communicate existing records; the Authority held these were not 'information' under Section 2(f). Aggarwal, by contrast, asked for copies of specific existing SEBI records—circulars, advisories, file notings, internal notes or regulatory communications—that define 'new business' or govern post-death distributor transactions, or confirmation that no such records exist. That is classic information held by SEBI. The Authority therefore did not apply the Section 2(f) objection; instead it found SEBI's Section 8(1)(a) exemption claim unsupported and remanded the matter for a fresh reply.
review_notes: Supported by Tripathi (Section 2(f) non-information) and Aggarwal (record request remanded under 8(1)(a)); clean contrast between clarification and held records.

question: On April 16, 2026 the Appellate Authority disposed of three first appeals—Appeal Nos. 6809, 6810 and 6811. Only one of the three was dismissed outright. Which appeal was dismissed, and what combination of reasons made its outcome different from the two remanded appeals?
answer_summary: Ajay Basudev Bose's Appeal No. 6809 was dismissed outright. Bose asked about Moongipa Investment Limited—ED/PMLA ECIRs, summons, attachments, SFIO references, Finance Ministry correspondence and the names/designations of SEBI officers. The Authority accepted that several queries pertained to bodies other than SEBI (ED, SFIO, Ministry of Finance) and that SEBI cannot create information it does not hold (CIC, Pattipati Rama Murthy v. CPIO, SEBI). It also upheld the personal-information exemption for officer names under Sections 8(1)(g) and 8(1)(j). In the other two appeals, the information was within SEBI's domain—Helios CIS prosecution/ROC correspondence in Tripathi's case and AMFI circular/internal guidance in Aggarwal's case—but SEBI's exemption claims under Sections 8(1)(h) and 8(1)(a) lacked sufficient justification, so those appeals were remitted for a fresh reply within 15 working days.
review_notes: All three orders support the outcome split: Bose dismissed on non-SEBI/jurisdictional and personal-info grounds, Tripathi and Aggarwal remanded for insufficient exemption justification.

question: A lawyer is reviewing three recent court orders that disposed of petitions in which SEBI appeared: Col. (Retd.) Harjit Singh v. WTM, SEBI (Bombay High Court); Samir Sudhir Porecha v. Geeta Jaswal & Ors. (Bombay High Court); and Nauman Zahid v. Allied Digital Services Ltd. & Ors. (NCLT). In tabular form, what did each petitioner seek, on what basis did the forum dispose of the matter, and which forum(s) expressly declined to decide the merits?
answer_summary: 1. Harjit Singh (Bombay HC, WP(L) 41355/2025, 10 Apr 2026): The petitioner challenged an impugned SEBI notice dated 19 Aug 2025. The court disposed of the writ after SEBI counsel stated that SEBI would not act in furtherance of that notice and would issue a fresh notice before proceeding. The court expressly said it had not gone into the merits, kept all rights/contentions open, and directed the order would not be treated as a precedent.\n2. Samir Porecha (Bombay HC, WP(ST/L) 3803/2025, 2 Apr 2026): The petitioner withdrew the writ because the parties had executed consent terms on 26 Mar 2026 in City Civil Court Suit No. 716/2025. The HC allowed withdrawal unconditionally; it did not adjudicate SEBI's position on the merits.\n3. Nauman Zahid (NCLT Mumbai, CP 137/2024, 11 Feb 2026): The petitioner sought transfer/demat of 14,90,000 shares into his beneficiary account, rectification of the register of members, and past/future corporate benefits. The NCLT disposed of the company petition because SEBI Circular No. HO/38/13/11(2)2026-MIRSD-POD/I/3750/2026 opened a one-year special window (5 Feb 2026 – 4 Feb 2027) for transfer/demat of physical securities sold/purchased before 1 Apr 2019. The tribunal expressly declined to express any opinion on the petitioner's entitlement to maintain the petition under Sections 58/59 of the Companies Act, 2013.
review_notes: Cross-case table verified against all three cited court orders; prayers, disposal grounds, and express non-merits language are supported. The three-order comparison is a distinct procedural-posture memory target.

question: A buyer holds original physical share certificates for securities purchased in 2018, but the corporate seller has gone into liquidation, making an ordinary dematerialised transfer impracticable. The buyer has filed a company petition under Sections 58/59 of the Companies Act seeking registration of the shares and past corporate benefits. Based on the Nauman Zahid NCLT order and the SEBI circular the tribunal relied on, what relief is the NCLT likely to grant and what conditions or exclusions apply?
answer_summary: The NCLT is unlikely to adjudicate the company petition on the merits. In Nauman Zahid (CP 137/2024), the NCLT disposed of the petition in view of SEBI Circular No. HO/38/13/11(2)2026-MIRSD-POD/I/3750/2026 dated 30 Jan 2026, 'Ease of Doing Investment – Special Window for Transfer and Dematerialisation of Physical Securities.' The circular opens a one-year window from 5 Feb 2026 to 4 Feb 2027 for transfer and dematerialisation of physical securities sold/purchased before 1 Apr 2019. Key conditions: original share certificates; transfer deed executed before 1 Apr 2019; proof of purchase by transferee; KYC documents as per ISR; latest Client Master List of the demat account (not older than 2 months); and an undertaking-cum-indemnity per Annexure-A. The securities must be credited in demat and locked in for one year. Important exclusions: cases involving disputes between transferor and transferee; and securities transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund. RTAs/listed companies must process complete requests within 70 days. The NCLT expressly stated that it was not expressing any opinion on the petitioner's eligibility to maintain the petition under Sections 58/59; the practical route is to apply under the special window.
