question: SEBI issued two investor-relief circulars in quick succession for holders of physical share transfer requests: the July 2, 2025 circular (SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD-PoD/P/CIR/2025/97) and the January 30, 2026 circular (HO/38/13/11(2)2026-MIRSD-POD/I/3750/2026). What changed in substance, eligibility cut-off, and duration between the two windows, and which of the two did the NCLT rely on to dispose of Nauman Zahid's company petition?
answer_summary: July 2025 circular (SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD-PoD/P/CIR/2025/97): It reopened a special window only for re-lodgement of transfer deeds that had been lodged before 1 Apr 2019 but were rejected, returned, or unattended due to documentary/process deficiency. Duration: six months from 7 Jul 2025 to 6 Jan 2026. Transfers were to be issued only in demat mode, and listed companies/RTAs had to publicise the window bi-monthly and report monthly.\nJanuary 2026 circular (HO/38/13/11(2)2026-MIRSD-POD/I/3750/2026): This was a broader 'transfer and dematerialisation' window for physical securities sold/purchased before 1 Apr 2019, not limited to previously rejected deeds. Duration: one year from 5 Feb 2026 to 4 Feb 2027. It introduced new conditions (original certificate, transfer deed executed before 1 Apr 2019, KYC, current CML, undertaking-cum-indemnity), mandated one-year demat lock-in, capped processing at 70 days, and excluded disputes between transferor/transferee and IEPF-transferred securities.\nThe NCLT in Nauman Zahid (CP 137/2024) relied on the January 2026 circular to dispose of the company petition.
review_notes: Both cited circulars verified; scope, eligibility cut-off, duration, and operational changes between the July 2025 re-lodgement window and the January 2026 transfer/demat window match the text. The NCLT reliance on the January 2026 circular is supported. Distinct version-delta target.

question: Three first appeals under the RTI Act decided on 27 and 29 April 2026—Mahesh Kumar Nama (Appeal No. 6816), V. answer_summary: Mahesh Kumar Nama asked about refunds to PACL investors. The Authority held that SEBI did not possess the information (the responsibility of disposal and repayment is with the Justice (Retd.) R.M. Lodha Committee) and cited the CIC decision in Sh. The Authority held the request was vague, non-specific and in the nature of seeking clarification/opinion, so it was not 'information' under section 2(f) of the RTI Act, citing the CIC decision in T. V. Sundaresan vs. CPIO, SEBI (November 24, 2021). Nikhil Mishra asked for dividend and correspondence details for State Bank of India shares. The Authority held the information was not maintained by SEBI in the normal course of regulating the securities market and cited the CIC decision in Lakshminarayanan R vs. SEBI (February 9, 2023). All three appeals were dismissed.
review_notes: Each of the three appeal classifications is directly backed by the cited chunks: Nama/PACL-Lodha/Rama Murthy, Mohan/vague s.2(f)/T.V. Sundaresan, Mishra/normal-course/Lakshminarayanan. All three documents are needed.

question: In two April 2026 RTI dismissals—Nikhil Mishra (Appeal No. 6823) and Mahesh Kumar Nama (Appeal No. 6816)—SEBI said it did not hold the requested information. Whom or what did the Appellate Authority direct each appellant to instead, and why were the two redirections different?

question: Compare the procedural chronology of the three RTI appeals decided in late April 2026—Mahesh Kumar Nama (Appeal No. 6816), V. Shankar Mohan (Appeal No. 6822) and Nikhil Mishra (Appeal No. 6823). In which case was the appeal dated before the CPIO's reply, and how do the other two differ?

question: Two PACL-related first appeals decided on 7 May 2026 - Appeal No. 6832 by Kedar Nath Yadav and Appeal No. 6833 by Rahul Sharma - were both dismissed, but the RTI requests were very different. question: Both 7 May 2026 PACL first appeals were dismissed even though one appellant asked about a specific Mohali plot and the other asked for documents and rules surrounding an allegedly mis-classified claim. question: Someone claims SEBI's CPIO sits on PACL RTI replies before first appeals. question: A lawyer is comparing the statutory counts in the three SEBI Special Court, Delhi sentencing orders for plantation/forest Collective Investment Scheme cases. question: Only one of the three sentencing orders states that the company fine already includes SEBI's cost of proceedings, and only two of the three direct that the amount deposited by the convicts will be transferred to SEBI's Investors Protection Fund. question: Three Bombay High Court orders published in January 2026 under SEBI's Orders of Courts involve very different proceedings: Biowin Pharma (India) Ltd. in liquidation, Abhishek R. The court allowed the Official Liquidator's report, dissolving the company (along with 33 other companies) and dispensing with winding-up compliance because there were no funds or recoverable assets; any preliminary deposits that could not be refunded could be transferred to the company liquidation account under Section 555 of the Companies Act, 1956. Abhishek R. Sheth vs SEBI: Bombay HC Ordinary Original Civil Jurisdiction, Interim Application No. 460 of 2023 in Suit No. 279 of 2022. question: In the January 2026 Bombay High Court orders in Abhishek R. Sheth and Karvy Realty, the court's disposition turned on SEBI's role in each case. In Karvy Realty, Defendant No.3 had sought leave to transfer its PMS business in reliance on an approval granted by SEBI. When counsel informed the court that SEBI had revoked that approval, the applicant sought leave to withdraw the IA with liberty to file a fresh application only if fresh SEBI approval was obtained. The court granted leave and disposed of the IA as withdrawn, expressly conditioning any fresh application on SEBI first granting a fresh approval.
review_notes: Both cited orders support the contrasted SEBI positions and the resulting dispositions; distinct from Q1/Q3 despite shared documents.

question: A 5 January 2026 order in Commercial Suit No. 98 of 2024 states that leave to transfer a PMS business was withdrawn because SEBI had revoked its approval. How does this outcome build on the 10 January 2025 order in the same commercial suit, and what does the 2 January 2025 SEBI adjudication order against Karvy Capital AIF/KCAP AIF reveal about the regulatory problem that shaped the approval history?
answer_summary: In the 10 January 2025 order (IA No. 35188 of 2024), Karvy Capital Limited withdrew its interim application after the time granted by SEBI expired on 31 December 2024. The court dismissed it as withdrawn with liberty to file afresh after obtaining SEBI's consent, and clarified that SEBI would consider all relevant factors, including the court's own orders in the suit. By 5 January 2026 (IA No. 6774 of 2025), the situation had worsened: the defendant's PMS-transfer application was grounded in a SEBI approval that had since been revoked. The court again allowed withdrawal with liberty, but made the condition explicit: a fresh application could be filed only if SEBI granted a fresh approval. The 2 January 2025 adjudication order explains the regulatory backdrop: Karvy Capital Limited was the manager/sponsor of Karvy AIFs, and its promoter Karvy Stock Broking Limited held approximately 100% of the voting rights in KCL. Following the SEBI final order of 28 April 2023 restraining KSBL from the securities market, KSBL no longer satisfied the fit-and-proper-person criteria under Regulation 4(f) of the AIF Regulations and Schedule II of the Intermediaries Regulations. To cure this, KCL arranged sale of its PMS business and obtained SEBI approval for the transfer on 21 March 2024, but continuing non-compliance/arising issues caused the approval to be withdrawn, leaving the commercial-suit application without the necessary regulatory foundation.
review_notes: The two Karvy court orders and the 2 Jan 2025 AO together support the PMS-transfer lineage; AO supplies the fit-and-proper/regulatory problem and the later orders confirm the revoked approval and conditional withdrawal.

question: Two company-petition orders published in early 2026 under SEBI's Orders of Courts both concern SEBI-regulated entities but were decided by different forums. Compare the Biowin Pharma dissolution order and the Nauman Zahid vs. Allied Digital Services order on forum, enabling provision, and the relief ultimately granted.
answer_summary: Biowin Pharma was decided by the Bombay High Court sitting in its Ordinary Original Civil Jurisdiction. The Official Liquidator's Report No. 160 of 2025 arose out of Company Petition No. 775 of 2001 under the Companies Act, 1956. The court allowed dissolution of the company (and 33 others) and dispensed with winding-up compliance because there were no funds or recoverable assets. Nauman Zahid was decided by the National Company Law Tribunal, Mumbai Bench, Court-V. The petition (CP No. 137 of 2024) was filed under Sections 58(3) and 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 seeking transfer and rectification of 14,90,000 shares. Because the shares had been sold/purchased before 1 April 2019 while still in physical form, SEBI's circular dated 30 January 2026 opened a special one-year window for dematerialisation and transfer of such securities. The NCLT disposed of the petition, making clear it expressed no opinion on whether the petitioner was eligible to maintain a Section 58/59 petition.
review_notes: Forum, enabling provision and relief comparison is directly supported by Biowin and Nauman Zahid orders; the NCLT forum contrast adds a different memorization target from Q1.

question: On 16 April 2026 the same SEBI Special Court convicted Chiranjit Mahanta and Rajlaksmi Bhattacharjee in Blue Print Securities and Shardaraj Tradefin, and additionally Sudip Nath in Sunshine Housecon. In all three cases the offence was non-payment of an adjudication penalty under Section 24(2) r/w Section 27 of the SEBI Act. State the fine imposed on each convicted director in each case and explain why the amounts differed even though the same pair of individuals was involved.
answer_summary: In Blue Print Securities (Special Case 1174/2021) the company penalty was ₹1 crore; Chiranjit Mahanta was fined ₹1 crore and Rajlaksmi Bhattacharjee was fined ₹50 lakhs. In Shardaraj Tradefin (Special Case 1172/2021) the company penalty was ₹50 lakhs; Mahanta was fined ₹50 lakhs and Bhattacharjee was fined ₹25 lakhs. In Sunshine Housecon (Special Case 1301/2021) the company penalty was again ₹1 crore; Mahanta was fined ₹1 crore, Sudip Nath was fined ₹50 lakhs and Bhattacharjee was fined ₹50 lakhs. The court held imprisonment inappropriate because the directors were only answerable for non-payment of the company penalty, but it differentiated fines according to the quantum of the underlying adjudication penalty and to the evidence of each director's role, noting 'overwhelming' incriminating material against Mahanta.
review_notes: Cited order paragraphs in all three judgments confirm the director-wise fines and the court's role-based differentiation, including the higher fine on Mahanta.

question: In the Blue Print Securities and Shardaraj Tradefin special cases the defence argued that the email communicating the adjudication order was not digitally signed and therefore did not amount to proper service under the SEBI adjudication rules. Did the Special Court accept that objection, and how did Chiranjit Mahanta's conduct in the Sunshine Housecon matter undermine the claim?
answer_summary: The court rejected the digital-signature objection. It held that the email in question was a pre-prosecution notice and was not mandatory, and that the lack of a digital signature therefore did not vitiate the prosecution. More importantly, Mahanta's own conduct showed actual knowledge of the order: he signed resolutions authorising the SAT appeals for Blue Print Securities and Shardaraj Tradefin, and himself moved an appeal against the same adjudication order on behalf of Sunshine Housecon. Those acts, together with the MCA director records and the common address of the companies, contradicted the later defence that he was merely a peon or employee.
review_notes: Chunk evidence confirms the court rejected the unsigned-email objection as a non-mandatory pre-prosecution notice and used Mahanta's cross-case SAT-appeal conduct to infer actual knowledge.

question: The Blue Print Securities, Shardaraj Tradefin and Sunshine Housecon judgments all trace to a common IPO-proceeds transaction. What was the shared fraudulent pattern, what amount within that pattern is attributed to each accused company, and how does each amount correspond to the adjudication penalty the company was ordered to pay?
answer_summary: The shared pattern was the use of fictitious inter-corporate deposits (ICDs) to round-trip proceeds of Brooks Laboratories Ltd's IPO through Suryamukhi Projects Pvt. Ltd. and other conduit entities. Blue Print Securities was shown to have routed back ₹1 crore via Mangalmayee Hirise and Suryamukhi Projects, and its adjudication penalty was ₹1 crore. Shardaraj Tradefin was shown to have routed ₹50 lakhs, and its penalty was ₹50 lakhs. Sunshine Housecon was shown to have routed ₹1 crore from Suryamukhi Projects, and its penalty was ₹1 crore. The three companies were part of a larger ₹8.25-crore network, and the reinstatement penalty in each case matched the amount attributed to that company.
review_notes: Cited factual paragraphs support the ICD round-tripping pattern, the company-specific routed amounts, and that each matched the re-imposed adjudication penalty.

question: Before the 16 April 2026 judgments, one accused director was discharged in each of Blue Print Securities and Shardaraj Tradefin, while no director was discharged in Sunshine Housecon. Identify the discharged directors and state how many directors were finally convicted in each of the three special cases.
answer_summary: In Blue Print Securities (Special Case 1174/2021) accused No.3 Manoj Shaw was discharged, leaving two directors convicted: Chiranjit Mahanta and Rajlaksmi Bhattacharjee. In Shardaraj Tradefin (Special Case 1172/2021) accused No.3 Ashis Das was discharged, again leaving two directors convicted: Mahanta and Bhattacharjee. In Sunshine Housecon (Special Case 1301/2021) no director was discharged, and three directors were convicted: Mahanta, Sudip Nath and Bhattacharjee. All convictions were under Section 24(2) r/w Section 27 of the SEBI Act.
review_notes: Accused-details tables in the three judgments confirm Manoj Shaw and Ashis Das were discharged and the final convicted director counts in each case.

question: Across the three 16 April 2026 SEBI Special Court judgments, the convicted directors argued that they were merely peons or employees and that the original PFUTP violations predated them. What Supreme Court precedent did the court rely on to reject that argument, and why did it impose the highest fine on Chiranjit Mahanta each time?
answer_summary: The court relied on S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals Limited v. Neeta Bhalla & Ors., (2007) 4 SCC 70, which draws a line between passive directors and managing directors, signatories, or persons in charge of and responsible for day-to-day affairs, who may be vicariously liable for company offences. The court held that the NI Act precedents cited by the defence were inapposite because the prosecution was under the SEBI Act. It fixed the highest fine on Chiranjit Mahanta because the record showed incriminating acts—signing board resolutions for Blue Print and Shardaraj SAT appeals himself, moving the SAT appeal for Sunshine Housecon, the common registered address of the companies, and MCA director records—proving he was the person in charge rather than a mere employee.
review_notes: Cited liability discussion confirms the court relied on S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals v. Neeta Bhalla for director liability and grounded Mahanta's higher fine in his incriminating cross-case acts.

question: In late 2024, the Principal Sessions Judge, Chennai delivered three judgments against plantation or agritech companies accused of unregistered collective investment schemes: SEBI v. Bon Plantations & Exports Ltd.; SEBI v. P.G. Fortune Agritech Ltd.; and SEBI v. Brammaputhra Plantations Pvt. Ltd. All three charged the accused under Section 24(1) read with Section 27 of the SEBI Act. Which specific accused were convicted, acquitted, or had charges abated in each case, and what factual difference led the court to sentence one managing director to imprisonment while the other companies and directors were acquitted?
answer_summary: Bon Plantations: Accused 1 (the company), Accused 2, Accused 4 and Accused 5 were acquitted; Accused 3 (Manikant Padmshi) had died pending trial and the charges against him abated. P.G. Fortune Agritech: Accused 1 (the company), Accused 3, Accused 4 and Accused 5 were acquitted; Accused 2 (VVLP Gupta) had died during the proceedings and the charges against him abated. Brammaputhra Plantations: Accused 1 (the company) was convicted and fined Rs.10 lakhs; Accused 2 (Jose Mathew) was convicted and sentenced to three years' simple imprisonment plus a fine of Rs.5 lakhs, in default one year's simple imprisonment; Accused 3 (Jolly Jose) was acquitted. The decisive factual difference was proof of who was in charge of the company and what happened to investor money: in Brammaputhra, voluminous prosecution documents showed Jose Mathew represented the accused company throughout and had admitted it collected money and refunded only a small part; in Bon Plantations, the prosecution failed to prove that the individual accused were directors or officers in charge at the relevant time, and no document was signed by Accused 3-5; in P.G. Fortune Agritech, the accused produced auditor-supported repayment correspondence and the court held any delay could be condoned, leaving the prosecution unable to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
review_notes: Directly supported by cited judgment chunks. Compares acquittal/abatement/conviction outcomes and the evidentiary reason for divergence across all three Chennai CIS judgments.

question: The three late-2024 Chennai SEBI collective-investment-scheme judgments all originated as complaints filed before the XXIII Metropolitan Magistrate, Saidapet, Chennai in 2002. What was the original C.C. number on the magistrate file and the later Sessions Court number for each of Bon Plantations, P.G. Fortune Agritech and Brammaputhra Plantations, and which accused died during the proceedings in each case?
answer_summary: Bon Plantations: the case was originally C.C.No.17/2002 on the file of the learned XXIII Metropolitan Magistrate, Saidapet, Chennai, and was later withdrawn to the Principal Sessions Judge, Chennai as C.C.No.79/2019. Accused 3, Shri.Manikant Padmshi, died pending trial and the charges against him abated. P.G. Fortune Agritech: the case was originally C.C.No.8803/2002 on the file of the learned XXIII Metropolitan Magistrate, Saidapet, Chennai, and was committed to the Principal Sessions Judge as Sessions Case No.135/2011. Accused 2, Shri.VVLP Gupta, had died during the proceedings and the charges against him abated. Brammaputhra Plantations: the case was originally C.C.No.8798/2002 on the file of the same Metropolitan Magistrate and was committed to the Principal Sessions Judge as Sessions Case No.454/2010. None of the accused died, and all three were tried to verdict.
review_notes: Court-file provenance and accused-death facts are supported by the opening/order sections of all three judgments. DISTINCT from q01/q03 because it targets procedural metadata.

question: Section 27 of the SEBI Act makes directors or officers who are in charge of a company vicariously liable for its offence. Using the three 2024 Chennai judgments—SEBI v. Bon Plantations, SEBI v. P.G. Fortune Agritech and SEBI v. Brammaputhra Plantations—explain why Section 27 liability attached to the managing director in one case but failed against the personal accused in the other two.
answer_summary: SECTION 27 LIABILITY ATTACHED in Brammaputhra Plantations because the prosecution produced voluminous documentary evidence showing that Accused 2 Jose Mathew consistently represented the accused company, signed letters addressed to SEBI and executed lease agreements as its Managing Director. He also admitted in his own deposition that the company had collected Rs.0.27 crore and refunded only Rs.2,62,000. The court held he was in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the company, and therefore vicariously liable under Section 27. SECTION 27 LIABILITY FAILED in Bon Plantations because, although the complaint stated that Accused 2-5 were directors, the prosecution adduced no acceptable evidence that they were directors or officers in charge when the CIS Regulations came into force, and none of the documents were signed by Accused 3-5. SECTION 27 LIABILITY ALSO FAILED in P.G. Fortune Agritech, but for a different reason: the company had wound up its schemes and produced auditor-supported correspondence showing that it had repaid investors, leaving only one unproved discrepancy. The court held the delay in repayment was condonable and the prosecution had not proved the case beyond reasonable doubt, so the directors could not be held liable either.
review_notes: Supported by the reasoning paragraphs on Section 27 vicarious liability in each judgment. Teaches a different memory target than q01 (legal test for director liability), so both can stand.

question: On April 10, 2026, SEBI's Appellate Authority disposed of three separate first appeals under the RTI Act filed by Ajay Kumar, Manoj and Kamal Kumar, all complaining that the CPIO reply would not open in the RTI MIS portal. Two appeals were received on March 18, 2026; the third was received on March 19. Which appellant filed the appeal dated March 19, and at what point did the Authority still consider all three appeals infructuous?
answer_summary: Ajay Kumar filed the appeal dated March 19, 2026 (Registration No. SEBIH/A/E/26/00111) in Appeal No. 6805 of 2026. Manoj and Kamal Kumar both filed their appeals on March 18, 2026. The Authority considered all three appeals infructuous because the CPIO reply had already been uploaded to the RTI MIS portal (March 17 for Ajay Kumar and March 18 for Manoj and Kamal Kumar), and the portal-access problem was traced to a technical issue on March 17-18, 2026, not to a missing reply; after confirming the reply was currently viewable, it enclosed a copy of the reply with each order.
review_notes: Supported by cited chunks; requires all three orders to map appellants to appeal dates. Distinct procedural-timeline target.

question: Three RTI first appeals decided by SEBI on April 10, 2026—by Ajay Kumar, Manoj and Kamal Kumar—shared a complaint that the CPIO reply was not opening in the RTI MIS portal. Two of the replies were recorded as uploaded on March 18, 2026, and one on March 17. Which appellant's reply was uploaded on March 17, and what uniform remedial step did the Appellate Authority take after confirming the technical issue?
answer_summary: Ajay Kumar's reply was uploaded on March 17, 2026, as reflected in Appeal No. 6805 of 2026. Manoj's and Kamal Kumar's replies were recorded as uploaded on March 18, 2026. The Authority attributed the access failure to technical snags in the RTI MIS portal on March 17-18, 2026. In all three appeals it disposed of the appeals as infructuous and, as a uniform step, enclosed a copy of the CPIO reply with each order while noting that the reply was currently viewable.
review_notes: Supported by cited chunks; requires all three orders to identify the March 17 upload outlier (Ajay Kumar). Distinct cross-reference target.

question: In the RTI appeals by Ajay Kumar, Manoj and Kamal Kumar disposed of on April 10, 2026, the Authority accepted that the CPIO had replied within the time stipulated under the RTI Act, even though the original applications were filed on February 19, March 10 and March 11, 2026 respectively. How did the Authority reconcile these different application-to-reply durations, and what single technical circumstance displaced the need for a delay-based ruling?
answer_summary: The Authority reconciled the varying durations by simply holding, in each of the three orders, that the CPIO reply dated March 17, 2026 was furnished within the RTI Act's stipulated time; it did not analyse the interval from application to reply. It displaced any delay ruling because the real dispute was a common allegation that the portal reply would not open, caused by technical problems in the RTI MIS portal on March 17-18, 2026. Finding the replies currently viewable, and enclosing a copy with each order, it treated the appeals as infructuous.
review_notes: Supported by cited chunks; compares varying application-to-reply durations and the uniform technical-issue reasoning displacing delay analysis. Distinct applied-compliance target.

question: The Bombay High Court dismissed two public-interest litigations against SEBI: one by Varun Dev Jha about the delisting of a corporate debtor's shares, and another by Chandrakant C. Shah about AMFI's mutual-fund advertising campaigns. What was the principal prayer in each PIL, and what separation-of-function concern led the court to refuse both?
answer_summary: In Varun Dev Jha (PIL/5/2026, earlier WP No. 3610/2021), the principal prayer was to declare Regulation 3(2)(b) including the first proviso of the SEBI (Delisting of Equity Shares) Regulations, 2021 ultra vires the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 and the SEBI Act. In Chandrakant C. Shah (PIL No. 84 of 2024), the petitioner sought a writ directing SEBI to revoke the liberty granted to AMFI to carry out investor-education/awareness programmes, and to restrain AMFI's 'Mutual Funds Sahi Hai', 'Mutual Funds Mein SIP Sahi Hai' and 'Be Patient and Stay Invested' campaigns. The Varun order held that a court exercising Article 226 jurisdiction cannot look to the wisdom of the legislature while framing financial or economic guidelines, nor direct the legislature/regulator to formulate policy or law. The Shah order held that no statutory breach affecting the public at large had been shown and that a PIL is meant for those unable to approach the court themselves. Both dismissals turned on the court refusing to substitute its judgment for SEBI's regulatory/policy domain.
review_notes: Supported by cited chunks; both PIL prayers and policy-deference reasoning confirmed. Distinct prayer/separation-of-function comparison target.

question: A prospective litigant plans to approach the Bombay High Court against SEBI's policy on delisting or on mutual-fund advertisements and claims to represent the public. Drawing on the dismissals in Varun Dev Jha and Chandrakant C. Shah, what credential or disclosure defect made the court question each petitioner's standing, and how did the two defects differ?
answer_summary: In Varun Dev Jha the court noted that the petitioners had not disclosed the extensive litigation background involving Yes Bank, DHFL and other entities, the CBI and Enforcement Directorate criminal cases and ECIRs, and the multiple proceedings taken by the parties. This non-disclosure of material facts was treated as fatal to the PIL. In Chandrakant C. Shah the court focused on the petitioner's personal credentials: he was a qualified chartered accountant, unemployed, with an annual income of about ₹3.5 lakhs, and he admitted he did not transact in mutual funds. Because he could not show he was impacted by the advertisements or that he possessed practical knowledge of their effect, the court held he lacked bona fide sufficient interest in the subject matter (following Ashok Kumar Pandey v. State of W.B.). The former defect was suppression of case history; the latter was absence of personal stake or genuine representative capacity.
review_notes: Supported by cited chunks; Varun non-disclosure of litigation/criminal history vs Shah credential/locus defects verified. Distinct standing/disclosure comparison target.

question: Before each PIL was ultimately dismissed, both matters went through earlier procedural stages. Trace the procedural history of Varun Dev Jha's case from its original case number to PIL/5/2026, and of Chandrakant C. Shah's case including the earlier PIL and Special Leave Petition. How did the later court use that earlier history in each case?
answer_summary: Varun Dev Jha began as Writ Petition No. 3610 of 2021. On 12 June 2024 a coordinate Bench of the Bombay High Court observed that the prayer and averments appeared to be a PIL and directed the Registry to place it as Public Interest Litigation No. 5 of 2026. The matter was dismissed on 10 February 2026 on the merits of regulatory non-intervention. Chandrakant C. Shah's PIL No. 84 of 2024 was accompanied by Interim Application No. 1504 of 2025; Shah had earlier filed PIL No. 26 of 2025 raising identical issues, which was dismissed by the High Court on 17 April 2025 ('keeping the issue open'). The resulting Special Leave Petition No. 13341 of 2025 was dismissed by the Supreme Court on 14 July 2025. In Shah, the later Bench treated the prior PIL and SLP dismissals as barring re-agitation of the same issues and additionally faulted Shah for suppressing that adverse history. In Varun Dev Jha the prior order was merely a procedural conversion; consequently the dismissal order concentrated on the substantive Article 226 non-intervention doctrine.
review_notes: Supported by cited chunks; procedural histories and their differing legal effect (conversion vs re-agitation bar) verified. Distinct procedural-chain/date-sequence target.

question: Both PILs sought affirmative relief, but neither succeeded. What final directions, if any, did the court issue in Varun Dev Jha compared with Chandrakant Shah, and what administrative note appears only in the Shah order?
answer_summary: In Varun Dev Jha the court simply dismissed Public Interest Litigation No. 5 of 2026 and passed no further directions or costs order. In Chandrakant C. Shah the court dismissed PIL No. 84 of 2024 with no order as to costs, and since the PIL did not survive, the connected Interim Application No. 1504 of 2025 was disposed of. The Shah order additionally recorded the court's appreciation of the assistance rendered by the learned amicus curiae, Shri Abhishek Venkataraman. No amicus note was recorded in the Varun Dev Jha order.
review_notes: Supported by cited chunks; final dispositions and the Shah-only amicus-curiae note confirmed. Distinct negative-check/final-direction target.

question: In April 2026 the Appellate Authority disposed of three first appeals under the RTI Act — Appeal Nos. 6807, 6808 and 6812. What was the central grievance raised in each appeal, what key factual finding led to the outcome in the first two, and why did the Authority reach a substantively different disposal in the third?
answer_summary: In Appeal Nos. 6807 (Dheeraj Dheeraj) and 6808 (Rakesh Hosmani) the appellants complained that the CPIO's reply, although uploaded to the RTI MIS portal on 17-18 March 2026, could not be opened because of technical issues affecting the portal on 17-18 March 2026. The Authority found the replies had been provided within time, were now viewable, and enclosed copies with the order; it therefore held nothing survived and disposed of both appeals as infructuous. In Appeal No. 6812 (Jagadish Vital) the appellant contested the substantive refusal of information across 13 queries about SMS Techsoft / MNCL recovery proceedings, internal file notes, auction details, settlement records and related matters. The Authority reviewed each cluster, upheld several exemptions and section 2(f) objections, but found that the CPIO had not justified the invocation of sections 8(1)(a), 8(1)(e), 8(1)(j) and 8(1)(g) for query nos. A1, A2, I(13) and B4. It remitted those four queries for de novo consideration within 15 working days and disposed of the rest of the appeal.
review_notes: Procedural comparison supported by all three orders. Portal-access/infructuous reasoning for 6807/6808 and substantive-remand reasoning for 6812 confirmed via cited chunks. Caveat: B4 was denied under 8(1)(e)/(g)/(j), not 8(1)(a); still functionally accurate.

question: Appeal No. 6812 (Jagadish Vital) was partly remanded while Appeal Nos. 6807 and 6808 became infructuous. Which specific queries were sent back for de novo reconsideration, and what defect in the CPIO's reasoning made remand appropriate rather than dismissal?
answer_summary: The Authority remitted query nos. A1, A2, I(13) and B4 for de novo reconsideration. It held that the respondent had denied information under sections 8(1)(a), 8(1)(e), 8(1)(j) and 8(1)(g) of the RTI Act but had not provided sufficient justification for invoking those provisions against these particular queries, so the queries had not been adequately addressed. The Authority therefore remanded them to the respondent for reconsideration and a fresh response within 15 working days. In Appeal Nos. 6807 and 6808 no substantive exemption claim existed; the only dispute was whether a timely portal response could be opened during a two-day technical outage, so once the response was reproduced and confirmed viewable the appeals became infructuous.
review_notes: Remitted queries (A1, A2, I(13), B4) and insufficient-justification defect confirmed in 6812. 6807/6808 provide necessary contrast to distinguish remand from infructuous disposal. Same caveat about conflated exemption sections for B4.

question: Across the April 2026 RTI appeal orders in Appeal Nos. 6807, 6808 and 6812, the Authority dealt with both access-failure and substantive-refusal cases. In the substantive refusal case, which clusters of requested information did the Authority hold were already publicly accessible or governed by an alternative procedure, and what SEBI circulars did it identify for certified copies of orders?
answer_summary: In Jagadish Vital's appeal the Authority held that query B3 auction-related information, including the Sale Confirmation Order, Sale Certificate, reserve price and e-auction notice, was already in the public domain on SEBI's website; the purchaser's bank account statement/UTR/TRN details alone were treated as third-party personal information. It cited the CIC decision in S. Rudraprakash v. CPIO and the Delhi High Court decision in The Registrar, Supreme Court of India v. R.S. Misra for the principle that certified copies of already-public information need not be supplied under RTI. For queries D7 and E, it held that enforcement actions against SMS Techsoft / MNCL were already public on SEBI's website and that certified copies of SEBI orders had to be obtained through SEBI Circular No. CIR/LAD/1/2019 dated 4 April 2019 and SEBI Circular No. SEBI/HO/LAD1/LAD1_DoP3/P/CIR/2023/88 dated 13 June 2023, not through the RTI route. It also relied on the Delhi High Court in Registrar of Companies v. Dharmendra Kumar Garg and the CIC in K. Lall v. M.K. Bagri for the proposition that information in the public domain is not information held by the public authority for RTI purposes. These alternative-route and public-domain issues did not arise in Appeal Nos. 6807 and 6808, which concerned only portal accessibility of otherwise timely replies.
review_notes: Public-domain/alternative-route clusters (B3, D7, E) and the two SEBI certified-copy circulars supported by cited chunks. 6807/6808 are used for the negative check that these issues did not arise there.

question: In Appeal No. 6812 the Authority refused to intervene over several queries it said were either not "information" as defined in section 2(f) of the RTI Act or fell squarely within specific exemptions. Which query clusters were those, and which precedent did it cite for treating the names, designations and signatures of SEBI officers as exempt?
answer_summary: The Authority held that queries C5, C6 and H12 were vague and not specific, essentially seeking clarification or opinion, and therefore not "information" as defined in section 2(f) of the RTI Act; it cited the CIC decision in T.V. Sundaresan v. CPIO, SEBI (24 November 2021). For queries F8, F9 and F10 it held that the appellant was seeking reasons or justifications for action or inaction, which were similarly not information under section 2(f); it cited Mahendra Kumar Mehta v. CPIO, SEBI (12 April 2021) and Dr. Celsa Pinto, Ex-Officio Joint Secretary (School Education) v. Goa State Information Commission (Bombay HC, 3 April 2008). For query G11, which sought the names, designations and signatures of officers who authorised recovery certificates, the Authority held the information to be personal information exempt under sections 8(1)(g) and 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act, citing H.E. Rajashekarappa v. State Public Information Officer (Karnataka HC, 1 July 2008) and Prerit Misra v. CPIO, SEBI (CIC, 21 November 2022). In Appeal Nos. 6807 and 6808 no such exemption or definitional analysis arose because the disputes were purely about portal accessibility.
review_notes: Section 2(f) and exemption clusters (C5/C6/H12, F8/F9/F10, G11) with cited precedents (T.V. Sundaresan, Mahendra Kumar Mehta, Dr. Celsa Pinto, H.E. Rajashekarappa, Prerit Misra) confirmed. 6807/6808 confirm no such analysis in portal-access cases.

question: Three older prosecutions from the Mumbai SEBI Special Court—M'Belle International (Spl. Case 352/2014), Money Management Services (Spl. Case 239/2020) and B.L. Investment (Spl. Case 448/2014)—each resulted in a 2024-25 judgment. Without assuming the same offence, identify the charging provision used in each, the form of the accused entity, and the sentence finally imposed. Explain why the statutory section differs between M'Belle and the two sub-broker cases.
answer_summary: • M'Belle International Pvt Ltd and its directors were prosecuted under Section 24(2) read with Section 27 of the SEBI Act, 1992 for failure to pay a ₹1 crore penalty imposed by the adjudication order dated 30.06.2004. The company was struck off and not represented; directors Gopu Parimal Belani and Anupama Motwani were convicted and each sentenced to pay ₹1 crore, in default six months' simple imprisonment, and half the fine was directed to SEBI as compensation. Rita Motwani was acquitted. • Money Management Services was prosecuted under Section 24(1) of the SEBI Act, 1992 (along with Rule 3 of the SEBI (Stock Brokers and Sub-Brokers) Regulations, 1992 and Section 17/23(1)(g)-(h) of the SCRA, 1956) for acting as an unregistered sub-broker. The partnership, through its director/partner Paul Donald Moses, pleaded guilty and was convicted and fined ₹5,000. • B.L. Investment (proprietary concern of Bajranglal Indermal Goyal) was likewise prosecuted under Section 24(1) of the SEBI Act, 1992 for dealing in securities as an unregistered sub-broker. The proprietor pleaded guilty and was convicted and fined ₹25,000, in default one month's simple imprisonment, with the fine payable to SEBI as compensation. The statutory section differs because M'Belle concerned non-compliance with a prior monetary penalty/adjudication order (Section 24(2)), whereas Money Management and B.L. concerned the substantive offence of operating without registration as a sub-broker (Section 24(1)).
review_notes: Cited chunks support all three cases' charges, entity forms, sentences and the Section 24(2) vs 24(1) distinction. All three seed documents are materially needed for the comparison.

question: In M'Belle International, three individuals were arraigned as directors of the accused company, yet only two were convicted. What specific finding about each person's tenure as director caused the court to convict Gopu Parimal Belani and Anupama Motwani but acquit Rita Motwani? Contrast this with how B.L. Investment's proprietor was held liable even though there was no company-director structure.
answer_summary: In M'Belle, the Special Court held that liability for non-payment of the adjudication order depended on whether the individual was a director of the company at the relevant time. Rita Motwani had ceased to be a director with effect from 16.06.1999, before the adjudication order was passed on 30.06.2004 and well before the compliance notices of 2007; no evidence showed she was re-appointed. The court therefore acquitted her because she could not be blamed for non-compliance. Gopu Parimal Belani was proved to be a director and had even filed a SAT appeal on behalf of the company, which imputed knowledge of the adjudication order to him; the court found he knowingly failed to pay the penalty. Anupama Motwani was appointed as a director on 15.06.2005 (per Form No. 32/ROC record) and led no evidence of resignation or cessation; the notices seeking compliance (Exhibits 66, 99 and 100 dated 23.04.2007, 21.05.2007 and 28.06.2007) were issued after her appointment, so she too was held liable as a director in charge at the relevant time. By contrast, B.L. Investment was carried on as a proprietary firm by Bajranglal Indermal Goyal. There was no separation between the accused firm and its proprietor; the proprietor himself ran the business, received SEBI's warning letter, chose not to apply for registration and voluntarily pleaded guilty. Consequently, no director-status inquiry was required—personal liability attached directly to the proprietor as the entity's sole operator.
review_notes: Director-tenure findings for Rita, Gopu and Anupama are directly evidenced in the M'Belle judgment, and the B.L. Investment proprietor-liability contrast is supported by the second order. Distinct memory target from q01.

question: The M'Belle prosecution and the Money Management prosecution both began with SEBI investigating possible market misconduct, but the prosecution routes diverged. Trace the enforcement sequence that led to the M'Belle case—adjudication, tribunal appeal, and prosecution—and explain why no adjudication order or SAT appeal precedes the Money Management case. What does that difference say about the type of violation each case addresses?
answer_summary: The M'Belle case arose out of non-compliance with an earlier civil penalty. SEBI first passed an adjudication order dated 30.06.2004 imposing a penalty of ₹1 crore on M'Belle International Pvt Ltd for non-cooperation in the Roofit Industries investigation. M'Belle (through director Gopu Parimal Belani) appealed to the Securities Appellate Tribunal in Appeal No. 154 of 2004; the SAT dismissed the appeal by order dated 13.11.2006. Even after the appeal was dismissed, the company failed to deposit the penalty within 45 days as stipulated, prompting SEBI to issue compliance notices in 2007 and eventually prosecute the company and its directors under Section 24(2) r/w Section 27 of the SEBI Act, 1992 for non-payment of the awarded penalty. The Money Management case, however, involved a substantive offence of operating without registration. SEBI received a complaint dated 11.05.2020 about the accused dealing as an unregistered sub-broker. SEBI wrote to the accused on 23.06.2020 asking it to obtain registration immediately and warning of penal action, and it had also published a public notice in December 2001 asking unregistered sub-brokers to apply. When no application was received, SEBI filed the complaint directly under Section 24(1) of the SEBI Act, 1992. There was no adjudication of penalty and no SAT appeal because the violation was the lack of registration itself, not the refusal to pay an already-imposed monetary penalty. Thus, the difference in enforcement route reflects the legal architecture: Section 24(2) cases typically follow a prior adjudication order that remains unsatisfied, whereas Section 24(1) cases punish the principal conduct (here, unregistered brokerage).
review_notes: Enforcement sequences for M'Belle (adjudication, SAT Appeal 154/2004, Section 24(2) prosecution) and Money Management (direct Section 24(1) prosecution for unregistered sub-broking) are both supported. Teaches a different procedural-lens target.

question: Three RTI first appeals decided by SEBI's Appellate Authority on April 1, 2026—Appeal Nos. 6792, 6793 and 6794 of 2026—each involved a different substantive complaint about information held by SEBI. For each appeal, what was the appellant's core request, and what was the Authority's distinct reason for upholding the CPIO's refusal?
answer_summary: | Appeal | Appellant | Core request | Authority's reason for dismissal | |---|---|---|---| | Appeal No. 6792 of 2026 | Aashish Pal | PACL investor seeking plot-allotment records, land-registry documents and possession-letter details for certificates on which refund was blocked because land had allegedly been allotted | SEBI did not hold the requested information. The Authority noted that disposal of PACL properties and repayment to investors is entrusted to the Justice (Retd.) R.M. Lodha Committee under the Supreme Court's February 2, 2016 order, and cited Sh. Pattipati Rama Murthy v. CPIO, SEBI (July 8, 2013) for the proposition that the CPIO cannot invent information not in SEBI's possession. | | Appeal No. 6793 of 2026 | B Narayan | Complaint that Larsen & Toubro disclosed PSU/PSE contract values only in bands (Significant/Large/Major/Mega/Ultra-Mega) rather than exact figures, and a request for SEBI to clarify whether this violated disclosure norms | The request was in the nature of clarification/opinion, not 'information' as defined in section 2(f) of the RTI Act. The Authority relied on Azad Singh v. CPIO, Oriental Insurance Company Limited (March 23, 2021), holding that a CPIO cannot create, interpret or compile information to answer such queries. | | Appeal No. 6794 of 2026 | Aadesh Motla | Inquiry about action SEBI could take regarding alleged disobedience of Supreme Court orders in the Sahara land-sale matter in Muzaffarnagar district | The CPIO had already given the information available with SEBI: the Supreme Court's conditions for Sahara property sales (furnishing valuation details, minimum 90% of circle rate, depositing sale proceeds in the SEBI-Sahara account, and a non-related-party declaration). The Authority found no deficiency. |
review_notes: Supported by all three cited orders. Each appeal has a distinct dismissal rationale and the table cleanly captures the contrast. Strong multi-doc coverage of the same-date batch.

question: In two of the April 1, 2026 RTI appeals the appellant asked about assets or proceeds tied to a Supreme Court-monitored matter (Sahara in one, PACL in the other). SEBI's response in the two cases was different: in one it gave detailed sale conditions, and in the other it said the information was not with SEBI. What factual distinction explains the different treatment?
answer_summary: The distinction is whether SEBI actually held the responsive information. In Aadesh Motla's Sahara appeal (Appeal No. 6794 of 2026), SEBI had itself been directed by the Supreme Court to implement the sale conditions and hold the proceeds, so the CPIO could list the four Supreme Court-imposed conditions (valuation details, minimum 90% of circle rate, deposit of sale proceeds in the SEBI-Sahara account, and a non-related-party declaration). In Aashish Pal's PACL appeal (Appeal No. 6792 of 2026), the asset disposal and investor repayment were entrusted by the Supreme Court to the Justice (Retd.) R.M. Lodha Committee, not to SEBI, so the requested plot-allotment records and registry documents were outside SEBI's records. The Authority cited Sh. Pattipati Rama Murthy v. CPIO, SEBI for the principle that a CPIO cannot manufacture information the public authority does not hold.
review_notes: Supported by Motla and Pal orders. The Sahara/PACL distinction turns on whether SEBI actually holds the information, which is a genuine multi-doc comparison.

question: An RTI applicant complains to SEBI that a listed company discloses PSU/PSE contract values only in bands and wants SEBI to state whether this violates SEBI norms. The Appellate Authority dismissed this appeal on April 1, 2026. On the same day it also dismissed another appeal even though the appellant had asked for concrete factual records. Contrast the two dismissal grounds and identify the precedent cited in each.
answer_summary: The first appeal is B Narayan (Appeal No. 6793 of 2026). The request was treated as seeking clarification or opinion on whether Larsen & Toubro's banded disclosure of PSU/PSE contract values violated SEBI norms; the Authority held this falls outside the definition of 'information' under section 2(f) of the RTI Act, citing Azad Singh v. CPIO, Oriental Insurance Company Limited (March 23, 2021). The second appeal is Aashish Pal (Appeal No. 6792 of 2026), where the appellant sought factual PACL plot-allotment records. There the Authority accepted SEBI's statement that the records were not available with SEBI and directed the appellant to the Justice (Retd.) R.M. Lodha Committee, which the Supreme Court had entrusted with PACL asset disposal and investor repayment; it cited Sh. Pattipati Rama Murthy v. CPIO, SEBI (July 8, 2013). The contrast is between a request that is not information at all (opinion/clarification) and a request for factual information that another body legitimately holds.
review_notes: Supported by Narayan and Pal orders. Contrasts a section 2(f) clarification/opinion exclusion with a non-availability redirect, teaching two different RTI Act grounds.

question: The three April 1, 2026 RTI appeals each ended in dismissal, but only two of them relied on an external precedent or alternate body to justify the result. Which appeal did not rely on such external authority, and what factual showing in the CPIO's reply made an external citation unnecessary?
answer_summary: Aadesh Motla's appeal (Appeal No. 6794 of 2026) did not cite an external precedent or redirect to another body. The CPIO had simply reproduced the four conditions imposed by the Supreme Court for Sahara immovable-property sales (valuation and sale-term details to the Court, minimum 90% of circle rate, deposit of net sale proceeds in the SEBI-Sahara account, and a declaration that the purchaser is not related to the Saharas). Because these conditions showed SEBI had already supplied the information it held, the Authority found no deficiency in the reply and dismissed the appeal without invoking an external authority. By contrast, B Narayan's appeal cited Azad Singh v. CPIO, Oriental Insurance Company Limited for the section 2(f) clarification point, and Aashish Pal's appeal cited Sh. Pattipati Rama Murthy v. CPIO, SEBI and identified the Justice (Retd.) R.M. Lodha Committee as the body responsible for PACL asset disposal.
review_notes: Supported by all three orders. The absence of an external precedent in Motla's order becomes meaningful only against the citations/redirects in the other two. Distinct negative-check memory target.

question: In the criminal writ petition Debprasad Nanda & Ors. v. The State of Maharashtra (Crl. W. P. No. 4101 of 2022), the petitioners asked the Bombay High Court for four specific reliefs connected to the Highbrow Market Research Investment Advisor Pvt. Ltd. affair. Map each prayer to the disposition recorded in the Court's 22 August 2025 order and identify the SEBI recovery certificate that confirms a quantified penalty was imposed on Highbrow.
answer_summary: Prayer (a) sought CBI transfer of D. N. Nagar FIR No. 120 of 2019 under IPC sections 420 & 406 read with 34 and consolidation of all cases against Highbrow—it was treated as satisfied because the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's earlier CBI-transfer order on 24 February 2025, permitted the appointment of a Special Investigation Team, and the High Court constituted the SIT by an order dated 8 April 2025; CBI had also concluded its investigation. Prayer (b) sought a time-bound SEBI inquiry into Highbrow—it was treated as satisfied because SEBI had completed its investigation, passed orders, and those orders were already under challenge before the Securities Appellate Tribunal. Prayer (c) sought court monitoring of the probe—it was declined as unnecessary because CBI had completed its investigation and the SIT had been constituted; the Court said any investor with future apprehensions could approach it separately. Prayer (d) sought reimbursement of losses from SEBI-frozen monies or the Investor Protection Fund during pendency—it was not pressed and recorded as such. The petition and all interim applications were disposed of. The recovery certificate confirming the penalty is RC No. 6925 of 2023 dated 20 July 2023, drawn against Highbrow Market Research Pvt. Ltd. for Rs. 5,26,000 (plus interest, costs and expenses), which was completed on 21 February 2024.
review_notes: Prayer-to-disposition mapping for Debprasad Nanda is directly supported by the High Court order chunks (clauses a-d) and the recovery certificate details (RC No. 6925/2023, Rs. 5,26,000, completed 21.02.2024) are confirmed by the third document.

question: Two 2025 Bombay High Court orders disposed of criminal writ petitions that listed SEBI as a respondent—Debprasad Nanda & Ors. (Crl. W.P. No. 4101 of 2022) and Alpesh Navin Chandra Gosalia (Crl. W.P. No. 293 of 2024). One bench treated the SEBI-related prayers as satisfied; the other refused to direct FIR/ECIR registration against SEBI and other agencies at all. What factual distinction led the two benches to reach opposite conclusions on Article 226 intervention in criminal matters, and which of the two petitions was ultimately dismissed rather than disposed of as redundant?
answer_summary: The opposite outcomes turned on whether an active, institution-led process already covered the grievance. In Debprasad Nanda, the prayer for a time-bound SEBI inquiry became redundant because SEBI had already completed its inquiry and passed orders that were before the Securities Appellate Tribunal; the CBI-transfer/consolidation prayer was also satisfied by the Supreme Court's 24 February 2025 order and the consequent SIT ordered on 8 April 2025. So the petition was disposed of as the prayers had become satisfied or unnecessary. In Alpesh Gosalia, the petitioner asked the Court to order multiple agencies, including SEBI, to register a fresh FIR/ECIR covering IPC 406/409/420/421/120-A read with 34, PMLA, PCA and FEMA. The Court held that Article 226 jurisdiction is not to be used to direct registration of a criminal case except in exceptional circumstances and compelling reasons, and that the petitioner had alternative remedies under the Criminal Procedure Code. The petition was therefore dismissed outright rather than disposed of as redundant.
review_notes: Cross-case contrast is supported by both orders: Debprasad Nanda was disposed of as prayers were satisfied (CBI/SIT/SEBI orders already passed), while Alpesh Gosalia was dismissed because Article 226 will not direct FIR/ECIR registration without exceptional circumstances and the petitioner had alternative remedies.

question: During the pendency of the criminal writ in Debprasad Nanda & Ors., the petitioners asked the Bombay High Court to direct SEBI to reimburse their losses from the monies frozen in the accounts of Highbrow Market Research Investment Advisor Pvt. Ltd. and its directors, or alternatively from SEBI's Investor Protection Fund. What did the Court do with that prayer, and what broader Article 226 limitation on directing SEBI did the same Court articulate in the contemporaneous Alpesh Gosalia matter?
answer_summary: In Debprasad Nanda, the petitioners' counsel stated on instructions that prayer (d) for reimbursement from SEBI-frozen funds or the Investor Protection Fund was not pressed; the Court recorded the statement. In Alpesh Navin Chandra Gosalia, the Court refused to direct SEBI and other agencies to register a fresh FIR/ECIR, holding that the High Court in criminal jurisdiction under Article 226 may not order registration of a criminal case except in exceptional circumstances and for compelling reasons, and that the scheme of the Criminal Procedure Code provides alternative remedies to an aggrieved person.
review_notes: The reimbursement prayer not being pressed is recorded in the Debprasad Nanda order, and the broader Article 226 limitation on directing registration of a criminal case is clearly stated in Alpesh Gosalia. Distinct negative-relief target.

question: Both Debprasad Nanda and Alpesh Gosalia involved allegations touching the same IPC offences—sections 406 and 420—but produced sharply different High Court results. In precise terms, why was the narrower 420/406 (read with 34) prayer in Debprasad Nanda treated as already resolved, while the far broader multi-statute prayer in Alpesh Gosalia was dismissed outright?
answer_summary: In Debprasad Nanda, the D. N. Nagar FIR No. 120 of 2019 was already registered under IPC sections 420 and 406 read with 34; CBI had concluded its investigation and an SIT had been constituted by an 8 April 2025 High Court order. Those facts made the corresponding prayers satisfied and the monitoring prayer redundant, so the petition was disposed of. In Alpesh Gosalia, there was no pending or subsisting FIR matching the prayer; the petitioner asked for a fresh ECIR/FIR covering IPC 406/409/420/421/120-A read with 34, PMLA, PCA and FEMA against many parties. The Court found no foundation: the relevant criminal complaint and further proceedings had already been quashed by an 8 April 2022 High Court order, the Supreme Court dismissed a related Special Leave Petition, the Enforcement Directorate's attempt to revive proceedings was rejected, and the issues were bound by decisions of the Company Court, NCLT, High Court and Supreme Court. The petitioner was not the complainant in the relevant FIR and could not claim to be an affected party merely because his steel-supply dues from the insolvent SRUIL remained unpaid. The Court also held that no one could insist on investigation by a particular agency. Thus the active 420/406 investigation in Debprasad continued into the SIT stage, whereas Alpesh sought to resurrect multi-statute allegations that had already been judicially closed.
review_notes: Offence-comparison answer is supported: the active 420/406 FIR in Debprasad had progressed to CBI/SIT, making prayers redundant, whereas Alpesh's multi-statute prayer sought to resurrect allegations already quashed and bound by Company/NCLT/Supreme Court determinations.

question: An AIF has been waiting since early 2024 for SEBI to process its application to change its investment manager. Its counsel cites the two July 2025 Bombay High Court orders in the SREI trust matters to argue that SEBI cannot simply sit on the request. What does SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012 require before such a change takes effect, and what specific procedural direction did the Court give SEBI in both the SREI Multiple Asset Investment Trust and SREI Alternative Investment Trust petitions?
answer_summary: Under the SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012 as in force in April 2024 (Regulation 20(13)), an AIF must obtain prior approval from SEBI for a change of Sponsor or Manager, or a change in control of the AIF, Sponsor or Manager. In both the SREI Multiple Asset Investment Trust (WP No. 3375 of 2025 / IAL No. 5222 of 2025) and SREI Alternative Investment Trust (WP No. 3359 of 2025 / IAL No. 5268 of 2025) petitions — which arose from applications dated 8 February 2024 seeking such prior approval — the Bombay High Court recorded SEBI's undertaking and disposed of the petitions by directing that: (i) if any further documents were required, SEBI would write to the petitioner within one week; (ii) the petitioner would have four weeks to furnish the documents; (iii) SEBI would dispose of the application after giving both the petitioner and the proposed intervenor a hearing; and (iv) the decision would be communicated after four weeks from receipt of all documents, after hearing both parties. The Court left all contentions of the parties open and did not adjudicate the rival controversies.
review_notes: Prior-approval rule under SEBI (AIF) Regulations, 2012 (Regulation 20(13)) and the Bombay High Court's procedural directions are supported by both the regulation chunk and the parallel court orders; strong rule-to-case mapping.

question: Two SREI AIF trusts separately moved the Bombay High Court in July 2025 against SEBI over applications filed on the same day in 2024. Identify at least three respects in which the two writ petitions are materially identical and two respects in which the court papers identify them as distinct.
answer_summary: The petitions are materially identical in that (i) both were heard and disposed of on 9 July 2025 by the same Division Bench of M.S. Sonak and Jitendra Jain, JJ.; (ii) both arose from applications dated 8 February 2024 seeking prior approval for a change of investment manager under SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012; (iii) both prayed only for a direction to SEBI to expeditiously dispose of the application; (iv) both had the same proposed intervenor, SREI Alternative Finance Limited, raising a prior civil suit at Alipore; and (v) both resulted in the same disposal order recording SEBI's undertaking on document request, hearing, and timeline. The court papers distinguish them by the petitioner name — SREI Multiple Asset Investment Trust versus SREI Alternative Investment Trust — and the case numbers — WP No. 3375 of 2025 with IAL No. 5222 of 2025, versus WP No. 3359 of 2025 with IAL No. 5268 of 2025.
review_notes: Comparison of the two near-identical petitions is supported by both orders; teaches distinct parallel-case identity and case-number disambiguation targets.

question: Three SEBI-linked court/tribunal proceedings appeared together in late 2025: P.S. Reddy vs. SEBI & Anr., Chitra Ravindra Dhavale and Ors. vs. SEBI and Anr., and Avil Menezes vs. Central Depository Services (India) Limited and Ors. For each one, name the court or tribunal, the procedural basis on which the petition/application was disposed of, and the substantive relief, if any, granted.
answer_summary: P.S. Reddy (clf-l2lbwikk8g2euym5fuzwu9sq) was before the Bombay High Court (WP 2719 of 2025). It was disposed of as withdrawn because Respondent No. 2 offered the petitioner a personal hearing; the court took an email dated 21 November 2025 from Respondent No. 2's advocate onto the record as Exhibit X. No merits were adjudicated and the interim application did not survive. Chitra Ravindra Dhavale (clf-l5accn6qt0abaofrcqs2suo5) was before the Bombay High Court (WP 2356 of 2015, with a Notice of Motion and two Chamber Summons). It was dismissed for want of prosecution because the petitioner was not interested to prosecute; the pending motions were likewise disposed of, with no merits relief. Avil Menezes (clf-jyrw5mjzmxhv4n05w5khp7p4) was before the NCLT Mumbai Bench-I (IA 2590 of 2025 in CP 1113 of 2022). The interim application was allowed on the merits and the tribunal directed BSE to vacate the debit freeze on Corporate Debtor demat Client ID 00009754 and issue necessary communication to CDSL within 15 days; if CDSL did not receive BSE's communication after that period, CDSL was directed to remove the debit freeze itself.
review_notes: Disposition basis and relief supported by each order chunk. P.S. Reddy was withdrawn after Respondent No.2 offered a personal hearing and email dated 21 November 2025 was marked Exhibit X. Chitra was dismissed for want of prosecution. Avil allowed IA with BSE/CDSL debit-freeze directions.

question: Only one of the three assigned 2025 orders resulted in a direction to lift an actual market-account freeze. Which proceeding was it, what originally triggered the freeze, and what SEBI/IBC overlap justified the lift? Contrast that with why the other two proceedings ended without comparable relief.
answer_summary: The relief-granting order was Avil Menezes (clf-jyrw5mjzmxhv4n05w5khp7p4). The Interim Resolution Professional of Future Corporate Resources Pvt. Ltd. discovered that BSE had instructed CDSL to place a debit freeze on demat Client ID 00009754, citing a SEBI Directive connected to non-payment of annual listing fees. The NCLT allowed IA 2590/2025 because the corporate debtor was under CIRP and the IBC Section 14 moratorium prevented enforcement of security interests. It also relied on SEBI's Standard Operating Procedure regarding Actions for Non-Payment of Annual Listing Fees dated 11 February 2021 (reference CFD/CMD/AAD/SGIBMIOV/038591/2021), specifically Clause 5, which lets stock exchanges keep in abeyance or withdraw action where a moratorium or tribunal/order exemption applies. By contrast, P.S. Reddy (clf-l2lbwikk8g2euym5fuzwu9sq) was withdrawn on the basis of a promised personal hearing, and Chitra Ravindra Dhavale (clf-l5accn6qt0abaofrcqs2suo5) was dismissed solely because the petitioner was not interested to prosecute; neither reached the merits and therefore neither granted any account-level relief.
review_notes: Avil is the only order granting account-level relief. Freeze origin (BSE instruction citing SEBI Directive / annual listing fee default) and SEBI ALF SOP Clause 5 plus IBC section 14 moratorium reasoning are confirmed. Negative contrast with the two Bombay HC orders is material.

question: All three assigned orders stopped short of deciding a contested dispute on the merits. What procedural reason did each forum give for that outcome, and why did only the Avil Menezes IA still contain an operative direction binding third parties?
answer_summary: P.S. Reddy (clf-l2lbwikk8g2euym5fuzwu9sq) ended without a merits decision because the petitioner sought leave to withdraw after Respondent No. 2 offered a personal hearing on the underlying grievances; the Bombay High Court granted withdrawal and disposed of the accompanying interim application. Chitra Ravindra Dhavale (clf-l5accn6qt0abaofrcqs2suo5) ended without a merits decision because the petitioner was not interested to prosecute; the Bombay High Court dismissed the writ petition for want of prosecution and disposed of the dependent Chamber Summons and Notice of Motion. Avil Menezes (clf-jyrw5mjzmxhv4n05w5khp7p4) also did not adjudicate a fully contested dispute because the tribunal was satisfied as a matter of law and precedent that the IBC moratorium and SEBI's ALF SOP required the freeze to be lifted; it therefore allowed the IA and gave positive directions to BSE and CDSL to remove the debit freeze on Client ID 00009754 within 15 days, making that order alone operationally binding on third parties.
review_notes: Procedural non-merits bases for P.S. Reddy and Chitra are evident. Avil's operative direction is supported by the order text. Covers a distinct angle from Q01/Q02 by contrasting non-merits closure with still-binding third-party directions.

question: Two of the three assigned orders proceeded through the Bombay High Court without any reference to parallel appellate proceedings, while the third explicitly discussed BSE's pending appeals. Identify that third proceeding and, relying only on the three assigned orders, state the two pending BSE appeals, the forums they were in, and why the existence of a Supreme Court stay did not prevent the NCLT from granting the IA.
answer_summary: Avil Menezes (clf-jyrw5mjzmxhv4n05w5khp7p4) is the third proceeding. BSE had filed Civil Appeal No. 7038 of 2025 before the Supreme Court of India, impugning an SAT order dated 30 April 2025, and the Supreme Court had stayed the operation of that SAT order. Separately, BSE had filed Company Appeal (Ins.) (AT) 1862 of 2024 before the NCLAT against an NCLT Mumbai Bench-III order dated 31 July 2024 in Mrudula Brodie v. NSE & Ors., but there was no stay against that NCLT order. The tribunal reasoned that the coordinate-bench Mrudula Brodie order was still operational and squarely covered the identical issue, so it directed BSE to vacate the debit freeze on Client ID 00009754 and require CDSL to act if BSE did not communicate within 15 days. The Bombay High Court orders in P.S. Reddy (clf-l2lbwikk8g2euym5fuzwu9sq) and Chitra Ravindra Dhavale (clf-l5accn6qt0abaofrcqs2suo5) made no reference to any such appellate context because both were simply disposed of as withdrawn or as dismissed for want of prosecution.
review_notes: BSE's Civil Appeal No.7038 of 2025 before Supreme Court (impugning SAT order 30 April 2025; stayed) and Company Appeal (Ins.)(AT) 1862 of 2024 before NCLAT (against NCLT Mumbai Bench-III order 31 July 2024 in Mrudula Brodie; no stay) are directly supported. The coordinate-bench/no-stay reasoning is correctly explained.

question: In early 2025, the Madras High Court was asked to direct the Tamil Nadu government to attach HBN Dairies & Allied Ltd.'s properties under Section 3 of the Tamil Nadu Protection of Interest of Depositors in Financial Establishments Act, 1997. Around the same time, SEBI published a public caution notice warning against dealing in HBN's properties. Why did the High Court refuse the TNPID-Act prayer, and why was SEBI, rather than the State, actively taking steps to sell HBN's assets?
answer_summary: The Madras High Court refused the prayer because it held that the Supreme Court of India was already seized of the matter in Civil Appeal No. 5089 of 2019 (see the Common Order in W.P. No. 9845 of 2024, paras 3-5). SEBI was active because the Supreme Court's order dated 14.05.2024 in C.A. No. 5089/2019 – SEBI v. Rohit Sehgal & Ors. specifically permitted SEBI to sell HBN's assets with the active involvement of the liquidator, Mr. Rohit Sehgal (SEBI public caution notice dated 18.06.2024). The assets were already attached by SEBI's Prohibitory Order dated 29.09.2017 under Section 28A of the SEBI Act, 1992, so the State-level TNPID-Act attachment route was held back in favour of the Supreme Court-monitored SEBI recovery process.
review_notes: Madras HC order confirms the Section 3 TNPID-Act prayer and refusal because the Supreme Court was seized of the matter; SEBI caution notice confirms Supreme Court-authorized sale and prior 29.09.2017 attachment. Both documents are needed for the answer.

question: In SEBI's recovery actions against HBN Dairies & Allied Ltd., the address 'Vardhman Chamber, Vikaspuri, New Delhi' appears in two recovery documents issued a few months apart. Which documents are they, what procedural steps do they record, and how is the Supreme Court's May 2024 order linked to the later of the two?
answer_summary: The property appears in (i) Prohibitory Order no. RO/NRO/1099/2024 dated 02.12.2024, which attaches 'Shop No. 301, 3rd Floor, Vardhman Chamber, G-Block, Community Centre, Vikaspuri, New Delhi-110018' under Rule 16 and 48 of the Second Schedule to the Income Tax Act read with Section 28A of the SEBI Act; and (ii) Sale Confirmation Order dated 02.04.2025 for Property Sr. No. 1, which confirms the e-auction sale of '302, Vardhman Chamber, Vikaspuri, New Delhi-110018' to Mr. Ravinder Singh for Rs. 41,30,000. The later sale order relies on the Supreme Court's order dated 14.05.2024 in C.A. No. 5089/2019 permitting SEBI to sell the corporate debtor's assets with liquidator Rohit Sehgal, and was confirmed under Rule 63(1) of the Second Schedule to the Income Tax Act.
review_notes: Prohibitory Order lists Shop No. 301 at Vardhman Chamber and traces attachment to Recovery Certificate No. 1216 of 2017; Sale Confirmation Order records e-auction of 302, Vardhman Chamber to Mr. Ravinder Singh under Rule 63(1). Cross-document property tracing is a distinct target.

question: By late 2024, SEBI had moved beyond attachment and issued a remittance direction to banks and mutual funds in the HBN matter, even as a Madras High Court petition seeking a TNPID-Act attachment remained pending. What does the remittance document direct, what is the total claimed due, and how does the interaction between the High Court and Supreme Court proceedings explain why SEBI – not the Tamil Nadu State – was handling the recovery?
answer_summary: The Remittance Advice dated 06.12.2024 (Attachment Proceeding Nos. 12582 & 12583 of 2024, Recovery Certificate No. 1216 of 2017) directs all banks and mutual funds to remit, to SEBI's 'SEBI Recovery Proceeds' account, any balance lying in the defaulters' accounts or units in their folios to the extent of the outstanding dues. The claimed dues are Rs. 1,136 crore plus further interest, costs, charges and expenses. The Madras High Court, by its order dated 07.01.2025 in W.P. No. 9845 of 2024, refused to order a TNPID-Act attachment because the Supreme Court was already seized of the matter in C.A. No. 5089/2019 and left the petitioner free to approach the Supreme Court. SEBI's actions therefore remained the operative recovery channel, resting on Recovery Certificate No. 1216 of 2017 and the Supreme Court's 14.05.2024 order authorising SEBI, with liquidator Rohit Sehgal, to sell HBN's assets.
review_notes: Remittance Advice directs banks/mutual funds to remit to SEBI Recovery Proceeds for Rs. 1,136 crore-plus dues, and Madras HC order confirms stay of TNPID-Act attachment because the Supreme Court was already seized. Combines amount/timeline with procedural channel.

question: Two coercive enforcement routes confronted HBN Dairies: a Tamil Nadu police Crime No. 3 of 2016 under the TNPID Act, pressing for attachment and a court-appointed administrator for depositors, and SEBI's Recovery Certificate No. 1216 of 2017 under Section 28A of the SEBI Act. What common factual premise links both routes, why did the Madras High Court not order the TNPID-Act attachment, and what remedy did it leave open?
answer_summary: Both routes spring from HBN's failure to return depositors'/investors' money. SEBI's Recovery Certificate No. 1216 of 2017 was drawn after the Whole-Time Member's order no. WTM/PS/71/CIS-NRO/FEB/2015 dated 12.02.2015 directed HBN to refund investors; the Madras High Court petition in R. Gayathri v. State (W.P. No. 9845/2024) sought attachment and disbursement for depositors in Crime No. 3/2016 involving the same company. The High Court declined to order TNPID-Act attachment because it held the Supreme Court was already seized of the matter in C.A. No. 5089/2019, and it left the petitioner at liberty to seek relief before the Supreme Court. SEBI's recovery certificate and subsequent attachment/sale proceedings therefore remained the active enforcement path.
review_notes: Prohibitory Order and Remittance Advice root Recovery Certificate No. 1216 of 2017 in the 12.02.2015 WTM refund direction; Madras HC order explains why the parallel TNPID-Act route was not ordered and the remedy left open. Distinct statutory-route comparison target.

question: A partner sends you a list of three SEBI Special Court, Mumbai judgments: (i) SEBI vs M/s Sagar Green Gold Plantation Group Pvt. Ltd. in Special Case 27 of 2014; (ii) SEBI vs Gopal Kupposwami Ramourti and Ors. in Special Case 391 of 2014; and (iii) SEBI vs Kanaiyalal Baldev Patel in Special Case 1592 of 2021. She asks which one was prosecuted and convicted under the Companies Act, 1956 rather than the SEBI Act, and the precise provision forming the basis of each conviction. What is the answer?
answer_summary: Special Case 27/2014 (Sagar Green Gold) was convicted under Section 24(1) read with Section 27 of the SEBI Act, 1992 for operating an unregistered collective investment scheme. Special Case 1592/2021 (Kanaiyalal Patel) was convicted under Section 24(2) of the SEBI Act, 1992 for failing to pay the adjudication penalty despite finality of the order. Special Case 391/2014 (Gopal Kupposwami Ramourti and Ors.) was the one convicted under Section 207 of the Companies Act, 1956 for failure to distribute a declared dividend within 30 days.
review_notes: Cited provisions matched in all three judgments; all three docs are needed to distinguish 24(1)/27, 24(2), and Companies Act Section 207.

question: Of all the individual accused sentenced across the three SEBI Special Court judgments, who received the longest term of simple imprisonment, and for what misconduct? Was a personal fine also imposed, and if so, how much?
answer_summary: Kanaiyalal Baldev Patel in Special Case 1592/2021 received the longest term: three years’ simple imprisonment for failing to pay the Rs.5 crore adjudication penalty even after SAT’s quashing was reversed by the Supreme Court and a demand notice was served. The court also imposed a personal fine of Rs.10 lakh (with six months’ simple imprisonment in default). The Twilight Litaka directors in Special Case 391/2014 received six months’ simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs.5 lakh each. The Sagar Green Gold directors in Special Case 27/2014 were sentenced to fines only (Rs.5 lakh and Rs.2 lakh).
review_notes: Sentencing terms confirmed in the order sections of all three judgments; multi-document comparison is essential.

question: In two of the three cases the accused challenged SEBI’s authority to prosecute. In Special Case 391/2014 the defence said SEBI was not properly authorized to file the complaint; in Special Case 1592/2021 the defence argued that the absence of a prosecution sanction under the Prevention of Corruption Act was fatal. How did the Special Court dispose of each objection, and what statutory basis did it rely on?
answer_summary: In Special Case 391/2014, the court held SEBI had valid authorization to file the complaint because Section 627 of the Companies Act, 1956 empowers SEBI as a regulator to do so, and the delegation of power was placed on record and proved. In Special Case 1592/2021, the court held that the Prevention of Corruption Act sanction requirements do not apply: under the SEBI Act, 1992 a complaint can be filed by an officer of SEBI, so the authority to prosecute was upheld without such sanction.
review_notes: Authority challenges are grounded in Special Case 391/#24 (Section 627 Companies Act) and Special Case 1592/#31 (SEBI Act officer complaint vs PCA sanction).

question: One of the three Special Court cases reached the Court only after a multi-stage appellate fight over an administrative penalty. Identify that case and trace the stages, then briefly contrast it with how the other two cases came to the Court.
answer_summary: Special Case 1592/2021 (Kanaiyalal Baldev Patel) went from an adjudication order dated 30.09.2011 imposing a Rs.5 crore penalty, to quashing by SAT on 09.11.2012, to restoration when the Supreme Court upheld the adjudication order, followed by a demand notice and eventually the criminal complaint. The other two were direct Special Court prosecutions: Special Case 27/2014 (Sagar Green Gold) arose from SEBI’s investigation of an unregistered CIS scheme in 1998-99, and Special Case 391/2014 (Twilight Litaka) arose from investor complaints about a declared dividend that was not paid.
review_notes: Patel appellate chain supported by the judgment; contrast with the direct prosecution backgrounds of the other two cases requires all three docs.

question: The Sagar Green Gold conduct dated back to 1998-99, while Kanaiyalal Patel’s adjudication penalty dated from 2011. A junior associate assumes the older violation should have drawn the heavier custodial sentence. Using the sentencing reasons in both judgments, explain why the Special Court imposed fine-only punishment on the Sagar directors but three years’ imprisonment on Patel.
