answer_summary: The Sagar Green Gold court considered that the matter was old, both individual accused were old, and they had led evidence of refund to investors; custodial incarceration was held inappropriate and the company and directors were sentenced to fines (Rs.5 lakh on the company, Rs.5 lakh on Kamal Kumar Jain, and Rs.2 lakh on Manoj Kumar Jain, with one-month default imprisonment). Conversely, the Patel court treated the failure to pay as a continuing economic offence affecting securities-market stability, noted the accused’s disregard despite the Supreme Court confirming the penalty, held leniency unwarranted, and sentenced Patel to three years’ simple imprisonment and a Rs.10 lakh fine.
review_notes: Sentencing rationales for Sagar (old age, refund, age of case) and Patel (economic offence, Supreme Court confirmation, disregard) are both supported.

question: Two of the judgments mention an accused who was initially charged but does not appear in the final sentencing order because the proceedings were abated. Name those accused, identify their cases, and state any reason for abatement that the record gives.
answer_summary: In SEBI Special Case 27/2014 (Sagar Green Gold), accused No. 4 Anoop Kumar Jain is described as having died after the charge was framed, so the proceedings against him were dismissed as abated. In SEBI Special Case 391/2014 (Twilight Litaka), the accused list marks Avinash Shantaram Chandvankar as abated, so he too is not in the final sentencing order.
review_notes: Anoop Kumar Jain (Sagar, died after framing of charge) and Avinash Shantaram Chandvankar (Twilight, marked abated) are documented in the cited chunks.

question: A compliance head notices that SEBI's August 2024 mass cancellation of depository participants and the 2025 mass cancellations of investment advisers and research analysts were all passed under Regulation 30A of the Intermediaries Regulations, 2008, but the underlying trigger is not the same. What factual breach grounded the DP order, and how does the breach differ from the common trigger in the IA and RA orders?
answer_summary: The DP order was triggered because the depository-participant agreements of each noticee had been terminated by the depositories (largely CDSL, some NSDL), so the noticees were no longer participants of any depository. SEBI held that they therefore ceased to satisfy Regulation 35(b) of the SEBI (Depository Participants) Regulations, 2018, which makes admission as a depository participant a condition of the DP certificate. The IA and RA orders, by contrast, were triggered by non-payment of the five-year renewal fee required under Clause 3 of the Second Schedule of the SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, 2013 and the SEBI (Research Analysts) Regulations, 2014, causing the certificates to expire. The DP order turns on loss of infrastructure-membership/eligibility; the IA/RA orders turn on non-renewal.
review_notes: Supported by cited chunks. DP trigger is agreement termination/Regulation 35(b) eligibility loss; IA/RA trigger is non-payment of five-year renewal fee. Cross-category Reg 30A comparison, distinct memory target.

question: Three Reg 30A class-cancellation orders were served on different entities for compliance monitoring: the IA and RA batches named BSE Limited, while the DP batch named another set. Who received the compliance copy in each case and why does the distinction follow from the nature of the intermediary?
answer_summary: The IA order requires a copy to be served on 'BSE Limited (being Investment Adviser Administration and Supervisory Body)' and the RA order requires a copy on 'BSE Limited (being Research Analyst Administration and Supervisory Body)'. The DP order requires a copy to be served on 'the Depositories'. The distinction reflects the regulatory architecture: BSE administers the IA/RA segments as the administration and supervisory body, whereas depository participants are governed through the depositories that terminated their participation agreements; the depository link is therefore the natural compliance channel.
review_notes: Supported by cited operative paragraphs. IA/RA orders copy BSE Ltd as IAASB/RAASB; DP order copies the Depositories. Teaches the regulator/recipient architecture distinction.

question: Two SEBI class orders cancelled Investment Adviser registrations under Regulation 30A for non-payment of renewal fees: one on September 10, 2025 and another on November 27, 2025. Affected advisers believe the later order carries the same post-cancellation wind-down duties (record preservation, investor-grievance redressal and transfer of client assets) found in the earlier order. Are they correct?
answer_summary: No. The September 10, 2025 order imposes express post-cancellation duties: the noticees must preserve records, redress investor grievances, transfer records/funds/securities of clients, maintain continuity of service, take necessary action regarding defaults/pending action, and abide by Regulation 30A(10) of the Intermediaries Regulations, 2008. The November 27, 2025 order is limited to cancelling the certificates with immediate effect and serving a copy on BSE Ltd (IAASB); it does not contain those continuing obligations or the 'not absolved from liability' language.
review_notes: Supported by September 2025 continuing-duty paragraphs and November 2025 bare cancellation order. Clear within-IA template lineage, distinct memory target.

question: The November 2025 mass cancellation of Investment Advisers is silent on whether the cancelled advisers remain liable for past violations. What do the contemporaneous Research Analyst and Depository Participant class orders say about survival of liability after cancellation under Regulation 30A?
answer_summary: Both the RA order (March 2025) and the DP order (August 2024) make clear that cancellation does not wipe away liability. The RA order states that the noticees continue to be liable for anything done or omitted to be done as Research Analysts, and the order does not absolve them from any securities-law violation committed as registered Research Analysts. The DP order similarly says the noticees remain liable for anything done or omitted to be done as depository participants, are responsible for outstanding fees/dues/interest to SEBI, and are not absolved of violations committed as registered depository participants. So cancellation stops future use of the certificate but preserves enforcement for past misconduct.
review_notes: Supported by RA and DP liability-survival clauses and the absence of such text in the November 2025 IA order. Well-formed negative/absence check.

question: How many intermediary registrations did SEBI cancel across the three class orders issued against Investment Advisers (November 2025), Research Analysts (March 2025) and Depository Participants (August 2024) under Regulation 30A?
answer_summary: 162 in total: 68 Investment Advisers (Noticees No. 1 to 68), 72 Research Analysts (Noticees No. 1 to 72) and 22 Depository Participants. The Research Analyst batch was the largest.
review_notes: Supported by cited enumeration clauses: 68 IA, 72 RA, 22 DP noticees. Simple numeric aggregate but still a valid multi-document corpus-count target.

question: I am preparing a compliance cheat-sheet of SEBI's recent Adjudicating Officer penalties against registered investment advisers found deficient during inspection. Map each of the three registered IAs—Growthlift Investment Advisories, Chenthil R Iyer, and Trade Nexa Research—to the core inspection deficiency, the exact penalty amount, and the SEBI Act provision(s) invoked.
answer_summary: Growthlift Investment Advisories Private Limited (reg. INA200014283): four deficiencies were established—not registered with CKYC/KRA during the inspection period; 98 client-facing employees lacked PAIA qualifications/certifications under Regulation 7(1)(c); charged more than Rs.1,25,000 per annum fixed fees from 16 clients and Rs.1,90,678 from 3 clients whose PAN details were not available; and failed to intimate FIU-IND about appointment of principal officer/designated director during the inspection period. Penalty: Rs.3,00,000 under Section 15EB. Chenthil R Iyer (reg. INA000008905): his NISM certificate expired on April 1, 2022, but he continued investment advisory services and collected Rs.46,86,601 in fees from April 1, 2022 to November 30, 2025 without valid certification, violating Regulations 7(1)(a) and 7(2) of the IA Regulations. Penalty: Rs.5,00,000 under Section 15EB. Trade Nexa Research Investment Advisor (Prop. Minakshi Asavani, reg. INA000009083): charged fees without/before executed client agreements (90 instances), failed to maintain call records/records of interaction, provided a free trial to a prospective client, and promised assured returns/loss recovery to clients. Penalty: Rs.5,00,000 under Section 15HA plus Rs.2,00,000 under Section 15EB, totaling Rs.7,00,000.
review_notes: Cross-entity table supported by cited chunks: Growthlift deficiencies, fee-cap and 3-client details, Rs.3,00,000 under Section 15EB; Chenthil Reg.7(1)(a)/7(2), Rs.5,00,000 under 15EB; Trade Nexa 15HA+15EB Rs.7,00,000. Requires all three AO orders.

question: In the registered-IA adjudication orders against Growthlift Investment Advisories and Trade Nexa Research, SEBI examined two different fee-related problems. What was the specific fee-amount or fee-timing irregularity in each case, and why did Trade Nexa face an additional penalty under Section 15HA that Growthlift did not?
answer_summary: Growthlift was penalised for breaching the annual fixed-fee cap: it charged more than Rs.1,25,000 per annum per client from 16 clients under the fixed-fee mode and collected Rs.1,90,678 from three clients whose PAN details were not available. The AO held this violated Regulation 15A of the IA Regulations read with Clause 1.2(iii) of the SEBI Master Circular for Investment Advisers dated June 15, 2023, and imposed Rs.3,00,000 under Section 15EB. Trade Nexa was penalised for collecting fees without executed agreements or before agreements were signed—90 instances were identified—in breach of Regulation 19(1)(d) read with the September 23, 2020 circular/master circular. Beyond the agreement/fee-timing breach, Trade Nexa was also found, through call recordings and WhatsApp chats, to have promised assured returns/loss recovery to clients. That conduct was treated as fraudulent/unfair trade practices, so SEBI imposed an additional Rs.5,00,000 under Section 15HA, taking the total penalty to Rs.7,00,000.
review_notes: Fee-axis comparison supported: Growthlift fixed-fee cap breach (16 clients, Rs.1,90,678 for 3 clients without PAN) and Trade Nexa 90 fee-without/agreement-before cases; additional 15HA penalty driven by call-recording/WhatsApp assured-return/loss-recovery conduct.

question: I am building a do-not-do list for client-facing staff by drawing only on the registered-IA Adjudicating Officer orders against Growthlift, Chenthil Iyer, and Trade Nexa. Which misconduct involving direct client communication or conduct was established only against Trade Nexa and not in the other two orders?
answer_summary: Three client-conduct violations were found only in the Trade Nexa order: (i) failing to maintain records of client interactions/call recordings, in breach of Regulation 19(1) read with the September 23, 2020 circular/master circular; (ii) offering a free trial to a prospective client in breach of SEBI circular dated December 27, 2019 and Clause 2.1 of the May 21, 2024 master circular; and (iii) promising assured returns/loss recovery to clients through call recordings and WhatsApp chats, which triggered Section 15HA. Growthlift's lapses concerned CKYC/KRA registration, PAIA qualifications, excess fixed fees, and FIU-IND intimation. Chenthil's lapse was rendering advisory services without a valid NISM certificate.
review_notes: Negative/absence check supported: only Trade Nexa has missing call records, free-trial offer and assured-return/loss-recovery conduct; Growthlift's and Chenthil's narrower lapses are correctly described and do not overlap.

question: A colleague argues that a registered investment adviser can continue advising existing clients without a valid NISM certificate as long as it stops charging fees. Does the Chenthil R Iyer AO order support that view? If the same adviser also tells a stressed client, 'I will recover your losses in a week,' what additional precedent from the Trade Nexa order should worry compliance?
answer_summary: No. The Chenthil R Iyer order holds that a registered IA must maintain valid NISM certification at all times while providing investment advice. Chenthil's NISM certificate expired on April 1, 2022, yet he continued advisory services and collected Rs.46,86,601 in fees through November 30, 2025. The AO found violations of Regulations 7(1)(a) and 7(2) of the IA Regulations and imposed Rs.5,00,000 under Section 15EB. The conclusion does not depend on whether fees were collected; the default is rendering advice without valid certification. If the adviser also promises loss recovery, the Trade Nexa order is the relevant precedent. Trade Nexa was found, through call recordings and WhatsApp chats, to have assured clients of returns/loss recovery. The AO treated that as fraudulent/unfair trade practices and imposed an additional Rs.5,00,000 under Section 15HA, beyond the Section 15EB penalty for the advisory-process breaches.
review_notes: Applied scenario supported: Chenthil order establishes valid NISM certification is required at all times while advising, regardless of fee collection; Trade Nexa order supplies the 15HA precedent for loss-recovery promises.

question: The three registered-IA AO orders against Growthlift, Chenthil R Iyer, and Trade Nexa were all issued after SEBI/BASL inspections. Which order records an interim settlement application, when was it rejected, and how do the inspection windows and order dates line up across the three matters?
answer_summary: The Trade Nexa order records that the noticee filed a settlement application and the proceedings were kept in abeyance; the settlement application was rejected by SEBI's letter dated June 25, 2025, and a personal hearing followed on July 18, 2025 before the order was passed on August 12, 2025. No settlement application is mentioned in the Growthlift or Chenthil orders. Inspection and order chronology: - Growthlift: inspection covered April 1, 2022 to October 31, 2023; order dated April 16, 2026. - Chenthil R Iyer: the non-compliance period ran from April 1, 2022 (NISM expiry) to November 30, 2025; order dated February 20, 2026. - Trade Nexa: inspection commenced March 5, 2024 and covered April 1, 2020 to December 31, 2023; after settlement rejection, order dated August 12, 2025.
review_notes: Timeline/settlement facts supported: Trade Nexa settlement rejected June 25, 2025 and hearing July 18, 2025; inspection/order windows for all three matters match the cited chunks and document metadata.
